Question: What do you do when you feel like you don't fit in anywhere?
Answer: I don’t think you’re supposed to fit in anywhere. At least, not perfectly. Here’s me: I’m the little guy on the right, although I’m not really little. That guy is just big. This was the quarterfinal round of one the biggest submission grappling tournaments in North America. I got 4th. I do Jiu-Jitsu, I wrestle, I lift weights, and I am definitely a jock. I’ve always been into sports for as long as I can remember. It was my first interest. But I also have other sides to me, and sometimes, these sides are at war. Here’s me also: I like to write — more than most people. Every day, I write articles, I’m working on a book, and I sometimes write Quora answers like this one. Part of the reason I love writing is because I love literature — currently, I’m reading like 5 different books. I love words and stories and sharing and consuming them. I won’t call myself a literature nerd because I did that once and people said I wasn’t a nerd because I am not a skinny geek, but whatever. That’s not the point. Sometimes I feel like I don’t fit in anywhere. I’m sometimes too nerdy for the jocks and too jock-ish (is that a word?) for the nerds. I feel like I don’t really belong anywhere. However, I’ve also felt this way long enough to realize that when I am feeling this way, it’s usually not because it’s true but instead because I am focusing more on what makes me different from people than what makes me like them. You have the confidence and the security in yourself to be yourself and be okay with being different from people while also working to connect with them. Don’t expect people who are living their own individual experiences to just meet you where you are because you think you’re special. If you feel like you don’t fit in anywhere, work to connect. When you do this, you might out new things about yourself that will make you connect more in one setting but less in another. This is the complexity of social interaction. It’s okay to not fit in, it’s not okay to wallow in your not fitting in. Also, a closing remark, if you really try to fit in somewhere and it just doesn’t feel right, there’s a chance that place is not for you. That’s okay too, but you won’t feel better until you leave.

Question: How do I get rid of jealousy?
Answer: Whenever I feel a pull of jealousy, I ask myself one simple question that stops the spiral: “Would I switch lives, 100%, with the person that I am jealous of?” See, at times, I feel jealous, but the truth is that I’m never really jealous of an entire person. I’m jealous of a moment they’re experiencing. I’m jealous of something they have. 100% of the time, the answer to the question is “no”. I feel jealous sometimes, but I am never so jealous of someone that I would want to switch lives with them 100%. This question is simple, but it helps me stay grounded and realize that I am very blessed. Jealousy is a normal human emotion. Just feeling it does not make you a bad person. The problems arise when you allow jealousy to consume you, which a lot of people do. The question above is my reframe.

Question: What is the main purpose of life to you?
Answer: Objectively speaking, there is no meaning to life. We must assign it a meaning. For me, I have experimented with many different meanings. I have sought meaning through things like: And much more — but nothing has ever really stuck. The other day, I came across a quote from CS Lewis that has been really helpful in putting into words the physical things that I have been working on for the last year or so. Here’s the quote, before I tell you my story: “To be happy at home, said Johnson, is the end of all human endeavor. As long as we are thinking only of natural values we must say that the sun looks down on nothing half so good as a household laughing together over a meal, or two friends talking over a pint of beer, or a man alone reading a book that interests him;” ― C.S. Lewis It’s a good quote. So a year ago, I was a ramblin’ man. Not really, but the sentiment remains the same. I’d quit my job, nearly given up on love, was traversing the United States training and competing in Jiu-Jitsu all the time, and I was unsure of what I wanted to do or where I belonged. I felt aimless. I did not have a home. My home was an Airbnb or hotel in whatever city I was training in. From Long Island, New York, to Toledo, Ohio — from Austin, Texas, to San Diego, California. I was all over the place. My income came from writing online (my expenses were low and I was ghostwriting), teaching Jiu-Jitsu when I could, and that was it. I really just focused on competitive success, new experiences, and exploring. And? Life was exciting, but I was miserable. I was not happy. I decided, eventually, that I needed “a home”. I settled in Austin, Texas — a city that I liked, but I didn’t know anyone. I chose this city because its Jiu-Jitsu scene is thriving and I had a big goal to qualify for this massive tournament in Jiu-Jitsu called “ADCC”. It’s been an obsession of mine for the last 3–4 years. I had also just begun a relationship with a woman who lived in San Diego. We were doing long-distance, and although I didn't know her super well at the time, I felt like there was something good about her. We did long-distance for a while, both of us not really sure where we were going and just enjoying the ride. The goal really, is to have a home that you can escape to. When I break down all of the things that I have listed above and all of the other meanings that I have assigned to my life, they, like the guy CS Lewis quotes above says, are really done to allow you to be happy at home. Ambition is done to make you happy at home. Pleasure is chased to make you happy at home. Everything worth doing is done to make one happy at home. And so in April, after about a year of doing long distance, my girlfriend moved to Austin, where we will reside together for the next year or 2. I’ve achieved many goals in my career and I will hopefully achieve more (I’ll be competing at that ADCC thing for the first time later this summer), but all of this is done just so I can be happy at home. When you’re happy at home, even bad days aren’t so bad. Don’t get so caught up in your ambition that you forget what really matters the most.

Question: What are the steps you take to get comfortable with being uncomfortable in the workplace?
Answer: "Get comfortable being uncomfortable" is an oversimplification. Comfort is not what you want when you're in an uncomfortable situation. If you're comfortable in a truly bad or uncomfortable situation, you don't perform better. You lose. You choke. You get choked. You fail. You DON'T want to settle or accept a bad spot too much. You need to work your way out. You need to scratch and claw and not accept the bad position. I get that this is a corny statement that people make to tell others to collect themselves in bad spots, it's also bad advice. When you're uncomfortable, this is not the time to be comfortable and chill. It's the time for calculated action. For constant productive movement. To be cool, collected, and focused. But comfortable? Never. Don't get comfortable being uncomfortable. Develop the ability to stay focused when you are uncomfortable. That is the real objective.

Question: What is the best way to live a happy and successful life?
Answer: Most people misunderstand happiness. People today often view happiness as the highs of life. People think that if you have good highlight reels of your life on Instagram, you’re happy. People think that you should always chase higher highlight reels. People act in a way that makes it seem like happiness is found in material things and the ego boosts you get off showing your material things to other people. A nice car? That’s so cool! A cool trip? OMG! I wish I was there! A picture with your beautiful partner? Wow, you must be so happy. We see these things and we think “Everything is perfect for them, and for me life sucks.” Therefore, I am unhappy. The thing is, this way of thinking isn’t really anyone’s fault. That’s just kind of how our society is. We all like showing off to each other. Before you were trying to keep up with your favorite influencer, you were keeping up with the Joneses. Before that, it was something else. For a long time, people have thought that boosting our own ego makes us happy. The truth is that it’s really the opposite. In my experience, happiness is when you take care of yourself to a certain point, and then start to make other people happy. Just because you can. The way you live a happy life is not to engage in these silly status games. Not to virtue signal too much. Not romanticizing everything. Not trying to “win” life. If you’re unhappy, try living authentically with who you are. If you don’t know who you are because you’re so caught in the societal trap, free yourself. Forget about the ideals for a bit. Quiet the mind and exit the system, rediscover your innocence. Learn to enjoy beauty for beauty’s sake — not because you want to show it off to other people. Learn to enjoy life just for the fact that you only have one. That’s what I’ve been trying to work on, at least.

Question: What's something I can do right now to increase my productivity?
Answer: I’ve been a writer and an athlete and running my own online business for the last few years, but it wasn’t really until the last few months that I was able to sustain consistent productivity the way that I am now. I was always: It was not fun. If you’ve followed me on Quora for a while, you probably remember when I had long “blonde” hair and wrote long-winded answers about ideas that I barely understood. It was a phase. A phase where I was very active in a lot of different endeavors, but I was not productive. See, I’ve always been a person who does a lot of stuff, but I don’t think I’ve really become productive until recently. My girlfriend showed me this super easy “productivity hack” that I’ve adapted to my evening routine starting at the beginning of this year (kind of like a New Year’s resolution of sorts) and it’s been huge for me. It’s really simple. Every night before bed, I pull out my little notebook and I write down the list of all of the projects that I am working on right now. Today, my writing list included: And that was it. Today was kind of an average day — plus Jiu-Jitsu training and a strength and conditioning workout — and I just woke up, looked at my tasks for the day, and got to work, checking them off as I went on. It’s stupidly simple, but most people don’t do this. Before you go to bed, make a list of all the things you need to do for the day tomorrow to get to where you want to be at the end of the week, month, and year. Then, put the notebook somewhere where you can see it in the morning, and then don’t worry about it anymore. Go to sleep. Then, the next day, wake up and get after it. Then, do the same thing the next day. That’s really all I got in terms of “productivity”. No fancy apps and Pomodoro timers for me these days. Just daily discipline and a daily to-do list that keeps that discipline in check.

Question: What are some good examples of "life isn't fair"?
Answer: Ernest Hemingway’s life wasn’t fair. His life was tragic. His dad was an abusive alcoholic who killed himself. He hated his mother for many reasons — perhaps in part because she dressed him like a girl when he was a boy — and he blamed her for the suicide of his father and resented her for it for his entire adult life. He expressed thoughts about killing both of his parents at different points in his childhood. Allegedly, 3 of his siblings also committed suicide. Still, Hemingway managed to do quite well for himself. As an adult, he lived a hyper-masculine, womanizing, adventurous life. He was in both world wars, survived 2 plane crashes, and held a lifelong obsession with bullfighting. He also was one of the most successful writers of the early 1900s. He’s a legend when it comes to writing. But his personal life was not good. His actions affected other people very negatively. He married 4 times and dealt with lifelong alcohol dependence. He was a cheater, a womanizer, brilliant, and likely manic bipolar like his father — although it was never diagnosed. He committed suicide by gunshot in middle age — just like his father. But did Hemingway ever really have a chance? His mother dressed him as a girl when he was in his earliest years and in the process of forming his identity. It’s no wonder he ended up going down a hyper-masculine route. He was abused, traumatized, and watched people around him kill themselves for his entire life. He was obsessed with death and suicide. He thought about it often. He also dealt with chronic pain, alcoholism (that he never got under control), PTSD, and after the plane crashes in Africa, a fractured skull among other injuries. Yes — Hemingway was a great writer — but did he ever have a chance of being “happy”? Of living a normal life? I’m not sure. The kind of pain that he experienced takes generations to unweave. In terms of having a happy and stable life, Hemingway was playing the game short-handed for his entire existence. He didn’t win, and he brought a lot of people down with him. Is it fair for us to blame Hemingway for everything that happened in his life? I don’t know. What I do know is that life isn't fair.

Question: Why is everyone in their 20s so confused?
Answer: In Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, there are 5 belts. Generally, it takes about 2 years at each belt (sometimes more) to eventually progress to your black belt. It takes a while to learn Jiu-Jitsu. When you’re a white belt, you don’t know anything. When you’re a blue belt, you think you know stuff, but you know way less than you think you do. Purple belt, you know a little more. Brown belt, you think you’re close to mastery. Then, you get your black belt and you realize that the only thing you know is how little you know. Likewise, life takes a while to learn about. Say you live to 100ish because you’re healthy and have good genetics or whatever. You’re going to spend 20 years at each belt of life. But realistically, most people don’t live to be 100. Similarly, most people who start Jiu-Jitsu don’t ever get their black belts. If you want to get your black belt in life, there’s really nothing to do but put in the time. To live. To experience everything day by day. If you’re in your 20s, you’re probably a blue belt. That means you’ve got the fundamentals down, but you’re still pretty clueless. You’re confused because you’re probably realizing that knowing the fundamentals alone doesn’t get you to a high level. You don’t know as much as you think. I am writing this as someone in their 20s. If there’s I’ve learned in the last few years it’s that I don’t know as much as I think I know. I wouldn’t call myself confused, but who knows what I think of my present self in 10, 20, or even 50 years from now. I’m a little nervous to find out. Maybe Quora will still be around and I’ll visit this answer to see how much I’ve learned compared to how much I thought I knew. “You must understand the whole of life, not just one little part of it. That is why you must read, that is why you must look at the skies, that is why you must sing, and dance, and write poems, and suffer, and understand, for all that is life.” ― Jiddu Krishnamurti

Question: What is your greatest fear?
Answer: We all think our fears are unique, but they’re really just different versions of the same story. We fear things like: The fears that we feel are not really so interesting. Everyone’s fears are pretty similar and they all illicit similar responses in us. My biggest fear is probably not achieving the goals that I have set for myself. Not “making it” in my own eyes. Typical, right? You probably saw that coming. That’s why I work myself into the ground, put myself out there as much as possible, and get so damn frustrated when it doesn’t work out. So what are we supposed to do about our greatest fears? Recently, I was reading a book by one of my favorite philosophers, Jiddu Krishnamurti. This guy, here: The book I was reading is called Freedom From the Known, and it talks a lot about fear, anxiety, and how modern society (the “known”) creates a lot of unpleasant sensations. I’m going to share some quotes from Mr. Krishnamurti that will help you deal with fear better. First, the setup: “Fear is one of the greatest problems in life. A mind that is caught in fear lives in confusion, in conflict, and therefore must be violent, distorted and aggressive. It dare not move away from its own patterns of thinking, and this breeds hypocrisy. Until we are free from fear, climb the highest mountain, invent every kind of God, we will always remain in darkness. Living in such a corrupt, stupid society as we do, with the competitive education we receive which engenders fear, we are all burdened with fears of some kind, and fear is a dreadful thing which warps, twists and dulls our days.” TLDR: Fear sucks, and until you’re free from it, your life will be kinda sucky. And here’s what Krishnamurti says you should do about fear at the end of the chapter: “When you see that you are a part of fear, not separate from it — that you are fear — then you cannot do anything about it; then fear comes totally to an end.” Your fears don’t exist unless you do. You shouldn’t fight them so much. You should learn to exist with them. To “let them be”. I should include that this is more about psychological fears than physical ones, but I hope that you’ve gathered that by now. Your fears are yours. They are part of you. When you let them be and don’t give them as much attention, they will begin to dissipate. Now I don’t know about you, but this goes against everything I’ve ever learned about fear. I was taught to “face my fears”, to fight the demons inside me, and to demonize all of those negative feelings I have that make me scared. No one ever tells you to basically learn to “love yourself” in the face of fear. It’s not really a thing, at least not in the Western world. However, that’s what I think you should do. Let your fears be. Live with them. Don’t waste time and energy trying to get rid of them. Just live. Just do the stuff that makes you scared with the fear present. Sometimes the fear doesn’t go away, but you have only one shot at this life. Are you really going to waste it obsessing over your fears and demons? I don’t think you should.

Question: I am 26. Am I considered old or young, and why?
Answer: I am also 26. According to my dad, who’s going to be 66 in September, I am a young man. According to Grandma and Grandpa who are in their mid-80s, I’m basically still a child. According to the 7, 8, or 9-year-old kids whom I used to coach in Jiu-Jitsu, I am very old. Last year, I had a Jiu-Jitsu match with a guy in his 30s. I felt like a young man. Also last year, I had a Jiu-Jitsu match with a 17-year-old kid. I felt like a grandpa. That was a trip. Say you live to be 80 — 26 is about 32% of the way through your life. That’s a low number out of 100%. If you Google “How old is the average person?” you’ll learn that the global median age is 38.5. At 26, you are still young, but just not younger than people younger than you. Wild concept, right? I’ll also use this time to remind you that age and wisdom are not the same thing. I’ve met some very wise 20-year-olds and some 60-year-olds who need to grow up. Life is funny that way. Don’t compare yourself to other people too much. Just live and learn. Relax. You’re not old, but if you keep going, you’ll get there eventually.

Question: What is the biggest misconception people have about life?
Answer: One major misconception people have about life is that you’re supposed to be “waking up” to a more “real” life. The idea that eventually, you will learn some fact or idea that will make you realize the “truth” about life. That you will become enlightened. That you develop wisdom. That life will be easy after you acquire this wisdom. I am here to tell you that that is bullshit. Wisdom is recognizing that there is no specific thing that you will learn that will fix everything. I used to struggle with a lot of anxiety. So much so that I couldn’t drink coffee in the morning, couldn’t sleep at night, and couldn’t function without acting like a complete train wreck all the time. I thought that I would learn something that would help fix my anxiety problems. I didn’t. I just practiced getting better at dealing with anxiety every day, and over time, I got better at it. I learned some useful ideas along the way, like meditation, the idea that anxiety and excitement are the same, and some Buddhist concepts that helped me unravel my “self” a bit, but there was no single idea that me “not anxious anymore”. For most people, the magic idea that solves all the problems does exist. This is because complex. In Jiu-Jitsu, this happens a lot too. People ask me questions like “What did you focus on to improve your competition skills?” or “What is the key to learning leg locks?” They hope that a “quick fix” exists that will help them achieve what they want without having to work really hard to deal with failure. This is not true. The reason I compete well in BJJ is because I do it often. The reason I am good at leg locks is because I practice them every day. The specific knowledge that you are missing is obvious to someone who has put in more volume than you. If you want to truly embody that knowledge, you must match their volume. You can learn facts, but understanding comes from action. From doing. This is why you train, not just think about training. There is value to mental training too, but you must physically train to execute on game day. Humans are hardwired to be looking for stuff. We used to look for berries or animals to eat. As we’ve evolved, we’ve started looking for things more metaphysically. We’re looking for meaning and understanding in our lives. But just like that search for berries, no find really provides lasting satisfaction. Just like that search for berries, the search for ideas is also risky. Bad berries will make you sick, and so will bad ideas. But then, when you find a good idea, just like a good berry, it won’t satisfy you forever. After a few hours, you’ll be hungry again. In times of scarcity, you might fantasize about that berry. You might dream about it. When I’m cutting weight for Jiu-Jitsu, I dream of lemonade waterfalls and chocolate croissants that are the size of a shopping cart. But once the cut is over, I hydrate and have my food, I have a great meal, and then I’m just back to normal. That’s it. Satisfying your fantasies will not give you lasting fulfillment. Nothing does. The pursuit of satisfaction is trite and neverending. The biggest misconception that people have about life is that if you just do “something” you’ll be good. You’ll be happy. Question: What is your favorite form of art and why?
Answer: I’m a writer, so most people think my favorite form of art is writing, but that isn’t true. The type of art I love the most is the kind that I cannot do well myself. It’s “envy”, I guess, but more so I think it’s appreciation. Most of my writing is nonfiction, but I’ve done a teeny bit of fiction as well. I love the craft of writing more than any other craft in the world — besides maybe Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. I love reading books, and I think that words are one of the most beautiful mediums of expression. But I also love music — I can’t sing well myself, but if I could, I probably would. I don’t envy musicians per se, but I am appreciative of the gifts that they have. Songwriting is a beautiful art. I also love movies. In high school, I wanted to be a film director or a screenwriter. However, I think my favorite form of art to consume is painting — visual art. When I was a kid, I loved making paintings. I loved art class in school. It was fun and therapeutic (even though I didn’t know what “therapeutic” meant at the time). I always felt better about myself after drawing and painting. Unfortunately, I wasn’t very good, and I was constantly discouraged in art class as I got older. One teacher literally asked me if I needed “special help” to finish my drawing, and another straight-up told me that my sculpture was “terrible”. I was devastated when these things happened. I was 10–12 years old, very sensitive, and definitely not strong enough to handle criticism from adults on my work. So after I finished art class in 7th grade (with a C, mind you), I never took an art class again. I took one photography class in high school for my fine arts requirement, and although I was decent at it for my class’s standards, I never really gave a damn about the class. I just took pictures and turned them in to get a grade. The teacher was nice and we bonded over a love for sports, and he gave me an A. Nowadays, as someone who writes for a living, I am deeply appreciative of the vulnerability and skill required to sketch and paint things. The skill of using your hands and your imagination to create the “unimaginable”. In particular, I like Salvador Dali. Surrealism is one of the most interesting styles of art out there. It reminds me of lucid dreams I’ve had. It reminds me of my favorite songs. It reminds me of scenes from my favorite movies. The ability to convey a message through a painting is beautiful to me. I took a class in college on art history (luckily no art making in that class), and I wrote all my papers on Dali and other surrealists. Recently, in Spain, I had the opportunity to visit the Dali Museum in Figueres. That’s where this picture was taken. Dali was brilliant — though very tortured. So, in conclusion, I think my favorite form of art is painting, but it’s really just whatever I don’t think I can do myself. My favorite form of art is the form of art that allows me to appreciate the skill and hard work of someone else. This inspires me to keep writing.

Question: When did you first know you wanted to be a writer?
Answer: During the Covid pandemic, I wrote a draft of a novel while at home for about 8 weeks in “quarantine”. I was a senior in college, and I finished my classes online while writing in the morning and evenings. I was bored, unable to go through my normal routine of doing Jiu-Jitsu every day, and I fell in love with the routine of sitting down at the keyboard each morning to write. It was the first time I’d ever done anything remotely “intellectual” and derived enjoyment from it. However, I didn’t think that writing was ever going to be something I’d pursue professionally until about 6 months later when I had my first job interview at a marketing agency. I had all the prerequisites for the job, I had an internship before the job that made me an ideal candidate for the job, and my interview went great. I’ve always been fairly good at job interviews. I could have gotten that job. The last phase of the interview was this survey, where I had to match “how I work” with that of the values and structure of the company. They told me that there wasn’t a right answer, but that wasn’t true. This was when I started to think about how much I was enjoying my daily writing routine. When I filled out that survey, I realized that if I wanted the job, all I had to do was answer properly and pretend that I was a good worker bee. That I work best when what I have to do is defined for me. That I’m a good rule follower and that I do as I am told. All I had to do was bullshit. All I had to do was lie. It was at that moment, as I was filling out this survey for this random company in Chicago, that I realized that I wanted to be a writer. I wanted to have control over my day. I wanted to tell stories that were interesting and inspiring to me. I wanted to be my own boss. I also realized that career unpredictability and “the risk of being broke” was worth the risk. Please remember that I was 22, educated, and had no family of my own before you decide to take this risk yourself. I realized that I wanted to create my own career instead of doing the one that was assigned to me based on my degree in school or what was available on LinkedIn. I spent the first 22 years of my life doing what people told me to do, and I wanted control over conventionality. That led me to the wild world of digital writing. I realized that all I really wanted to do with my life was write and train in martial arts, and I just decided to do whatever I could to make that dream work. It might sound a little bratty and selfish, but I’d do it again in a heartbeat. So what did I do about that job? I’m not proud of this, but I sabotaged the final part of my interview. Instead of filling out the survey the right way and turning down the job (how would I tell my parents that I turned down a good job?), I answered the assessment in a way that made me seem like a loose cannon. I made myself seem borderline unstable. In the end, I didn’t get the job. The following week, I started writing on the internet. I got my first freelance job about 10 days later. Within a year, I had a growing freelancing business. Within 2 years I was ghostwriting. It wasn’t without trials and tribulations, but a few years later, I am a full-time writer, Jiu-Jitsu athlete, and entrepreneur. I’ll be releasing my first book in a few months. I’m so glad I took the chance to dive into a profession I am passionate about, especially at the time that I did. Apart from the few times that I’ve nearly lost everything and failed, I have never considered doing anything else. (I won’t lie to you and tell you this oath has been easy) Some other day, I’ll tell you those stories. Oh, and that novel? I’m still sitting on it. Should I release it?

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: I want to change my life. How do I start?
Answer: When people want to change their lives, they usually start out by thinking about the different things that need to be added to their lives to get to where they want to be. They need to add a workout program, a mentor, a new job, new friends, new habits, etc. They add, add, and add some more until they’re just constantly in motion all the time. They’re not a different person and their life hasn’t changed for the better — they’re just busier. I know I thought like this when I first started my self-improvement journey. I started waking up early. I started listening to self-improvement podcasts. I started reading books. I started meditating. Journaling. Following a more dedicated workout program. I did a lot of stuff. But you know what? Although my life changed, it didn’t change how I wanted it to. I just became busy. I still had anxiety. I still got really sad. I still had bad friends and shitty relationships. I still spiraled the same way. The truth is that changing your life is not about what you do, it’s about what you stop doing. Removing bad habits is how you actually have lasting change. This is how you make lasting progress toward goals. This is how you change the person you are in a sustainable and manageable way so that you skip the period where everything comes crashing down. You skip that phase where you’re just an overwhelmed mess all the time. You get some peace. You learn to embrace boredom. You learn that boredom elicits creativity. You learn to drop your bad habits instead of just following new havits to cancel out the bad ones. It’s the equivalent of doing a bunch of burpees to hopefully cancel out a whole pizza. Just don’t eat the whole pizza. True self-improvement is not about what you do, it’s about what you stop doing. It’s about quitting. Let’s make quitting cool again.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: If someone asked you for dating advice, what would you say?
Answer: There are a few big ideas that stand out to me that I’ve learned over the years. I’ll give you 3 of them: Before my first date with my girlfriend, I was nervous. I was staying in a new city (Austin), and she was flying all the way from California to meet me. It was a big risk for her, and I was very scared to f*ck it up. I also hadn’t been on a date in a while. We both were nervous that our first date — something we both were taking a risk in doing — was going to be a flop. We hit it off over the phone, but being in person is different. I wanted to make sure I said all the right things (I didn’t), and so did she. We both were more interested in being perfect being our imperfect selves. This is normal — at first — but you shouldn’t try to be perfect all the time. You should just be natural. This might get you rejected in the short term, but it will lead to deeper relationships in the long term. You’ll filter out people who aren’t actually interested in you, you’ll click faster with the people you’re supposed to click with and best of all, you won’t have to deal with a lot of the “bullshit” in the modern dating world because you’re being yourself. Relationships that are built around authenticity are the ones that are built to last. Rule 1: Don’t play a character. Probably the biggest flaw that I have in relationships is a strong desire to never have conflict. I hate fighting. It’s exhausting. It’s not fun. I don’t think anyone likes it. Most of the time, fights I have are because of something my unpredictable self has said or done on impulse, and it always makes me feel bad about myself. I used to run from this feeling, probably because it reminded me of getting yelled at as a kid or bullied in 5th grade or something stupid like that. I’m not sure. Either way, I’ve always been the kind of person who’s tried to avoid hard conversations because I don’t want to have them. Because they make me uncomfortable and tired. They suck. The irony is that by avoiding certain topics with a partner, although you’re not technically lying, you are still guilty by omission of the truth. Sometimes, you’re going to fight. Sometimes you are going to have disagreements. In the early stages of your relationship especially (probably the first few years, if we’re being honest), this will be a big test for you as a couple. How do you handle conflict? The longer you avoid the truth, the more likely you are to have the natural “fights” you are going to have with your partner blow up into something big. Don’t let resentment fester. Talk it out. Rule 2: Tell the truth. Avoiding the truth is lying. Let’s talk about those “fights” real quick for our last point because they’re very important. At least, how you react to them is very important. When you fight with your partner, where does your mind go? If you’re like most people, you probably go straight for ego protection. You probably go straight to make yourself “win” the argument, and you don’t care about the safety of your relationship. You just want yourself to be “the good guy/girl”. The truth is that when you’re fighting with a loved one, there’s no “good guy”. Everyone is a loser. You are a team, and the sooner you both switch your mindset from “Me versus You” to “Us versus The Problem”, the more likely you are to work through big fights, hurt feelings, and resentment. It’s also good to make sure you don’t run the second you have fights. I used to do this because I was taught to have “an abundance mindset” when it came to relationships. I was raised to believe that losing a girlfriend didn’t matter because there were “plenty of fish in the sea”. While this is true and while a breakup won’t be the end of you, you can’t think this way if you want love that lasts. The reason a relationship is valuable is because you can lose it. Rule 3: Don’t run away the second it gets hard. Before you go, here are the 3 rules, side by side: Hope this helps :)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do you come up with writing ideas?
Answer: I actually use Quora a lot for help coming up with writing ideas. I just search up words of things that I’m thinking about — “dating”, “life”, “self”, or “fitness” — and find a question that I can write about from there. It’s a pretty reliable strategy for finding writing advice. Quora is a pretty valuable writing tool in that regard. But the truth is that writing on Quora is really just a structure that I use for coming up with writing ideas. There’s really something deeper going on. The truth is that the way that you really come up with consistent writing ideas is by sitting down and writing every day. Writing is like fitness in that regard. Think of the quality of your writing ideas like the amount of weight you bench press. If you show up to the gym every day, over time, you’re going to get bigger muscles. You will be able to handle more stress “weight” on your lifts. Writing ideas are the same. When you start writing, you will pretty much be stuck with surface-level ideas — which are basically going to be your ideas of other people’s ideas, and your own personal experiences. Over time, you’ll start to gain access to better-quality ideas. This comes through practice. You’ll digest your experience, and learn from other people’s experiences, and you’ll also create hypothetical experiences in your head that you’ll want to learn about and talk about. Part of growing as a writer is learning to write about things that are not affecting your directly right now. Take one of the most successful authors/idea-sharers today — Malcolm Gladwell — for an example. When you read one of Gladwell’s books, if you like to write, you might catch yourself thinking “Wow that’s a great story idea, I wish I had thought of that…” But you didn’t, Gladwell did. But how did he do it? It wasn’t just this God-given talent and he probably didn’t learn much about idea generation in school either. Schools tend to do a terrible job of producing good writers. In reality, was from writing at a newspaper and needing to have a story every day at the end of the day. This is the equivalent of Gladwell going to the gym every day and getting his reps in. Learning how to think deeply about things. Learning how to work under pressure. Learning how to take surface-level ideas and dig past them. It was training. It was consistency. That’s how you really come up with writing ideas.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What do fit people think about overweight people at the gym?
Answer: When I think about overweight people at the gym, I feel happy for them. I want them to keep going to the gym. To keep doing things that are good for their physical health. The worst part of the fitness industry is its unnecessary exclusivity. The amount of body-shaming that happens in fitness is insane. But at the same time, for better or for worse, I don’t think much about overweight people at the gym. I feel like it’d be weird if I had a really strong opinion on this either way. Overweight people are just other people who are also at the gym. I don’t think about the other people at the gym unless they’re taking an obnoxious amount of selfies or screaming/grunting. When I’m at the gym, I mostly try to focus on myself, think about ideas that have been circulating through my mind, do my workout, and then go home. That’s just me.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some words of wisdom for men?
Answer: Growing up, I always wanted to be a certain kind of man. A strong man. A leader. A man who was powerful, but gentle and kind. A man who could be soft, but not weak. A man people looked up to. A man people were proud to have around. That was my vision. My life, however, has not always been like that. At times, even now, I am very stupid. I am naive. I get angry. I get sad. I feel weak. I feel scared. I want to give up. I think that the kind of man that I want to be exists in someone’s future, but not mine. I feel like a burden, a weakling, and an overgrown child. I don’t feel a man worthy of giving advice to other men. But then, on other days, I feel great. I do great. I make a positive impact. I make someone happy. I show someone how to do something. I feel safe and strong at home. I feel like I’ve learned a lot and I have lessons to show other people. Usually, I write them down in a post like this or a newsletter or something. Life is good. And then, it swings back the other way. Some days are not so good. But really, your perception of how you are doing comes through your expectations for yourself and how you feel you stack up with those expectations. When you’re early on in the process, you won’t really know a lot of things. You’ll struggle more. If you have high expectations for yourself and you’re struggling a lot, you’re going to feel like crap about yourself. If there’s anything I know, it’s that. I’m only 26 — so that excludes me from giving qualified advice on things like fatherhood, husbandhood, or a bunch of other things, but I have lived enough to know that life is hard. Life is hard, at pretty much every stage. The only thing to really do is keep on moving. Of course right now is imperfect — you’re too early on in the process to have life exactly how you want it. The only way to get to where you want to go is to stay the course. The best wisdom I have for men (or I guess really anyone) is simple: Don’t give up. You’re going to get to where you want to be, but only if you don’t give up. That’s the “wisdom” I wish I’d heard more of when I was younger. That’s the wisdom I wish I heard more of nowadays.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best way to stay fit?
Answer: The best way to stay fit is to be LESS competitive. When I was in the early stages of my fitness journey, I became very competitive with myself. I wanted to always beat my previous day’s workout totals. In the early stages of fitness, being personally competitive was good. It made it pretty easy to come back to the gym every day. Over time, however, this obsession with “being my best” actually made me less than my best in terms of fitness and strength. I tested my one-rep maxes too frequently. I trained to failure too often. I overtrained because thought that if I did more, I’d get stronger. I also eventually became obsessed with combat sports, which dramatically altered the way I viewed my fitness journey. I had to become stronger to beat someone else in a wrestling match. I needed to have better isometric strength to fight off submissions in Jiu-Jitsu for longer. I “needed” a lot of things to consider myself fit, and I pretty much always fell short. This is naturally what happens when you have high expectations for yourself. You’re never going to be strong enough, fit enough, or lean enough. It’s a never-ending cycle. So what I’m trying to work toward for myself of late is finding a new definition of fitness. A definition of fitness where despite not being able to deadlift 400 pounds multiple times anymore, I’m still strong. I’m still healthy. I’m getting stronger in new ways. I’m excited to go to the gym every day. I don’t hate myself when I can’t do as many pull-ups as I could before. If anything, I see it as data that I need to change something or a sign that maybe I just had “an off day”. I’m trying to train in a way that compliments my sport, not viewing strength training as a specific sport for me to compete against myself until I herniate all my discs. This idea doesn’t just apply to athletes. If you want to be fit, you need to work on training in a way that makes you able to train often. You need a training method that is sustainable. Sure, it’s good to be competitive, but I feel like everyone else in the fitness industry is already telling you that. Today, I’m telling you to be less competitive. To train in a way that allows you to train more, even if you don’t have chiseled abs and a 500-pound bench press.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the dark side of being an entrepreneur?
Answer: I have many friends who are small business owners who are miserable. They hate their business. They wouldn’t encourage anyone to start a business. They think it’s a terrible idea. They want easier ways to make money, feed their families, and make a living. The dark side of being an entrepreneur is that there is an extreme amount of discomfort in this world. There is anxiety. Failure. Frustration. The thought of giving up. It’s terrible at times — especially when it’s not going well. Sometimes, it’s even terrible when it IS going well. It’s overwhelming. You shouldn’t do it. Unless of course, it’s something you can’t stop thinking about. Our culture seems to romanticize the idea of a self-made entrepreneur. Of someone who starts a small business to chase their dreams and do what they love. Of someone who creates a startup to “change the world”. Of someone who dares to live “on their terms”. But here’s the harsh truth: Doing something you’re passionate about — like a startup, small business, or even just any other passion-based pursuit — is only really worth it if you are deeply invested in it. If you are doing it to the best of your ability. If you’re not being lazy. If you’re not taking shortcuts. If you’re not being reckless. If you’re not half-assing anything. The dark side of being an entrepreneur is that you are responsible for everything. Every failure, problem, and hiccup is your responsibility to bob and weave through. You might lose things — money, sleep, peace, friends, partners, and more. It’s hard. People might talk crap about you until you start doing better than them. Then, when you do, they’ll put you on a pedestal. You’ll feel awkward. If you’re not ready for that, I suggest you choose a different career. But of course, it’s not all bad. Running my own business has led me to: There’s more, but these are the highlights. The dark side of being an entrepreneur is the extreme personal responsibility required to survive and thrive in the field. However, if you can live with this, you’re on the path to joining a life that others are going to be jealous of. You’ll probably be too happy to even care that they’re jealous.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some weird things you did as a kid?
Answer: I’ve always been “a dreamer”. Ever since I was a kid. When I was younger, I used to construct fictional worlds in my head. I imagined realities with people who were not like the people in the world that I was living in. In hindsight, these imagined realities were my ways of escaping from the anxiety and depression that I felt as a kid. As an adult, in times of intense anxiety or stress, I long for the worlds that I created in my head. The order that existed because I created it. The chaos that was really just order in disguise because again, I created it. The structure. The peace. The tranquility. Lots of children play in their imaginations, but my imagination was a bit more vivid than most. I wrote everything down in notebooks. I created explanations for everything. Before I learned to understand myself in the adult world, I first learned to understand myself in the fictional one that I created in my head. I tried on different personalities. Different careers. Different adventures. I tasted so much — but none of it was real. But still, it was fun. Peaceful. Exciting. Although, at times it was a bit lonely. I eventually stopped creating these imagined realities in my head because it became inconvenient to have these imagined realities and also to try to exist in the “real world”. Anyway — constructing elaborate imagined realities was a weird thing that I did as a kid.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the definition of mature love?
Answer: Sometimes in relationships, when things are going well, we get afraid that we or our partner is going to get “bored”. I get it. I’ve been in relationships in the past and I’ve felt “bored”. I’ve also been in relationships that were anything but boring, but they were not happy. There was no peace. There was no joy. In hindsight, I’m not sure if there was really love. But recently — in the last almost year — I’ve learned a lot about building a stable, happy, “mature” love. Mature love requires one to be a mature person. It also requires one to be with a mature person. A happy, healthy love is not something that “makes your life exciting”. You should have an adequate life before the other person enters the picture. Your love should simply compliment you. Allowing your love to make or break your happiness is a dangerous step. You’re the chips and your lover is the guacamole. Or the salsa. Or whatever else you like on your chips that make you (already a complete snack in your own right) even better. A mature love should make the dark days not so dark and the good days so good that you stop and think “Damn, is this life I’m living real?” Mature love, in part, comes from gratitude. But a mature love ain’t all sunshine and rainbows all the time, either. There will be disagreements at times. Arguments. If you never argue with your partner, you’re probably either some idealized person who doesn’t need to read an answer like this, or you're both holding back. In that case, you really need to read this answer. Mature love is not boring. It’s not perfect — it acknowledges the imperfections of life. Mature love is what happens when 2 people who are looking for the same thing come together and try to build a future together. Mature love is the love you wanted as a child, perhaps as a reward for doing all the work to become an adult capable of having such relationships. Mature love is learning that you learn more about love every day that you’re in it. P.S. — We’re having coffee outside in the sun in February… Texas is RAD!

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the secret to insane productivity?
Answer: The most productive people that I know are not so because they follow a perfect morning routine, work smart as opposed to hard, or because they have every single stupid optimization tool or supplement on the market. Yes — some people I know utilize productivity tools, supplements, the power of routine, or smart work — but there’s so much more to being productive than that. Or should I say, there’s so much LESS to insane productivity than that. The real secret to insane productivity and insane output is simply working more than other people. In other words, there’s no secret. Productivity is not based on routine except for the fact that you need to sit down and work every single day on your craft. Productivity is not based on working smart instead of hard except if you are already sitting down and working insanely hard every day. Productivity is not about supplements or gadgets — unless you are already working insanely hard every day. Most of the “secrets” that people look for are just distractions from the inevitable requirement for more work. Want to be great at what you do? Want to produce more great work? Want to produce higher quality work? Same. I get it. The easiest way to do this is to do more. Get uncomfortable. Push your limits. Don’t waste your most valuable resource (time) worrying about the best way to optimize your work life. Work insanely hard until you have the luxury of “focusing on working smart”. You could probably write this off as toxic hustle porn, but the question wasn’t “How do I have the best work-life balance”, it was “What is the secret to insane productivity?” The secret is to get work.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the one thing that should be taught in school that isn't already?
Answer: Martial arts, in some capacity, should be taught in schools. I don’t know if we should be teaching flying crane kicks to 5-year-olds on government money, but especially as kids age into adolescence, the need to learn self-defense becomes higher and higher. I was fairly troubled when I was younger. I got in fights at the playground, dealt with lots of bullying, and wasn’t confident in myself in any aspect of my life. Martial arts training — first wrestling for me and later Jiu-Jitsu — was extremely helpful for me. When I started training martial arts, I became more self-reliant (less bullying), better at avoiding physical violence when there was conflict, and most importantly of all, I became more confident so that in the case of a possible physical confrontation I knew how to handle myself. Martial arts training was one of the most valuable additions to my life that I made as a young person. But here’s the problem (at least here in America). When I wrestled, it was very cheap. Wrestling is a pretty inexpensive sport and not a lot of equipment is required. I just wrestled at my school every day after school. Eventually, I started training martial arts, and the first thing I learned was how expensive it can be. $125 for gym membership (usually more). Training gear — another few hundred. Commuting to and from the gym. If you want to compete in Jiu-Jitsu, it’s at least $100 per tournament. I didn’t start training martial arts very much until I landed a job at a local restaurant near the gym. I was also living with my parents and going to the local community college, so I didn’t have a ton of extra expenses at the time. I was also one of only 2 or 3 people from my high school graduating class (over 1000 people) who ended up learning Jiu-Jitsu. The lessons you learn from martial arts training are priceless, but they aren’t available to everyone. Wrestling — like I said — was pretty cheap, but the wrestling experience I had wasn’t available to everyone. Women — people who arguably need to learn self-defense the most — generally don’t even consider joining their school’s wrestling team. And even if they do, wrestling is more of a sport than it is a martial art where you are learning to defend yourself. A lot of people are turned off of the valuable skills of wrestling because wrestling workouts are extremely challenging (because it’s a competitive sport). It’d be cool if more high schools had martial arts — things like Jiu-Jitsu, Muay Thai, and Judo — available for students. I think it’d make the world a better place.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Which is the best self help book you've ever read?
Answer: Most self-help books are hot trash. As someone who writes a lot of “self-help”-esque content, I get it. The industry is terrible. It’s a bunch of mantras, corny stories, silly quotes, and annoying ideas that end up just making you more angry than anything else. I’ve read too much self-help. So much so that eventually, I graduated to philosophy — things like Nietzhsce, Viktor Frankl, etc. Then, I moved on to Eastern philosophy. The ideas that I learned from people like Confucius, Thich Nhat Hanh, Jiddu Krishnamurti, and more were all very helpful in getting me to learn to better deal with anxiety in my early 20s. Recently, I’ve moved on from reading philosophy and I’ve been reading a lot of classic novels. I’m just following what sparks my curiosity. Books like: Have been some of my favorites of the last year or so. I like fiction for self-improvement because the lens of a story is for some reason less insufferable to me than some guy sitting on his high-horse telling me what to do and how to do it. But there’s one book that trumps all the rest for me when it comes to self-help, and honestly, it’s not even a self-help book. It’s not Western philosophy, either. Nor is it Eastern philosophy. It’s a strength and conditioning book. If you’re interested in fitness, improving your life, and living well, I highly recommend that you check out 5–3–1 by former powerlifter Jim Wendler. The thing is, if you’re looking for playful anecdotes about personal development, life-changing revelations, and other typical self-help book things, you won’t find it in Wendler’s book. Instead, you’ll get something that reads a little bit more like this: “You want science and studies? Fuck you. I’ve got scars and blood and vomit.” ― Jim Wendler There’s something refreshing about blunt honestly when it comes to “improving yourself”. I don’t want the truth sugarcoated. I want you to tell me how it is. Jim does that in 5–3–1. Oh, you’ll also learn a thing or 2 about weightlifting along the way. Paperback, ebook, and audio versions are available here. Trust me, after this one, you won’t need another self-help book :)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is one piece of simple advice that actually changed your life?
Answer: One simple piece of advice that I got from a friend of mine who is a Jiu-Jitsu world champion a few years ago: When you need a break, just take a damn break. One day, I was visiting and training with a friend of mine for a week, and one day in the middle of the week, he just didn’t show up to training. He stayed home, watched TV, ate some food, and rested. In the middle of the week! While the rest of us were busy working our asses off. When I asked him if he was “okay” he said, “Yeah, I just needed a day.” He was back to training the next day as if he’d never missed a single session. Here’s what I learned from that: Ambitious people tend to get married to their work and their schedules. As an athlete, I sometimes become married to following my daily training schedule. I don’t “feel right” if I don’t follow it. As a writer, I sometimes feel a bit neurotic about meeting a daily word count quota. I don’t “feel right” if I don’t reach it. Even if I’m tired. Even if I’m burnt out. Even if I want to do anything but train and work. But the highest-level performers out there understand something that most ambitious people don’t. I definitely didn’t understand this at first. The best of the best don’t try and outwork everyone, they try and out-perform everyone. Doing the most work does not mean you are going to do the best work. Yes — hard work and elevated performance are deeply connected — but it’s not that simple. In reality, hard work and elevated performance are only correlated up to a certain point. Eventually, start working yourself into the ground. The best of the best understand that there reaches a certain point where you are going to get diminishing returns on your efforts. Plus, obsessively following your work schedule is generally not the best thing for quality of life or happiness. Decreasing quality of life and happiness, in my experience, makes you perform worse.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I develop self-confidence and self-esteem?
Answer: In Jiu-Jitsu, we do this thing called “specific training”. Essentially, what you do during specific training is you pick a specific position or objective, and you play an iterated game. For example, sometimes a specific training round could be starting in a locked-in submission or a leg lock. It’s the equivalent of playing chess and allowing your opponent to start having already taken your queen. You start the game in a situation where you are at a disadvantage. What happens in specific training? Well, at first, it’s pretty awful. You get tapped out a lot. You lose (although, you can’t really “win” in practice). You get frustrated. You cuss under your breath. Then you cuss out loud. You sigh. You think about how if you weren’t doing specific training — deliberately putting yourself in bad positions — you’d be doing great! This is step 1. Then, you come back the next day. You do more specific training. You thought you’d learned from yesterday and that today was going to be better, but it’s worse. You get tapped out even more. You almost lost your temper. You might have even slapped the mat in frustration once or twice. It’s okay. We’ve all been there. This is step 2. You keep coming back and doing this type of training where you are putting yourself in terrible positions. Over time, you start learning to survive. A few times, you even manage to escape the bad positions. You sometimes even escape in situations where you weren’t expecting yourself to. Nice work! This is step 3. Eventually, you’re not just escaping those bad positions. You’re excited to train in those bad positions because you are so confident in your ability to escape bad positions. Eventually, your escapes become one of the best parts of your game. When you compete, you sometimes get put in bad positions too, but it’s no matter. You’ve spent hours there and you don’t mind getting stuck in bad spots. You have built self-confidence in a particular skill. Life is the same way. Jiu-Jitsu training is not always the perfect metaphor for life, but it’s a really good one here. In order to develop confidence in any arena, you have to practice the skill over and over again. If you want confidence to talk to people, for example, you need to talk to lots of people. At first, you will struggle and feel uncomfortable. You will be awkward and weird. You won’t know what to say. You’ll come back to this Quora answer and curse the stupid author for telling you just “get out there!”. But you still keep trying. You talk to someone new every day. Most days, it goes badly. “Why are you so awkward?” you ask yourself. But over time, it starts to get better. You start to pick up on social cues faster. You start to anticipate interactions better. You start to realize that a lot of people are just as anxious and unconfident as you are. You start to realize that many people are more anxious and unconfident than you are. You just want to tell them to try more and “build social skills”, but you don’t want to come off as patronizing. And I guess that's the point of this post. Confidence comes from skills. Skills come from elongated periods of deliberate practice. Over a period of time spent doing anything, you will start to become more confident in your abilities. You’ll start to figure things out. You’re probably smarter than you think. Eventually, you reach a period where you have quite a bit of self-confidence. Enough that it doesn’t go away after a bad day. That, in my experience, is self-esteem.

Question: What is a short, useful, and generally applicable piece of wisdom?
Answer: If your friend only reaches out when they need help, they’re not a good friend. On the flip side, if your friend is there for you when you need help, they’re an extra good friend. You should make sure to be there for them if they ever need help. It’s also okay to give without expecting anything in return — to a point. Eventually, you’re putting yourself in harm's way. Quality friendship is a two-way street. Not all friendships require you to talk daily, but pretty much all friendships require you to be open to connection. If someone is closed off until it’s inconvenient, make room for and invest your energy into better-quality friends. Oh, and if your friend has a cooler beard than you, ask them for beard care tips. Follow their advice.

Question: What are the most difficult and useful things people have to learn in their 20s?
Answer: This is an idea I read somewhere a while ago, and it’s been really helpful for me in developing patience: Most people completely overestimate how much they can do in a day, but underestimate how much they can do in a year. In just a day, you can’t change much. Say one day, you go to the gym, eat healthy, sleep 8 hours, talk to a girl you have a crush on, and work on your business for a few hours. You do some breathing exercises you found on YouTube, read a book, and even call your mom and ask her about her day. You had a great day. But at the end of the day, you’re frustrated because your life is pretty much the same. You still kind of suck. You’re still a mess. Your muscles are still small and you’re still overweight. Your business is still in the red. The girl you have a crush on still keeps forgetting your name. You still have anxiety, your mom is still worried about you, and reading the book was hard — there were a lot of words you didn’t know. “Fuck this!” you think. You want to give up because you’re frustrated by how little progress you’ve made. A whole day of work, and you weren’t rewarded… What the hell? Right? Wrong. Positive results come from compounded efforts. Most people understand that things like fitness or weight loss take time (if you don’t, you should get that in your brain) but we often lose patience when it comes to other things. Things like: ALSO take a long time to build. These skills are a result of mental fitness, business fitness, social fitness, etc. The most important thing you can learn in your 20s (or any age, I think) is the value of patience and persistence. After a year in the gym, you’re still not at your goal weight, but you’re close. Your confidence has improved. You know the names of all exercises now and you know what muscles they work. When you walk into the gym, you have a plan. The guy at the front desk remembers your name now. After a year of working on your business, you’ve turned it around. You’ve made dozens of mistakes, lost clients, made marketing errors, and nearly given up 100 bajillion times, but you didn’t. You’ve been rewarded with your first high-paying client. When you got the Stripe notification from them, you cried. Baby steps. That girl you have a crush on doesn’t just know your name now, she’s in love with you. You’ve been together for almost a year. Working up the courage to “talk to her” became working up the courage to ask her out, then the courage to kiss her. You’re happy. You want to marry her one day. Those books you read have gotten a lot easier to read. You actually enjoy reading now. You look up fewer words. Each book teaches you a new lesson — even if sometimes the lesson is just “some ideas are not worth writing books about”. Your anxiety has gone down a lot too. You’ve done those breathing exercises every single day. You’ve learned that it’s called “meditation”, and whenever you feel stressed about work or your relationship or anything else in your life, you try and practice it. It doesn’t always “fix everything” but it usually helps. It also helps you realize that progress is a neverending journey. There’s something infinite about sitting in a finite space and doing nothing but existing. Oh, and your mom? She’s still worried about you because that’s your mom. She’s never not going to worry about you. But hey, we covered most of our bases, didn’t we?

Question: What is the single insight that most changed your life?
Answer: About 8 months ago, I decided to move to Austin, Texas. I struggled with anxiety about the move for months — from April to July. I’d lived in Chicago for roughly 20 years and wanted a change. I also was struggling to find world-class training for Jiu-Jitsu in Chicago. I also was sick of freezing my booty off every winter. I was terrified that the fear of not making my move “work” would stop me from making it at all. In the end, I just packed my car and drove all the way down to Texas to begin a new life. I left my friends, family, and everything I knew behind and “gave it a shot”. Instead of quitting when things got hard (although I definitely wanted to at times), I kept going. As of today, I have been living in Austin, Texas for 7 months. About 9 months ago, I met my girlfriend. I struggled with anxiety about my new relationship for the entire first few months of it. Fear of past traumas ruining a good thing before it began. Fear of the relationship failing despite the obvious potential it had. Fear of having everything I’d ever wanted in a partner and still not being happy. I was terrified because I cared. Despite my fears, I decided to carry forth in my relationship and do my absolute best. I decided to love openly despite being scared of being burned. I decided to try. Today, I’m in the happiest relationship I’ve ever been in. About 11 months ago, I started writing my first book. I struggled with a lot of anxiety about the book for a very long time. The fear of the book not being good. The fear of the book being good but not selling well. The fear that my stupid ADHD wouldn’t let me even finish the book in the first place. I was terrified of doing something I had always wanted to do. Nonetheless, I kept putting one word in front of the other and writing. Then, when I’d finished writing, I started editing. The book will be available in a little less than 3 months. About a year ago, I quit my job. I struggled with a lot of anxiety about it for weeks and weeks. I lost sleep over it. I worried about becoming broke and unemployed and “a bum”. I was taking a big leap and essentially trying to make a full-time living through Jiu-Jitsu seminars and writing on the Internet. I was terrified that fear wouldn’t “let me” quit my job and chase my dream. In the end, I went up to my boss and told him I was quitting and why, and he was cool with it. Life’s been good since. The lesson is this: The human experience is so much more customizable than most of us are aware of. You can quit jobs, move cities, and meet new people. You can write books, make art, and do all the things you’re afraid of. Yes — sometimes things don't work out — but realizing that you have more control over your life than you think is deeply empowering.

Question: What's the hardest truth of life?
Answer: We live in the most distracted time in all of human history. There has never been a human society that is less present than we are today. And look — there are a lot of great things that modern society has figured out. Things like: Before you yell at me to “Get off my high horse!” or make some snobby comment about how I think I’m better than other people for daring to even acknowledge this, understand that I am not saying I am free from this. I struggle with it a lot myself. Scroll. Like. Refresh. Repeat. It’s an addictive cycle that preys and feeds on your dopamine receptors until they don’t work anymore. Until you’re so addicted to scrolling that the mere idea of “thinking for yourself” is exhausting. Doing this all day long is changing your mind in a way that most people do not understand. Is reading harder for you today than it used to be? Is your anxiety stronger than it used to be? What’s going through your mind? Worries. Plans. Reminiscing over past happenings. We live in a world where people are less mindful than ever, which means that despite having more access to communicate with each other than ever, we are less connected than ever. This, in my experience, is one of the hardest things for many people to accept. The solution? I’m not entirely sure, but here are a few things that work for me: Learn to control your focus and you will learn to control (more of) your life.

Question: How do you know if you are in an unhealthy or toxic relationship?
Answer: Healthy relationship: open communication, occasional disagreements, hard conversations about the future, trust, laughter, joy, empathy. Unhealthy relationship: lack of communication, constant disagreements, only surface-level conversations about everything, lack of trust, misery, lying. In a bad relationship, the conflicts are always “me versus you”. In an unhealthy one, the conflicts are “us versus the problem”. If you’re miserable all the time and you feel “trapped” in your relationship, that is a good sign it’s a crappy one. If you look forward to the future with your partner, I think that’s a good sign it’s a good one. Listen to how you feel. “There is more wisdom in your body than in your deepest philosophy.” — Nietzsche

Question: How much should an average person have accomplished after 26 years?
Answer: I’m 26, and I’ve done a lot. Yet simultaneously, I’ve done nothing. Today — I wrote for 3 hours, went to Jiu-Jitsu practice, got a big ole black eye, came home, talked to my girlfriend, went to the gym to lift weights, dropped a weight on my foot (ow!), did laundry, got a burrito for dinner, and now, I’m sitting at home writing this Quora answer before I shut off my computer for the day. In the first 26 years of my life, I’ve: And more. Compared to some people, I’ve done and achieved a lot. Compared to others, I’m very average. Unfortunately, the way the brain works, most of us spend most of our time comparing ourselves to the people who have done more than us. This is not healthy and not ideal. The truth is that at the end of my life, the only thing that will really change between now and then is that I will have a longer list of things to tell you I’ve done. Hopefully things like “Dad” and “Novelist” will be on my list one day. But of course, compared to some people, I’ll still have done nothing. Someone my age will end up being president. Another will end up a famous musician. There will always be someone more impressive than everyone. Someone who’s accomplished more than everyone. I mean, for crying out loud, there are nearly 8 BILLION people on earth. Trying to avoid the comparison trap. It will never make you feel better. It will often make you feel worse.

Question: What small thing can tell you a lot about a person?
Answer: One small thing that I pay attention to in people is how they react when small things go wrong. There’s a long line in the coffee shop. Traffic. Someone cut them off on the road. A lot of people nowadays freak out when things like this happen to them. I think that there is more insight into who someone is when small things go wrong than there is when things go right. I also think catastrophic incidents (losing loved ones, accidents, etc) are a bad time to judge character. But when something small goes wrong, the strongest people I’ve met are completely unfazed. They simply adjust and go about their business. “A long line in the coffee shop? That’s okay. I’ll wait.” “Traffic? I’ll put my book on and let everyone know I’ll be late.” “Someone cut me off on the road? That’s okay. They must be in a hurry.” Before you can become truly strong — the type of strong where major problems don’t phase you — you must first become strong enough to deal with minor inconveniences. It’s kind of terrifying to me how many people nowadays can’t handle something small going wrong.

Question: What motivates people for self improvement?
Answer: What motivates people to do something so uncomfortable and inconvenient like improving their lives is not what you think. I would love to tell you that what motivated me to get into “improving myself” was a book, a breakup, or being overweight, but that would be a lie. I don’t think there’s every one thing that motivates people to get their shit together. I think most motivational speakers take too much credit. What generally provokes someone to actually change their life is rock bottom, or something close to it. The breakup, plus losing a job, losing a longtime partner, losing some money, being out of shape or overweight — or any combination of several of these things. The greatest motivation for self-improvement is getting smacked in the face by life and realizing you need to get stronger. Usually, after a bunch of bad shit happens, people start looking into self-improvement content. Then, the motivational speakers take credit for “changing people’s lives”. Don’t get it twisted. Speakers, authors, and bloggers can help you change your life, but if your life sucked and then you did the work and improved it, that’s because of you. You did that yourself. You had help, but give yourself some credit. You’re on the path.

Question: How do I find someone who makes me happy?
Answer: Finding someone who truly makes you happy is dumb luck. Or is it? Part of it is, but most of it is on you. You have to work on yourself. You have to stop doing stupid shit. You have to break your bad habits. You have to become the kind of man or woman who can truly make someone else happy so that someone else can make you happy. You also have to make yourself happy with or without the other person. If you’re anything like me, you probably have to improve yourself before you can find someone who makes you happy. Then, you have to put yourself out there. You have to try. You have to take risks. You might have to kiss a few frogs to find your prince or princess. You might have to get your heart broken into a bazillion pieces a time or 2. What? You thought this was going to be free? You will probably cry — tears of joy and sadness. You will probably fail. You will probably lose. The journey to finding love is like so many other journeys in life. It’s complicated. It’s non-linear. Sometimes you take 2 steps forward and then one step back. You’re probably going to screw up at times and take a few wrong turns down long windy roads that seem to lead to nowhere. But you know what’s funny? On one of those long, windy roads, you might find someone who’s on the same path as you. Someone who, as you get to know them, inspires you to keep going. Someone who sees something in you that sometimes can’t see in yourself. Someone who makes you laugh and smile and think about the world in a new way. Someone who likes you just because you’re you. Someone who doesn’t want to change you to fit their mold. Someone who’s beautiful, thoughtful, and kind. Someone who you know deserves nothing but your best. And luckily, because of all the work you’ve done, you’re able to give it to them. Luckily, because of the trials and tribulations you’ve experienced, you know how valuable what they give you is. So yeah, part of it might be dumb luck (we just happened to be on the same long, windy road), but there’s a lot of hard work and steps to getting that dumb luck dice roll to land in your favor. PS — We met on Twitter. It’s better than Tinder ;)

Question: What are some of the best ways to find inner peace?
Answer: Inner “peace”, despite the name, is a very active process. The moments that I feel the most peace are moments of stillness of the mind. Things like: The actions decrease overall anxiety and help me get more in tune with the finer things in life, like nature, spirituality, connection, and camaraderie. However, living a peaceful life is a lot of hard work. Most of us can’t just sit in meditation our whole lives. That type of peace — the kind that eventually begins to adhere to more Hedonism than Buddhism — tends to create problems because it’s so far disconnected from the reality that most people are living. Yes — meditation makes you more peaceful — but a life in meditation is not a possibility for most of us. Most of us meditate and then get yelled at by our bosses. We go for a walk and then stress out about our taxes. We do a hard workout and then have to deal with the stresses of family life, work, or school. We meditate and take care of our minds, but that doesn’t mean we’re free from stress, anxiety, or anything else that disrupts the inner peace we all want. So what do you do? You need to pair your peace with strength. Build the ability to let go of the ego. To feel free from anxiety. To move through the perils of life without becoming bitter and cold and constantly anxious. Enjoy that peace you get from those walks, but become strong enough to not let anyone take it away from you. You might not ever become a monk or a Zen master, but isn’t being a peaceful human enough? Get strong, get peaceful, and get on living.
