Question: Why it is so easy for some to find love, while for others it takes ages or can't find at all?
Answer: In my experience, the harder something is to get, the more valuable it is. Eating Doritos, for example, is easy. Doritos are yummy snacks that feel good to eat at the moment and are easy to obtain (they’re literally at every store). Home-cooked meals, on the other hand, aren’t as easy to have. You have to go to the store, walk past the Doritos, buy fresh ingredients (sometimes the store doesn’t even have the right ingredients so you have to improvise), take the ingredients home, cook them, serve them, and then hope that the food is good. It’s easier to screw up a home-cooked meal than a bag of Doritos. If you want to eat nothing but Doritos, your life would probably be easier… But would it be better? Love is like a home-cooked meal, not a bag of Doritos. If anyone claims that their relationship has been completely effortless, I question how deep the connection is. I’m not saying you need to make extreme sacrifices if you want to find love, but you do need to work. You do need to forget about the romantic equivalent of eating Doritos. You do need to prioritize a long-term relationship. Love is built over time. Love is built through hard work. I don’t believe love at first sight exists. I believe infatuation at first sight is confused with love. Love is not just enjoying the good days. Love is not what you see on an Instagram post or even a sappy Quora answer like this one. Love is “I’m not sure, but I’m going to keep going”. Love is a risk that you take despite being scared or afraid or even traumatized. Some people seem to find love easier than others, but that’s just like how some people are better at cooking home-cooked meals than others. But I like to believe that everyone can learn to love. Maybe your love won’t look the same as everyone else’s. Maybe it’ll be a little different. But it’ll be yours. Maybe that’s okay. Maybe, if you stop comparing yourself to everybody else all the time, that’s good enough.

Question: How do I stay motivated?
Answer: In my experience, inspiration comes from 2 sources: However, the motivation that’s being referred to here is a different beast entirely. If you want to “stay motivated” (over long periods of time), it has nothing to do with how much you think or how much you consume. Staying motivated is all about output. It’s all about what you do. The ability to “stay motivated” doesn’t really have anything to do with inspiration. Reading this Quora answer right now (the one where I’m trying to fire you up) won’t help you stay motivated. Even coaching can only do so much to help you stay motivated. The only person who can truly keep you motivated is you. I guess that’s a bit corny, but it’s true. Sustained motivation comes from seeing progress. It comes from working toward goals. It comes from taking chances, making efforts, and building confidence. It comes from doing things that you are proud of. For me, if I’m experiencing a period of low motivation, it’s pretty much always because I haven’t done anything that I’m proud of in a while. I haven’t really worked. However, when I have positive momentum (the foundation of sustained motivation), I feel unstoppable. I’m self-aware enough to know that I’m not unstoppable (I experience failure very often), but my hard work gives me the sensation that I’m headed in the right direction. Hard work is the best way to stay motivated. That’s kind of the problem, however. If you want to learn how to stay motivated, you’re probably not doing anything. If you knew how to stay motivated, you’d never ask. You’d be too busy doing the work — regardless of how motivated you felt. That’s why inspiration is important, too. Inspiration gets you started, but discipline keeps you going when times are hard. Discipline helps you create positive momentum, and that’s the key to staying motivated. I challenge you to do something today that you’re proud of. Baby steps. Do one thing today you’re proud of. Then do it again tomorrow. Before you know it, you’ll be spiraling in the right direction. Question: How do you know when someone really loves you?
Answer: One way that I know I’m loved is in the aftermath of the moments when I don’t feel lovable. When life is hard — too hard. When thick becomes thin. When I’m drowning. When I’m anxious or afraid. When I’m sad or depressed. When I feel like crap about myself. When I feel like a loser or a failure. When I look at her and think “Why are you still here? She loves me on the good days and bad days. Those bad days are the surest moments I have. When I know that she really loves me. I’m grateful.

Question: What makes you enjoy being alone?
Answer: The biggest misunderstanding people have about solitude is that people who enjoy being alone are “loners”. That’s not true at all — at least not for me. I enjoy my alone time. My quiet time. I was on a trip to Italy recently with my girlfriend (see picture), and I still made sure to carve out some to sit by myself, write, and enjoy a crispy, crunchy Diet Coke. Part of this is because writing is my job and I have to write my newsletter every Friday, but I also enjoy having these periods of solitude and silence. I like having time for myself and making myself a priority. I like having time to think. Time to create. Time to organize and understand my thoughts. I like having time by myself. Also, in my opinion, one of the best ways to improve your life is time by yourself. When you’re alone, you can understand the inner workings of your mind better. You can create new projects that can allow you to live more on your terms. You can learn things about yourself and the world around you. You can read, write, meditate, walk, or think. Solitude is the original most powerful source of inspiration, novelty, and creative action. In a world where everyone insists on an obsession with appearances, external validation, and “connection”, dare to spend time alone. Dare to sit with your thoughts for a bit before bringing them to the public. It’s especially true with the internet. Do not settle for insincere connections because they are convenient. Have the courage to wait. Have the courage to go inward. Your brain is already full of novel ideas, frameworks, lessons, and life-changing revelations. The only way to reach them is to cut out the noise. Also, when you don’t mind spending time alone, you choose better people to keep company with. One of the best parts about my relationship with my girlfriend is that we prefer to spend quality time together instead of maximal time. We’re content to be in the same room doing things in silence. The same things we’d be doing if the other wasn’t there. We also both appreciate our solitude when the other isn’t around. Me a little more so, but still. The older I get, the more I recognize the value of solitude. It’s important to me to have a partner who respects this. I’m blessed to have someone who enjoys her solitude too.

Question: Was the first book of any famous writer not successful?
Answer: Anthony Bourdain is the first one that comes to mind. People always talk about Bourdain’s wildly successful memoir, Kitchen Confidential. Rightfully so, if you asked me. Kitchen Confidential is a good book. It’s raw, fun to read, and you learn a lot of things about the culinary world — not all of it good. Some of the stuff that’s happening to your food before it’s served to you is wild. “An ounce of sauce covers a multitude of sins.” — Bourdain, Kitchen Confidential One thing that was notable to me about Kitchen Confidential is how well-written it is. The metaphors are deep. The descriptions are vivid. It reads like someone who’s put time into the craft of writing. This begs the question: Was Bourdain naturally such a good writer that his first book was a massive success and a future cult classic? Not exactly. Kitchen Confidential was published in August of 2000, and it was actually Bourdain’s THIRD book. Before Kitchen Confidential, Bourdain wrote a book called Gone Bamboo, published in 1997. It’s a crime thriller about a retired CIA agent who gets caught up in mobster stuff. It performed poorly in sales. Before that, Bourdain published a book called Bone in the Throat, a culinary mystery novel about a young chef in Manhattan’s Little Italy who, again, gets caught in the mob. Bourdain paid for his own book tour on this book, and it also ended up performing badly. Before he published any book at all, Bourdain submitted work to literary magazines in New York City. He wrote for 5 years for various magazines and eventually managed to get a small book advance from Random House. Before Kitchen Confidential, Anthony Bourdain was a writer, but not a mainstream one. He was an author, but no one knew who he was. He was not successful. I haven’t read his literary magazine work, but I’m assuming that long before Bourdain was crafting those soothing opening sentences for his popular TV show, Parts Unknown (or any of the shows before that) he wasn’t even a great writer. Reading Kitchen Confidential is reading 10 years of dedication to the skill of writing. Writing is a skill that takes time, experience, and maturity to build. Bourdain is one of many authors who published several books before becoming a successful writer. Oh, and want to know something funny? In 2015, Bourdain’s first novel Bone in the Throat was made into a movie, directed by a guy named Graham Henman. The film only has 3 reviews on Rotten Tomatoes, and it has a 6.0/10 on IMDB. The more you know.

Question: What is a ghostwriter? What is the difference between a ghostwriter and an author?
Answer: Ghostwriting gets a lot more hate than I realized, but that’s because most people don’t understand what it really is. If you’re a skilled writer who’s interested in working with people, ghostwriting is one of the best ways to make money by practicing your skills. My first 2 ghostwriting jobs actually came from right here on Quora :) However, ghostwriters (and the people who work with them) tend to get a bad rep. People think it’s “not real writing”. As someone who’s ghostwritten hundreds of articles online (and one ebook), I’ll tell you this: the writing that ghostwriters do is very real, and if the ghostwriter does their job, that writing is a lot better than whatever the subject probably would have written on their own. Everyone has a story, but not everyone can write. Some people need help. Ghostwriting is the perfect way for people who have compelling stories to work with writers who have the ability to tell those compelling stories. I mean, think about popular biographical films, like The Social Network or Money Ball. Just because Mark Zuckerberg and Billy Beane didn’t write the screenplays for those films, does that mean those stories have no credibility? Not at all. Will Smith’s memoir — Will — had a ghostwriter. A lot of your favorite bloggers and content writers have ghostwriters. They simply get too busy and have to hire someone to lighten the load — like me :) Ghostwriting is not lying. It’s not a dirty word. Ghostwriting is someone taking your story and helping you bring it to life. If you’re looking for someone to help you bring your story to life through digital writing, check out the link below.

Question: I exercise all the time. Why am I not losing weight?
Answer: Just like with pretty much any sort of endeavor where the goal is progress toward a main goal, a lack of progress means that you are either doing the wrong things or not enough of the right things. If you were doing the right things and the right volume of them, you wouldn't be dissatisfied with your progress. You'd be confident that you were doing everything you could. That feeling probably seems impossible to you right now. I get it. Unfortunately, the only ways to figure out if you are truly doing the "right things" are either coaching from reliable sources or continuing to do what you are doing and seeing if it gets you results. You pay the premium to skip the extended trial and error phase. If you’re exercising “all the time” and not losing weight, you’re either not really exercising all the time, you are not doing the right exercises (strength training or cardio — most people are slacking on one), or your diet sucks. Or, you haven’t been “exercising all the time” for long enough. P.S. This answer is about more than just weight loss ;)

Question: How can one make money starting a blog?
Answer: Blogging is dead. Okay — it’s a little more complicated than that. There are some people out there who use blogs and have a well-established readership. They simply write an article, hit the “publish” button, and their article will then be viewed by thousands, hundreds of thousands, or even millions of people. They monetize the site with ads, by selling a product or service, or through affiliate marketing/sponsorships. This used to be “the way” to make money writing online. But times have changed. When was the last time you read someone’s blog? Or, an even better question: When was the last time you read someone’s blog who you hadn’t heard of? That’s the big problem with traditional blogs on WordPress or Squarespace — discoverability is very low. It’s really hard to get traffic to your blog just by writing consistently. When I was in college, I wrote on a blog for about 6-months (it was part of a class), and despite publishing every week, I struggled to get more than 10 to 15 page views on my site. Even after optimizing things and reading some basic stuff on SEO, I never got much more than that. It takes time to build a blog. It takes hard work to build a blog. It takes a bit of “dumb luck” to build a blog as well. Blogging is great if you have a well-established audience of millions of followers and readers, but if you’re a “normie” like you and me, blogging is not the way to make money through digital writing. Instead, learn to use “digital writing platforms”. Sites like Medium, Substack, and Quora offer writers the ability to make money directly from their sites. I currently make a few hundred bucks per month from Medium and a few hundred bucks per month from Substack. I only make about $15 per month from the Quora Partner Program, but there’s more to writing on Quora than just the Partner Program. What I really like about Quora, X, and LinkedIn is that although there is no way to make a lot of money directly, there is a high rate of discoverability on these platforms. It might be hard to make money with these platforms directly (with X you need to get more than 3 million views over 3 months to monetize), but it’s fairly easy to reach a high amount of people and then plug a product or service. This is why I’m writing daily on Quora and Twitter, and I also write on Instagram. It’s a great time to be a writer, but not the best time to be a blogger. If you’re a beginner looking to make money with a blog, write on social platforms, create helpful products, and offer valuable services.

Question: I am 30 and still not able to figure out what is my passion in life. I am just going where life is taking me. How do I discover my passion?
Answer: From the outside, it looks like my entire life is me “following my passion”. I’m a professional martial arts athlete and coach, and a writer. For the last few years, I’ve been traveling the world competing, teaching, and writing about it here on Quora and on other sites, like Medium and Substack. I’ve been living a lot of people’s dream life. The part that fills me with a sense of imposter syndrome is that while I’m immensely grateful that I get to do what I do, I didn’t exactly dream this up when I was a kid. Real life is not as black and white as following your passion or not. When I was a kid, I liked reading books, watching movies, and immersing myself in stories. I also wanted to be a professional baseball player. Then, I wanted to be an NFL quarterback. Unfortunately, I lacked the talent to play professional baseball, and because I stand at about 5′10, 185 pounds, and was not particularly fast or athletic, NFL football was out of the question. It was after getting cut from my school’s basketball team that I found my way onto a wrestling mat, which led me onto this journey of martial arts and self-improvement. It was that journey that eventually sent me into the world of writing and storytelling. But I didn’t set out to “find my passion”. I live a passionate life. If you’re lost and struggling to find a passion, just do something. Act. Move. Live. The passion will come. However, if you just sit at home and ponder “What am I passionate about?” you’ll never find it.

Question: What is the best way to stay healthy?
Answer: The best way to stay healthy has nothing to do with sun tanning your balls, eating raw testicles, or getting up at 4 am to flip tires as a workout. It doesn’t matter much what your diet is, it doesn’t matter what your exercise routine is, and it doesn’t matter how many water fasts you do. Health is boring. The trick is that the “out there” stuff that you see health bros talk about online is only really talked about for “shock value”. If Liver King didn’t eat liver, he’d just be some crazy guy on a bunch of steroids. But… Is a guy like that… Healthy? I don’t think so. The best way to stay healthy is to develop this itty bitty little thing called “discipline” or “self-control”. The best way to stay healthy is to have a couple of slices of this lovely pizza in front of me, but not the whole thing. To never go “off the rails”. To indulge — but not to excess. To view food as a part of life, not a drug that you base your whole life around. To view exercise as a vehicle for health, not as torture for bad eating. To always bounce back after a bad day. To exercise even when you don't want to. To not drink too much alcohol (it’s easier to have 5 drinks than 1). To have 1 cookie for dessert, not 11. The best way to be healthy is to develop a “diet” and “lifestyle” that you don’t need a day off from.

Question: What are some intense life quotes?
Answer: Here are a few quotes that have made me re-examine the way I think about pretty much everything. “It is no measure of health to be well adjusted to a profoundly sick society.”—Jiddu Krishnamurti “It’s dark because you are trying too hard. So throw away your baggage and go forward. There are quicksands all about you, sucking at your feet, trying to suck you down into fear and self-pity and despair. That’s why you must walk so lightly. Lightly my darling...”― Aldous Huxley “Wisdom cannot be imparted. Wisdom that a wise man attempts to impart always sounds like foolishness to someone else ... Knowledge can be communicated, but not wisdom. One can find it, live it, do wonders through it, but one cannot communicate and teach it.”― Hermann Hesse “Whoever fights monsters should see to it that in the process he does not become a monster.” — Friedrich Nietzsche “The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation” — Henry David Thoreau "If you're twenty-two, physically fit, hungry to learn and be better, I urge you to travel – as far and as widely as possible. Learn from them — wherever you go." — Anthony Bourdain “The meaning of life is that it is to be lived, and it is not to be traded and conceptualized and squeezed into a patter of systems.” — Bruce Lee “The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts.” — Marcus Aurelius “Those who have a 'why' to live, can bear with almost any 'how'.” — Viktor Frankl “Think lightly of yourself and deeply of the world.” — Miyamoto Musashi

Question: What did you look like when you were depressed?
Answer: Depression takes many forms. When I was dealing with severe depression from 2015 to 2019, I was still a fairly high-achieving individual. I became top 10 in the world in Jiu-Jitsu at my belt rank, won a world championship at another belt rank, and I was in college. I also worked some part-time jobs, taught a few private lessons, and taught some BJJ classes. I was a pretty high-achieving individual, but that doesn’t mean I wasn’t dealing with depression. See for me, the achievements that I earned while I was depressed were pretty much the only thing that kept people from worrying about me. Apart from working on my goals, all I did was sit at home, sleep, and essentially “be depressed”. I didn’t have friends during this time. I didn’t date. I was too sad. I was angry all the time. No — I didn’t gain or lose a bunch of weight like some people do when they’re depressed, but why would I? I compete in a sport where I have to obsessively monitor my weight. I had to be fit and physically healthy, and if I didn’t maintain that, I knew people would worry. When I was depressed, the last thing I wanted was people worrying about me. But anyway, here’s a picture of me when I was dealing with the most severe depression of my life. I was fit, healthy, and even had a six-pack, but I was miserable. I was planning to kill myself during this period. Depression takes many forms.

Question: I am 23 years old and unemployed. I still live with my parents. I want to follow my passion but can't because of my depression. What do I do?
Answer: This advice might seem counterintuitive, but I don’t think you should “follow your passion”. At least, not right now. Here’s my story: When I was 23, I also lived with my parents for about 1 year and 2 months. It was after college, I had no idea what I wanted to do with my life, no job, no real skills, and the longer I stayed with my family, the more depressed I became. It was a terrible period for myself, my mental health, and my relationship with my family. I’m lucky I got through it. Here’s what I did: I also wanted to “follow my passion” — the passion of writing, traveling, and doing Jiu-Jitsu full time. I was so obsessed with this passion that I completely refused to do anything that wasn’t “my passion”. I distanced myself from people who weren’t in line with my goals. I self-isolated, self-medicated with extreme exercise and drinking, and I wrote self-loathing articles on the internet for an entire year, hoping that I’d “crack the code” and write a viral hit that would “change my life”. But that didn’t work. What worked instead was focusing on creating something of myself that was at least kind of valuable. Instead of writing articles about myself, I started a freelance copywriting business and started cold-emailing local businesses. I started teaching Jiu-Jitsu, and the way I got my first job teaching was by literally asking everyone in my city on social media if they were looking for an instructor. I ended up getting a steady job teaching Jiu-Jitsu for a summer that turned into a long-term gig. I started teaching private lessons. My freelance business grew to the point where I had so many clients that I was paying my sister to help me with content creation. Then, I moved out of my parent’s house and I’ve been living ever since. If you’re young, depressed, and anxious, the best thing you can do is aim to create value, acquire skills, and build a network. If you’re severely depressed, you need to treat your depression, and then focus on the bolded point above. It’s all about building a foundation. When I started writing and building my teaching network, it was a survival mechanism. I didn’t have “passions” anymore, I was just trying to monetize the only skills I had. However, as I started to do better (freelance writing became “ghostwriting”), teaching kids Jiu-Jitsu classes became teaching private lessons at a premium rate and seminars for enough money to pay my rent in an afternoon, my “dreams” started to come back. I started to want to travel. I started to become passionate about creative work. I started writing essays like the one you’re reading right now. Don’t “pursue your passion”. I mean, that itself might be the reason you’re depressed. Acquire skills. Help people. Learn. Create a life worth living. “Passion” is not something to follow, it’s something to find.

Question: What is the secret to success?
Answer: If you look for the secret to success in the processes of the single most successful people out there, you probably are going to be frustrated. If you look for the secret to success in Michael Phelps’s diet or Michael Jordan's basketball journey, you probably won’t learn much about success and you probably will be pretty disappointed. This is why, instead of obsessing over the “hack” that will make you the best you can be, aim to cultivate self-awareness. Cultivate the ability to learn your weaknesses and improve on them. Become self-motivated, not driven by desired results and victories. Avoid an “all or nothing” approach, because having this approach will only make you miserable. If failure at any point in the process kills the dream, the dream probably was never that strong. The best success comes from working your hardest, improving your weaknesses as much as you can, and learning to simply “let it fly” when the time is right. You need to understand yourself just as much as you understand your given skill. That is “the secret” to success.

Question: Why do I suck so much?
Answer: You don’t suck, you’re just early in the process. When I was 12, I joined my middle school’s wrestling team. In my first year of wrestling, I sucked. I won 4 matches and lost 14. I got pinned (put on my back and held there against my will) a lot. I got pinned more times than I won matches. I finished the season and hoped that next year, I’d be better. Everyone I talked to about wrestling said that it takes a while to get good at the sport. My second season was worse than the first. I won 4 matches again, matching my win total from my first year, but I lost 28 matches. I got pinned several times more than I won. It was undeniable. It my second year of wrestling, I cemented the fact that I sucked. I don’t really know why I didn’t quit then, after that miserable 4–28 season, but I didn’t. I kept training, kept wrestling, and desperately tried to get better. Over the next 4 years, I wrestled in several hundred more matches. I was never a state champion wrestler. I never even had dreams of wrestling on the Olympic team. By my senior year of high school, I was decent. That was it. Years of training, hundreds of matches, and hundreds of losses, and all I ever got to be was decent. Kind of sucks, doesn’t it? But my wrestling experience became about so much more than just trying to “not suck” at wrestling. When I finished wrestling after my senior year, I was done. I didn’t want to wrestle anymore. I had no interest in being on a mat. I went into a boxing gym one day a few months after my final wrestling match, and from there, my love affair turned marriage to Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu started. Jiu-Jitsu was and has always been fun for me, but what I loved about BJJ from the start was that I was good at it. I picked things up faster than most people. I was tougher than most people. I was more athletic than most of my training partners. I was just better, and I excelled quickly. The reason? Wrestling. I spent all those years trying to be “okay” at wrestling, and the skills that I learned from wrestling — specific things like base, posture, and takedowns plus mental things like toughness, discipline, and grit — allowed me to improve at a very high rate compared to the average BJJ practitioner. This culminated when I won a world championship in BJJ at my belt rank with just a few years of training. I later have become a professional Jiu-Jitsu athlete, have competed in some of the biggest grappling events in the world, and have been able to make a career for myself using BJJ. At first, however, I sucked at competing in grappling. I was able to manufacture an “advantage” for myself through years and years of hard work, despite sucking for a good percentage of time along the way. But that’s kind of the thing about, well, everything. When you start out, you suck. When I started writing, I was terrible. Reading my early articles and posts here on Quora makes my skin crawl. When I started trying to have romantic relationships, I was also terrible. My trauma and anxiety determined everything. It was miserable. When I started cooking, I was awful. I broke my mom’s blender the first time I tried to make a smoothie in high school for crying out loud. Skills take time to develop. The more difficult the skill (something like love or grappling people, for example), the longer it will take you. You need to respect that. You need to respect the game. It’s the only way you’ll ever stop sucking at anything worthwhile.

Question: What are the best romantic relationship tips?
Answer: Having better romantic relationships has not come easy to me, but I’ve learned a lot over the years — mostly by screwing up. Here, I’ll give you 3 of my most important rules for healthier, happier, and longer-lasting romantic relationships: Before my first date with my current partner, I was nervous. I was staying in a new city (Austin), and she was flying all the way from California, literally just to meet and go out with me. We both were nervous that our first date — something we both were taking a risk in doing — was going to be a flop. We hit it off over the phone, but being in person is different. We were both smart enough to know that. I wanted to make sure I said all the right things (I didn’t), and so did she. We both were more interested in being perfect being our imperfect selves. This is a normal feeling, but you should still fight it. Don’t try to be perfect. Be natural. It’s corny, but you have to “be yourself” at the beginning of a relationship if you want to have romantic relationships with high compatibility. This might get you rejected in the short term, but it will lead to deeper relationships in the long term. You’ll filter out people who aren’t actually interested in you, you’ll click faster with the people you’re supposed to, and best of all, you won’t have to deal with a lot of the “bullshit” in the modern dating world because you’re being yourself, not the person that people expect you to be. Relationships that are built around authenticity are the ones that are built to last. Rule 1: Don’t play a character. Probably the biggest flaw that I have in relationships is a strong, deep-rooted desire to never have any conflict. I hate fighting. It’s exhausting. It’s not fun. It makes me feel embarrassed, guilty, and icky. Most of the time, my fights are because of something my unpredictable ass has said or done, and it always makes me feel bad about myself. I used to run from this feeling, probably because it reminded me of getting yelled at as a kid or something. I started to do whatever I could to avoid conflict in relationships, and a funny thing happened: I’d have no conflict for a while, but then when I did have conflict, I’d have the worst fights imaginable. I only know that now because when I have fights with my current partner, they’re very mild and easy to work through. Sometimes, you’re going to fight. Sometimes you are going to have disagreements. In the early stages of your relationship, this will be a big test for you as a couple. The longer you avoid the truth, the more likely you are to have the natural “fights” you are going to have with your partner “blow up”. Don’t let resentment fester. Rule 2: Tell the truth. Avoiding the truth is lying. Let’s talk about those “fights” for our last point because they’re very important. At least, how you react to them is very important. When you fight with your partner, where does your mind go? When you struggle with keeping your relationship going, do you fight, or do you give up? I’ve come to believe that there’s a little bit of “struggle” that’s involved to keep a romantic relationship alive and healthy. You have to work for it. This is part of what makes relationships worth having — they’re not easy. If you’re like most people, you probably go straight for ego protection. You probably go straight to make yourself “win” the argument, and you don’t care about the sake of your relationship. You just want yourself to be “the good guy”. The truth is that when you’re fighting with a loved one, there’s no “good guy”. You are a team, and the sooner you both switch your mindset from “Me versus You” to “Us versus The Problem”, the more likely you are to avoid big fights, hurt feelings, and resentment. It’s also good to make sure you don’t run the second you have fights. I used to do this a lot because I was taught to have “an abundance mindset” when it came to relationships. I was brought up to believe that losing a girlfriend didn’t matter because there were “plenty of other fish in the sea”. While this is true and while a breakup won’t be the end of you, you can’t think this way if you want love that lasts. Rule 3: Don’t run away the second it gets hard. Fight. If you fight and fail, and least you can give up with no regrets. Also, learn the difference between “toxicity” and “a tough time” — but I guess that’s really another post for another day.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What makes a writer great?
Answer: When I learn about highly successful writers, pretty much all of them have one thing in common: An insane amount of volume at their craft. There’s a story about Stephen King that I think summarizes this pretty well. Every time he got a rejection slip from a publication on a story, he’d attach it to a nail that he stuck in his wall. Here’s what he had to say about that nail and his writing volume (as just a kid!) in his memoir, On Writing: “By the time I was fourteen the nail in my wall would no longer support the weight of the rejection slips impaled upon it. I replaced the nail with a spike and went on writing.” He put an insane amount of volume into making himself incredible at his craft. He got the 10,000-hour rule. He worked his ass off. Blah blah blah. All the corny stuff. But the truth is that when it comes to greatness, there’s something to be said about the corny stuff. There’s gotta be a hint of neuroticism there, maybe some demons, but most of the time, truly great art doesn’t just come from pain or being sad or “talent”. It comes from the ability to express the innermost thoughts and feelings that come with being a human being. That can only be done with practice. You can’t be great at anything until you master it. The way you master it is through a high volume of “deliberate practice”. Are there exceptions to this rule? Of course. There are exceptions to anything. However, I don’t think writers who are looking up “what makes a writer great” are going to be those exceptions. For most of us who want to get better at writing, it’s about putting in the time, taking failure and rejection on the chin, and just inching forward — day after day.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the must see attractions in London?
Answer: I was born in London, and although I live in the US, I’ve been to London 4 times in the last year and a half. There is a lot to do here. I’ll give you just some notes on things I’ve done. The riverwalk is wonderful, even on a rainy day. I was in London for a Jiu-Jitsu match, and the day after the event I went for a lovely (and long) walk along the Thames River. Because it’s Christmas time, there’s a cute little Christmas market set up along the river with shops, food vendors, and more. They also play Christmas music all day long, if you’re into that sort of thing. The food at the market is decent, but if you really want the London culinary experience, you need to try some Indian food. English food tends to get a bad rap, and honestly, if you’re eating normal English food, it’s deserved. However, Chicken Tikka Masala is the National dish of England, and some people say it was invented there (by Indian chefs, of course). It’s closely related to Butter Chicken. I stumbled into this place called “Dishoom” by accident, and it was really yummy and seemed to be pretty popular. I went at about 10:30pm, and I had to wait nearly 30 minutes for a table. The restaurant had a really nice aesthetic as well, a great bar, and an extensive menu. Although Dishoom has many locations in London, I went to the one in Shoreditch, which is kind of a trendy, artsy area a bit North of the river. If Dishoom seems too fancy for you (it’s described as a “retro-futurist cafe”), there are a ton of great curry houses in London. Specifically, you should check out the suburb of South Hall or on Brick Lane, which is just a few minutes from the aforementioned Dishoom location. After you’ve gotten your food, let’s get back to the riverwalk. If you start at Tower Bridge and walk for like, a really long time, you’ll hit Big Ben and the London Eye. The London Eye is that giant Ferris wheel thing (below), and it’s kind of an expensive ride. I guess it’s a bucket list thing, but I haven’t been on it (or desired to go on it) in any of my 4 trips here. I went on it with my dad when I was 10 though. I don’t remember it being particularly memorable, but nice views I guess. Honestly, the river and the Indian food are enough to keep you occupied for at least an afternoon, maybe a full day. But what else can you do in London? If you like shopping and eating, check out Camden Market. (above) There are dozens of food vendors and dozens more shops. It’s a bit packed. It’s “happenin’”, as my dad would say. He would know, he used to live near there in the 90s. Camden Market has something for everyone, and it’s definitely worth spending a few hours there wandering around and seeing what it has to offer. I picked up a little gift for my girlfriend there and my friend got some beard oil. One of the coolest parts about London is the complete vastness of it. The city is huge, and getting around is going to feel like a bit of a daunting task. Take the tube, the famous red double-decker bus, or, if you’re ballin’ and in a hurry, a black cab. These are just a few of the things you can do in London, but the possibilities for how you can enjoy the city are endless. What’s your favorite travel memory from London?

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best comeback for "All men are the same!"?
Answer: There are roughly 4 billion men in the world. Here’s a bit of a visual representation of what 1 billion dollars looks like. Multiply that by 4 to imagine what 4 billion looks like. Then, zoom out and remember that we’re talking about people, not dollars. I won’t say that all men are completely different because doppelgangers exist, people act alike, and biologically, all men are very similar (although still different), but all men aren’t the same. Some men are monstrous. Other men are incredible. Some men are power-hungry. Other men swear off material possessions. Some men cheat on their wives. Other men do not. Other men don’t even have wives. Some men don’t have wives because they have husbands. I can’t even confidently say that “all men have penises” thanks to a rare congenital condition called “Aphallia”. Click the link, if you’ve got the balls. Now, let’s reverse the roles for a moment: I don’t think all women are the same because I don’t think I, one man, can confidently make generalizations about billions and billions of people. I’m not that intellectually lazy. Not all men are the same. Not all women are the same. Not all people are the same. We’re all similar, but we’re not the same. This isn’t some snowflake BS either. There’s literally too much variance among humans (and men, and women) to make sweeping generalizations about behavior. Saying “All ______ are the same” is an emotional statement, not an intellectual one.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I begin as a writer?
Answer: You begin by writing. There’s nothing else to do if you want to “begin”. You don’t need to read. You don’t need to be “inspired”. And for crying out loud, you don’t need to ponder. I started writing during the COVID-19 pandemic when I was stuck at home and bored and unable to do Jiu-Jitsu all day. I, like a lot of people, always wanted to “write a book”, but I couldn’t stand the idea of not ever trying to do it. So, one night, I sat down at my computer and tried to “write a book”. I think I watched 2 YouTube videos before I jumped in. From there, I tried to articulate a story. From my experience in wrestling and Jiu-Jitsu, I knew that the way to get better at something was to practice every day, so every night I’d sit down at my computer with sparkling water and hammer out 500–1000 words. After about 2 months of practicing every day (thankfully the pandemic gave me a lot of time to practice), I had a 60k-word novel. I never published the novel. I’ve revisited it a few times, but it’s kind of a trashy book. I’m a little embarrassed by it at this point. Still, it’s important that you know before I published anything, I wrote 60,000 words for myself. This was when I started to fall in love with writing. I wrote that novel draft 3 years ago. Those were the early days of my writing journey. A few months after that, I started writing articles on a website called Medium dot com. About a year after that, I started writing here, on Quora. Since then, I’ve published 3 ebooks, ghostwritten blogs, and newsletters on personal development, and used writing to start and build my first business. Writing has changed my life, and the only reason that’s been able to happen for me is that I began. I didn’t tell people I was beginning, I just began. I just started practicing. I fell in love with the craft for the sake of the craft. I learned to love the ins and outs of the game. I learned to respect how hard writing is and how hard it will always be. The way you begin is by sitting down and getting some words out on a piece of paper or an open word document.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Life: What one piece of advice would you give to your younger self?
Answer: Stop trying to be like people around you, and start trying to find people like you. One thing I struggled with a lot when I was younger was a fear of loneliness. The fear of not fitting in. Dealing with bullies. Social anxiety. I thought that the way to free myself from anxiety was to “fit in”. To be more like the people I was already around. To mimic them to the point of losing myself. But what I found was that the harder I tried to “fit in”, the more unhappy I was. The more unnatural my life was. The more frustrated I became. Trying to fit in and be “one of the cool kids” was exhausting, and I never really felt “cool” while doing it because I felt like I was wearing someone else’s skin. Instead, over time, I’ve learned to march to the beat of my own drummer a bit. I explored my interests. I dove headfirst into the things that I loved (writing and Jiu-Jitsu), and I got pretty good at them. I pursued the lifestyle that I wanted and let a lot of people go in the process. In the pursuit of trying to master these skills and live the life that I am blessed to live, I’ve met some of the best friends I could ask for. People who don’t want me to change. People who don’t care if I’m “cool”. People who like me for me. One key piece of advice I’d give my younger self would have been to skip the “trying to fit in” phase. I might have met my friends sooner. But at the same, I might have needed that place to get to the one I’m at now. Either way, today I’m happy. I wish my younger self new that that was a possibility.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: If you could tell your younger self one thing, what would it be and why?
Answer: Don’t just blindly “follow your passion”. When I was younger, I, like most young men and women in the Western world, was bombarded with messages about how if I were to find a fulfilling career or a job that I didn’t hate, I was going to be miserable for the entirety of my adult life. I had options for what I could become, but because of that, I was terrified of choosing the wrong thing. What if the thing I chose (Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, and later writing), didn’t end up being my passion? What would I do then? I spent my early 20s in this constant state of panic — that I had to either “achieve my dreams” and “find my passion” or else I’d be unremarkable. Social media made this problem even worse for me. On social media, you only really see “the outliers”. The small, loud minority of people who have found their passion, achieved success, and are “living their dreams”. You think that in order to be happy, you have to be like that. But you’re not supposed to base your own life on that of the outliers. If you’re an outlier yourself, you probably don’t need this advice. If I could tell anything to my younger self, it’d be to spend less time worrying about “finding your passion” — which led to this perilous and toxic journey through the self-improvement world — and focus on what you’re doing right now. Stop speculating so much, and start living. Be present. Be more mindful. Instead of focusing on a specific activity that is “your passion”, try to find activities that are in line with your values. Find things that bring out the best in you. For me, my passions for Jiu-Jitsu and writing started not because I love fighting and writing, but because I enjoy improving myself. I enjoy building skills. I enjoy working with people (Jiu-Jitsu) and I enjoy thinking deeply about the world (writing). Thanks to the Internet, you can build nearly any life you want. That doesn’t mean it’s going to be easy, but it sure as hell is possible.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Love: What are some good photographs depicting friendship?
Answer: I started doing Jiu-Jitsu with these guys when I was just 17 years old. The guy on my left is 10 years older than me, and the guy on my right is 15 years older than me. When we met, we were all beginners in Jiu-Jitsu, but they were grown men and I had barely finished puberty. They had man strength, and I had nothing but a stubborn resilience to try to keep fighting them. Our friendship started off with them literally beating the crap out of me on the mat every day. But over time, things started to change. They went from their early 30s to their mid/late 30s. I hit my early and now mid-twenties. We traveled the US and the world together. I went to India, England, and Poland with the men in this picture. For them, life started to change. One of them got married. The other started several successful business ventures and became busier. I started traveling the world doing Jiu-Jitsu, training, and competing, while they were busy with other kinds of adventures that life has to offer. But that didn’t change our friendship in the slightest. We all had a love for Jiu-Jitsu that made sure that we saw each other at least a few times a week. Now, when we spar, I may get the better of them, but when it comes to real life (you know, the one that happens outside of a gym), I need these guys more than I can express here today. They’ve taught me countless lessons about friendship, life, business, and even relationships. I feel lucky that while a lot of people my age were out partying and drinking, I spent my early 20s working on building my skills in BJJ and spending time with amazing people who actually want me to succeed. Nowadays, we don’t get to see each other as much. I live in Texas and they live in Chicago. They have more responsibilities because they’ve reached that phase of life. My own life has been crazy as well — I’ve got a new girlfriend, I’ve been working like a maniac on my first book and redesigning my life in Texas, and I’ve been doing Jiu-Jitsu all over the world. We had every excuse to not see each other as much or not talk to each other as much. And yet, that didn’t happen. I still managed to get back to Chicago last weekend to see them get their black belts in Jiu-Jitsu. My friend on the right still managed to take the week off work to come to England with me this week. This picture alone might not depict friendship, but I wish I could tell you everything that each of us went through to make this picture possible. Being there for someone through everything is, in my opinion, the best depiction of friendship that exists.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why some people prefer not to talk about themselves?
Answer: I travel the world teaching Jiu-Jitsu seminars often. I do a lot of speaking, but pretty much all of it is about Jiu-Jitsu and none of it is about myself. My seminars typically consist of about an hour and a half to 2 hours of technical instruction, followed by a Q&A session, followed by open training with the seminar attendees. Basically, a bunch of people pay money to learn Jiu-Jitsu from me and then try to fight me afterward. It’s a great time. I’m also paid well for these seminars, so I make sure to go above and beyond and deliver a good time for the attendees. I keep the environment pretty laid back because I never want people who attend my seminars to think I have this aura of superiority. I’m just like them, only I’ve done Jiu-Jitsu a bit longer than them. Here’s what my seminar looks like: I don’t even like standing, partially because I’m tired, but also because I’m not a motivational speaker. As a seminar giver, I’m barely even a teacher. I’m more of a guide trying to help someone find out if Nonetheless, a lot of times, I get asked very personal questions. Things like dealing with anxiety, finding motivation, or even things like balancing personal life and training life. Sometimes, it’s funny to me because I’m 26 and I’ve barely figured out my own life. I don’t know if I have the qualifications to tell other people what to do, and I believe that it’d be irresponsible for people to do exactly what I do. When I’m speaking or talking to people I try not to talk too much about myself. I try to ask them about themselves first. I try to speak from a place of helping them than I do a place of imposing my own ideas. This isn’t because I think I’m better than anyone, it’s because I don’t want to impact people in a way that makes them exactly like me. In my head, I prefer the idea of helping people discover what techniques, philosophies, and ideas work for them than I do the idea of creating a bunch of clones who believe exactly what I believe. Plus, I talk about myself and my life quite a bit when I write. It seems like it’d be a bit self-centered to talk about myself all the time in real life, too. Question: What is the best strategy for boosting self-confidence?
Answer: A lot of the answers to this question make me laugh. Stuff like buying fancy clothes, taking cold showers, or following a morning routine won’t help you build genuine confidence. Confidence that lasts during hard times. The truth is confidence is not easy to obtain. It can’t be bought or sold, it can’t be found in the shower, and confidence doesn’t give a damn what time you wake up. Confidence is built through hard work. Here’s a short story about how I built confidence in combat sports. When I was a kid, the moments before wrestling matches were always heated and hectic. Angry music. Frantic pacing. Uncontrollable anxiety. It was never "fun". I did not enjoy competing for a long time. As I transitioned to Jiu-Jitsu as a young adult, I experienced this anxiety at different times and in varying severities throughout my competitive career. It's a normal feeling, but there's something problematic about normalizing it too much. For a time several years ago, I thought that my nerves were because I was unconsciously aware that I wasn't good enough. It turns out, about 7 years later, that I was correct in my initial observation. At the time of those matches when I felt extremely anxious, I wasn't good enough. The reason? I wasn't preparing enough and I wasn't preparing properly. I was going into matches with gaping holes in my game and I was terrified that those holes were going to be exposed. Nowadays, however, it's different. This is pretty much entirely because over the last half a year, I've been truly giving my all in preparation for the events I compete in. It’s not that I didn’t train hard before, but I’ve reached a new level. I’m literally giving it everything I’ve got. I don’t think I have much more in me to give besides what I give now. This has been huge for my confidence. The opponents I compete against now are better than the opponents I went against in my youth, and yet I feel more calm and excited to compete than ever. I think this illustrates an important lesson on confidence. You are not entitled to feel confident just because you're you. This is delusion, and it's a problem. You get to feel confident because you do the work prior to the thing that you're nervous about. In school, when you study for a test, you're less nervous. In grappling, when fully believe you give your all in training, you get to feel more confident in your skills. When you don't hold back, you know that all failure is final. There's no "what if". The big difference for me in the last 5 months has been simply doing everything I possibly can - all the time. It's an exhausting way to live, but when I do that, I get to sleep easy before the big days. Life is more fun. I'm happier. Things bother me less. This isn't just about competing in wrestling matches.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I make my life like a movie?
Answer: Your life is already kind of like a movie. Your life has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Even if you don’t know when the middle and end days are coming, they will eventually. But, like a good movie, the ending of your life isn’t really supposed to be the point. You’re not supposed to watch a movie for the end, you’re supposed to watch it to enjoy the whole story. You’re supposed to see the whole story play out. This, in my opinion, makes our lives and the movies we watch very similar. However, in the age of social media, I think people forget about a key difference between the movies we watch and our actual, real lives. A movie is created to be watched by an audience. A movie that no one likes watching is bad. In your real life, however, no one is watching, most of the time. In reality, it’s pitiful to live your life for an audience, because the audience doesn’t exist. That’s what makes social media so sad to me sometimes — people start to live authentically because they care so heavily about an audience that doesn’t even exist in their real life. They want to make their life like a performance, even though the entire audience is empty. The truth is that no one thinks about you more than you do. However, in a world obsessed with social media and the internet, everyone seems to think they’re the star of their own movie. And yes, it’s kind of true — minus the audience. Minus the lights. Minus the linear storytelling that makes sense all the time. Your life is not always like a superhero movie where you fight the dragon, get the girl, and ride off into the sunset. There is no sunset, and no one cares if you get the girl but you. Your life is kind of like your own movie, but no one else is watching it except for you. The problem nowadays is that the internet/social media makes people think that everyone else is watching their movies, all the time. If you can, embrace anonymity. Be faceless. Do the things that rattle and destroy your sense of self. Have an ego death. Sprints. Hard workouts. Difficult conversations with a lover. Writing and bleeding on the page. Realizing your limits and realizing that no one thinks about them except for you. The humility you get from this kind of thing is the key to truly focusing on improving your life. Ironically, that’s how you get a life that other people become envious of.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What surprised you the most about living alone?
Answer: Living alone is the bomb diggity — sometimes. I like having “my space”. A workspace. A bedroom. My special chair in the living room. My kitchen is like my special food sanctuary. These things are really nice for me and make me feel safe and secure, but as I’ve gotten older, I’ve found that I’m less married to my routine and more open to accepting others. I love when my girlfriend stays over and I’m sure we’re going to love living together, but even when that occurs I’m going to make it a point to have my own little space. Something that’s “mine”. I'm not sure if this will work in reality, but in theory, it’s what I want. I think that the biggest thing that surprised me about living alone has been all the cleanup. When you have roommates or live with your family, you all (hopefully) share the chores. Someone takes out the trash. Someone does the dishes. Someone cleans the toilet (worst job). When you live alone, all the clean-up is on you. This isn’t a problem unless you’re messy. One of two things will likely happen: You’ll either stop being messy because you don’t want to clean up, or you’ll succumb to your mess and live in filth. If you ever want to get married, I think the first is better. Here’s me, doing the laundry. Cleaning clothes. Livin’ the dream.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Are some people destined to be unhappy, regardless of life circumstances?
Answer: I struggle with this, especially when I’m at my happiest. Sometimes I think it’s all my fault. It’s hard to allow yourself to be happy when you’ve been depressed and anxious. The hurt you feel when you’re sad becomes kind of like a monster that you’re trying to outrun. You don’t know when it’s going to come back and get you, there’s just a part of you that’s certain that it will. You spend your days trying to cement yourself further and further away from this hurt, but the holes it left are still there. You start to fear that the hurt is just a part of who you are. That it will never go away. You start to fear that the hurt is engrained in your DNA and that no antidepressant or therapy session will ever help. You start to think that it will not only ruin your life again but the lives of the people you love most. The people who support you and keep you afloat when you’re losing control. The people who you literally can’t live without. You become so engrossed in this grand act of protection (although you’re not sure who you’re protecting) that you start to distance yourself. You isolate. You run — although you’re not moving your legs. This is when it’s a good time to zoom out. Go for a walk. Take some space. Do some Jiu-Jitsu. Workout. Eat some food. Watch your favorite show. Maybe drink a cold can of sparkling water (I’d recommend laying off the booze if you’re feeling sad). Read some stuff. Maybe this Quora post is doing it for you. Realize that the unhappiness that you feel despite a seemingly happy life isn’t new to you. This is part of why I like sad music and books. It helps me realize that I’m not a crazy person. You’re not ungrateful. You’re not a brat. You’re dealing with stuff. That’s okay. Almost everyone deals with stuff sometimes. Realize that you maybe aren’t destined to be unhappy forever, regardless of life circumstances. You’re just unhappy right now. You’re just having a tough day. You can pull yourself out of it. When I’m depressed, anxious, or embarrassed, I try to remind myself that I don’t want an easy, happy life. I want the strength to endure and transcend a difficult one. This, for now, is working for me. I’m happier than I’ve ever been, even on my bad days. It’s been this way for several years now.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the best towns to visit in Italy?
Answer: My girlfriend and I spent 3 days in Ravello earlier this year, and it ended up being my favorite place we went to on the whole trip. Here’s the sunrise view from our hotel room on the morning we left. Ravello is known for its views, lemons, and its popular yearly summer music festival. According to the research I did before going on this trip, Ravello is called by some as “la città della musica” — the city of music. But whether you go to the music festival or not, Ravello is a great place to visit. It’s a small town — with a population of around 2500. The food is good (as it is almost everywhere in Italy), the views are stunning, and you’re also kind of… “off the grid”. I loved this. I mostly just hung out with my girlfriend, hung out by the pool, did some journaling, and went on a couple of hikes. I never got bored of the view. Since you’re on the coast, the seafood is a must-try. I forget what this dish was (I don’t speak Italian), but I loved it. In addition to the pasta and the seafood (the pizza is good too), Ravello has a lot of lemons. Well, technically it’s the whole Amalfi Coast that has a lot of lemons, but the lemon craze is really concentrated on “the path of lemons” — which goes from Maiori to Minori and through Ravello. The abundance of lemons means lots of “limoncello”, which is a very popular liqueur, but I’d never had it before going there. I don’t know if any limoncello I have now is going to live up. Here’s a limoncello spritz (a popular limoncello cocktail) that I had with my lady. And here are some funny dick-shaped limoncello bottles we saw at a local shop. Viewer discretion is advised lol. I highly recommend seeing the Amalfi Coast at least once in your life. If for no other reason than to pretend like you’re a character in a Christopher Nolan movie (parts of Tenet were filmed in Positano, another town on the Amalfi Coast that’s WAY more expensive than Ravello). What’s your favorite town to visit in Italy? Next time I’m there, I want to visit Lake Como.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the most underrated cities I should visit in the United States?
Answer: I’ve lived in the US since I was 5 years old. It’s an incredible country, but most tourists only visit the big cities and the “famous” places. They miss out on some of the best in the country. Most folks only go to places like: These cities are all pretty cool for their own reasons, but there are a lot of other really great cities in the US that I’d recommend you visit when you plan your trip here. Here are my top 5 cities that I’ve been to in the US that aren’t exactly tourist hubs: 1. Arizona Honestly, before I went to Arizona for a friend’s wedding this year, I completely despised the entire state. I went once as a kid, and all I remember was being sweaty all the time. It was kind of terrible. Then, I went to the wedding, and I didn’t want to leave Arizona. The scenery is incredible, the weather in the winter and fall is really nice, and the food in the city is good too. I highly recommend checking out the Grand Canyon (obviously) and also the Desert Botanical Garden. I loved it so much that I’m going back for a BJJ competition next month! Skip Vegas and go to Arizona. 2. Austin, Texas I moved to Austin, Texas, this year, so I’m definitely biased, but this city has a lot to offer. It’s one of the most booming cities in the country right now as well, with more people moving to ATX every day. Austin has a great food and live music scene, and there’s a whole lot more to it than just BBQ, Tex-Mex, and country music. Living here has been the most fun I’ve had in a long time. It’s kind of hip, very modern, and there is a lot happening. I usually tell people that Austin is like if Texas and Portland had a baby. Just make sure that when if visit in the summer that you remember that it’s going to be hot! 3. Milwaukee, Wisconsin Most of the midwestern cities that surround Chicago are all pretty nice. This includes Kansas City, Columbus, and Louisville, Kentucky, but there’s more. I just like these the best. They remind me of the gritty, Midwestern feel that you get in Chicago, but it’s a bit less crazy. Milwaukee is especially nice — and it’s only about an hour and some change away from the Windy City. Milwaukee has a great food scene for such a small city, and the Miller Brewing Company is located there too. If you’re traveling to the US and plan on seeing Chicago, I highly recommend a day or 2 in Milwaukee. 4. Seattle, Washington I lived in Oregon for a year and a half when I was 18, and I managed to take one trip to Seattle during my time there. (I was in college and balling on a budget, but I made one trip happen) The Pacific Northwest is beautiful, and in my opinion, Seattle is the coolest city in the PNW. Starbucks was founded there, so you can go to “the original Starbucks” as well. Right around that is the Pike Place Farmer’s Market, the gum wall, and then from there you can go to the Space Needle, which is a cool attraction that is unique to Seattle. Plus, you’re not far from some beautiful hikes and lots of other fun outdoorsy stuff. Just make sure to bring an umbrella if you go in the winter months, it gets rainy! Unfortunately, my pictures from my trip to Seattle are on my old laptop, so here’s a random picture of the space needle :) Unfortunately, I left out the northeast because I haven’t explored it very much, and the non-mainland spots (Hawaii and Alaska), but they’re amazing regions as well. I also really recommend visiting the state of Montana, the state of New Mexico, and parts of Canada, too. If you can, also try to go to Puerto Rico! What’s your favorite city to visit in the US?

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: All I do is go to work at 8:00 and am home by 6:00 pm. The shops and other places in the city where I reside all close early. I watch TV and read and go to bed. What can I do to make my life more interesting?
Answer: One great way to make life more interesting is to start fighting people! Okay — kidding. Kind of. One of the best ways to make your life a bit more interesting is to try new hobbies. Another one of the best ways to make your life more interesting is to try social hobbies — things where you have to talk to and work with other people in order to develop. Jiu-Jitsu is great in that regard. You might make some new friends, you’ll get in better shape, and you’ll learn a skill that could save your life one day! Look. I’m all for things like book clubs, taking a music class, or whatever other hobbies other people recommend (maybe some people can recommend things in the comments here?), but I think something like Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu is a great way to improve your social network while also making your life more interesting. Just be careful — you might get addicted ;)

Question: I am 21 years old. Is it normal to think that I haven't achieved anything in my life, and feel self-pressured to do something?
Answer: Here’s me at 21. This was the first day of an internship I had that a friend got me that I quit eventually. Being 21 sucked. I hadn’t finished college yet, so I couldn’t really get a job that was “enjoyable”. I also wasn’t smart enough to know what “an enjoyable” job was. I couldn’t have good relationships with women because I was too anxious to approach them. I didn’t even have good relationships with friends because I had a deep-rooted belief inside me that “the world was out to get me”. It was a whole thing. To top it off, the only thing I was good at the time was Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (I was a purple belt and competing in tournaments all over the US), but I hadn’t even really done anything remarkable in that either. I wasn’t making money from it, I was losing money on it! And this was the only thing I was really “good” at. Being 21 is a weird time in your life because people will tell you “You’re young, you have time!”, but you can’t let this get to your head because before you know it, you’re going to be in your mid-20s. Then your late 20s. Then your 30s. Then, before you know it, you’ll be an old man with a cane and a long grey beard. That’s why you feel the “pressure to do something”. You only get one life, and although you feel you haven’t achieved anything, you are not a kid anymore! The other big mistake a lot of 21-year-olds make is they compare themselves to people like Warren Buffett or Elon Musk. These are people who weren’t exactly late bloomers, but even they weren’t really doing anything remarkable at 21. 21 is an age that’s still pretty much dominated by the prodigies. Very few people have “a body of work” in their early 20s. You simply haven’t had enough time to become someone remarkable. But that’s okay. Plus, when you start achieving stuff, you will realize that that’s really not what life’s about anyway, but I think that’s a different post for a different day.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some good habits to become a good writer?

Question: What is the key for a healthy relationship?
Answer: I don’t know all the keys, and more of my relationships have been bad than good, but I’ll let you in on a secret: A huge key to having a good relationship is being the kind of person who does the things that lead to good relationships. It’s just like basketball or any other team sport. You need to get the fundamentals down before you can be a player that others want on your team. Be a person who doesn’t get jealous over little things. Be a person who doesn’t play games. Be a person who thinks about conflicts as “us versus the problem” as opposed to “me versus you”. Be loyal, honest, and an open communicator. Relationships are hard work. The relationship I’m in right now has challenged long-held beliefs about relationships that I’ve thought of as law since my childhood. I’m learning new things every day. I don’t know everything about relationships, attraction, and love, but I do know that the person I was a few years ago wouldn’t deserve the relationship I have now. I’m happy in my relationship, for the first time ever — and it’s because I’ve started to get good at the fundamentals of loving.

Question: How do I get stuff done when I have too much on my plate?
Answer: This year, I’ve had way too much on my plate: Btw, if you like those mugs, they’ll be available soon :) Anyway: This has been my least productive year in a long time. I’ve simply been traveling too much to work the way that I used to. Ironically, I’m traveling more for work, but actually working less. Here’s a really important lesson about productivity that I’ve had to learn the hard way: The 2 most important requirements to do things (and to do them well) are time and energy. If you don’t have time — either because you’re stuck on an airplane like me last week, distracted by other pressing matters, or because you struggle with time management — and you don’t have energy — because you’re jet-lagged, exhausted, sick, etc. — you will not get the things you need to do done. You need to have time and energy, otherwise, you will be scatterbrained and unproductive. This will create a cycle that will spiral out of control until you deal with it. I have ADHD, so I’m naturally pretty scatterbrained as it is, and the constant travel I’ve been doing has been terrible for my focus and productivity. Naturally, this way of thinking is what has led me to believe that putting an end to my nomad days is what I really need to do. I’ve thought that if I want to live a productive life, I must stop traveling and embrace the monotony of routine. But is this really true? What I’ve learned in the last year is that it’s not about living an exciting life or a boring one, it’s about building a life with the kind of work and the amount of work that you can handle. About working toward doing more of what you love and less of what you don’t. If you want to get stuff done when you have too much on your plate, focus on your energy levels, manage your time well, and optimize your “recovery”. Sleep well, eat well, and don’t work so damn much. If you can’t do these basic things, you will always struggle to be productive.

Question: How do most people waste their life?
Answer: I don’t think most people waste their lives. (The glass is root beer. Hehe.) “Most people waste their lives” seems a bit harsh. I think that most people do end up dying with unfulfilled dreams, incomplete bucket lists, and regrets, but I don’t think that means these people are “wasting their life”. Wasting your life, to me is what happens when you don’t make an effort to live it. It’s not that hard to not waste your life. You just need to try to do your best with what you have. You just need to avoid sabotaging yourself. It’s easier said than done, but it’s really worth it. Just because you don’t realize all your dreams doesn’t mean your life is a waste. People who live unremarkable lives have plenty of people who love them, things they like to do, and goals they aspire to. This alone is, to me, enough to make a life worth living. Just because not everyone wants to be a billionaire, a celebrity, or even have the same life you do does not mean that their life is “a waste”.

Question: What foods are good for losing weight?
Answer: Would you believe me if I told you that when I was in Italy, I lost weight while eating pizza, pasta, gelato, and drinking alcohol — every single day for about 2 weeks? Maybe you’ve heard of this phenomenon. Maybe, you’re like me, and you’ve heard of people losing weight while traveling in Europe and thought it was a lie. You thought they had some fancy genetics or a metabolism that runs like wildfire. You thought they were “lucky”. I’ve never been the guy who magically loses weight, so when I lost nearly 2 KG (about 5 pounds) from my trip a few weeks ago (and I’ve kept it off since then), I thought it was too good to be true. Here are a few hard truths about which foods are good for losing weight: All foods are bad for losing weight when you eat too much of them. I ate 4 pizzas in 5 days. There was an abundance of pizza. Pizza is my favorite food. I swear I’ve written about that before. Either way, something strange happened because of the abundance of pizza. Because pizzas in Italy are smaller and because I had the option to eat one every single day, I didn’t really overeat outside of this one pizza meal. I’d have a light breakfast, go on an adventure with my girlfriend, and then either have a snack or lunch and then we’d go for dinner. I ate what I wanted, and because it was really delicious and satisfying, I didn’t overeat. Your activity level determines everything. If you live a sedentary life, you’re not going to be able to eat very much if you want to lose weight. What kind of life is that? When I was traveling, the lifestyle my girlfriend and I lived was very active. We walked 5–10 miles per day, every day. We hiked up stairs and hills to catch cliffside views of the mountains — like this one: We were incredibly active, to the point that at the end of each day, my legs were kind of tired and my feet kind of hurt. But you know what? Each hour of walking that you do burns around 250 extra calories. This makes the sedentary nature of American life that much more disappointing. If you can, get up and go on adventures. Your waistline will thank you. Avoid processed things. Most of the restaurants we went to in Italy were older than me. I’m 26. Some of the restaurants we went to were twice, even 3 times my age! These are places that have been in business for a long time, and they focus on using the best quality ingredients for their dishes. Pizza that had fresh cheese and tomato sauce — nothing else. Carbonara that had high-quality prosciutto and egg, like this: Gelato from a cow — but neither I nor my girl got sick. I’m not big into the conspiracy that American food is poison, but I ate pizza and gelato for a week, felt great, and lost weight. Kind of makes you think a bit. Avoid eating too much, stay active, and try to avoid eating stuff you can’t pronounce. If you’re looking to read about the rapid weight loss I do for martial arts matches, check out this article:

Question: How do I live a good life of travels and tourism?
Answer: I’ve been on 21 trips this year. It’s not all it’s cracked up to be. This photo is from Burano, Italy, where I spent a day a few weeks ago with my girlfriend. It’s a beautiful, small town just outside of Venice. We had to take a boat taxi to get there. How did I get to live a life of travel and (relatively frequent) tourism? Well, it was pretty simple. You can probably do it too. First, I was a brat who decided that he didn’t want to work “a real job”. When I was younger, I worked normal young person jobs, but there’s a gap on my resume from the time I was 22 onward. I worked in a restaurant when I was younger. I was a camp counselor. The reason? I became a “professional Jiu-Jitsu athlete” and “internet writer” instead. I gave up the stability to teach kids Jiu-Jitsu, private lessons (through word-of-mouth marketing alone), and create an online content portfolio. For a few years, my parents thought I was out of my f*cking mind. I lived in a shitty studio apartment where my rent was incredibly cheap — although, when I moved in, I couldn’t even afford it. A story for another day. On the side, I wrote copy for small businesses. I hustled like a maniac. My personal development routine bordered on insane. I woke up at 6am every day and either wrote or worked out. I wrote and trained Jiu-Jitsu all day long. I didn’t have any money, so I just threw myself into my crafts — writing, competing in Jiu-Jitsu, and teaching. It was stupid. I wouldn’t recommend anyone live like this. I was unstable because I was financially unstable. I did not socialize. I had no friends (except my friends from Jiu-Jitsu). I trained so hard that my body broke and I wrote so much that I had wrist injuries. When this happened, I kept working and training. I was determined to do “something” for myself. In the end (long story short), the hard work paid off, and I was gifted the opportunity to travel full-time for about 6 months. During this time, I had pretty much every experience you can imagine. I had my heart broken. I fell in love. I failed and spent thousands of dollars on investments that I still haven’t seen a dime of return from. I achieved some major goals, like placing in one of the biggest martial arts tournaments in Europe (despite going up in weight and being injured). I also had some really fun travel experiences, like spending a week in Italy with my girlfriend, walking the sunny beaches of San Diego, road-tripping across America and listening to one of my favorite novels, or crossing the border south and seeing Mexico for the first time. I’ve gotten to do the whole “travel the world” thing like my old hero, Anthony Bourdain, and I didn’t have to inherit a bunch of money, have rich parents, or even get a high-paying job. I nickeled and dimed my way all the way across the world, a handful of times. I traveled the world while being an online writer and competing in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu — a grappling art that you probably have never heard of. That’s pretty cool to me. But that’s not the end of the story, unfortunately. Or, fortunately, depending on how you look at it. When I was younger, I wanted my life to look just like the movies. I wanted to fall in love in Venice (I did), I wanted to work on my first book on a rainy day from a cafe in London, and I wanted to sip coffee with an eager grin while overlooking the Rocky Mountains. I wanted all these idyllic, movie-esque experiences, and I got them because I sought them. But they did not make me happy. They did not heal the wounds in my heart put there by past torments. Travel did not make me a happy person. You don’t need happiness or the novelty of travel to be complete, you need meaning. The problem is that a lot of us are so disconnected from meaning in our daily lives that the only place that we truly find it is through travel. When I was traveling the world, you know what I longed for? To be somewhere like where I am now, relaxing after a hard workout, writing something that interests me, and sipping a hot coffee while my beautiful girlfriend reads in the other room (she took this picture). Home is here. Travel is fun and can offer some fun experiences, but home is here.
