Question: How can I become socially confident?
Answer: The most common questions I get asked are about managing anxiety and building confidence. Ever since I started posting writing in 2020, I've gotten hundreds of messages asking about being more confident. Timidity is an epidemic, and most suffer in silence. It's tragic irony. I struggled with confidence my whole life. It was debilitating in my early 20s. I sort of still deal with anxiety, but it's a minor player for me now because of the work I have done on my brain for years. Here are 4 actionable tips to help you become more confident: Get some advice from someone who knows more than you. Most mental health/dating/life advice online is nauseating. People are unqualified and just trying to make money off you. Take everything you read with a grain of salt. And look, I'm not saying I'm qualified to help either. I grapple and I write. I'm not great at much else. I'm just saying that maybe taking advice from a dude whose profile picture is a Greek warrior or an AI-generated version of himself is maybe not the way to get a strong mind. Read some books. Try therapy. Make friends. Think. Become competent. People always make it seem like you need confidence to develop competence. "If you want to be great, you have to believe in yourself" or whatever. That has not been my experience. I couldn't lie to myself and be confident without having data on my skills. This was big in competing in BJJ. My first gold medal was the hardest to win. After I got my first, winning became more of a habit. It’s not easy, but it’s a lot harder to do something you’ve never done before. You can do all the mantra BS you want, but the best way to develop self-belief is to get good results. Have some fun. If you take everything extremely seriously, you're definitely going to be more anxious. Anxiety = decreased confidence. Yes, you need to take yourself seriously and you need to work hard but RELAX. No one cares about you as much as you do (maybe your mom). The obsession with mediocrity prevention in my opinion screams insecurity. The more you enjoy life (and the things you do in it), the more confident you can be. Anxiety and excitement are basically the same. Live excited so you don't have to live scared. As your confidence builds, make sure you keep failing. Confidence that goes away the second you start failing was never "confidence" in the first place. Avoid complacency. Constantly seek out new challenges to make sure your confidence is not misplaced or based on lies. This is why I spent the spring getting my ass kicked at one of the best BJJ gyms in the world. I trained like a maniac and I stacked up well with a lot of the best guys in the world. Right now, I am more confident than I've been in years. "Losing" can be excellent for confidence. Hope this helps :)

Question: For life advice, what are some smart moves a 22-year-old can make as soon as he/she starts earning?
Answer: If you haven’t already, start putting yourself out there more. If you want to earn more, experience more, smile more, and build a better future for yourself, the most important thing you can do is learn how to put yourself out there. Yes, this is scary. Yes, this is not without risk. However, complacency will kill your spirit sooner than anything else. Most people give garbage advice to people in their 20s. I’ve read some of it on this very answer page. And more. Fuck that. Yes, you need to make smart financial decisions, but it’s not freakin’ rocket science. I actually recommend reading some books (finance, philosophy, and psychology) instead of taking advice from random people on Quora (you should see how easy it is to add qualifications to your Quora profile). Yes, you probably aren’t going to get married anytime soon at 22–25 (but props to you if you do!). Yes, you probably won’t have the resources at 22 to buy a fancy car or a yacht. But that doesn’t mean you need to live like a loveless hermit. It doesn’t mean you to need to put happiness on hold until you’re older. I’ve been having the time of my life for the last several years. I’ve fallen in love and gotten my heartbroken. I’ve traveled and done martial arts all over the world. I’ve made incredible friends. I’ve explored some of the most magnificent places in the world, from the shoreline of the Amalfi Coast to the jungle of India. I’ve also worked insanely hard. I write 1000+ words every day (7 days a week!). I train Jiu-Jitsu 6–7 days a week. I lift weights. I run sprints. I date. I spend time with my friends. I fucking hustle, because you're 20s are the time when you have the most energy to put into that hustle. Instead of spending my early 20s and playing it safe so I could have a better future, I’ve chased every single possible opportunity that I can. The result is that my options for the future are a lot better than they are if I had played itself and lived frugally. My only big piece of advice to my 22-year-old self would be to put myself out there more. I could have saved myself a lot of head and heartache. I could have gotten here a lot faster. Sometimes people tell me I sound young and arrogant in some of my answers. I may be arrogant, but I’m also confident. If you don’t put yourself out there and really test yourself, you’ll never get to feel the same way. Cheers.

Question: How do I really enjoy living? My life had been pretty monotonous for the past 17 years, and I’d prefer that not to be the rest of my life.
Answer: “Enjoying life” can be a painful undertaking. The problem is that what most of us consider “happiness” is pretty damn wrong. At least, it is for me. (Before you write a douchey comment — happiness is subjective!) As a society, we tend to think of happiness as an all-you-can-eat buffet, a pile of money, 500 women chasing after you, and consuming as much as we can as fast as possible. We think of happiness as flooding our system with dopamine so that we feel great for a few moments, but like crap in the long run. This is not good. This is an existentially broken way of living. To me, enjoying life is the act of doing things fully — whatever I’m doing. Enjoying life just means living as fully as I can. Chasing my dreams. Doing things I love. Lifting weights. Writing honestly. Pushing myself in the gym and in my personal life. Putting myself out there. Being vulnerable. Being strong. Getting humbled by life. Sometimes, that means I have to suffer, but a little pain isn’t a bad thing. It just makes me stronger. Here’s the hard truth about joy, suffering, and modern society: People don’t usually love when you tell them to suffer. They get mad because they want to “feel good” right now. Being hedonistic is more trendy and sounds sexier than putting your nose to the grindstone over and over again. The problem is that it’s the latter that makes you happier. You don’t just get to feel good for free. Sorry. You were probably told to “Just love yourself!” or whatever they say on Instagram — as if perceived self-love alone is enough to complete a being’s existence. They were wrong. It’s hard to love yourself when you don’t even respect yourself, and it’s hard to respect yourself when you don’t have the values to qualify the standards you deem respectable. It’s hard to love and respect yourself when you haven’t earned the love and respect you so desperately crave. Growth and happiness are more complicated than one-sentence mantras that you can stick on your water bottle or use as an Instagram caption with some fucking mountains. You wanna enjoy life? Break the monotony. Go do shit. Just try things. Even if it sucks. Even if you get hurt. Even if you don’t get what you want sometimes. What you’ll learn is that joy is found in individual moments. What you’ll learn is that a joyous life contains a great deal of agony. What you’ll learn is that if you’re okay with it, that’s totally okay.

Question: What's the best relationship advice you can give someone?
Answer: I used to think that relationships were the way they seem on the internet. Like this picture, for example. Doesn’t it look nice? These 2 people look so in love. But relationships, I have learned, are not like pictures. Relationships are a bit more like this thing: This is a bonsai tree. Under the right conditions, a bonsai tree can easily live for 100+ years. They’re very cute too. If I wasn’t constantly traveling, I’d have one of my own. You need to care for your tree every single week. You need to look at it every day and make sure it’s doing okay. You need to water it, trim it, and give it sunlight. You need to nurture the tree so that it can grow, live, and thrive. Relationships are the same way. In the beginning, the work you have to do in relationships is relatively easy. It’s fun. You’re excited and they’re excited and everything is new. Life is good. However, as time goes on, we get used to things being as they are. We become comfortable. Comfort breeds carelessness. You might forget to water the tree for one week. Then 2. Then you forget to trim it. Then you forget you even have the tree. Then, one day, you remember how important the tree is, but the tree is too far gone to be saved. Love is kind of like a bonsai tree - you need to tend to it to make it grow. When cared for, romantic love can last 100+ years, like a bonsai tree. When ignored, the future becomes unpredictable. The tree could get pushed over and die at any moment. Negligence causes more heartbreak than personal failures.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What was the best relationship advice you ever got?
Answer: The best relationship advice I ever got came from someone who I will never get to thank. I’d never experienced the death of a friend until this year. I’ve been lucky in that regard. However, one of my friends and training partners from my Jiu-Jitsu academy back home was tragically hit by a car and passed away earlier this year. It was a really hard time for me and all of my friends back home. This man was my training partner at my first Jiu-Jitsu class ever, and despite being 30 years older than me, we connected quite a bit over a mutual love for writing, martial arts, and self-improvement. We’d gotten lunch outside the gym together a few times, and each time he’d ramble on to me about life advice, love advice, and how I needed to open a 401k. I mostly just laughed and said “I’ll get on that this weekend!”, but I never really did. I still haven’t opened a 401k, but one time my friend did say something that really made me think about romantic relationships and how to have better ones. It’s interesting to me because this relationship advice goes against a lot of what I read online. It’s not the purest advice, but it might be the best relationship advice I’ve ever gotten. Before I give you the advice, I need to tell you about myself. I’m sorry in advance — I’m not the main character in this story, but I’m still making it about me. But I think this is important because the reason this relationship advice stood out to me so much was that it was applicable to me. It was like without knowing it, my friend had analyzed all of my bad relationships and knew what I needed to do. See, growing up, it was really hard for me to feel love from anyone. I didn’t feel it from my family, I didn’t feel it from my girlfriends, and I didn’t even feel it from my friends really. I even felt like my dog hated me at times. This is in part due to some trauma, and also in part due to anxiety and depression that I’ve dealt with for my entire life. I’ve always struggled to make connections because I get stuck in my damn head all the time. As a response to this, I would go all-in on my relationships because I thought the validation I’d get from them would make me finally feel the love that I couldn’t give myself. It was a vicious cycle that made me get hurt over and over again. This was why I started to look for validation from my relationships in the place of love because validation has always been easier to understand than “love”. In the aftermath of the worst relationship I had, I became hyper-independent to protect myself. I put love on the back burner and all cared about was looking perfect. That’s why the advice I got from my friend one-day last spring changed everything for me. First, he stressed the importance of the decision to choose a life partner. Who you marry is one of the most important decisions you’ll ever make. You have to see them like, every single day. You’ll sleep with them basically every night. You’ll have dinner with them basically every night. You might make people together or raise a family. It’s probably obvious to you, but it wasn’t to something I really thought about at 23: Marriage can get really serious. You’ll do some important shit together. And that’s if it’s going well. At the time, I was downplaying the importance of whom you choose to date/marry. I was downplaying the importance of relationships because I got hurt. I was training myself to believe a relationship wouldn't ever make me happy, and that all of my happiness was going to be internal. I was trying to be a good self-help boy so that the big bad world couldn't hurt me anymore. F*ck that. This, while partially true, is an oversimplification. As I’ve seen with my own family, a relationship can’t make you happy, but it can make you pretty damn unhappy. This taught me a valuable lesson about priorities. My friend told me he dated “a lot” when he was younger. This is maybe weird but I feel like it’s really helpful. It made me finally feel like it was okay not to know exactly what I was doing. It made it feel like my not-knowing was just a step in the process of knowing. I wasn’t born with the ability to have great relationships. I’m imperfect, and culture today does a terrible job of allowing us to be imperfect without a great deal of shame. You can thank the internet for that. I’ve constantly felt that every relationship had to be perfect all the time. I’ve constantly felt like a deranged lunatic running around with a bucket trying to save a sinking ship. Learning that my friend didn’t just marry his high school sweetheart and that he dated a lot (you know, like practice?) to get better at having relationships made me realize that relationships are so much more complex than people let on. The perfection we see online is imagined. My friend dated “a lot” and eventually found a woman that he loved more than anything. By the time he did, he was ready to settle down and have children and build his life with her. He wasn’t a child, he was a man. He also put in the work on himself (through writing, martial arts, and more) so that he could be the kind of man she deserved. His wife was equally as devoted to him as she was to her. He shared his life with her. They had 3 amazing children. His funeral filled up the synagogue with tons of people he touched and people he cared about. It was standing room only. I trust my friend’s advice when it comes to life and love. He was a great man who led by example. In a world full of 25 year-old-bros online preaching dating advice to other 25-year-old bros, it was refreshing to get some advice from someone who actually had built a life he was happy with. He gave me the advice my parents could never give me. So what’s my advice to you? I, like most people, have exes. I, like most people, am imperfect and have had bad relationships. My advice to you would be to stop thinking relationships have to be perfect. Stop thinking you have to be perfect. Purity, perfection, and all that other nonsense create more harm in us than love, and this is exactly what we don’t want. I’d rather be flawed and loved than perfect and alone, and since perfection doesn’t really exist, it’s really the only option. Live, learn, and keep living. Don’t forget to love along the way. RIP to my friend Warren. Thank you for teaching me what no one else could.

Question: What is the best mindset to have before going into a relationship?
Answer: I used to go into relationships completely open-minded - ready to experience anything and everything with a new person. Not anymore. I’m just 25 so I can’t call myself old without making everyone roll their eyes at me, but I’m definitely more cynical now. I don’t really want as many new experiences anymore with relationships. I’ve had too many of them. At a certain point, new experiences stop making you interesting and they start making you damaged. If you have too many experiences, you’re eventually very likely to experience some “trauma”. You might not even notice that this is happening until you go to therapy or journal and notice all your unresolved trauma. This makes everything a bit more complicated. That’s why the best mindset to have to go into a relationship is “skeptical optimism”. You must be positive, but you must be vigilant. You must be open to new experiences, but you must know what you want — and almost equally as important — what you don’t want. Pessimism is very unattractive and should be avoided. Doom and gloom makes you a contagion to be around, and not the good kind. That being said, blind optimism — the way I used to be — will make you more susceptible to getting hurt — the way I used to get hurt. You can’t hope to fix people or to be their saving grace. You can just hope to coexist happily with them. If you do enough work on yourself, you’ll realize that this is enough.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the deep secret of life?
Answer: A lot of the deep secrets of life lie in comedy. The things we joke about often have deeper meanings. We joke about things we’re insecure about, things that make us uncomfortable, or even our hidden desires. This is really interesting to me, because oftentimes, an audience or even just your friends laugh at something, but the reaction is so unconscious that we don’t think about why we laugh or how we’re able to make someone laugh. What makes people laugh is a combination of surprise, tragedy, and relatability. Sometimes, we’re laughing because we can’t muster the energy to cry. I’m not a master comedian and never have been, but I’ve noticed this a lot from watching comedy specials. The deeper you think about some of the jokes, the more grim it becomes. Here’s a quote from Jerry Seinfeld (before you hate — he’s not my favorite comic, either) as an example: “According to most studies, people’s number one fear is public speaking. Number two is death. Death is number two. Does that sound right? This means to the average person, if you go to a funeral, you’re better off in the casket than doing the eulogy.” This little “bit” has it all: The deeper we think about comedy, the more we can learn about other people, life, and ourselves. This hidden dark side of comedy isn’t always true, but I’ve found that very often, it’s more true than we’re willing to admit.

Question: Have you been in a relationship with an older woman?
Answer: A few times. There tend to be problems, however. I’m 25, and I’ve dated older women several times. The largest age gap was 12 years, but there were a few instances with women who were 8 years older than me. These women claimed that I was mature for my age. I’ll flatter myself and say that they were right, but unfortunately, emotional maturity alone doesn’t make for great relationships. In some ways I’m mature, and in other ways, I am a 25-year-old professional athlete and internet writer. I can express myself fairly well, I am a good listener, and I am fairly romantic when I like someone, but I’m not perfect. At times, my real life catches up with me. This tends to create problems for me in relationships with older women. I’d like to have kids one day, but I am 25 and just not ready mentally or financially. It would be irresponsible for me to try to have a serious relationship with someone who wanted children soon. Unfortunately, when dating older women, this tends to be an issue. Realizing this made me seek to stop dating older women. Older women in my experience either have decided they don’t want kids (which makes us incompatible for a serious relationship), or they want kids too fast. The whole biological clock thing. Question: Why do women *hate* nerdy men?
Answer: Maybe I’m not nerdy enough (I can’t code and I don’t even watch anime anymore), but I don’t think women hate nerdy men. The girl I’m seeing took this picture. I look like a fuckin’ dork. Me wearing a cowboy hat is not a cool look. But here’s the thing: I am kind of a fuckin’ dork. I just try to own it. Women don’t hate nerdy men. In my experience, girls often like smart guys (I as a man also prefer smart (nerdy?) girls, but that’s not the question). Being smart and being nerdy is actually attractive. I, for example, am obsessed with Jiu-Jitsu - I love telling stories about matches I’ve watched or competed in years and years ago, or just explaining why I find the outside ashi to be such a dominant leg-locking position (you’ve got great heel hooking opportunity and it’s very easy to transition to aoki locks!). I also know a lot about books and literature, as I’m someone who makes part of my living with writing. This gives me 2 things to “be a nerd” about. But no girl has ever hated me because I’m nerdy about stuff. They’ve hated me in the past because I was insecure. They’ve hated me in the past because I have a big mouth. They’ve even hated me in the past because they didn’t like themselves very much. But no woman has ever “hated me” because I’m a nerd. You can be whatever you want to be, you just have to own it. Women hate insecure men.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Is happiness linked to success?
Answer: There’s a quote from Mike Tyson that I love that explains how I feel about this: See, Mike Tyson was (and is) a pretty mean-looking dude. This picture is from before he had that scary tattoo on his eye, and even then, he was pretty mean looking. But here’s the thing — looking mean, being mean in the ring, and even living like you have something to prove (all things that would make you a better boxer) are great for being successful in the boxing ring, but don’t they don’t have much to do with your happiness. You can be mean in the ring and happy in life. This is not a paradox. And actually, if you’re miserable, you probably won’t have the resolve to do something as crazy as getting in the boxing ring and fighting someone who wants to hurt you just as badly as you want to hurt them. “There's nothing like fighting when you're young and you're happy. There's nothing more dealy or more proficient than a happy fighter. Everybody believes the mean, and the serly fighter, is the tough fighter but that's not true. The guy who's most relaxed and loves what he does, and is happy to be in there doing what he does.” — Mike Tyson When you’re happy, your anxiety is lower. This makes you fight (or do whatever you’re trying to do successfully) better.

Question: Can money really buy happiness? If yes, then how and if not, then what can bring happiness?

However: Money can buy you the delicious chicken curry you see above (and the other curries next to it), and you can go out to a restaurant with your friends and talk, laugh, make memories, and enjoy the ambiance of a restaurant. Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are you up to?
Answer: On September 9th of 2021, I challenged myself to write a Quora answer every single day for 6 months. During this writing challenge, I stayed consistent. From September 9th to March 9th, I didn’t miss a day of publishing on Quora. After about 3 months of obsessively posting, I went viral. After 4 months, I had a following. After 6 months, I took a self-assessment and decided that I was going to consolidate my efforts and focus on other platforms — namely Twitter and Substack — in addition to my writing on Medium. After a few weeks of posting infrequently, I went back to Quora like a college sophomore goes back to his crappy ex-lover. Quickly, I got sucked back into the Quora rabbit hole. I got nearly 14 million views on my work and gained more than 7000 followers. I did well on this site. Today, however, after months of going back and forth, I decided that I’m officially leaving the site. Here’s why: Problem 1: Quora is kind of crazy. In my early 20s, I was attracted to crazy. I liked excitement, I wanted adventure and new experiences, and I didn’t mind getting hurt in the name of “trying something new”. I’ve grown up a little bit and I’ve changed the way that I think about this. I don’t want to deal with people who cause me unwanted stress and anxiety anymore. I joke that I’m getting old or something. After someone commented on several of my answers this summer telling me to “kill myself”, I’ve changed the way I feel about crazy commenters. There’s a lot of drama on Quora and I don’t want to be around it anymore. Problem 2: Quora isn’t fun anymore. I’ve been having a blast writing on Twitter. I like writing jokes, writing threads, and taking ideas from my writing and breaking them down to 280 characters. It’s a game and it’s fun. For the most part, the readers have been supportive. I like it. On Quora, if I wrote something that was “niche” like stuff about Jiu-Jitsu, anxiety, or mental health, I was met with constant crazy comments from people and hate from people who have never met me in real life. I can deal with bullshit, but I can’t deal with bullshit from every platform I write on. I think Twitter is a better long-term investment than Quora, and while both might have their fair share of crazies, Twitter has a far greater upside than Quora. There’s a reason many of the top writers on the internet (like Nicolas Cole or Tim Denning, to name a couple) have either stopped writing on Quora completely or still do it sparingly. Quora was one of the first writing platforms I fell in love with, but we’ve drifted apart. We’ve changed. I’ve grown, and honestly, Quora hasn’t. Problem 3: Quora doesn’t really pay you. I got an awesome ghostwriting job off Quora this year. That is the only thing that’s happened from Quora that led me to make money off the site. Other than that gig, I’ve been scraping and grinding on the site for a whopping total of $142. I have 13.8 million content views, I’ve monetized a lot of my answers, and I haven’t even made more than $150 from the site — in a full year! I’ve made more than $200 on Medium every month since February of 2021. The ROI on Medium is so much higher than Quora, and until Quora does something about that (and you know, pays people who write there), I’d rather just look for a better way to make money. Quora was great for my ego (it’s cool to say you got more than 13 million views), but it’s just a vanity metric. It doesn’t help me live a better, happier life. I don’t need my ego stroked, I need to pay my bills. I need to make a living with my words, not use them to stroke my ego. That’s another reason why I’m leaving. Problem 4: I have other projects I’m working on. Every high-level writer that I know and follow has had a phase of writing on Quora. All of them, besides Sean Kernan (who’s arguably the top writer on the site), have left Quora. For the most part, the top writers on Quora and the top writers on Medium are completely different people. I haven’t talked to all of them, but for most of us, it’s because we’ve found other, less stressful, and more rewarding ways to spend our time. I’d rather get really good at Twitter, Substack, and Medium than write original stuff on Quora. Closing Thoughts This doesn't mean I’m abandoning Quora forever. It might not be goodbye, but it’s definitely see you later. The new year is a time for new beginnings and painful goodbyes, and for me, it’s time for a painful goodbye with Quora. It’s not you, it’s me. We’re done — at least for now. I might still use Quora as a writing tool here or there (writing on Quora has helped me get writing prompts when I feel writer’s block), but I won’t write daily on Quora anymore. I’m done. My heart isn’t in it anymore. It’s been a wild year. I went viral more times than I can count, I connected with some incredible people, and I developed a lot as a writer while I was using Quora. But now, it’s time for me to move on. Here’s to finding out what’s next. If you guys want to keep in touch, my newsletter is a good thing to check out (it’s in my bio). If not, I’ve been very active on Twitter recently as well:

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Where do I start to get my life together?
Answer: When I was 17, I was severely depressed, chronically anxious, and lost as to what I was going to do with my life. Then, a few weeks before I graduated high school, I started learning Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. What happened next is a long journey and an even longer story that spans 8 years, from the time I was an anxious schooler to today, where I’m 25, doing what I love full-time, having great mental health, and “living the dream”. Living my dream. It’s partially because of Jiu-Jitsu, partially because of writing, and partially because of my disciplined effort over years and years. Here’s what happened: This story has been told before, and it will be told again. You’ve probably read or heard a story like this one before — about someone who was a mess and how martial arts (or some other craft) “saved their life”. But I wasn’t a mess. I was a decent high school wrestler, I was going to college, and I was dating my high school sweetheart. I was doing okay, but I was just lost, sad, and more anxious than I could possibly understand. I wasn’t a mess, I was just having a hard time. I was having a hard time until I started to learn Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Jiu-Jitsu became the band-aid for all of my personal problems and anxieties, and I drank the Kool-Aid (and a lot of it). After I started competing in Jiu-Jitsu, my grappling addiction took over my life. I moved back in with my parents, started training full-time, and “punted” everything else. I started winning tournaments and matches at the lower belts of Jiu-Jitsu. I became pretty good. However, my early success didn’t last. I started to struggle. My mental health was catching up with me. My neck, my back, my anxiety attacks. Around that time, the depression that I’d been treating with a big ole Jiu-Jitsu band-aid started to seep through into my personal life. I had toxic relationship after toxic relationship. I cheated on my partners. I dropped out of college and then re-enrolled — twice. I failed my exercise science program and had to choose a new major. I couldn’t keep a part-time job without butting heads with my bosses. I wasn’t really doing anything well in my life, but I had a decent armbar. Then, in the midst of a series of serious physical injuries, a few tough defeats on the mat, and some other personal issues at home, I spiraled out of control. I experienced a rare mental condition called “depersonalization”, and at 21, I came close to committing suicide. I even wrote a note. Then, 12 months after I wrote a suicide note in my parent’s basement, I won the IBJJF No-Gi Worlds at purple belt. This was a great moment, but it made me realize how naive I was being about so much in my life. Winning the tournament was both inspiring and humbling. It was inspiring because it taught me that I was capable of a lot more than I thought. It was humbling because I realized that for the most part, no one gave a shit. I realized that I was fighting for myself (and only myself) and that selfishness wasn’t a sustainable source of motivation. On paper, the biggest win of my life didn’t change my life at all. That’s when I started to grow. After winning the Worlds, I was also now 22, and my friends were getting jobs, living in nicer apartments, and some were even getting married. I was a Jiu-Jitsu bum who couldn’t see anything past his next tournament. In my old circle of friends, Jiu-Jitsu went from being my cool hobby to a reason that I wasn’t growing up. I drank the Jiu-Jitsu Kool-Aid so hard that now, I was choking on it. After this, I became incredibly interested in ways to make a living while doing Jiu-Jitsu, instead of making a living from doing Jiu-Jitsu. I started to leverage the only other skill I sort of had: writing. After a few months of helplessly trying to freelance, I started a blog on Medium at the end of 2020. Within a few months, I became obsessed with writing. I wrote about everything I could think about — from Jiu-Jitsu to philosophy to love to mindset. I wrote about stuff I knew and stuff I didn’t. I wrote a lot. And? In time, with practice, patience, and a lot of hard work, I became a writer. Writing gave me a new identity and a new job, and it also taught me what Jiu-Jitsu is really about. I fell in love with writing as deeply as I fell with Jiu-Jitsu, and I found myself in a strange position. I was the only person competing at the higher levels of Jiu-Jitsu who was also writing about it (and making money from it). For a while, I felt like I was cheating reality. After a while, I realized that I was happy with what I was doing. I was so fucking happy. The more I wrote, the harder I trained, and the better I got at both of my passions. Eventually, I gained more than 10 million views on my online writing and became ranked in the top 15 in the world in Jiu-Jitsu. Now, I write/ghostwrite professionally, teach Jiu-Jitsu, and compete in professional Jiu-Jitsu events. Though I’m not exactly where I want to be, in a way, I made it. I forget that sometimes. That’s pretty cool to me. But what’s the point? I’m happy. So what? This article isn’t really about me. I’m the writer so I get to be the main character of my own story, but this story is not about me. This story is about life, love, and learning. That’s what writing is about. That’s what Jiu-Jitsu is supposed to be about. I see a lot of bullshit online about how “writing saved my life” or “Jiu-Jitsu saved my life”. Give yourself some credit — a craft doesn’t make or break your existence. Jiu-Jitsu didn’t “save my life”, but it did give me a framework to grow up into a person I’m proud to be. It also gave me a job, a sense of purpose, and a great set of friends. Writing gave me all that, and the ability to tell stories about the stuff I do. That’s how I got my shit together. Hopefully, this isn’t just me ranting and praising my own hard work. Hopefully, this helped you a bit. Have a great day.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What makes you happy?
Answer: “You have power over your mind — not outside events.” — Marcus Aurelius Let’s turn back the clock to last October. I’d just moved into my new apartment a few weeks earlier. I was writing 2000–3000 words per day, I was freelancing for 11 clients, I was training Jiu-Jitsu 2–3 times per day, and I was on the mend from a devastating week where I injured my back, neck, and ribs, all in the same week. Life was different then. It was a simpler time, but not really in a good way. I was desperate for any glimpse of success, and achieving that was all I wanted and thought about. I was working my butt off, I wasn’t making that much money in reward for my efforts, and I didn’t do anything besides work for a long time. I barely saw my friends besides my gym friends at the gym. I couldn’t really afford to date. All I could do was eat (mostly beef and broccoli), sleep, train, and write. That was my life for about 8 months — 12–16 hours per day, 6-7 days per week. It was tough. It was gritty. My days weren’t glamorous, they were monotonous. Everything was difficult, pretty much all the time. But strangely enough, I look back on those days now and I miss that struggle and blind motivation. I miss not making enough money to date and barely seeing my friends and having to work 12 hours per day. I miss only being able to eat beef and broccoli and being too anxious about money to take myself out for a coffee in the afternoon. I miss all this stuff. What the heck is wrong with me? I‘ve felt this way before. When I look back on the last year, I reminisce the same way I reminisce about my last season of wrestling when I was in high school. Wrestling was hard. During my final season, I was cutting weight constantly to make the 160-pound weight division (yo-yo dieting — gaining and losing 8–10 pounds per week), I was dealing with college applications and school, and I had my first girlfriend ever. There were a lot of things happening at once, and life was overwhelming. All I really wanted at that moment was for the wrestling season to be over, to be done with school, and for my girlfriend to give me a break. I wanted these things, and eventually, I got my wish with all of them. My wrestling season ended — although not the way I wanted it to. I graduated from high school — although again, not really the wanted to. My girlfriend and I broke up a few weeks before we left for college and I didn’t handle the breakup the way I wanted to either. It took a while to hit me, but in the weeks before I left for college that fall, I started to realize how much time I had wasted wanting things to be over. It was also depressing because everything I had used to build my identity was gone and I didn’t know who I was anymore. I wanted the tough days back because I defined my identity and gave myself self-esteem from my ability to overcome struggles. I had to find new struggles to help me define and identify myself. You can have anything, but not everything. With fewer exceptions than you realize, you can have anything you want. The problem for most people is the sacrifice that comes with having what we want. We want to be fit, but we don't want to give up junk food. We want to have less anxiety, but we don’t want to sleep better or make time for a weekly therapy visit. Everyone gets excited about doing stuff, but no one gets excited about the discipline aspect of becoming good at things. This is what happened to me over the last year. In the early days of my journey to trying to make a living for myself through Jiu-Jitsu and writing, I struggled with giving up my free time to work more and working when others were enjoying themselves. I also just struggled because I working full-time on 2 projects at the same time. Most people can’t write or do martial arts at a high level. I was trying to do both at the same time. Over time, however, these perceived limits didn’t matter anymore. My work started to pay off. I got better competition results, my writing got more views, and I started to make more money. Life became less difficult and more fun. I got to do more fun stuff and less work stuff. This culminated in me taking myself on a trip to Europe back in May. It was my way of rewarding myself for 8 months of working like a lunatic to build “the life I wanted”. It was nice, but I felt like something was missing while I was on vacation. The messed up thing is, when I was on that trip in Europe, all I could think about was how I wanted to go home and train and write. I missed struggling. For a while, I thought that this was because the only way to feel fulfillment and peace was through doing hard things. This is not the case. Now I’m going to tell you what took me the entire summer to figure out. The problem is that we have activity-based identities. How do you define yourself? A writer? An athlete? A teacher? A trauma survivor? A hard worker? People use all these words to describe themselves because these words give them a sense of power. They make them feel like they are in control of their lives. They make them feel like the things they do matter. But really, the question shouldn’t be “How do you define yourself?”. The question should be “Why do you define yourself?” You’ll find more from answering that than in any label. Why do you define yourself? Why do you need a label? Is there any other value besides a false sense of comfort that that label gives you? Labels provide comfort, but they do little else for us without living in accordance with those values. People in married relationships still cheat. People who call themselves writers still give up on writing. People who are athletes eventually give up their athletic careers. Because we use labels to build our identities, we become attached to times in our lives when our identity is strongest. After a big win in Jiu-Jitsu, I feel especially validated as an athlete. After an article performs well, I feel validated as a writer. After the girl I like tells me she thinks I’m cute, I feel attractive. The problem is, this validation is fleeting. You have to constantly feed that need in order to feel happy from it. That’s why you have to find another way to keep yourself happy. You have to develop lasting motivation in a way that combats your fleeting identity. If you lost everything tomorrow, how would you rebuild? If you tore every ligament in your knee and you could never play sports again, what would you do to pass the time? If you had to stop writing or painting, how would you express yourself? If your partner left you, how would you rebuild? These are dark questions and maybe they seem rooted in scarcity, but it’s essential to think this kind of stuff about if you want to build a strong sense of peace. By diving into the scarcity of reality, you find an abundance of peace. I don’t care about your identity. I don’t want you to build a strong identity. I want peace. Peace comes from climbing a mountain without constantly thinking about how you’re going to feel when you reach the top. Peace comes from finding flow in the act of climbing the mountain. That is how you become happier through the pursuit of your goals. “For man is always bound so long as he depends for his happiness on a partial experience; joy must always give way to sorrow, otherwise it can never be known as joy.” — Alan Watts

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Is the "never give up" attitude always helpful?
Answer: No. Sometimes you should let yourself give up. In fact, I wrote an article the other day about how I was quitting writing. It’s still in my drafts folder. I almost gave up. I really did. I’m not saying that for attention — I was really done with writing for like a month. There wasn’t anything in particular that led to that decision, but over the last few months, I haven’t been able to feel calm and clear-headed enough to write anything I’d consider “good”. Life has been crazy, and as a result, I’ve been moving around like crazy. This year, I’ve been on 20 trips for Jiu-Jitsu. Some trips have been to train, some have been for competitions, and others have been to teach. They’ve all been exhausting in their own way. In addition to doing Jiu-Jitsu all day, I’ve been writing on the internet as “prolifically” as I possibly could. All year long, I’ve been writing on Medium, Quora, Twitter, and Substack, and I’m ghostwriting for a few clients as well. It’s been a lot. Thanks for listening to my sob story. Here are the mindset shifts that have helped me pull myself out of the creative funk that I’ve been in over the last few weeks. Whatever you’re doing — it’s not that serious. Maybe it's because as I’m writing this, I’m tired from training, but when you're fighting people all day, every day, it is very easy to start to view your life distortedly. You start to view conflicts as extreme because your entire day is just you engaging with conflicts. You’re constantly fighting, so when you’re not fighting, the one thing that you want to do is not fight anymore. You become conflict avoidant. People say that martial artists are some of the most “laid back people” because we know how brutal fighting is and we don’t want to do it if we don’t have to — but as you progress through life, you start to realize that it’s more about knowing when to fight that it is avoiding fighting at all costs. You have to fight sometimes (for your livelihood, for things you believe in, or if you’re threatened), but most of the other times, you have to chill. You have to be present and not fight. You start to realize that nothing is that serious when you really think about it. You start to learn how to pick and choose your battles. “Writing online” or “blogging” sound like they’re very serious. “Posting your thoughts on the internet for money” sounds much less serious. “Professional Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu athlete” sounds very serious. “Guy who wrestles people for a living” is a bit less serious, and it’s closer to the truth. This helps me put anxiety in perspective. It helps me relax. The problem is that you’re constantly being told how much everything matters by everyone, all the time. Whenever I open Twitter or Medium, I see articles about the shit I need to do to have “a better life”. Things I need to do to make more money, live better, be happier, get laid more often, etc. These articles are designed to pray on my pain points. They pray on common insecurities to get you to click on them and read them all the way through. For me, my pain points as an aspiring athlete and writer are making money and improving my skills. As someone who’s battled severe mental illness being happy is another pain point. As someone who’s had plenty of crappy relationships, getting better at dating is another pain point. The problem is, all of these articles are putting thoughts in my head, but these thoughts are not building me up. These thoughts are breaking me down so that I’ll buy someone’s course or ebook or whatever. That’s how a lot of online writers work: they try to play on your pain points to get you to buy their crap. And? Financially, this is probably a good decision. It’s kind of how copywriting works. Ethically? It’s kind of fucked up. Nothing matters that much. Existentially, barring the improbable existence of a god or some sort of afterlife, there’s nothing that matters more than right here, right now. Still, the human brain was designed to get you to spend the present worrying about the future. This is how the species continues to survive. However, if you can get past that worry your life gets a whole lot better. Still, it’s not easy. Caring about things is essential to living a good life However, caring about things too much is the precursor to anxiety. Anxiety is a mental condition that essentially impacts your ability to enjoy the present by placing you in uncomfortable future and past situations. Anxious people typically spend a lot of time thinking about things that do not directly relate to the present. Trust me — I have anxiety too. I get it. When you’re like me, dealing with that anxiety makes it impossible to relax, to think, and unfortunately for me, to write. So what did I do to give myself the freedom to write again? I told myself I was quitting writing. I gave myself permission to be a quitter and a failure. I let myself feel sorry for myself. I gave in to my weakness. You probably won’t see that in a self-help book or in a motivational speech, but it helped me. It helped because, after spending just a few hours feeling sorry for myself, I realized something very important: I didn’t like how it felt to feel sorry for myself. I don’t like feeling like a failure. I don’t want to be someone who gave up. And so, after taking a few days off (resting, not quitting — what a concept), I started to find the energy to do my things again. Funny how being nice to yourself can actually make you more productive. I’m feeling less burnt out from work, but I am still very burnt out from motivational speakers on the internet. I’m tired of writing-oriented hustle porn. I’m tired of being told that I have to 10x my productivity with some stupid routine. I’m tired of getting nutrition tips from people who have never taken a nutrition class in their lives. What I realized is that when I’m feeling tired of these things, I just need to unplug. I need to turn off the phone, put down my books, turn off the TV, and just sit there. I need to act like a cat. I need to allow myself to feel tired and overwhelmed and done with all the bullshit I deal with every day. I need to process my emotions. If you let yourself process those emotions, they stop weighing you down. Most of the people who tell you otherwise probably haven’t processed their emotions themselves. How do you expect to do anything worthwhile if you can even deal with yourself?

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What life lesson did you learn the hard way?
Answer: For most of us, the “path to success” is non-linear. We always think that we’re going to go from point A to point B to point C, rounding the bases of life smoothly and passing each test throw at us with flying colors. The reality is a bit more complicated. We always hear about and praise prodigies, but their results are not realistic for the common person. That’s why we praise them. What seems to have happened is that we live in a culture today where everyone aspires to be a prodigy. Everyone thinks and wants to be the best, and they want to get there in the easiest way possible. Life doesn’t work this way for most people. Skills are hard to learn. This is why they’re called skills. I remember when I was a kid and riding my bike and learning to tie my shoes seemed so hard. They seemed like “adult skills”. Learning to ride my bike involved a lot of falling, bleeding, some crying, and slow progress toward a goal. Now, the skills I’m worried about are budgeting, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, and writing, but the game is still the same. For whatever reason, a lot of people change their expectations when they become adults. They think that now that they’re a “grown up” and living on their own, that doing hard skills should be easier. That’s not how it works. Progress is nonlinear. Take my friend Ramses, for example, from the picture above. Ramses started training with me just over 2 years ago. He had never done a leg lock in his life. He was terrified of them. He tapped ridiculously early. He was so bad at leg locks that I stopped using them on him in training because it wasn’t even a fair game. That was 2 years ago. Now, Ramses is tapping people with leg locks in competition. He did that on Saturday, and he was rewarded with his black belt on the mat. His progress at leg locking has been non-linear. There were periods where he was getting better, but then the stress of running a business or the pain of an injury would take him off the mat for a while, and his progress would slow down. Day by day, he didn’t really feel like he was getting better. Last weekend at the competition, he made his opponent look the way he did when I first started training with him 2 years ago. For my own sake, I’m anxious and excited to see where Ramses’ leg lock game is 2 years from now.

Question: What is the one habit you believe contributed the most to you becoming a great writer?
Answer: One habit that made me a better writer is that I really don’t think I’m a great writer. Not great at writing, but really good at looking like a douche with sunglasses. I work at writing, I do my best, and I practice nearly every day, but sometimes, I just feel like a hamster stuck on a wheel. Today is actually one of those days. I feel like I’m working my butt off and not making any progress. I start to wonder if maybe I’m not getting better because I’m just not that talented. I don’t feel talented or great. I do feel like I have to make up for a lack of talent for writing by working my freaking butt off. I’m not talented at writing. If I don’t use Grammarly and read my posts aloud before I post them, I post shit that has dozens of spelling and grammar errors. I’m a “Top Writer” in 5 of the more competitive categories on Medium and I can barely spell without the help of my computer. Don’t believe me? Go back and read what I wrote before I downloaded Grammarly in January of 2021. If Grammarly misses it, so do I. I never wrote for a school newspaper. I got a C in college writing. No teacher in school ever suggested to me that I might have a way with words. As a writer, I started as a 23-year-old with a big mouth and a Medium account. That was it. The only habit that made me better at writing was putting in the fucking work. Some days, the words pour out of me. Other days, I dig and dig, and nothing’s there. It doesn’t matter. I still write because I want to be good at the skill. The only habit that’s made me a better (not “great”) writer is writing every single day. The only mindset trick that makes me eager to practice every single day is the knowledge that I can always get better at writing. Fuck talent. Write. Erry day. I’m big into Twitter right now. Question: How do I stop letting people's negative comments toward me affect me so much?
Answer: I don’t read my comments as much as I probably should, but a few weeks back, a reader told me to “kill myself”. People get weird in the comments. Maybe that’s why I avoid them. (Me not killing myself and being happy ☺️) The irony of writing about mental health is that if someone says something that affects your mental health, it’s best if you don’t say anything about it. You aren’t supposed to give them leverage. The other day, when that commenter said I should “kill myself”, I couldn’t respond the way I wanted to. Instead, it was better for me to not say anything at all. If I had decided to engage with this random stranger and talk about how what they said was both problematic and deeply upsetting to me, they would just have fuel for their fire. They would win because they knew that they had gotten under my skin. Writing about mental health is great, but writing about mental health and talking about mental health are not the same things. Writing about mental health is for everyone. Talking about it is for you. You have to remember when to keep things private. Thank God this wasn’t 4 years ago. 4 years ago, I was dealing with a rare mental condition called “derealization”. I was in a constant state of anxiety, dissociation, and “unreality”. The world was a scary place. I didn’t feel safe in my own body or my own skin. I hated everything about life. I was very miserable. I wanted to be dead. Mentally and spiritually, my back was up against the wall. I didn’t feel like there was a way out. Over time, I found a way out. Today, I’m pretty peaceful and happy, for the most part. So when I get a comment like this now, it makes me think a bit more than if I was just getting hate on the internet for my character or my writing abilities. Comments like these make me think about the entire scope of my mental health experience. The comment isn’t really “triggering” for me, but it does show me how far I’ve come. Now, when someone tells me to kill myself, I think it’s empowering in some twisted way because I know I won’t. I didn’t always have that luxury. Writing on the internet changed my life. I feel like the cliches about how writing on the internet can change your life are romanticized and embellished a bit. I make a decent amount of money from my writing, but it doesn’t make me rich. Writing didn’t change my life in that sense. I still drive the same car I did 2 years ago and about half my income still comes from teaching people Jiu-Jitsu. What writing online did teach me goes beyond the scope of cash in my pocket. I’ve never had to lie when I write stories about life and mental health, and the result of “telling the truth” has been incredibly empowering. Writing online made me feel seen for the first time in terms of mental health. It made me feel like my struggles were valid. It made me feel like I wasn’t the first person to struggle with anxiety or derealization or depression. I knew I wasn’t before, but when you’re alone in hell, you think you’re the first one there. Writing online gave me a community that I felt connected to, and now, I don’t feel like I want to kill myself anymore. So when I read comments that tell me I should kill myself or jump off a bridge or stop writing and die in a hole, I don’t feel scared anymore. I feel sad for the people on the other end of the keyboard, because they’re projecting their word vomit onto me, and I’m going out for coffee and a walk in the sunshine. I’m doing Jiu-Jitsu and writing articles that are fun for me. One of us is doing a lot better than the other. When I first started writing, I doubted myself every step of the way. I thought that if I wrote about things that I struggled with, people would invalidate them. I thought if I wrote about being anxious or depressed, people would tell me to “shut up and deal with it”. I thought that people would use the same weapons that my anxiety does to invalidate me and make me further doubt myself. Some people say shitty things, but you learn to realize that these comments are more about them than you. What I realized through writing is that the only person who really wanted me to stop writing was the voice in my head who couldn’t stand the thought of me growing into the person I’ve always wanted to be. 99% of the comments I receive from other people validate this way of thinking. That’s why I feel sorry for the reader who told me to kill myself.

Question: How should a young person invest money?
Answer: Here are the best investments of time and money I’ve made before I turned 25: Actual investments I’m not an accountant, so I won’t tell you where to invest your money. My dad worked in the stock market for decades and he told me to invest $100 per month to get started. If you save $100 per month for 40 years, you’ll have almost $50,000. If you invest that money, you will have about $1 million. At the very least, investing just makes you feel like you’re being smart with your money. Writing online for a year. When I downloaded Medium, I was hesitant about paying the monthly $5. It’s the best investment I’ve made in my career. I’ve made thousands in return and it’s only been 2 years. I have hundreds of email subscribers, average tens of thousands of monthly views on Medium, and I get about 1 million views per month on Quora (for now I guess, haven’t been writing here very much lately). I’m not saying that to brag. I’m saying that because it’s shocking to me that so many people would ever view my words. That’s the beauty of writing online. The best way to improve your thinking and the quality of your ideas is to publish them in written form. Give it a year. It takes at least 6 months for anyone to notice you—sometimes more. After that, you’ll probably get addicted. Training Jiu-Jitsu I’ve spent a lot of money on Jiu-Jitsu training, traveling to train, and competing. I saw no financial ROI before this year. Some of the friends who I started with or who haven’t stuck with training are still white belts because they refused to consistently invest time into training. I’m a black belt and I teach and compete all over the world. My black belt has opened doors for me in the Jiu-Jitsu world and given me a career. It’s also made me more confident, more intelligent, and most importantly, it’s taught me how to overcome adversity in ways life couldn’t. I’ve also made the best friends I’ve ever had. That’s the icing on the cake. The best time to start Jiu-Jitsu is 10 years ago, the second best time to start is today. Luckily for me, I started 7 years ago. Therapy A lot of men (and women) still stigmatize talk therapy. This is strange to me. I go pretty much every Friday morning when I’m home, and the ideas that come out of therapy are the subject matter for a lot of the stuff you see in my writing. I wish people didn’t stigmatize because therapy can make your life a lot much better. If you think therapy is dumb, it’s probably because you need it and you don’t have the guts to go. To put it bluntly, therapy helps you figure out where you’re fucking up, and you develop strategies so you don’t keep doing that. Therapy is the reason I’m not chasing my ex-girlfriend around and working myself into the ground masochistically anymore. Weight lifting 3x per week Everyone should invest in a gym membership. I only lift weights 3 times per week because most of my exercise is Jiu-Jitsu training, but I still make sure that I lift heavy stuff every week, multiple times per week. Still, 3 times in the weight room every week is better than most people. Dozens of people have written articles about the benefits of lifting weights for your physical health, but I also think having the discipline to get in the weight room and push yourself gives you an incredible mental edge in your life. Plus, just think about how great you’ll look and feel after years upon years of maintaining a gym habit. Quitting gi Jiu-Jitsu (this bugs people, but that sport is a dead-end financially) This investment is really niche and doesn’t apply to most people, but perhaps the concept is valuable. In Jiu-Jitsu, the sport has gi competition (kimono) and no-gi (no kimono). The sport is growing financially on the no-gi side, and it’s stagnating in gi. About a year ago, I decided to quit the gi and focus on no-gi, because I was better at no-gi and there was more money in it. After a year of this, I became ranked in the top 15 in the world and I was able to actually make a living doing Jiu-Jitsu. The lesson here is that you should invest your time wisely. Specialize. If you’re world-class at what you do, the specialist out earns the generalist, every single time. Hopefully, these investments will make you think about more than just where you’re putting your money. Also, you probably shouldn’t take financial advice from random people on Quora ;)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I make my life more interesting?
Answer: Well, you could do what I did this morning and drop your breakfast plate. That was pretty interesting because I had to waste 10 minutes of my life picking up the pieces and then vacuuming up all the shards. Okay — don’t do that. Don’t drop your plates. Or, in other words, don’t do dumb shit just to make your life more interesting. You probably agree with me, but how many people still do stupid things just to “stir up drama”? Kind of a lot, if you asked me. Look at the culture. And look, I get it. Life is kind of lame sometimes. I don’t know anyone who actually wakes up every single day with a pep in their step singing to themselves about the adventure of life. Maybe people like that exist, but I don’t know them. I do know some pretty happy people, however. Happy is more valuable than interesting. In fact, I think that people who are happy are incredibly interesting. I try to surround myself only with people who fit this type of interesting. So yeah, life is kind of uninteresting. You wake up, every damn day, and you have to “do stuff”. Doing stuff is exhausting. But on the other hand, not doing stuff is boring. It’s a Catch-22. You have to work. You have manage your finances. You have to take your kids to wrestling practice (I don’t have kids, but you can bet your behind if I did I’d try to put them in wrestling before soccer or basketball). You have to do all this shit, and it gets boring because it feels like the same shit every single day. Only, it’s not. Life has a lot of variety. You have to take some time to notice it. Every day, the clouds look a bit different. You can get a different coffee drink each time you go to the shop. You can mix and match your outfits in like a bazillion different ways. Life is really interesting, you just have to dig a bit. If you’re happy with what you have, you’re probably not seeking a “more interesting life”. If you’re unhappy because your life is boring, breaking your routine is a great place to start. Try something new. I’m my happiest when I’m finding the uniqueness in each moment. This morning I had a weird acai-match-vanilla infused coffee. It wasn’t my favorite, but it was kind of “interesting” to try. If you do a tiny interesting thing every day, before you know it, you’ll have a pretty interesting life.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some of the best life-changing books?
Answer: When the pandemic started and forced me inside a few years ago, I decided that I was going to read at least 2 books per month. It was a small goal at the time, but I’ve stuck with it. The beautiful thing about habits is that when you stick with them, they compound. Now, in the last 2.5 years, I’ve read nearly 75 books. I’ve read books on philosophy, writing, self-improvement, science, and more. I’ve read fiction and non-fiction. I’ve read a lot. These are the 10 books that made the biggest impact on me. For One More Day — Mitch Albom I just finished this one on the plane. It made me cry. I’ll spare you a lengthy write-up and leave you with the question the book focuses on: What would you do if you could spend one more day with a lost loved one? Think about it. “One day spent with someone you love can change everything.”― Mitch Albom, For One More Day Man’s Search For Meaning — Viktor Frankl Man’s Search For Meaning is one of the best Western philosophy books of all time. The first chapter is one of the most powerful book chapters I’ve ever read. This book should be required reading for everyone from ages 18–22, and if you’re struggling to be happy, I’d recommend this book right away. “Love is the only way to grasp another human being in the innermost core of his personality.” — Viktor Frankl, Man’s Search For Meaning Siddhartha — Herman Hesse I’ve always liked the idea of being “Zen” and less anxious, but I never really understood what that meant until I read Siddhartha. As far as philosophical novels go, this is one of the best. They might call it a classic, but learning to think a bit more like Siddhartha will put transport you to new heights spiritually, emotionally, and intellectually. “Seeking means: having a goal. But finding means: being free, being open, having no goal.”― Herman Hesse, Siddhartha Striking Thoughts — Bruce Lee When I found out Bruce Lee was a philosophy writer, I pretty much snorted. “You mean, the guy from Enter the Dragon?” Yes. That’s the guy. He was a philosophy writer, and he wrote some good philosophy. Turns out, the most famous martial artist of all time was also pretty damn smart. “It’s like a finger pointing away to the moon. Don’t concentrate on the finger or you will miss all that heavenly glory.”― Bruce Lee, Striking Thoughts Can’t Hurt Me — David Goggins I’ll never forget when I finished Can’t Hurt Me because I was on my way to a Tinder date. I showed up with red eyes from crying and was entirely inspired to improve my self-discipline. Not the best way to impress a pretty girl, but that’s what happened. It was an appropriate response to the story of David Goggins and how he came to be the man he is. This book is inspiring as hell. “You are in danger of living a life so comfortable and soft, that you will die without ever realizing your true potential.” — David Goggins, Can’t Hurt Me The Book of Life — Jiddu Krishnamurti I wrote a whole article on The Book of Life last week. I’ve never dedicated a whole article to one book before. This book is simple, but it’s that powerful. 365 daily meditations on life, spirituality, happiness, and more. You’re supposed to read meditation one per day. I read them all in about 6 weeks because I couldn’t get enough. Be warned, however, this book just might shake your worldview. I know it shook mine. “If you have no love, do what you will — go after all the gods on earth, do all the social activities, try to reform the poor, the politics, write books, write poems — you are a dead human being.” — Jiddu Krishnamurti, The Book of Life A Wrestling Life — Dan Gable When I was wrestling growing up, Dan Gable was the wrestling’s equivalent of Chuck Norris or Steven Seagal. The stories and legends of what he did are ridiculous. His autobiography brings the legends of my childhood to life in a way that we can all appreciate, whether you’re a wrestler, combat sports fan, or just someone interested in improving your mental toughness. Gable was an incredible athlete, coach, and human being. This book gives him the time in the lime-light that he has always deserved. “Gold medals aren’t really made of gold. They’re made of sweat, determination, and a hard-to-find alloy called guts.” — Dan Gable, A Wrestling Life Greenlights — Matthew McConaughey I listened to this book on Audible, and it was probably the single-most enjoyable download I’ve made on that app. The way Matthew McConaughey told his life story inspired me to both write more honestly and to live more openly. Greenlights is such a fun book. It’s a must read for anyone feeling lost, alone, or confused. It’s a light in the dark or a blanket in the cold. It might just be exactly what you need. “I believe the truth is only offensive when we’re lying.” — Matthew McConaughey, Greenlights The Old Man and the Sea — Ernest Hemingway This is the story of an old man’s crazy dream to catch a giant fish. Reading it inspired me to keep chasing my crazy dreams. The dream of chasing a giant fish feels just like trying to win a huge Jiu-Jitsu tournament or write a great article. Keep at it — you never know what can go right. But man is not made for defeat,” he said. “A man can be destroyed but not defeated.” — Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea The Almanack of Naval Ravikant — Eric Jorgenson I read all these inspiring books from all these different periods and people on happiness, making money, and living a better life, but I never had a guide to doing it in the modern world. Naval seems to me to have figured life out pretty well, and Eric Jorgenson’s collection of Naval’s thoughts, blogs, and interviews gave me that guide that I was looking for. This book is essential for anyone interested in being happy and making money. “If you’re not willing to do a wholesale, 24/7, 100 percent swap with who that person is, then there is no point in being jealous.” — Eric Jorgenson quoting Naval Ravikant, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant These are just 10 of my favorite books from the last few years. However, I definitely wasn’t able to cover every inspiring book in this list alone. If there’s a book that’s inspired you that I haven’t listed, let me know in the comments — I’m always looking for new books and new stuff to learn about. Thanks for reading. 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What makes you hate Quora?
Answer: Today is my one year anniversary of writing on Quora. I decided a year ago that I was going to publish an answer on Quora every day for 6 months. I wanted to try something new and challenge myself to write more. Well over 400 answers and 11 million views later, here we are. I like Quora a lot. I’ve gotten a couple content writing jobs through Quora. I’ve made some coffee money with the QPP. I’ve read some really interesting answers and interacted with some great writers. Hell, I even used Quora to get through and process the break up that I had last year. If you’ve been following me for a minute, you probably know about that and have read about it. Good times. I also hate Quora sometimes. Here’s why, in a nutshell: I wish the platform had a greater ROI for the writers. Quora is a great platform with a lot of potential, but it’s difficult to make money here. From what I understand, even the top Quora writers aren’t making that much directly from Quora either. You don’t want to choose relationships based on potential, and you maybe shouldn’t choose platforms based on potential. Call me a soulless bastard, but making money makes me want to stay on a platform. That’s why I like Medium and Substack and that’s why I’m investing a lot time in my Twitter and Instagram accounts right now. But I stay on Quora despite the lack of cash because it’s a fun platform. I enjoy writing these answers. Trying to go viral on Quora is a fun game I play a few times per week. What I really don’t like about Quora are the extreme, negative comments. I get more hateful comments on Quora than any other platform I’ve posted on. I’ve gotten plenty of hate on Medium, but no one’s ever told me to kill myself. I don’t know if it’s because of the format of the platform or the culture that the users have created, but Quora reminds me a bit of the wild west of internet writing. There are actual crazy people on Quora, and as a writer you kind of have to keep your guard up. I’ve connected with some awesome readers and writers on here, but I’ve also been accused of killing someone’s dog, I’ve be insulted, and I’ve been told to kill myself multiple times. That’s what I hate about Quora. I wouldn’t leave the platform over a lack of cash, but a lack of cash paired with a bunch of people who want to fuck, marry, and kill me makes me anxious. That’s what I hate about Quora. I’m still posting on Quora when I have time, but I’ve putting a lot more time into Twitter the last few months. Tweet at me here!

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is wrong with our society today?
Answer: Society is sick, but there’s more to it than a contaigous virus. We’re sick spiritually, existentially, and socially. Society is sick because when an anorexic loses 23 pounds in 2 weeks, we tell her that she looks great and nothing else. Society is sick because when depressed 21 year old drinks so much that throws up all over his bed sheets, we will him that he’s “having too much fun”. Society is sick because when a burnt out college student working a job and internship collapses with their face in their laptop keyboard, we say they have an “inspiring work ethic”. Society is sick because there are thousands of gay little boys and girls who live in a world where killing themselves seems like an easier solution than trying to be themselves. Society is sick. The globe literally has a fever. Most of us ignore this in our daily lives. A lot of people think that climate change is hoax. Society is sick because our values are sick, and we don’t really know what to do about it. We struggle and we fight to fit into our fucked up society because we’re told that that will make us happy and peaceful, but that doesn’t really fit the problem. Being at complete peace in today’s world probably means you aren’t paying attention to what’s going on around you. “It is no measure of health to be well adjusted to a profoundly sick society.” — Krishnamurti So what do we do?

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What diet should I eat to reduce belly fat?
Answer: I’ve followed a lot of diets in my life. Most of them don’t work. Usually, I end up eating crap like this, no matter what diet I’m following. It might partially be a discipline issue, but I think my dietary struggles are deeper than that. I think our diet culture makes it especially difficult to follow healthy and balanced diets. But can a cheeseburger and fries even be apart of a balanced diet? I think maybe they can be. The truth is, before I had my In-N-Out burger today, I can’t remember the last time I had a cheeseburger and fries. I’ve been to California 3 times this year, but I haven’t had In-N-Out once. I’m not saying this as an accomplishment or anything, I’m just saying I don’t eat burgers and fries that much. But today, I wanted the burger, so I bought it ate it. I took a picture of it because it looked good. I posted it on my Instagram story because I’m annoying and basic like that. And what did I do afterwards? I moved on with my life. I didn’t get mad at myself and binge eat more crap because I was upset. I didn’t freak out. That was my last meal of my vacation, so I just ate it and moved on. The best diet to reducing belly fat is the one that leads to a sustainable restriction of calories. In my experience, extreme rigidity is usually followed by extreme chaos. In the long run, these extremes are very bad for both your health and your waist line. If you eat too many calories, you’ll get fat. Learn to stop eating too many calories. Learn to have one burger and fries every once in a while. Not 3 burgers every weekend. Don’t be an emotional eater, either.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are your techniques to improve writing?
Answer: I barely got a C in college writing. I have ADHD and I forgot to submit one of the important assignments on time. I also never wrote for my school newspaper or had anything published anywhere before I started writing on Medium in 2020. My biggest writing accomplishment prior to writing online was that I got a B on my Junior theme in high school. I wrote 3 posts on a blog when I was 19 and then quit and deleted the site after no one read them. Not even 2 years ago, I posted my first article on Medium. I figured no one was going to read it anyway, so I gave it a shot. Today, I make half my income writing on the internet about things that are interesting to me. The other half comes from fighting and teaching people how to fight. This is a career that is only possible because of the internet. Cute story, ain't it? The moral of me bragging here isn't that I'm awesome, the moral is that it doesn’t matter if you don’t have writing experience or life experience. Writing online is beautiful because you don't need qualifications to "get your foot in the door". Everyone seems to think that to write, you need to be special. You need to have won an Olympic medal, ran a 6-figure business, or at least need to have "talent" like Orwell or Hemingway. That's crap. All you need to write is to show up - every single day. Everything else is semantics. You don't need connections, a $1000 course, a mentor, or any of that other stuff you see people talk about on success podcasts or in self-help books. I was 23 with a big mouth and a Medium account, and I put a lot of time in. I STILL put the time in. I've published 332 articles on Medium as of this morning, more than 400 answers on Quora, and more than 100 posts on Substack. I've written well more than 1000 articles when you count articles I've written for clients and the articles I've never published. And like I said, I still haven't been doing this for 2 years. This is repetition. That's ALL it is. I'm traveling right now to train and film a Jiu-Jitsu instructional right now, but I still got up this morning and got my reps in. (See above: I’m squinting at the sun, not taking a dump) I can't imagine waking up and doing anything else. (I PROMISE I only put the laptop on the ledge for the picture… lol.)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is some good advice and tips for traveling alone?
Answer: Traveling alone is hard. I did the math today, and I’ve been on 19 trips this year for Jiu-Jitsu competitions, seminars, and training trips. I’m in San Diego right now, for the third time since June. The city is starting to feel familiar. I can get around parts of it without using my maps app. This trip is a little different than the last time I was here though, because I’m traveling by myself. It’s cool to get in a new place and do my favorite thing—I’m here to train and film an instructional DVD for my Jiu-Jitsu—but it’s a little lonely when I’m not at the gym. Last week I was in Toledo, Ohio, for training. It was fun to train and I definitely got better, but I missed my friends. The other night, I drove home to Chicago, and then the next morning I hopped on a plane and flew out here to SD. Loneliness in the road can be difficult to tame. I chose this life, I’m just a little lonely sometimes lately. Part of me longs for somewhere that feels like home. I’ve been on the road so much this year I don’t really remember what home feels like. One tip that’s helped me mentally when I travel alone has been learning to address my emotional needs by myself. If I’m lonely, I find someone to talk to. This is essential for me. If there’s no one to talk to (the 2 people I’m friends with in San Diego were busy today), I find some work to distract myself. I’ve been working a lot lately—-writing, training, teaching, etc. I’m not posting as many original Quora answers lately in part because I’m kind of sick of getting yelled at by people every time I open this app, but also because I’m focusing a bit more on the writing that is going to help me grow my career a bit.
