I’m trying to next the step, and I feel I’m getting closer. That’s why I keep traveling. I’m focusing on the mission. The mission requires travel, even when the beauty of travel is gone. Another tip for traveling alone is to remember why you’re traveling. Don’t forget what you want. If you haven’t figured out what you want, stop acting as if traveling to a new place is going to give you peace. Sorry that this answer became a diary entry. Hope this helps at least a bit. 😅

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is happiness for you?
Answer: You’re supposed to want to be the best. At least, that’s what I was told to want. Wanting and expecting anything less than the best from yourself goes against the very essence of what you’ve been told life is all about. Progress toward goals is supposed to be the single most important quality in determining the quality of your life. But is it really? Is life really just going from one pursuit to the other, grinding away at monotonous till you die? Is that all there is? The answer is complicated, but these are the questions that have been keeping me up at night lately, and the lack of sleep is making the already exhausting habits I have to maintain to chase my goals even more exhausting. I’m starting to think that success alone is not what I actually want out of life, and in my circle, I feel like that makes me weird. I feel like the only person in my inner circle who doesn’t want to constantly chase success, but it doesn’t matter, because I’m still constantly chasing success. Life isn’t always a hero’s journey. I’ve always loved “hero’s journey” novels, like The Alchemist, The Hunger Games, or the Harry Potter books. They follow a traditional story arch that’s easy to follow. The hero does a thing, he becomes a better person, gets the girl, and then he lives happily ever after. Life is nice when you’re a hero. Real life, on the other hand, is different. Real life has some “heroes’ journeys”, but it also has a lot of other things happening too. In real life, you have bills (I’ve never once heard Harry Potter discuss his 401k), you have responsibilities, and you have this horrible thing called “limits” following you around that heroes don’t seem to have in books and movies. When I’m training Jiu-Jitsu and my body is breaking down, my muscles are spasming, and I’m completely at my limit, it’s really hard to feel like I’m the Rocky Balboa of Jiu-Jitsu. You need to find another way. Real life is more complicated than just trying to be the hero all the time. Real life has subtle nuances and complexities that many of our foundational stories do not account for, and this leads many of us down the wrong pathways for how we want to spend our lives. I thought I had to win to be happy. For my entire life, I thought that after achieving certain goals, I’d finally have peace and happiness. I thought that once I won more Jiu-Jitsu tournaments, I’d make more money and be happy. I thought that once I started dating my dream girl, I’d never feel lonely again. I thought that once I got 1 million eyes on my writing, I’d be a successful writer. This is the trap of modern society. We convince each other that in everything we do, we need more to be happy. You need another championship. You need to write another bestseller. You need to date a hotter girlfriend and drive a fancier car. These were the things that I thought were going to make me happy. In reality, all I was doing was pushing the goalpost on allowing myself to feel content and happy in my life. I was chronically unhappy with my progress because I thought that the only way that I’d be worthy of love, happiness, and satisfaction was through achieving more and more stuff. In my own way, I was getting lost in my own sort of trap. You can have your goals AND be happy too, it’s just a little harder. There is a better way to go about it. The thing is that while success won’t make you happier in the long term, it’s easier to pursue the things that will make your life happier and more fulfilling when you are also immersed in goals and pursuits that you are connected to. Goals are a component of happiness but are not the whole pie. The biggest existential mistake that most people make is thinking that their success will be the cause of their happiness. It won’t, and if you don’t address this issue, your success is actually going to make you more miserable than you were before. When this happens, life starts to look grim and feel miserable — no matter what you do. Everyone constantly talks about “achieving their dreams”, but then we’re confused when our achievements make us unhappy. This is because our approach to life is incomplete. Success can help make you happy, but the things in your life that will really make your life “happy” do not come from conquering goals and overcoming the human condition. Happiness is mostly about love, and we forget that because we’re scared to love. We’re scared to be vulnerable. “If you have no love, do what you will — go after all the gods on earth, do all the social activities, try to reform the poor, the politics, write books, write poems — you are a dead human being.” — Jiddu Krishnamurti Happiness is simple. We just make it complicated. To me, a happy life boils down to just a few key components, several of which are articulated in this quote: “A fit body, a calm mind, a house full of love. These things cannot be bought — they must be earned.” — Naval Ravikant You can’t get “a fit body, a calm mind, and a house full of love” just by trying to be successful by the conventional definition of success that society portrays in the media. You have to be different. Most of us say we want to be sports champions, bestselling writers, and million-dollar business leaders, but I’m not sure how many people are saying that because it’s what they want and how many people are saying that because it’s what they were told to want. I mean, think about it. If you had your physical health, a calm mind that is content, and a home full of people who love and care about you regardless of what you’re driving or making, what else would you need? You’d probably find that many of your “goals” would fade into oblivion. What would you do then?

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I escape my comfort zone with social anxiety?
Answer: In my experience, you never really “escape” your social anxiety. It doesn’t really go away, but you can become so good at dealing with it that you stop noticing it. Take this Jiu-Jitsu match, for example. At the time, it was one of the biggest matches of my life. There were thousands of people in attendance, and even more were streaming and watching online. I’d come out of nowhere and made the semifinals in a bracket of 256 competitors. People literally thought I’d come off the street to upset 3 of the top 16 seeds. So, I was dealing with the regular anxiety of competing in front of people, but I was also dealing with the fact that I was thrust into this big stage match, and to most people, I had no business being there. Hell, one of the media guys at the event accidentally tried to kick me and my cornerman out of the backstage warm-up area because we were that much of an unfamiliar face. We were nobody, and it was all up to me to prove that we were somebody. If I got embarrassed during a match like that, I’d be humiliated. I’d have blown my shot. I was nervous. My palms were sweating. Knees weak. Arms heavy. Thank God I didn’t have any spaghetti. However, as the anxiety went through me, I didn’t freak out. If you saw me at the match, you wouldn’t have been able to tell that I have anxiety. I didn’t have a panic attack. I didn’t lose my mind (even though I was scared I was going to). I just noticed the crazy thoughts going through my brain and thought “damn, those are some crazy thoughts, this is my anxiety. It’s not real.” Through practice, you can learn to process your social anxiety. Because really, if you think about it, performance anxiety is really just a more rational form of social anxiety. I get more nervous from talking to pretty girls than I do before matches like the one above, and it’s taken me a long time to realize that these 2 sensations have the same root cause. Both of them stem from a fear of judgment. What I’ve been working on is having the same “growth mindset” in my personal life as I do before ginormous Jiu-Jitsu matches. It’s been an interesting experiment these last few months. I lost the match that day by 1 takedown and I took 4th in that huge tournament, but I learned a pretty valuable lesson throughout that weekend. First, I learned that when I’m healthy, in charge of my anxiety, and on top of my game, I’m one of the best 170-pound grapplers in North America. I also learned that when you learn to disconnect your anxious thoughts from accurate interpretations in the real world, good stuff can happen. Sure, bad things can happen, but I can tell you pretty confidently that your likelihood of success goes down significantly when you start to deal with your social anxiety. The best way to deal with social anxiety is to confront it. Sorry, there isn’t an easy solution for this one.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why is it so difficult to maintain a good work/life balance?
Answer: Through the constant chaos of living a life full of constant competition and fighting, I’ve somehow found myself really interested in Eastern philosophy this year. I guess it’s becoming an “ideal” way of living that I’m trying to shoot for. My life is full of competition and hustle and trying to win and create better things, and Eastern philosophy preaches the dulling of the ego for a sense of peace. I like that. I try to apply these ideas to my daily thinking and living. I’m starting to realize the flaws in my life, and that’s why I’m drawn to the thinkers and books that I am. These ideas are the peace to my chaos. It’s through seeking that balance that I’m able to feel more at peace in my daily life. I used to think that winning championships or becoming “a famous writer” or whatever would make me free of anxiety, imbalance, and all other negative emotions. I’ve since realized that negative emotions are just a part of being a person. I’m trying to allow myself to feel them — even if they’re uncomfortable sometimes. To me, that is why balance is important. Today, instead of working all afternoon I went to the harbor to read. Trying to be more relaxed and less hustle obsessed. Bugs kept biting me and I got grass stains on my cool white shoes, but it’s fine. I still had fun 😂

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Is Jiu Jitsu the best martial art for self-defence?
Answer: Like… kind of? People get mad when I write answers about how awesome Jiu-Jitsu is because they think that most Jiu-Jitsu training looks the way it does in the picture above. And let me tell you, as a Jiu-Jitsu black belt, I personally would absolutely never do something like… Wait… How’d that get in there? Before I talk about the perception that people have of Jiu-Jitsu, let’s talk about what’s actually the best martial art for self-defense. If someone attacks you with a knife, Jiu-Jitsu probably isn’t the best art. If someone tackles you, on the other hand, learning to fight off your back can be life-saving. If someone tries to punch you, Jiu-Jitsu is probably not your friend. The first best martial art for self-defense is not being an idiot who gets into fights. The second best martial art for self-defense is running away. The third best martial art for self-defense is a well-rounded study of various different martial arts, so that you can be prepared for a lot of different scenarios. Now that we have established that Jiu-Jitsu alone is maybe not the best art for self-defense, can we talk about why Jiu-Jitsu is awesome? Most people’s perception of Jiu-Jitsu comes from watching sport Jiu-Jitsu competitions, where strikes are not allowed. The rules of these competitions allow for a great deal of versatility. They allow athletes to do things like spinning on their heads, diving for leg locks, or throwing up buggy chokes in order to win the match which would certainly be stupid to do in a street fight. You can chose to view these techniques as impractical, but I view them as beautiful displays of athleticism and what the human body is capable of. Grappling is literally one of the oldest sports in human history. People have been wrestling each other for like, a really long time. These fun variations of techniques and different expressions of the human body make Jiu-Jitsu a lot of fun to participate in. These movements are the reason that the sport has steadily been growing in popularity for the last decade or so. The thing is, a lot of people think that because people who compete in Jiu-Jitsu would do these things in a street fight. I’m going to be completely honest with you: if you think I’m going to spin on my head in a street fight like I did in the picture above because “that’s my instinct”, you don’t know anything about martial arts. I wrote an answer once about how Jiu-Jitsu is more fun than Judo, and someone told me it was “the worst answer they’d ever read” because it didn’t talk about self-defense at all. And look, I get it. If I never actually trained martial arts either, I’d get really mad when people talked about things in martial arts that I didn’t understand, like inverted heel hook entries, buggy choke setups, or scrimmage wrestling. People have this misconception of Jiu-Jitsu, and it’s strange to me. You can sit around here on Quora and talk about how Jiu-Jitsu sucks because it has no emphasis on knife defense or whatever. If you need me, I’ll be at my Jiu-Jitsu gym, scooting on my butt and spinning on my head. Take a guess who’s having more fun (and also not getting into street fights 😬).

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the ways to end loneliness?
Answer: If I had to describe my life from 18–23 in just one word, that word would probably be “lonely”. (This isn't a picture of me, I just think it’s cool 😂 I found it here.) When I was living a lonely life, it wasn’t that I never had any friends — although, there was definitely a period like that — but it was more so that I didn’t feel connected to anyone I interacted with. I was interacting with people every day at school, Jiu-Jitsu, and the different little jobs I did, but I had a profound sense of loneliness because I felt disconnected from everyone. This, paired with the already constant social anxiety that I’ve had for as long as I can remember left me feeling miserable all the time. Anxiety paired with loneliness is a hell that I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemies. But luckily for me, there was a light at the end of the tunnel. This is how I found my way out of chronic loneliness. Working your way to a lonelier life. After I graduated high school, I did what most high seniors did. I went to college. However, when I was in college, I didn’t live the way most people did. I didn’t do the whole “go to class, study with classmates, and then blow off steam on the weekend at parties and bars” thing. I didn’t interact with people at school because I didn’t feel like we had similar interests. I decided this, and therefore, it was true. I was only 18, but I swore my mind was older. I swore I was destined for bigger things than a bachelor’s degree. Instead of enjoying my youth, I was obsessed with achieving outside goals that I had set for myself. The thought of social interaction was so uncomfortable (thanks, Anxiety) that I decided to throw myself into goal-oriented pursuits instead of doing anything else in my life. I became obsessed with Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Every day, 2–3 times per day, I was in the gym either training Jiu-Jitsu, lifting weights, or working on wrestling. I was obsessed. Once I started competing, I had to find a way to make some money so that I could pay to go to competitions, so I became obsessed with finding ways to make money on the internet. All I did was train martial arts, go to my college classes, and obsess over entrepreneurship on the internet. This might surprise you, but this made me very lonely. I was lonely because I thought that there was no one like me. There’s only no one like you because you are not looking for people like you. When you read that little story, you might think something like “well, your loneliness was your own fault. You didn’t do anything.” If you’re older, you probably think that I’m a spoiled brat who should have just been more grateful for the opportunity to do cool things like chase goals and do Jiu-Jitsu. You’re probably right, but that doesn’t really matter. I was still depressed. I had this delusion in my mind that there were no people who could understand what I was trying to do. I didn’t think that anyone my age would understand what it was like to want to be a world-class Jiu-Jitsu athlete, so I just didn’t talk to anyone about trying to be a world-class Jiu-Jitsu athlete. My beliefs about friendship were self-fulfilling. I went to school, trained, and sat at home being sad whenever I wasn’t chasing my goals. I lived my life on social autopilot. I was married to my routine because I thought that deviating from my routine would make me fail at my goals. I thought I was too ambitious to have friends. I thought I couldn’t date anyone because dating would kill my dreams. I created a reality that was based on my beliefs about goalsetting and success which I had learned from watching YouTube videos and scrolling through Instagram. My naivety to believe everything I saw online helped create a very depressing, and isolating reality. Your phone is not your friend. I made my first social media account when I was 14. I made a Facebook account because I wanted to play the “ESPN U Collegetown” game with my friends. Soon after that, I made a Twitter account. After that, I made a Snapchat. Then, I joined Instagram. A year or so after that, I was graduating high school, so I created a LinkedIn profile. I’ve grown up with digital communication and I’ve used a smartphone since I was a teenager. I’ve communicated through iMessage since it came out in 2011. My last 2 romantic breakups have started over things that were posted on social media. For years, I thought that my phone was my friend because it was connecting me with my friends and the world. The reality is more complicated. Your phone doesn’t make your social connections stronger. Your phone does help you maintain bonds, but the best way to build bonds that help enhance your sense of connection and happiness is through face-to-face communication. Call me old-fashioned, but after years of feeling alone and addicted to social media, I prioritize in-person communication over digital communication every single time. I think a lot of people feel this way, but I also think that our world is being engineered to force us to prioritize the digital over the physical. We feel that there’s no one like us because we’re not around each other as much. I used to feel lonely all the time, but I don’t feel that way anymore. I feel lonely sometimes, but I know how to handle it now. One of the most common and heartbreaking messages that I get from people who read my writing is something like “I wish there were more people like you”. This is weird to me because I’m really not super unique. I mean, I have an anxiety disorder and not everyone has an anxiety disorder, but still, 20% of people in America have anxiety. You could walk outside and scream “I have anxiety!”, and the odds that a person who has anxiety will hear you are incredibly high. What makes us lonely today is not that we are different from each other. What makes us lonely is that we do not talk to each other. Given the statistic above, I’d reckon that we probably aren’t talking to each other very much because we are all too nervous to talk to each other. We think that there’s “no one like us” because we’ve been taught to focus on our individuality from the time we are children, but the reality is that we’re all quite similar. We’re individuals, but we’re also part of a group. Perhaps instead of constantly celebrating our differences, we could take a few moments to celebrate all the things that make us the same. There are millions of people like you. You just have to be bold enough to go out and find them. Modern society has a loneliness problem. While our mental health problems are incredibly valid, I think that our society’s mental health problems could be greatly alleviated by working together to fix our collective loneliness problem. This starts with a mindset shift: don’t focus on all the things that make you different, focus on all the things that make you similar to the people around you. Make a deliberate effort to not be unique, at least, sometimes. That doesn’t mean you’re going to become best pals with everyone, but I promise that if there are people like me, there are people like you. There are people like all of us, we just haven’t found them yet. Have the audacity to seek connection in a world that preaches about the importance of solitude and “focus”. Have the courage to be vulnerably human. “A friend is someone who knows all about you and still loves you.”― Elbert Hubbard

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I find work-life balance?
Answer: This question has been on my radar for a long time, but mostly as a viewer. I didn’t want to answer something I felt I had no idea talking about. That said, I’ve learned a lot about balance this year. This is what most days look like for me—sort of. (It’s not usually this staged but we had to get that content for the IG 😂) For me, it’s really easy to overwork. I’m 25. I’m a competitive grappler, Jiu-Jitsu instructor, and writer. I don’t have kids or a mortgage at the moment. All I do is work and spend time with my friends when I can. The main reason I overwork so much is that I love what I do all day. Everything I do is something I like doing. That sounds corny, but it’s honest. My job is dope. There’s also a deeper reason, but we will get to that in a second. What really bugs me is that sometimes I have to do a little more of it than I’d like. I wish I could have success with less work, but I’ve found that it just doesn’t work like that. For writing, I usually write around 2500-3000 words per day. If I don’t train I usually have the brain power and endurance to get up near 5000. More writing than this usually burns me out, but a lot of pro writers online write way more than I do. For training, I usually do Jiu-Jitsu sparring, technique drilling, and weight training all on the same day. Usually, 3–4 hours per day are spent on physical activity of varying intensity. More training than this usually breaks my body down. Less training impacts my improvement and fitness compared to the other top guys I have to go against in competition. I try to prep all my meals on the weekend so I don’t have to cook during the week, and I make sure to prioritize sleep, stretching, sauna, and taking time to be mindful every day. I also try to keep my social life these days low stress so I don’t feel strung out. I do all the right stuff because if I don’t, I start to feel like my life is falling apart. But here’s the thing. You don’t care about my stupid fucking productivity routine. You don’t care about how often I stretch, how many pages I read per day, or how many words I slam onto the keyboard every day (it’s a lot to all of them). What you care about is how I stay balanced. How I do everything I do without losing my damn mind. I used to struggle a lot with my mental health, primarily because of my lack of balance. It’s not as much of a problem anymore because I’ve figured a few things out about myself. It’s really hard for me to stay balanced because, for the longest time, I thought that my success defined me. I used to prioritize success over everything, and this made me very unhappy. This made me unhappy because though my life was full of excitement and adventure, there was no love in my life. I had no work-life balance because I had no life to look forward to outside of work. Everything I did was work-related because I was scared that if I stopped chasing success, people wouldn’t think I was successful anymore. If they stopped viewing me as successful, I wouldn’t have an identity anymore. My whole life has been very achievement-oriented, and in order to develop balance, I had to realize this and then make active attempts to push back against it. The way that you create “work-life balance” is not by “working” on your balance. If that’s what you’re doing, you’re missing the point. Work-life balance is not something you work at. Most of us don’t need to get better at working, we need to get better at living. You don’t need to work more, you need to live more. You need to laugh more. You need to cry more. You need to think more. You need to align with all the things that make you human. There's something very human about avoiding what makes us human, but that’s what you have to stop doing to have balance in your life. You have to stop trying to be superhuman.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What do you consider your strength and why?
Answer: If you asked me a year ago, I would have told you something like “strength is the ability to transcend pain”. My view of strength was all about suffering. I used to think that strength could not exist without pain and suffering. I’ve changed my mind a bit. Today, I think that strength is different. Whether you’re a man, woman, puppy, or goldfish, the foundation of strength does not change. Whether you are lifting weights, overcoming anxiety, or facing adversity in your life, strength is not about pain. Strength is about what you do in the face of life. To me, strength is the ability to endure and transcend the human condition. Strength isn’t about what you’re going through, it’s about what you do. Strength is the ability to do difficult things with a smile. It’s the ability to talk to strangers even though you’re nervous. It’s the ability to be confident when inside you’re more anxious than a puppy on the 4th of July. Strength is the ability to be yourself in a world that would prefer if you’d just shut the fuck up and fit in. “The people's champ must be everything the people can't be.” — Chance the Rapper

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the best inspirational books that you ever read? And how were they inspiring?
Answer: Here are 5 inspirational books that have helped me get my life together this last year. Here’s my lovely bookshelf made out of Tide pods. Not all the books on this list are in the picture. The Midnight Library — Matt Haig When I read The Midnight Library last fall, I was in a phase where I was terrified to “start”. The Midnight Library tells the story of a woman named Nora Seed, who was also terrified to take action in her life. She was so terrified, in fact, that she tries to take her own life in the opening chapter of the book. This suicide attempt sends her to a place called “The Midnight Library”, where she has to determine both how and why she wants to live her life if she’s granted another chance. I wasn’t suicidal like Nora in the novel, but I was terrified to take the next steps toward living. I didn’t think I was worthy of living the life I wanted. I thought that I was special in how inadequate I was. The Midnight Library made me feel like my anxiety wasn’t isolating. It made me feel validated, and this gave me the strength to take the shots that I was afraid of taking. “The only way to learn is to live.”― Matt Haig, The Midnight Library The Almanack of Naval Ravikant — Eric Jorgensen Ever since I heard him on Tim Ferris’s podcast a few years back, I’ve had 2 main feelings about Naval Ravikant: That’s why when I heard about The Almanack of Naval Ravikant, I was immediately skeptical. I didn’t like the idea that some guy had just taken all of Naval’s ideas and made them into a book. It seemed like a cop-out. I figured that Eric Jorgensen would twist Naval’s words to fit his personal narrative and that the book would be terrible. I’m a skeptic like that. I was very wrong. This was the best book I read last year, not only because it gave me a detailed framework to build wealth and improve my life, but also because it gave me a reading list that I was able to use to find some other great books that changed my life (2 of which are on this list). “The reality is life is a single-player game. You’re born alone. You’re going to die alone. All of your interpretations are alone. All your memories are alone. You’re gone in three generations, and nobody cares. Before you showed up, nobody cared. It’s all single player.”― Eric Jorgenson, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant Striking Thoughts — Bruce Lee Ever since I first saw Enter the Dragon when I was a kid, I’ve been fascinated by Bruce Lee. Bruce Lee did everything. He was an athlete, a martial artist, a writer, an actor, a director, and a philosopher. He was a multi-talented man who lived a life of discipline and dedication to his craft. That is why he became the best in the world in pretty much everything he did. That’s why martial arts schools all over the world still teach his style of martial arts to people today. That’s why we still watch his movies and read his books. Once I saw Striking Thoughts on Naval’s reading list at the end of the “Navalmanack”, I decided to download it on Audible and play it during a drive to Toledo, Ohio earlier this year for a weekend of Jiu-Jitsu training. I’m really glad I did. I hadn’t read much great philosophy in nearly a year, but Striking Thoughts gave me a new, refreshed perspective on Eastern philosophy that both made me think and motivated me to keep striving on the path I am on. This was the book that made me know that it’s okay if you don’t know. “The meaning of life is that it is to be lived, and it is not to be traded and conceptualized and squeezed into a patter of systems.” — Bruce Lee The Book of Life — Jiddu Krishnamurti This is another book from Naval’s reading list. Krishnamurti’s life is fascinating to me. In his early life, he was believed by the Theosophical Society to be a vehicle for the new “World Teacher”. Basically, he was groomed to be a cult leader, and even at a young age, he didn’t like that. Instead, he made the decision as a young man to reject this and go his own way. He withdrew from the spiritual organization. The irony is, though he didn’t become the “World Teacher”, his writings and philosophies still taught millions of people in the 1900s and today to live better, happier, and more peaceful lives. He wrote many books and gave many talks during his life, but one of his best-known books is The Book of Life, which consists of 365 daily mediations on spirituality, life, love, and pretty much every other topic under the sun. Each meditation is just one page long, which makes this a great, digestible read for anyone who’s interested in philosophy but worried about material being “too dense”. “You only learn when you give your whole being to something.” — Jiddu Krishnamurti Siddhartha — Herman Hesse This year I’ve been very focused on spirituality more than normal because I had some experiences last year that made me feel that my mind and body were not working together. My mind wanted a healthy body, healthy relationships, and to build a future for myself, but my body still was living in the destructive patterns that I used to follow in my adolescence and early adulthood. Basically, I had a period where I was full of shit. I was talking the talk about happiness and self-development, but I wasn't walking the walk because I didn’t know how to walk the walk. I was trying to live a healthy, balanced life, but I didn’t know how. Siddhartha was one of the books that helped me realize what spirituality really is. It’s a short read (I read the whole thing during a 2-hour and 45-minute flight to Austin earlier this year), but it’s jam-packed full of insight on living authentically, living spiritually, why certain pursuits (like money, for example) make us feel the way that they do. The way the book is written makes each reader see parts of themselves in Siddhartha, Hesse’s main character whom the book is named after. This book will make you think, cry, and hope. It might even make you change your life. “Knowledge can be communicated, but not wisdom.” — Herman Hesse

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the five most important things for a man to learn in life?
Answer: Without learning these 5 lessons, I’d be completely lost today. Learn how to control your own mind. If you don’t control your mind, it will control you. A man who is a slave to his primitive desires and urges is not a man, he’s a boy. ”He who cannot obey himself will be commanded. That is the nature of living creatures.”—Nietzsche This quote might be a bit more intense than what I was going for, but it does lead you down some interesting thought tangents. Either way, the point is simple: master your mind. Mental mastery is the pathway to freedom. Learn how to treat the opposite sex properly. I don’t get crushes very often. For whatever reason, I’m difficult to impress. Then in the past, when I would finally crush on someone or start to have feelings for them, I would be all in way too quickly. I wasn’t the guy who yelled at his girlfriend or was rude to her, I was the doormat type of guy because I was scared of being hurt. We worked on this in therapy, and I learned how to stand up for myself without becoming an asshole or acting like a doormat. Both being overly aggressive and overly submissive in relationships is bad for your self-esteem, the stability of your relationship, and your happiness in your life. Learn how to treat a woman right without treating yourself like crap. “Respect is one of the greatest expressions of love.” — Miguel Angel Ruiz Learn how you learn stuff. Doing Jiu-Jitsu changed my life, but not in the way you might think. Jiu-Jitsu didn’t make me a millionaire. For years, all Jiu-Jitsu did was damage my body and take my money. I thought I was a crazy person for spending so much time obsessing over how I could get better at fighting. Then, I started writing. What happened was kind of interesting. I applied the same principles that I used in Jiu-Jitsu to writing. So far, it’s working out better than the early years of my Jiu-Jitsu career because I’ve been able to skip past all the guesswork that I did in the early years of Jiu-Jitsu. Learning how to learn is the ultimate key to improving your confidence, your career prospects, and your personal life. “If you know the way broadly you will see it in everything.”—Miyamoto Musashi Learn how to carry yourself properly. Most young men seem arrogant. This is because they are unconfident. When I was 18–22, this was me. I walked around like I owned every room because inside, I felt like a child in a man’s body. I was in great shape, I was winning Jiu-Jitsu tournaments allover the country at the highest levels I could, and I was young. It was supposed to be the prime of my life, but I wasted it by being anxious Learning how to carry myself confidently without coming across as arrogant was difficult for me, but I feel that in the last few years I’ve gotten a lot better at it. Confidence will open doors for you. Arrogance will close them. "With realization of one's own potential and self-confidence in one's ability, one can build a better world." - The Dalai Lama Learn how to develop hobbies. One thing that was hard for me when I was younger was that I thought that I had to be the best in the world at everything I did. I thought that if I couldn’t be the best in the world at something, there was no point in doing it. You can probably see the holes in this way of thinking, but for me, it was very difficult. I never thought about my own joy or happiness. I only thought about winning and getting results. This did help me win a lot of martial arts tournaments and build my writing business in the early days, but it also made it very hard for me to avoid burnout, build interpersonal relationships, and manage my mental health. Recently, I’ve picked up my guitar again for the first time in nearly 3 years. I’m never going to be a professional guitarist, but playing the guitar is fun for me. Hobbies are great. Non-destructive hobbies will make you better at your professional work. “Today is life - the only life you are sure of. Make the most of today. Get interested in something. Shake yourself awake. Develop a hobby. Let the winds of enthusiasm sweep through you. Live today with gusto”― Dale Carnegie Oh, and yes, all of these things can be applied to women too. Have a great day 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What keeps you strong, even though you're actually very tired?
Answer: The last thing I wanted to do today was go to the gym. I’ve been dealing with a back injury recently that keeps flaring up, and it’s made me a bit anxious during training, a bit miserable during daily life, and the thought of doing my current least favorite thing (driving with pre-existing back pain) makes me visibly upset. Today, my friends at the gym wanted to train in the gi (the bathrobe things we’re wearing). I hate training in the gi. It’s my least favorite. I like trying to be explosive, scrambly, and athletic during Jiu-Jitsu. Gi training is slower and more technical. For me, it’s less fun right now. However, a few of my friends are getting ready for the World Masters Jiu-Jitsu tournament in a few weeks, so we had to train gi to get them ready. I didn’t want to do it. My back hurts. I’m starting a new diet this week. I’ve got a lot of writing to get done. As grateful as I am for everything, life is stressful right now. I still went to the gym today because I my friends were expecting me there. I still had a good time, didn’t sit out during training, and pushed myself, even though I’m tired. What keeps me strong even when I feel weak is all the people who have similar goals to me. “Family” isn’t the proper term, I guess, but it’s the only one that comes to mind.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do you deal with problems in life?
Answer: Yesterday, I went to my car to drive to Jiu-Jitsu, and someone had smashed my window. They didn’t steal anything because I don’t have anything valuable in my car, but the fact that I now had to deal with a smashed window was kind of a pain in the butt. It was a Sunday, meaning most repair shops were closed. I posted a photo of the smashed window on my Instagram because I needed help finding someone who could repair the window, and the comments I got from people were very interesting to me. Most people didn’t know any places I could get the window fixed, but everyone was freaking out the fact that my window got smashed. I guess I get it—a picture of smashed glass is kind of freaky looking—but I don’t really understand the “freak out sympathy” approach to problem solving. When something happens to someone, most people tend to react emotionally to the situation, even if the situation doesn’t require an emotional reaction. People told me things like “God why are people so awful?”, but honestly, I didn’t want to think about the guy who broke into my car. I just wanted a new window. That doesn’t mean emotional reactions to situations are always wrong—there are certainly times to be emotional. I just feel like most people go around letting their emotions dictate their approach to problems. So, what do I do about problems in my life? I try to approach them objectively. I try to stay focused on solving the problem, not dealing with how the problem makes me feel. Yesterday I drove around with a smashed window for like 3 hours, and that made me a bit anxious. A lot of times, when I used to get really anxious, I would stress eat. The problem is, eating cookies doesn’t cure your anxiety. It doesn’t fix your problem. It just distracts you from the problem. Freaking out about how people are terrible when they smash your window is kind of the same way. I don’t know who smashed my window. I’ll probably never meet them. I don’t think I want to meet them. Meeting them won’t get my window fixed. The best way to approach problems in your life is to approach the problems head on, and stop focusing your energy all the things that aren’t directly your problems. You’ll probably notice that in time, this approach will help you get rid of those unrelated issues as well.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I stop doubting myself?
Answer: Here’s 8 things I do that help me stop doubting myself. Understand that doubt is really a fear of vulnerability. I’ve always admired people who do slam poetry. Slam poets stand on a stage and speak (and sometimes shout) some of the most raw powerful sentences you can imagine — to a room full of strangers. The thought of doing this puts my stomach in knots. Slam poetry is an insanely vulnerable experience. The people who do it are courageous because they confront the innate human fear of vulnerability. They’re courageous to me because, if the content of their work says anything, it says that they aren’t free of doubt and anxiety. Learning to lean into vulnerability is one of the first ways you can start to ease your anxiety and self-doubt. Put your doubts on trial. Sometimes, I have the most ridiculous doubts in my head that are completely disconnected from reality. I doubt myself in dating because I’m awkward, but no one thinks I’m as awkward as I do. I doubt myself in Jiu-Jitsu because I’m not that good, but my record on the mat and my friends say otherwise. I doubt myself in writing because I don’t make as much as Tim Denning or Nicolas Cole, but I’ve only been writing for 2 years. I doubt myself, but when I put the doubts into the world, I realize that they’re, for the most part, all in my head. Jump into the deep end. In addition to sharing your doubts with people in your life, another great way to overcome your doubts is to just start fighting them. When you’re anxious to talk to someone, go do it anyway. When you’re doubting your abilities before a match, a date, or publishing an article, just do the damn thing. It’s okay if you don’t believe in yourself. Contrary to popular belief, you don’t have to believe in yourself to be successful. Believing yourself just makes life more pleasant. Avoid people who feed your doubts. Everyone experiences that “friend” who doubts them. Not everyone wants you to be successful because, for insecure people, your success is seen as a threat. You have to learn how to read people. The first step to doing this well is to overcome your desire for attention. When you are no longer desperate for attention, it’s easier to view people objectively. This allows you to better analyze the intentions of your closest friends. Learning how to recognize these people is the first step to avoiding them. Break the comparison trap. If you’re like most people, social media is probably making you compare yourself to other people more than you should. I’ve heard people argue that this comparison is “motivating”, but I think that for most of us who struggle with anxiety, the constant comparison just feeds our doubts. This makes us more anxious, insecure, and eventually, depressed. The successful people I’ve gotten to know in the writing/entrepreneurship world barely use social media for any reason other than for business. The most successful people don’t use it all. The goal is to be rich and anonymous. That’s where peace comes from. Make an impact on other people’s lives. This might seem contradictory to the “rich and anonymous” comment I just made, but you really don’t need a large following to impact people. I’m the 13th-ranked Jiu-Jitsu athlete in my weight class and I compete in pro events all over the place, but the 7-year-old students in my kid’s class don’t really give a damn about what I win. They don’t know what that means, and I still make a positive impact on their lives. The other day, one of the parents in my class said that their son “adores me”. That made me really happy. That made me doubt myself a lot less. Develop an abundance mindset. When I started competing in Jiu-Jitsu, I thought that the top spots on the podium were reserved for “special” people, and I knew that I definitely wasn’t special. I was just a regular guy with a dream that he assumed he wasn’t going to achieve. I’d never achieved anything else before, so I figured Jiu-Jitsu wouldn’t be any different. It took winning a world championship for me to realize that my potential is not limited by the ideas in my mind. You can do a lot more than you think because there is plenty of success to go around. Call me a naive idealist, but I like to think that everyone can be happy, healthy, and wealthy. Develop hobbies. This might seem completely unrelated to mental training or overcoming doubt, but it’s been really important for me the last few weeks. I’ve been working so much on training, writing, and “trying to be more”, that I’ve completely forgotten why I do any of this. I forgot how much I love what I do. I deal with burnout a lot from overwork. But doesn’t doing what you love to the point of being miserable defeat the purpose of doing what you love? Taking time away from your work (whether you love it or not) is crucial for easing the intense emotions that we get from the stressful parts of our lives. I’ve been playing the guitar again lately for the first time in 3 years, and I’m really enjoying it. The most important habits for helping me overcome my doubts are writing and working out, but there is a lot more to it than just picking up weights and writing words. When you’re dealing with crippling anxiety (like I did a few years ago), you can’t just work out and write your doubts away. You have to put in real work for long periods of time. You can’t change your life in a day, so why would you be able to change your mind in one? This is a process. This is a lifestyle. But when you get started, and start to see results, you’ll start to feel that there isn’t any other way to live.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best way to grow up?
Answer: The best way to grow up is to partially grow up. Here’s me, yesterday. To an outside observer, it looks like I sit around on my ass and do Jiu-Jitsu all day. “Jiu-Jitsu bum” is a real thing, and a lot of people think I am one. They’re partially right. I do Jiu-Jitsu pretty much every day, usually times several times per day. Jiu-Jitsu is my playtime. It’s my job (I just booked a really important match that’s coming up this fall), but it’s also my happy place. When I’m at Jiu-Jitsu, I don’t feel like a “professional” or “a grown-up”, I feel like a kid playing his favorite game. But then, training ends, and I have to come home. I have to come back to real life because I don’t live in Neverland. I have clients I write for. I have lessons to teach. I want to make money doing what I love, and that requires a lot of hard work. A friend once told me that Jiu-Jitsu is like Neverland, and I partially agreed with them. That’s why I try to make an effort to do more than just martial arts all day. I don’t want my entire experience to come from fighting people. I don’t want to be a lost boy. I don’t want to be a Peter Pan, but I also don’t want to lose the ability to have fun. And that conundrum is pretty much how I ended up here. When I got deep into the Jiu-Jitsu world at 19, I also started reading and learning about philosophy because I dealt with depression from the time I was 10. I felt strange because in Jiu-Jitsu, I was supposed to forget all my problems, but the advice I was getting from the philosophers and self-help folks I was reading told me to confront my problems. I’ve found that what you really need in “growing up” is balance. You need to be a person who can “have fun” when it’s time to play, but you also need to be someone who can pay rent, make a living, and contribute to society. If you don’t you’re a man-child. Or a woman-child. Whatever. “Forget them, Wendy. Forget them all. Come with me where you'll never, never have to worry about grown-up things again.”—Peter Pan Don’t be like Peter. Grow up. Peter Pan was weak. The world is cruel to all of us, but it takes a truly weak mind to run away from that. It takes a very weak mind to never grow up. There is pain and tragedy everywhere. More than 100,000 people die every day. That’s fucking heartbreaking, but I can’t change that. I’m just one guy. If there’s a way I can change that, let me know. Until then, I feel a little helpless when I look at all the problems in the world. But that doesn’t mean that I don’t just run off to my Jiu-Jitsu Neverland and forget about the world. I try to make an active effort to do something positive every day for others. I try to do something to make sure I have my shit together every day. I work every day like a lunatic because there is so much fucked up shit in the world, and I just really don’t want to be someone who makes it worse. Don’t be like Peter. Grow up. I teach kids martial arts classes, and my kids always tell me about things their parents tell them about how “being an adult sucks”. Their parents complain about bills, traffic, and work. I’ll admit, all these things do kind of suck, but I really don’t miss being 10. I don’t miss having to ask permission to go to the bathroom. I don’t miss puberty. I don’t miss the bullies. I don’t miss getting in fights at school because another kid had called me fat. I’ve done the work, and honestly, for me, being an adult is so much better than being a kid. I tell my kid students something like “being an adult is hard, but being a kid is hard too, it’s just a different kind of hard”. I try to make sure that the kids know that growing up isn’t going something to run from. Life is beautiful, and I hope more people think that way. The last thing I want is to be a part of a generation of people who hate their futures. Let’s make growing up cool again.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is one of the best examples of tough love that you’ve ever seen?
Answer: Here are 10 pieces of tough love that have really helped me in the last year. You’re probably being too nice. Being “too nice” used to be a big problem for me. It wasn’t because I was weak, it was because I was afraid. I had the strength to deal with confrontation, but I didn’t do it because I was afraid I didn’t have the strength to deal with confrontation. The fear of the problem was worse than the problem. The problem created by constantly avoiding confrontation is that you lose control of the flow of your life. Confronting things is the best way to ensure that actual change happens. Passivity leads to inaction, and eventually resentment. If you don’t confront things you’re unhappy with, I can guarantee that they won’t change. Your self-worth impacts your net worth, not the other way around. I know plenty of rich people with low self-esteem. I also know plenty of not-so-rich people with low self-esteem. Self-esteem is important, but you can’t get it from making money or earning status. On the other hand, if you have high self-worth, you’ll find it easier to make money and improve your status. You’re not afraid of rejection, you’re afraid of vulnerability. Failing makes you vulnerable. Failure exposes your limits. But the fear we feel isn’t really a fear of failure, the fear is looking like someone who isn’t capable of doing everything. This is a bit silly, because all humans fail. Failure is a part of the human experience Being afraid to fail is being afraid to be human. Social media is probably making you dumber. I used to wake up every morning, and the first thing I’d do was turn my alarm off. The second thing I’d do is open Instagram and check my direct messages. The third I’d do would to be checking my Instagram story viewers to see if the girl I have a crush on viewed the story. It took me a while to realize it, but starting your day with a cheap dopamine rush is never a good idea. Social media is easy to consume, and frequent consumption of social media will make difficult things (like reading books, for example) more difficult. Long story short, social media probably makes you dumber. Everyone says they work hard. Not everyone works hard. In competitive fields, everyone says that they work hard. Saying you work hard is a way of fitting in. Some people do work hard and still fail, but there are a lot of people who work moderately hard and say that they’re giving “everything they have” when in actuality, they’re holding back. “Everything I have” is self-fulfilling. Most people are holding back. Are you? Just because you took the time to make something doesn’t mean anyone will care about it. I put out an ebook in January, and I sold like 11 copies. I considered the ebook a flop. I put a lot of time into the book, poured my heart into it, and because of a variety of factors (primarily a lack of commitment to marketing on my part and a crappy title for the ebook), the book didn’t sell well. What I learned from this is just because you make something doesn’t mean anyone will care about it. You have to make them care. You have to create value to sell products and ideas. Dumb habits make a smart person stupid. Ignoring nutrition and not prioritizing your sleep will break you down very quickly. The older you are, the faster negative habits will catch up with you. Checking your phone first thing in the morning isn’t awesome for your mind. Not reading will stagnate your learning. Eating like crap will make you fat. Eventually, all these will make you stupid. Sorry for being blunt. I don’t care how smart you are, if you do dumb things, your quality of life will reflect that. People who care about you will show you that they care about you. I used to think that the word “love” meant something. I’m not so sure anymore. We throw around the word love so much that for most of us, the word doesn’t have any meaning anymore. The easiest way to see who really loves you is to see who helps you out when you’re struggling. Who still supports you when you’re down? Who goes out of their way to make you happy? You shouldn’t have to ask people to show you that they love you. You don’t have money because you don’t have time, not the other way around. Time gives you the ability to create more sustainable income streams and better habits. Running around like a lunatic without planning, strategizing, and thinking about ways to genuinely improve your life is a fast track to finding yourself caught in the same behavior patterns over and over again without even realizing it. Use your time wisely. Use your time to develop wisdom. You can have almost anything you want, but not everything you want. Specialization is the single most important thing that I have done in my life. The second most important thing was realizing that I could do things without trying to be the best in the world at them (these are called “hobbies” apparently — I’m new to them). In Jiu-Jitsu, choosing to focus on no-gi competition sent me from a decent level brown belt to one of the top 15 ranked grapplers in the world in just 9 months. By trying to do everything at a high level, I was limiting my potential in everything. I was also more stressed and strung out. Learning how to quit effectively will change your life.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is your dream job? Are you already doing it?
Answer: When I was 5-years-old, I decided that I wanted to be a professional athlete. To be specific, I wanted to be a baseball player. My parents gently explained to me that I should have “a backup plan” because not everyone gets to be a professional baseball player. They said that lots of other little boys wanted to be professional baseball players, and some of them might be better than me. I understood what they meant, but it still bugged me. It felt so obvious to me that I was going to compete in sports at a high level someday. I was mad that they couldn’t see it. For me, it wasn’t a dream, it was a vision. I later realized that they weren’t “not believing in me”, or anything like that. They just couldn’t fathom the idea of the person they made doing could do something that they had never even fathomed for themselves. I’m not the most talented athlete. I’ve always been a bit of a late bloomer. My parents are not athletes. My dad is too anxious to even exercise anymore. I have a bit more anxiety than the average athlete. It doesn’t look like it when I’m competing or training because I hide it well, but there are times when the anxiety is so bad that it comes pouring out of me like a waterfall. If my parents taught me anything, it’s that not everyone gets to do their dream job. You have to work your ass off. You have to get lucky. You have to have the right connections. You have to be in the right place at the right time. You can even do all these things and still come up short. But the thing is, for me, the dream was always to be a professional athlete. Ever since I was 5, I’ve had tunnel vision on this as a career. Someone asked me the other day what I’d do if I didn’t do Jiu-Jitsu full-time. I said I’d write, but I honestly have no idea what life would look life it wasn’t different from the way it is. Writing is just something I picked up along the way to make ends meet while I was coming up. I guess I kind of made it some ways, but simplifying the whole journey into that one sentence — “I made it.” — doesn’t do the journey justice. It took more than a decade to find a sport I was above average at. It took a decade after that to develop the skills to do that sport at a high level. It took even longer to figure out a way to make the sport my job and compete at the professional level. The journey has been so long. It’s kind of overwhelming to think about everything that’s happened along the way. That’s why I’m so grateful for every single little thing. Every match offer, every sponsorship request, and every fan or follower who sends me a message. It all makes me so happy because it’s what I wanted ever since I was swinging my baseball bat in the backyard impersonating my favorite players. Maybe I’m the only one who feels this way, but I still get the feeling that I shouldn't be here. I still feel like an imposter—like I shouldn’t be where I am. My biggest fear about working my dream job is that one day, someone’s going to try and take it away from me. I guess maybe that’s what I’m fighting for.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are three habits that highly productive people have on a daily basis?
Answer: I’m a professional athlete who writes between 2500–3000 words every day. Here are the 7 most positive ROI habits that I have in my daily life (cuz 3 is too few): • waking up at the crack of dawn and wrestling (3 times per week) • lifting weights (3 times per week) • spending time outside every day • writing (on the internet) every day • reading every day • Jiu-Jitsu training/teaching • asking for help when I’m struggling I don’t really do anything crazy, I just do the same things every day. My friends joke that I’m predictable. The things is, the habits themselves are not really that important. My daily habits look very different than most people because my job is very different from most people. What is important is the fact that I have these daily habits and that I maintain them, rain or shine, happy or sad, eager or uninterested. Productivity is the result of consistency. Everything else is fluff. I could sit here and tell you about cold showers, meditation, affirmations, and all that other stuff, but I’d be lying. There’s nothing wrong with using tricks to help you build your discipline, but if you want to be highly productive, you have to show up and work every day. That’s the game. If you want to understand why you are where you are, take inventory of the last 6 months of your life. If you want to see where you're going, look at your habits. If you want to take control of where you're going, take control of your habits. Here's a photo from morning wrestling today. There's just something about getting your hardest workout of the day done before most people have finished their coffee. Here’s an article I wrote on Medium a few weeks back on habits that have helped me get better at stuff faster. If you’re interested, check it out.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: I have fallen in love with a girl, but she has a boyfriend. What do I do?
Answer: I didn’t “fall in love” with her, but I met a really sweet girl today and immediately I developed a crush on her. I knew she had a boyfriend, but I bumped into her at a Jiu-Jitsu event, so we started chatting a bit. I’d known of this girl through the Jiu-Jitsu scene for a while and thought she was pretty, but I didn’t have a crush on her or anything. Then, she started talking, and I started getting those nerves you get when you’re talking to someone you’re attracted to. She wasn’t just cute. She was really good at Jiu-Jitsu. She was really smart. She was a catch, and I really wanted to get to know her better. I felt myself turning pink while we talked. I was excited and anxious and all those other fun feelings for the first time in a while. I don’t get crushes often anymore, so it’s really fun when I do. I get insecure about stupid things. “I can’t believe I’m wearing Avatar: The Last Airbender shorts,” I thought, “I look like the world’s biggest dork.” I’m not sure if she noticed my Avatar shorts. We had a nice chat. It wasn’t super eventful I guess, but it was nice. Then, the interaction ended. It wasn’t weird. Nothing happened, except for that I walked away realizing I definitely had a crush on that girl. She definitely has a boyfriend, and I definitely felt myself getting a crush on her. That was, to put it lightly, a bummer. Did I mention that she was cute as hell? And really good at Jiu-Jitsu? And really smart? I’m a simple man. I wasn’t walking around looking for love that day, but there was a period of about 3 minutes when I thought I’d stumbled upon it. I think this is my biggest flaw as a human. In my late teens/early 20s, I was kind of a scum bag. I liked chasing unavailable girls because I was insecure and chasing them made me feel valuable in some demented way. I thought that a man’s value was measured by his body count and his life was the story of how he went from escapade to escapade without getting caught. I didn’t want to be happy, I wanted to be interesting. Except, in the end, all that really happened from this way of thinking was that I hurt a bunch of people and got hurt a bunch. See, I’ve always had a desire to pursue “what was right” in everything in life, except when it came to women. In romance, I’d throw all my morals away for a cute smile and a fit body. I didn’t care. I couldn’t control myself around beautiful women. It wasn’t that I didn’t care about the people I was hurting. I did. I just felt so insecure about not feeling loved in my life that I wanted to take that love away from others. If I could be happy, no one could be. That’s how the bullied become the bullies. Between impulsivity and insecurity, I had a lot of bad relationships. I had mostly bad relationships. I worked on it through therapy, journaling, and reflecting on my choices for a long time because I didn’t like who I was. I decided I wanted to be better. Impulsivity is my biggest character flaw. My therapist says it’s an ADHD thing, but she also says that ADHD isn’t an excuse to be an asshole. When I compete in sports, being impulsive helps me. I just go for things during my Jiu-Jitsu matches. In writing, it’s great too. I just write stuff that I feel and don’t hold back. In dating, however, it’s not always best to just do what you want at the moment. It’s smart to think about what you want. I know there are some old-school dudes out there who will tell me to “take what I want”, but I’m not sure taking things is always the best move. So what did I do about the girl today? Well, if she messaged me right now asking what I was up to, you’re damn right I’d respond. However, that hasn’t and probably won’t happen. I’m probably going to have to get over it. It probably wouldn’t be wise for me to “just tell her how I feel”. That’s okay though. Not everyone needs to know how I feel all the time. Some feelings are best kept to yourself. The thing that bugs me, I guess, is that my lil’ sensitive kid heart is still full of love. I still have a lot of love to give, I just can’t give it to that person. That’s okay though, that’s why I found this question on Quora and started writing an answer. Instead of being thirsty in people’s DMs tonight, I wrote a Quora answer. Find better ways to use your energy. Goodnight 😴

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best way to make money?
Answer: Making money is harder when it comes from something you love. I’ve been doing Jiu-Jitsu for about 7 years, competing for more than 6 years, and competing at the “world level” for about 5 years. I didn’t start making enough money to live as an athlete until this year—2022. Originally, I thought that money didn’t exist in Jiu-Jitsu. Jiu-Jitsu, as I understood it, was an amateur sport. Then, I realized something. I didn’t realize it on my own, either. I realized it because of a friend who was a few steps above me in his career. He had a much more professional approach than I did. Jiu-Jitsu was an amateur sport for me because I was competing in amateur events. I wasn’t getting paid because I was taking every opportunity to compete possible. I didn’t really care if there was money on the line, a gold medal, or just some social clout. I loved Jiu-Jitsu, so I just fought because I loved it. I wasn’t a professional though. Looking back, this approach had some great benefits (I got a lot of experience, became good at competing, and became good at handling competition nerves), but it also had some drawbacks too. I got injured a lot, didn’t make money most of the time, and I spent a lot of my own money and time traveling to events, training myself, and working weird jobs to pay for competitions and travel. What a lot of people don’t realize is that most of the medal pictures I post on here won me zero dollars. I used medals as a way of building my teaching pedigree, but I didn’t get paid directly from competition until earlier this year. The only thing that changed was my mindset. I stopped viewing myself as “a grinder” and started viewing myself as a racehorse. I started viewing myself as a prizefighter. If that sounds pretentious to you, don’t worry. I didn’t like it at first either. In sports, it’s not smarter to fight every weekend. UFC fighters fight 3–4 times per year, and that’s a very active year. Jiu-Jitsu is less taxing than MMA, so I figured I could compete every couple of weeks without a problem. I had a meeting with a strength coach, and when I told him about my competition schedule, he basically laughed at me for thinking it was possible to be at my best every weekend without consequences. He told me about a bodybuilder who was hustling like a lunatic, trying to maintain peak performance every weekend, and using small shows (where he was paid $500 or less) to make his living. After about 6 months, he died. So what’s the point? The point is that you can’t nickel and dime your way to big success. You need to take stepping stones, but if you never take big shots, you’ll never get the big wins. I ain’t rich, but I’m also not fighting for free anymore. I make several times what I did last year and I’m doing the same things. The best way to make money is to know your worth and not accept anything less that what you are worth. If you can do this, you will get ahead of most people. Oh, but there’s a caveat. If you think you’re worth $1000 per hour, you better work like someone who’s worth $1000 an hour. You better deliver at least $1000 per hour worth of benefit to your customers. Skill pays. If you want to make money, do whatever it is you do really fucking well.

Question: How important is routine in life?
Answer: It’s not as important as people think. I’m a pro athlete who writes 3000 words every single day, and yet my routine is complete garbage. According to what most productivity experts say, I shouldn’t be able to get anything done. My morning routine is all over the place. Most mornings, I start writing articles that I haven’t planned at all. I don’t use any productivity apps. I procrastinate on difficult tasks sometimes. Yet still, my writing output is more than most writers online. I still train more Jiu-Jitsu than most pro-Jiu-Jitsu athletes. I do more on a daily basis than most people in both fields that I operate in, yet I lack the infrastructure that many insist is a requirement for a productive lifestyle. So what’s the deal? My approach to staying productive is a bit unorthodox, but as someone who’s had ADHD their entire life [ https://chriswojcik.medium.com/5-things-i-want-you-to-know-about-adhd-434f9cfc7306 ], I think that it has to be that way. This is about how I stay productive, despite many days feeling like a chicken with its head cut off.  Lesson 1: Before I work, I warm up. Some of my best writing sessions come from waking up early, making a pot of coffee, sitting at the keyboard, and starting off my morning with a brief journaling session. In anything you do, you have to warm up. It’s silly to expect your best work to just pour out of you first thing in the morning. After my journal session, once I start feeling warmed up, I’ll write an article — 1000–1500 words. Sometimes, I’ve planned this article the night before. Other times, I wing it. Either way, I get the article done. That’s the key. This writing routine is great, but there’s also a big problem: For me, almost every day is different. I can’t follow the same morning routine every day, because my lifestyle doesn’t allow me to do the same things every day. As someone with ADHD, my variety in routine is awesome and keeps me engaged and inspired in my life, but you won’t see a deviation in routine prescribed in most productivity advice articles. Some days, I have to train at 7 am, so I can’t wake up and write. Other days, I have to be at the gym by 8 am to teach a private lesson. Occasionally, I’m out late teaching, so getting up early isn’t exactly the most appealing idea for me. That’s why my routine isn’t strict. Instead of following a strict routine, I have extracted the micro-routine that I need to have good writing sessions. That micro-routine is warming up and finding a flow state. I can do this at any time of day. When I’m training Jiu-Jitsu, I always warm up. Why would writing be any different? My best writing sessions don't come from cutesie-tootsie routines where I meditate and read Meditations and make tea and journal long-hand. My best writing sessions come from warming up before diving in. It’s that simple.  Lesson 2: Solitude is your friend. Currently, I live alone. This is nice. However, I started my productivity routine when I was still living with my family, and I’ve maintained it as I have had partners come and go. I’ve had to find ways to get my alone time. I force alone time into my life. It’s a priority for me. It helps me recharge. I’m a more introverted person than not, which means that if I don’t get my alone time every once in a while, I become tired, burned out, and socially exhausted. This doesn’t mean that I don’t like people. I love them. I see people every day. All it means is that it’s really nice for me to have a few hours every few days of solitude.
