Question: What advice would you give to your 18-year-old self?
Answer: If I could go back in time, I force my 18-year-old self to do these 18 things to change the direction of his life. 1. Delete all your social media — for at least 6 months. Social media isn’t great for anyone, but for young people, social media is like poison. If I had taken a significant break from social media during my early 20s, it would have made me happier and less anxious, but most importantly, it would have made me much more grounded in the world that I was slowly learning about. Given that I later experienced dissociation due to severe anxiety, this would have been nice. 2. Go to therapy. Men especially don’t talk enough about mental health. The best way to get over that hump is to go to therapy and force yourself into a situation where all there is to talk about is mental health. 3. Start a side hustle — just one. When I was in college and trying to make it as a professional martial artist, I was obsessed with trying to find ways to monetize activities in my life. I tried everything from blogging to flipping my old martial arts gear to teaching private lessons to ghostwriting riflescope reviews. None of them were successful, in part because I wasn’t serious about any of them. Pick one side hustle and do it well. 4. Start getting comfortable with social rejection. After my first breakup, I was so scared to date that I didn’t ask anyone out for 3 years. I was too scared. This 3 year period did a lot more damage to my social life than that breakup ever could have. Learning to accept and bounce back from social rejection will give you the ability to navigate all of the most beautiful aspects of the human experience. 5. Learn how to eat properly. Wrestling definitely gave me a strange relationship with food. “Eating disorder” isn’t the right word, but from the time I was 14-20, I weighed myself 5–10 times per day. I was obsessed with monitoring my weight, and this obsession had a negative effect on both my physical and mental health. This is why now, my physical is very important to me. 6. Prioritize your sleep. The dumbest things I did in college weren’t going to some party or skipping classes or almost dropping out after every semester. I did those things, but they didn’t really impact my life that much. The dumbest thing that I did in college that actually impacted me was that I developed a habit of trying to sleep 6 hours per night while also trying to maintain peak performance. When you’re 18, you can away with things. When you’re in your early 20s, you think you can get away with the things you got away with at 18. Quicker than you think, not sleeping catches up to you. At 25, 7–9 hours of sleep every night is essential for me. 7. Commit to reading 25 books per year. I’m a slow reader. I’ll never be someone who reads a book a week. However, a few years ago (2020), I made a commitment to read at least 25 books every single year. 2 years later, I’m still going strong. If I had started this habit at 18, I’d have read at least 175 books by now. Habits compound. 8. Start writing online. Writing is the single most positive ROI habit that I’ve ever adopted. Writing has given me a job, an audience, and peace of mind. At 18, I had an urge to tell stories, but I thought I didn’t have the “life experience” to tell stories worth reading. This belief was self-fulfilling. I don’t care how old you are. Start writing if you want to. 9. Test your limits. I was always more scared of what I couldn't do than what I could do. I had this fear that if I tried to live up to my potential, I would fall short of the goals I had in my imagination. I thought failure would break me down before I even got going. I was naïve. The goals you have are less important than you think. What is important is the self-knowledge you acquire through the pursuit of those goals. Finding the limitations of your abilities will both humble you and inspire you. 10. Plan a trip to somewhere cool. Go on it. I wanted to travel ever since I was a kid. I thought traveling would make life feel complete. In particular, I wanted to see Europe, Asia, and Australia. I didn’t see any of them until this year when I went to Europe. The trip was fun, but at the end of the day, my trip didn't make me a happy person. I wish I had traveled sooner so that I could have gotten it out of my system and focused on long-term goals. 11. Identify your priorities. I was very passive when I was 18. All I really wanted was to get through life without causing trouble or getting yelled at. I hate getting yelled at. Because of this, I ended up putting up with a lot of crap that I didn’t need to. By actively identifying your priorities and sticking to them, you filter out a lot of bullshit in your life. 12. Stop questioning everything and start questioning yourself. I thought I was smart because I questioned everything around me. I realized pretty early on that everyone was just a person and no one really knew what they were doing, so I questioned their behavior. I didn’t trust people. I could have saved myself a lot of time if I started to really question myself with the same intensity. 13. Stop treating sex like a competition. At 18, I thought that having sex with someone was the peak of the male experience. Getting laid was one of my ultimate goals as a young man. I thought that sex would make me happy just like how social media and the society around me told me it would. The result of this mindset was mostly empty and lame sex. Sex is a valuable part of the human experience, but it isn’t everything. Don’t chase sex like a gold medal. You will be bored. 14. Learn to trust your gut. I went against gut feelings for years because of my anxiety and insecurity. I stayed in bad relationships because I thought that I couldn’t do any better. I knew the relationship was bad, but I thought that maybe I was wrong. Every time without fail, my gut was right and I just didn’t trust it. Have the confidence to trust gut feelings. 15. Get rid of your loser friends. I was kind of a loser, so I hung around people who were also losers. I wasn’t friends with drug addicts and criminals (besides a weird stretch when I was about 21— we’ll talk about that some other time), but I was friends with people who didn’t have very high expectations for themselves. I didn’t really like myself, so I surrounded myself with people that I didn’t like. Don’t do that. Surround yourself with people who add value to your life. Everyone else is a waste of space. 16. Stop waiting for permission. For years, I waited for someone to give me permission to try and do Jiu-Jitsu at the highest levels and to let me try to write. I thought that one day someone would come and say “you’re pretty good at this, you are now allowed to give it your all”. That day never came. I had to make that day for myself. 17. Learn how to rest. I’ve always been hyperactive, so I never actually learned how to rest until my body started to physically break down from martial arts competition. I wish I had learned how to rest sooner. This would have increased my productivity at work, made me better at school, and made me a better and less injured Jiu-Jitsu athlete. 18. You have value. Start giving back now. I used to think that because I was “a kid”, I had no value. I thought that I couldn’t have value until I “did something”. I guess that’s why I spent years traveling all over the country chasing plastic medals for external validation. While I don’t have regrets about my years spent competing all over the place, I didn’t need to do that to have value or knowledge to give to people. If you have the desire to give back, you have the obligation to. Not helping others by sharing what you know is spiritual suicide. For me, 18 was the first year of my life that I really felt that the world was expecting anything from me. I felt a lot of pressure, and unfortunately, in a lot of ways, I feel I crumbled under that pressure. I made horrible social decisions. I made stupid career decisions. I made a lot of mistakes. People see wins in Jiu-Jitsu or views on articles as metrics of success, but I don’t think these metrics tell the whole story. If I had done the 18 things I listed above sooner, I wouldn’t just be making more money or winning more Jiu-Jitsu tournaments. I’d have become happier sooner. That to me is the most important metric of progress.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What can I do to reduce anxiety?
Answer: Anxiety sucks. Here are 5 things I do to make my anxiety suck less. I seek failure. Physical limits are very real, but you really shouldn’t be afraid of them. The fear of failure causes a lot of people a great deal of anxiety. People are scared to lose matches in sports, they’re scared to perform badly at their job, they’re scared to not make enough money, or they’re scared to get rejected by a pretty girl. Failure is everywhere, and on a micro-scale, failure is akin to dying. I used to joke that failure was “dying-lite”. But at the same time, failing makes you realize something very important: Failure makes you realize that failure isn’t so bad. After a while, you’ll realize that in real life, it’s not scary to lose, get rejected, or fail. You recover from pretty much every failure — even the really bad ones. What’s really scary is living in the constant agony that comes when you don’t try to confront your anxiety. Failure is worse in your head than in real life. Seeking failure in endeavors like exercise, dating, or business helps you realize this. I don’t freak out when I break my discipline. I’m not a Navy SEAL. I’m never going to sit here and tell you that in order to succeed you need “unmitigated daily discipline in all things”. I can’t tell you that because I don’t have unmitigated daily discipline myself. Yesterday, for example, I forgot to meditate. The day before, I forgot to read. Saturday last weekend I didn’t write a single damn word. If you saw how much cake I ate on my birthday, you’d probably look at me like I’m insane. However, when it comes to having a good routine, I never give up and I don’t beat myself up for forgetting to do something. Every time I get knocked off the wagon when it comes to reading, meditating, or journaling, I get right back on as soon as I can. While my discipline isn’t perfect, I never stop trying to do the things that are hard for me. I don’t want to wake up early and train and then write all day and teach all night while also squeezing in time to read, study Jiu-Jitsu, and take care of my mind, but I do it anyway. It’s not about never stopping, it’s about never quitting. I’ve found that not doing the hard things is worse than doing them. I’ve also found that beating yourself up for not doing things doesn’t make you want to do them anymore. I don’t care about being the best anymore. I’m a little scared to write this one. In competitive sports, being the best is supposed to be your obsession. You’re supposed to hate losing more than dying and you’re supposed to never accept failure from yourself. You’re supposed to do these things, but I’ll tell you this — that’s an exhausting way to live. Instead of obsessing over who the best is (which is hard because typically “the best” changes depending on a lot of factors), I’m a lot more interested in being the best that I can be. That might sound corny, but this is much more pleasant and actually makes me better in the long run. I have limits. Every time I get a comment from a hater that I should “kill myself” or feel something in my joints snap or pop in a way it’s not supposed to, I’m reminded that I’m not Superman and I can’t do everything. It’s humbling, but my limits are definitely real. Instead of constantly comparing myself to everyone around me, I’m more interested in pushing my own physical and mental limitations for me. In order to have longevity, I’ve needed to drop the constant need for validation to focus on long-term goals. I do something mindful every day. Writing is my job, so a lot of times writing doesn’t make me more mindful. Jiu-Jitsu is also my job, so a lot of times Jiu-Jitsu or working out doesn’t make me more mindful. Having a job that you love is great, but you have to realize that no matter what you do for a living, you need stress relief. You need breaks — probably more than you’re taking. That’s why I take time to do mindfulness every day. I’m not religious about it, but it’s a habit. The problem is, sometimes I get stuck working at the gym for 5 hours in the evening or I get caught up training all day long, and I just don’t have time to sit down, pull out my little cushion, and meditate. If you work a 16-hour day, you’ll understand what I mean. That’s why sometimes, I get my mindfulness through walking. Other times, I get it through driving in silence. If I have time, I like to do the whole “cushion and guided meditation thing”, but what I do isn’t really the point. The point is, every single day, 7 days a week, I take at least a few minutes to be mindful of the world around me and where I am in it. This is the best habit I’ve ever developed for getting out of my head. I call myself out on my BS. From late February to early May of this year, I was constantly dieting and obsessing over my weight for Jiu-Jitsu competitions. I hated it. I hated monitoring my water intake, I hated counting all my calories, and I hated waking up in the middle of the night with a stomach ache from hunger pains. After my last competition where I had to be at my low competition weight, I let myself go a little bit more than normal. I stopped giving a damn about what I ate, how much I ate, and how much salt was on my food. My Yin was extreme rigidity and a religious diet of chicken and broccoli, so my Yang was chocolate chip cookies every night. And? I got kind of chunky. I gained about 8 pounds, give or take, and almost none of it was “good weight”. It was “happy weight”, but definitely not good weight. While there’s nothing wrong with a little “fat and sassy season” (as my mom calls it), I’ve sort of realized over the last few weeks that I am not at my best in terms of being a lean, mean, fighting machine. I don’t feel like I’m as fit as I’ve been earlier this year. For my big competitions this fall, I’m going to really dial in on my nutrition and improve my habits. I’m even working with a nutrition coach for the first time in my career because I know that dieting and weight cutting have always been a challenge for me. This is just one example of how I try to “call myself out on my BS” in my life. Doing this makes me a lot less anxious about anything I am struggling with. I feel like every answer article is the same. Journal. Meditate. See a therapist. Do this. Do that. I get it. At this point, I’ve tried all of it. At this point, I’m kind of tired of the typical anxiety treatments that people describe because I feel like they are devoid of any real insight or value. That’s why for this article, I wanted to focus on concepts instead of habits. You can call yourself out on your BS in a journal, in therapy, or on social media. You can forgive yourself in any area of your life. You can escape competition through authenticity in everything you do. These are concepts, not behaviors. We all have different lives and different habits, but the fundamental concepts that will help you get past anxiety are very similar for all of us. These are the 5 concepts that have worked for me.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can we always stay focused and motivated towards our goals?
Answer: This morning, I hit 10 million views on Quora. My first 89 answers on here were viewed a total of 6000 times (about 67 views per answer). I’m kind of competitive, so this was a bit humbling. I felt like I was shouting into the void on the internet and no matter what I said, no one would hear me. I used to feel jealous of the other writers who were getting hundreds of thousands of views per answer, while I was posting every single day to only an audience of one follower. My first follower was my friend Ramses, who doesn’t really use Quora. He just made an account and followed me to be a supportive friend. It was a nice gesture, but only having one follower who doesn’t even use the site doesn’t really help you in the algorithm 😂 Eventually, people started to read my answers. I guess now I can say I have a nice little audience. I appreciate everyone who reads my stuff. However, as the views started to tally up on Quora, I started to realize that for the most part, views, followers, and all those other stats that people use for clout in the digital world aren’t really anything except vanity metrics. I wish I didn’t have to get it myself to realize that, but I did. I never was popular in school and I never had a lot of followers on any other site, so I felt really cool when I hit 1k on Medium last summer and when I hit a million views on Quora last fall. I felt cool, but the cool feeling wore off after a few hours. Then, I was chasing the next vanity metric. In the early days, I was very motivated by these external metrics. Interestingly enough, the same is true in Jiu-Jitsu. When I started training, all I really wanted to do was fight and win medals. However, once you start to taste “success”, you realize that most success tastes the same. I’ve won a world championship in martial arts. I’ve competed in Jiu-Jitsu at the highest levels. I’ve written things that have gotten several million views. None of that shit really matters. Most of it is just to satisfy your ego. When I started writing on Quora, I was making like $1500 per month doing copywriting for like 10 different clients. Now, I get paid more to work on more interesting projects, I get more money from my blog, and I get more recognition in Jiu-Jitsu for the years of hard training I’ve done. But that doesn’t make me happier. What makes me happier is the fact that I have less anxiety. I have less anxiety because I’ve done a lot of work to work on my anxiety. I’ve worked hard on happiness the same way that I work at success. This question asks about focus and motivation, but I think that the key to staying focused is to forget motivation. Motivation is external. It comes and goes. Focus can stay. You can be focused on something even when you aren’t motivated to do it. Focus is what makes you keep writing even when you’re getting 11 views on your articles. Focus is what gets you in the gym when no one else is there. For me, my focus comes from passion for the craft, not motivation for the results. If you don’t me believe that’s fine. We’ll see who’s still trying to do this a decade from now.

Question: What are the best tactics if you get in a fight?
Answer: If you get in a fight, the first thing you should do is run away. You don’t know how much the other person knows, if they’re armed, or if they are a crazy person who wants to cause serious damage to your body. The second thing you should do, if you can’t run away, is to try to de-escalate the situation. Words are the first defensive weapon everyone should use. If you disagree, you’ve probably never been in a real fight. The third thing you should do, if the fight turns physical, is to use the self-defense lessons that you’ve learned from training in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, Krav Maga, Muay Thai, Jeet Kune Do, or Boxing to control your opponent and restrain them without hurting both of you. Maybe carry a pocket knife or a gun or something if you’re really worried about weapons. What’s that? You’ve never trained martial arts before? Then don’t get in a fight. It won’t end well. If someone wanted to know the best way to write a song on their guitar that would help them serenade their lover, I wouldn’t say “read shit from people on Quora and give it a try”. I’d say take a guitar lesson and practice a lot. Similarly, if you want to know the best way to defend yourself in a fight (you know, like an actual dangerous situation), I wouldn’t say to read Quora answers from keyboard warriors. I’d say to go to a gym and learn from someone who thinks about fighting all day long. Just an idea! 😂

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I get over my anxiety of going to the gym alone?
Answer: I used to be so anxious to go to the gym alone that if I couldn’t find “a gym buddy” I just wouldn’t work out that day. Now, I usually prefer to go to the gym alone. I like going to the gym alone because I like having the time to think. A lot of people like to blast music while they work out, but I don’t. I usually will workout with just whatever’s playing in the background. I have big cauliflower ears so I can’t actually fit ear buds in my head, and most headphones fall off while I’m lifting or using a machine. I’m at the gym to workout, not to listen to the same Drake song on repeat 367 times. I take my time at the gym to just be mindful and to focus on my exercises. If I do end up going to the gym with a friend, I’ll talk to them inbetween exercises. That’s a nice benefit of a gym buddy. Another thing I like about having a gym buddy also is having access to a spotter if I need one. If you ever decide to go for max effort lifts in the gym, you’re going to want at least one spotter. However, when I’m in the gym by myself, working out feels like more of a mental exercise for building self-control and staying focused. I like this. Here’s the step by step process that I used to get over my anxiety of going to the gym alone: “Going to the gym alone” anxiety is similar to any other form of social anxiety. The way that you attack this anxiety is not by reading Quora answers like mine on how to get past anxiety. The best way to confront any form of social anxiety is through exposure to the thing that scares you. If your anxiety is very severe, you might have to work your way up to working out at the gym alone by first walking to the gym alone, then going in the door fo the gym alone, then walking in the gym alone, and finally exercising in the gym alone. If you feels that you, then take it in steps. However, most of us allow our anxiety to talk up our fears. Once you get going, you’ll probably realize that you aren’t as afraid of working out in public as you thought. Plus, once the endorphines kick in, you’re on a fast track to a temporary bliss of zero anxiety. It’s almost like your brain was designed to do physical activities, even if other people are around. When you get that sensation, enjoy it. Exercise can change your life.

Question: Do you consider yourself a optimist or a pessimist?
Answer: Growing up, my dad used to go on these ridiculous rants at the dinner table about how the world was a horrible place. Usually, it was toward the end of the meal, when he was half drunk, half joking, and making a deliberate effort to piss everyone off. I wish I could say that I just laughed at these rants, but the problem was that his pessimistic rants usually brought up some good points. I always thought about them longer than I probably should have. We were all going to die. The world was (and is) kind of messed up. People everywhere do treat each other like garbage, every single day. It’s tough to argue with logic. Despite those lovely articles from HumanProgress.org [ https://www.humanprogress.org/ ], there are some real problems in the world today. It’s naive to not acknowledge this. Humans might reach immortality someday [ https://www.livescience.com/could-humans-be-immortal ], but there might not be a planet for those immortal humans to even live on. Without oxygen, no one’s immortal. So how can we be rationally optimistic in a world that’s completely falling apart? I’ve come up with a system to outreason my own pessimistic tendencies.  I’ve thought about death a lot. When I tell older people about how I’ve thought about death a lot, they usually just laugh at me and say something like “you’re only 25, you don’t have to worry about that yet”. Except, when you’re living in a world like the one we have today, it’s kind of hard to not think about your death at all. Everything is kind of fucked. The anxieties and fears that we have about the world, the people around us, and our social insecurities are extremely valid. When you look at the modern world objectively, it’s strange that there are people who walk around every day not feeling anxious. Most of our communication happens through screens in our pockets. The planet is heating up [ https://www.amnesty.org/en/what-we-do/climate-change/#:~:text=The%20effects%20of%20climate%20change%20are%20already%20being%20felt%20now,climate%20change%20can%20be%20exhaustive. ]. We’re working our way through one pandemic while another might be just getting started. In my state, Illinois, they just declared a state of emergency for monkeypox [ https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/monkeypox-has-been-declared-a-public-health-emergency-in-illinois-heres-what-that-means-for-residents/2904052/ ]. I had Covid 3 weeks ago. This is getting out of control, and it kind of freaks me out. So, forgive me for being so audacious, but the world that I’m living in has me thinking about the end sometimes. That’s why I’ve had to become an optimist.  At first, thinking about death was too much. When I was about 9 years old, I figured out that I was going to die one day. My dad had made some comment about how everyone dies eventually, and I just kept thinking about it. I’ve always been an overthinker. This freaked me out, but it didn’t make me cry. What did make me cry was the fact that my parents were going to die too — probably before I did. The fact that my baby sister won’t even live forever sent me over the edge. Death is overwhelming. That’s why we don’t think about it or talk about it very much. However, I believe that the fact that we don’t think about death is the reason that we’re so pessimistic as a culture. People don’t realize how fleeting their lives are because they spend so much time wr...

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I cope with being ghosted?
Answer: Ghosting is the most annoying part of dating. (^ my face, after getting ghosted) Especially if you’re an anxious person, being ghosted probably leaves you with more questions than answers. The thing is, to the ghoster, it doesn’t feel like that. Someone who ghosts you doesn’t think they’re “being indirect” or “being rude”, they probably just think you should “take the hint”. I hate admitting this, but I ghosted people quite a bit in my early 20s. It was just easier than having an honest conversation about how I didn’t see a future with them. At the time, I thought that this was a necessary evil of dating. Then, I found myself on the opposite side of the ghosting equation—multiple times. Ouch. I probably deserved it, I guess. For a long time, getting ghosted made me really insecure. I hated going on dates with people because I knew that at any moment, they could just be gone from my life without explanation. When you’re anxious or predisposed to anxiety, being ghosted hurts a lot. The thing is, ghosting is kind of traumatic. I’m sure I’ll get some comment from some angry dude on this about how I should just “grow up” after being ghosted, but I don’t really think that’s how it works. Getting ghosted sucks because it’s usually unexpected. I got ghosted recently by someone who I’d been talking to every day for nearly 3 weeks. We talked about everything under the sun. We talked about life, sex, memes, food, jokes, and everything else you can think of. I thought it was going well, but I guess I was wrong. That’s the problem with digital communication. We made plans to go for pizza, I texted her to confirm the time and meeting place, and never heard from her again. Such is life. The way I learned to deal with ghosting was by learning to accept that there’s nothing wrong with getting rejected, but there is something wrong with ghosting. I don’t ghost people because I know what it’s like to ghost and be ghosted, and I wouldn’t be able to look at myself if I acted like that anymore. Ghosting is childish and disrespectful, and to be frank, it hurts people’s feelings. I can’t get too mad at ghosters because I’ve been one myself, but I really try to not do that anymore because it just adds negativity to a world that already has plenty of it. I understand rejection—not everyone is everyone's match—but that doesn’t mean it’s okay to just ghost someone who might really like talking to you. People don’t ghost you because they don’t like you. I’ve dated plenty of people as an adult and decided I didn't like them. I didn’t ghost them. I just told them it wasn’t a good match for me. Ghosting is done as an attempt to control a relationship. Ghosting gives you power in a kind of fucked up way. I stopped letting ghosting bother me when I stopped looking to control people in my relationships. Plus, one great sign of mental strength is to continue to pursue romantic relationships, despite the possibility that you might get ghosted.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the saddest truth about life?
Answer: The saddest truth about life is that most people are living it on autopilot. Today, you’re reading this answer from some know-it-all white kid on Quora. “This guy is an idiot!” you think, and keep scrolling. A week from now, you’ll be going through your life, and maybe not much has changed. Then, maybe a month from now, your girlfriend leaves you for another man. Ouch. She’d be cheating on you for months. Double ouch. A year after that, you meet someone new and you decide to get married. A few years after that, you have a kid. This changes everything. It usually does. A few weeks after you have a kid, you realize that having a kid is stressful. Kids are a lot of work. You need to take yourself more seriously. You work. You really fucking hard. You build a successful business. You start to make some money. You make some investments. You get a house. You get yourself a better car—a better one than your neighbors at least. Your kid starts to grow. 10 years of driving him to soccer practice later, next thing you know, he’s going off to college. You worked your ass off to make sure he could go to college, and he’ll never know how much time you put into building him a nice life. You can’t think about this though, because you have to make sure he gets through college. You have to make sure your family is okay. A few years after that, you turn 65. Your back pain is really bad now. A few more years pass and you’re 80. Damn dude, you’re old. You and your partner play golf or whatever it is you want to do to pass the time. You go to the grocery store together. You attempt to rediscover the love you had that was destroyed through the tumultuous experience of raising children. Maybe you do. Maybe you don’t and you become bitter. Then your partner gets sick. They die. Then you die. And… that’s your life. How many minutes of that life were mindful? Very few. Just about everything that happened in this fictional life I just created happened on autopilot. The sad thing is that the fictional life isn’t too different from many people’s actual lives. In the picture above, I’m doing what most people spend their whole lives doing. I’m partially working on my phone and checking emails, partially scrolling Instagram, and slamming another coffee to fuel my ambition and to help me get through the day. I’m not being mindful. I’m barely paying attention to my sister who’s taking the picture. That was sort of the point (this picture may have been staged 😬). Don’t be like me in the picture. Be present in as many moments as you can. It’s hard to be entirely present all the time, but making an effort to be more present can make a real difference for you. You don’t want to live your life by just going from activity to activity, checking boxes, and making progress. Having a great job, making money, and raising kids can be rewarding, but if you don’t take the time to be mindful, you’ll miss all of the parts of these experiences that make life beautiful. The saddest truth of life is that most people live their entire lives and never even start to think about why they’re doing the things they’re doing. Most people are living lives they were told to live, not lives they’re interested in living. That’s heartbreaking. Thoughtlessness in our lives destroys the world. Many people have kids because society told them to have kids. This leads to unhappy kids and parents. People chase money over happiness because society told them to. Indirectly, leads to capitalism killing the planet. Most people let external factors dictate the course of their life. To me, that is the saddest truth of life. “Many young men die at age 25, but are not buried until they're 75.” — Benjamin Franklin

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: If someone doesn't reply to my comment on their answers, does that mean they think that the comment isn't worth their time?
Answer: I think I should answer this one, because I’ve been thinking about it a bit lately. I’m not the most popular writer on Quora by any means, but recently I’ve started to reach the point where I’m getting too many comments and it’s overwhelming to keep track of all of them. I feel bad when I get nice comments that I don’t pop up in my notifications or get hidden in the collapsed section. I also get some crazy comments where people just basically insult me to make themselves feel better, so I try to avoid going through the comments section—unless I’m bored. Usually, however, I’m a busy guy. Here’s my day to day: I’m busy. Most days for me are 12–16 hour days from the time I wake up till the time I go to bed. I only go through my comments when I have some time, often on the weekend or on the occasion that I get an easier day. I’ve got some readers on here who have been replying to my answers since the beginning. I recognize their profiles by now and will reply sometimes when I see their answers. If I upvote your comment that means I saw it and I appreciate you. I occasionally will respond to a crappy comment with the same level of maturity as the commenter. Usually, I’ll just ignore the comment because no one’s ever changed anyone’s mind through a war in the comments section. I have nothing but love for everyone who reads my answers and I love all of you guys who write comments on my stuff. The support is really motivating and it keeps me going on here. ❤️

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I stay motivated in life when it's all going to be gone eventually anyway?
Answer: On paper, optimism doesn’t really make sense. Why would you ever be happy when every single thing you know and love about life is going to die one day? All your friends and family will die. You will die. Sooner or later, the world is going to end. Why should you do anything? What’s the fucking point? These were the questions I used to ask myself every day when I was severly depressed. I don’t feel that way anymore, and part of it is because I’ve thought a lot about death. I’m not scared to die anymore. Not in a stupid, crazy sense (I still look both ways before I cross the street and I still wear my seatbelt), but more so in the sense that I’m not really scared of rejection and failure anymore. I’m not afraid of killing my ego. I spent so much time holding myself back and allowing my anxiety to dictate the flow of my life. I wasted years in fear. From the age of 10–22, pretty much everything that I did was something that someone else told me to do. I never really thought for myself. When I did think for myself, I didn’t act on my desires because I assumed that I couldn’t actually achieve anything. The photo in this for this answer is from the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington DC. I was there in March this year. I didn’t take the picture (because taking a picture there just didn’t feel right), but I found the memorial to be very moving. I was staying with friends, and we spent pretty much all of our time joking around and laughing except for the few minutes that we walked through the monument. Those moments and the moments after were silent. I don’t use the memorial as examples because I’m some crazy patriotic dude who wants to celebrate his country. I’m not super proud of my country’s history. However, what the memorial does is individualize all of the people who died during the wars. Every name on the memorial was a person with a family and hopes and dreams. Many of the people who fought in the war didn’t know what they were getting into. Seeing all of these names makes me remember that my life isn’t really just about me. It’s a momentary detachment from the individualistic nature of American culture. It’s temporary detachement from my ego. It helps me realize that I’m not the center of the world. Detaching from your ego makes life a lot nicer. I’m not accusing anyone of being arrogant, either. The ego isn’t just walking into a bar and thinking you can beat the heck out of anyone who looks at your girl the wrong way. The ego is the thing that clings to your identity. The ego is the little voice in your head that says “I’m a manly man, see!” or “I’m super smart and self-aware, it’s crazy how smart I am”. The stronger your sense of identity, the more fleeting everything around you becomes. When you detach from this, you start to look at the fact that everything around you going to go away one day a little different. You start seeing the fleeting nature of reality as not a stressor, but a stress relief. I’m going to die one day, so I might as well make the most out of my time before they put me in the ground. I might as well love people with my all my heart. I might as well take every shot at being the best version of myself that I can be. If everything is going to end one day, I can either make my life as great as possible, or I can sit around and be miserable. The solution to existential depression isn’t antidepressants. The solution to existential depression is getting yourself moving, connecting, and feeling. Go get your heartbroken. Go write a book. Go take your first martial arts class. Whatever scares you, give it a try. Fuck it. We’re all gonna die anyway.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How long would it take to become a black belt in Brazilian jiu-jitsu?
Answer: I got my black belt in 7 years. Here’s me, on the day I got my black belt: I trained nearly every day to get my black belt for almost exactly 7 years. I think I got my black belt about a week or so after my 7 anniversary of training. I had a few breaks because of injuries, but for the most part, I trained through and around my injuries. The longest I’ve gone without training since I started in 2015 was about 3 weeks, after I had meniscus surgery in 2018. I was training and competing about as close to full-time as it can get, and I got my black belt in 7 years. The average hobbyist will get their black belt in about 8–10 years, if they stay consistent. There are stories about guys like former UFC champion BJ Penn, who got his black belt in just 3 years. You don’t see these stories much anymore because in the 2010s that set in place time limit requirements for each belt. In 2022, the fastest you can get your black belt in BJJ while following these requirements is 4.5 years (2 years at blue, 1.5 at purple, 1 at brown), but that assumes that you spent zero days as a white belt. I spent 13 months as a white belt, 2 years as a blue belt, 2 years and 3 months as a purple belt, and 1 year and 8 months as a brown belt. I don’t usually plug products, but I’ll leave this link here because this product is free. Here’s a short ebook I wrote a year ago on ways that you can learn Jiu-Jitsu faster. They helped me go from complete beginner to world champ in just 4 years.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How much can your life change in just one year?
Answer: You can’t change everything, but you can change your life quite a bit in one year. (Long post alert)**** For example, around this time last year, I was losing my damn mind. Here’s a random picture from last fall. I don’t know what I’m doing. You can’t tell how anxious and tired I was by the photo, but I was miserable. I was freelance copywriting for 11 different clients for a little more than minimum wage, writing 4–6 articles on Medium every week, working on my first ebook, teaching Jiu-Jitsu for 3–4 hours a day, and training myself 1–3 times per day. It was crazy. I was running from something, and at the time, I didn't know what. Looking back, I don’t know how I kept up this workload for months on end. Looking back, I’m not surprised that around 6 weeks after this time last year, I herniated a disc in my back, aggravated a disc in my neck, and popped my rib — all in a 4-day span. I learned a valuable lesson from that period of my life about pushing limits, achieving goals, and working hard. I learned that I had to change my lifestyle, and I didn’t have much time to do it. I was only 24 at the time, but the pain in my joints and the dullness in my mind made me feel older. I was on a crash course to burnout and quitting everything I loved. These are the 10 ways that I changed my life in the last year: 1. I specialized. When my body broke down on me and I finally had some time to think, I realized that the biggest mistake I was making was that I was trying to do everything at a very high level. I was trying to write fiction, nonfiction, ebooks, and copy for clients. I was competing in Jiu-Jitsu in gi and no-gi. I was even trying to deadlift 400 pounds during my strength and conditioning workouts. I did everything to an extreme. I had too many goals. I thought I was superhuman, and the world showed me that I wasn’t. Once I killed some of my dreams, this made space to bring the most important goals in my life to fruition. 2. I wrote on the internet every single day. A lot of writers write about how writing online every day can “change your life”. A year ago, I thought this was a cliche, but now, I’ve realized that there is truth to this — writing online can change your life. In the last year, I’ve published on either Medium, Quora, Substack, or Twitter basically every single day, and the audience that I’ve built from this daily writing led me to eventually quit all my freelance copywriting jobs. It also gave me access to a whole new world of people who I’d never otherwise get to interact with. It made me happier and it made me more money. 3. I got some thicker skin. Getting yelled at by crazy people on Quora every single day has made me nearly immune to crazy shit that people say to me both online and in real life. It’s hard to be phased by someone making a snarky remark when you just got accused of killing someone’s dog on Quora or got called an idiot by some tech bro on Medium. Getting thicker skin has made my normally sensitive soul much calmer in the erratic world I inhabit. 4. I learned better ways to improve my skills. Maybe you have no interest in fighting people or doing Jiu-Jitsu ever. That’s okay. Nonetheless, everyone can benefit from optimizing the ways that they try to improve in the different areas of their life. For me, learning how to structure my Jiu-Jitsu training for specific competitions and injury avoidance has changed the way that I approach all work that I do. In the last year, I’ve learned how to write better while writing less, get stronger while lifting less volume, and how to improve my Jiu-Jitsu skills without destroying my body (at least, not as much). 5. I failed at one of my biggest goals. I’ve had a lot of failures this year, but my biggest failure was probably my trip to Europe in May. I had a bad weight cut and a mediocre tournament performance. In the end, I fell short of my goal of qualifying for the ADCC World Championships. Instead of competing in the biggest tournament in Jiu-Jitsu history Las Vegas in September, I’ll be watching it on TV at home. Ouch. That failure hurt a lot. My entire Europe trip cost me around $3000, and it didn’t make me any happier or more successful. However, this failure did make me a lot more comfortable with throwing some money down and taking shots at big goals. It made me comfortable with having skin in the game. It made me realize that big failures really aren’t that bad. 6. I bet on myself. Quitting my freelance clients to “write online and do Jiu-Jitsu” was the scariest thing I ever did. Over the course of just a few days, I lost several thousands of dollars in monthly income, and there was no guarantee that it was going to be replaced. A couple of days after I announced my “hiatus” from freelance copywriting, I took 4th place in the biggest grappling tournament in North America. This led to seminar and competition opportunities that I’d never previously had. A few weeks after that, I beat a super high-level black belt who outweighed me by 20 pounds to win a $5000 cash prize tournament in Minnesota. 3 weeks after I quit my job, I made about $10k in one week. I took a shot, and within weeks it paid off. This wasn’t luck though, this was a result of years of hard work, tons of clear-mindedness, and a wee bit of luck. 7. I made a habit out of giving back. I still teach kids Jiu-Jitsu classes. I will for a few more months. I’m currently the 13th-ranked grappler in the world in my weight class, and my day job is teaching 10-year-olds how to fight. For people who don’t understand, I guess it’s kind of the equivalent of being a professional writer who teaches 5th grade English. A lot of my “colleagues” on the competition scene are surprised I still teach kids. I make a bit of money teaching, but at the end of the day, teaching kids classes isn’t exactly my dream job. It’s something that I do because it makes me feel good. It makes me happy to be a positive part of my kid-students lives. I’ve only got a few more months left at this gig before it’s time to move on, but making a habit out of helping other people has made me more empathetic, more conscientious, and a happier human. 8. I cut a bunch of people out. This was a hard one. I lost a lot of “old friends” this year that I was holding onto for no reason other than sentimental purposes. Some of my friends actually acted like they were jealous of or threatened by my success and newfound happiness. Some of my friendships just weren’t stable enough to survive both of us having busy schedules. Either way, my social circle has changed a lot in the last year. I’ve made some of the best friends I’ve ever had. I feel really lucky, but part of me knows that I earned my good friends. I sacrificed bad friendships for good ones. 9. I went on an adventure. After I went all the way to Europe only to not win that Jiu-Jitsu tournament, I went on an adventure through Europe. I saw parts of Poland, Rome, the Amalfi Coast, and my birth city of London. I took 2 and a half weeks off of work and training to travel. I thought that maybe traveling would give me some insight into why I’d felt so unhappy and burned out in the past. I thought traveling would make me happy, but it didn’t. I’m glad I went on my little adventure because it made me realize that while adventures can be an important part of life, meaning comes from the connections you make at home. Traveling just made me want to find somewhere where I really feel at home. “Wherever you go, there you are.” — Jon Kabat-Zinn 10. I healed a broken heart. I had a tough breakup last year, and it took me more than a year to really feel like I recovered from it. I journaled, went to therapy, wrote about my ex on Medium and Quora, wrote to my ex in love letters (not a good idea), and even tried to rebuild the relationship, but nothing healed me quite like taking the time to learn to enjoy my own company. Silence was a better treatment than therapy for me. I made some errors in my recovery (I probably jumped back into dating sooner than I should have), but in the end, taking the time to heal my heart was the best thing that I did this year to change my life. It was the catalyst for all of my growth because it taught me the value of patience. I’m far from perfect, and I’m far from where I want to be, but in the last year, I’ve come a very long way. I make more money, I reach way more people through my writing, and I do Jiu-Jitsu at the highest levels. This was the first year that I finally felt comfortable calling myself a “pro athlete” and a “pro writer”. I felt like I made it in a lot of ways. It took a lot of work, a lot of discipline, and a rollercoaster of a year, but in the last year, I’ve changed a lot about myself and my life. If effort on projects compounds over time, the possibilities for where I’m at a year from now are limitless. If it doesn’t, I know that at the very least, I’m enjoying every second of the ride. That’s good enough for me for now.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is it like to live in Chicago (city)?
Answer: I’m in an abusive relationship with Chicago. From the months of January through April, living in Chicago is next to impossible. In January, our winters are nearing their worst points, and we’ve lost the “winter wonderland” feeling you get from those early snowfalls and the holiday activities that go with them. January in Chicago kind of sucks, and it’s a sign of things to come. February is brutal. I’m a professional athlete, which means that most days, my first activity is getting to the gym for a workout. I love that I get to call working out “work”, and I nearly always spring out of bed ready to start the day. However, not in February. In February, when I wake up for morning training, it’s still dark and cold. When I walk to my car to shovel the snow off of it, it’s still dark and cold. When I get to the gym, it’s still dark and cold. After training, there’s usually a bit of sunshine, but the cold doesn’t fade for months. This daily routine makes me feel like I have to earn my sunshine. The Chicago weather toughens you up a bit. March is tough too, but usually only because pretty much every winter in Chicago lasts longer than it’s supposed to. Whoever our Groundhog is, he sees his shadow every damn year. It’s rare, but it’s not unheard of for us to get snow in April, or even early May. Every Chicago winter that I endure makes me ready to leave this city that I’ve lived in for 20 years. Then, the summer happens, and boy does Chicago become beautiful in the summer. Chicago in the summer is a tough place to leave. It makes the winter worth it. Chicago in the summertime is my favorite place in the world. The city is really beautiful year-round, it’s just a bit easier to appreciate the beauty when the air you’re breathing doesn’t freeze your lungs. Chicago’s culture runs deep, and the summertime is a great time to experience that. Don’t let the media narratives about constant shootings and murders in the city terrify you from visiting. The danger in Chicago is pocketed in a few areas on the South and West sides. Here’s a murder map, to help articulate what I’m trying to say. If you visit, I’d say that you go to the following areas: A few of my favorite neighborhoods in Chicago are Pilsen (I used to live in Chinatown for a year in college, which is right near Pilsen), Wicker Park, Lincoln Park, and the West Loop. I also lived in West Town during my senior year of college, so that area has a special place in my heart. That’s where I was when the pandemic started. We’ve also got a nice Little Italy, a nice Chinatown, and an area you can get some of the best Indian food you’ll ever have on Devon Avenue in Rogers Park. The “Mag Mile” is very pretty too, it’s just a bit touristy for me. Maybe I’m just a grumpy old man now 😂 I used to see a girl who lived down there so I was down in Streeterville/River North pretty often, and I didn’t much like paying $20 for parking or having to bob and weave through seas of tourists. The views, however, were incredible. Last weekend, a friend rented a sailboat for his birthday and took us out on the lake. That was the first time in 20 years of living in Chicagoland that I got to go on a boat on Lake Michigan. It was cool as fuck. Sweet home Chicago… There’s so much more to Chicago than deep-dish pizza, hot dogs with a lot of toppings, and an atrocious amount of violence. I’m biased, but it feels to me that the world has never given Chicago the respect it deserves. Chicago does have rough, blue-collar pockets, but it also has so much more. There are millions of people that live here. You’re bound to get a bit of everything. Chicago also has the fancy-schmancy areas that remind you about how strange humanity can be (I avoid the magnificent mile at all costs unless a friend is coming in town and they want to see “The Bean”). It also has beautiful architecture, some fascinating history, and some of the best food in the whole world (and no, I’m not talking about the pizza). Chicago is a world-class city in the middle of America. Chicago is a world-class city that isn’t located where you’d expect a world-class city to be located. If you get on the expressway and drive an hour outside of Chicago, you’ll find yourself in a cornfield. Apart from Chicago, the rest of Illinois isn’t particularly impressive. (Starved Rock is a cool park though if you’re in Illinois and looking for hiking) Because of its location and its downsides, people often forget about Chicago. A lot of people I’ve talked to about cities in America love to romanticize New York or LA, but they look at me weird when I talk about Chicago. Chicago isn’t like New York or LA. Why? Well, first of all, it’s way more affordable. But the truth goes deeper than that. I think it’s because Chicagoans don’t walk around telling people about how great their city is. We don’t act like Chicago is the best city in the world because we know that our city has it’s flaws. Chicago does have its flaws. Chicago isn’t the safest city in the world. Our mayor is kind of a lunatic. The winters here aren’t for the faint of heart. It’s a tough city. I guess I’ll use this part of the essay about why I love my city to say that I’ll be moving to San Diego the 6 months. I love Chicago, but I’m leaving. I’m a wee-bit terrified. I’ve lived here for 20 years. I’m not leaving because I have a problem with anything about Chicago that most normal people would have. I’ve learned to find beauty in the winters, avoid the dangerous pockets, and live my life despite our crazy politics. However, one of the problems with Chicago for me has always been the tininess Jiu-Jitsu scene. It’s a bit small here, and for me to take my grappling career to the next level, I have to move somewhere where the Jiu-Jitsu is at a higher level. I don’t think this will be “goodbye” to Chicago, but it is going to be a “see you later”. I’d like to raise my kids in Chicago I think. And hey, perhaps when I come back, I’ll be able to build the Chicago Jiu-Jitsu community into what I’ve always thought it could be.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best life advice you would give?
Answer: Let’s talk about pleasure and how it relates to a good life. My whole life, I was taught to demonize things that felt good. Early on, this way of thinking was helpful. It made me stop eating so much junk food. It made me stop flooding my brain with porn. It made me stop chasing people who were bad for me. But over time, I started to get depressed from all of the self-inflicted constraints that I put on my own life. I removed all of the immediate pleasure from my life in the name of self-development, and I fucking hated it. People seem to think that there is an inverse relationship between success and pleasure, but is this really true? I think it’s partially true. Our ideas of pleasure are also heavily influenced by religion, past experiences, and stuff we see online. Honestly, today I’m just fed up with all the self-help bullshit I see from startup bros on Twitter that tells me that I have to take cold showers, wake up at 4 am, and chant positive affirmations into the mirror like the characters in Candyman chant for Candyman to appear. You can’t make your life better by just saying positive shit to yourself. You have to talk nicely to yourself, and then you have to go out and do nice things for yourself. A better life doesn’t come from waking up at 4 am every day or optimizing your optimized morning routine for the 42nd time, it comes from having the discipline to weather any storm you go through. Discipline is tough to sell, so people give it fancy packaging. The measure of discipline is not through how you spend the The real test of discipline is not the ability to abstain from pleasure or things that feel good. It’s pretty easy to abstain from things once you get in the habit of abstaining from them. The real test of discipline is the ability to do things that feel good every once and a while without over-indulging to the point of excess. Try to eat one Oreo. Try and take one day off work. Can you do it? For me, it’s hard. It’s easier to just burn myself into the ground. I’ve been on both ends of the spectrum, and for me, discipline to the point of excess is not a whole lot better for happiness than eating pizza to excess. You’ll just dig your own grave in a different part of the cemetery. The best life advice that I would give is to strive to be reasonably disciplined in your life. You don't need to take cold showers. You don't need to do intermittent fasting. You don't need to wake up at 4 in the morning. You don't need to do what the self-help Twitter guy tells you to do. You need to be disciplined, not drastic. Drastic behavior is a sign of projection. The second best piece of life advice that I would give is to never sit on social media and tell people to take cold showers and wake up earlier.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is your opinion on antidepressants?
Answer: I’ve taken anti-depressants every day for several years. I’m actually going to start weaning off of them soon. In the last 3 years, my opinion on antidepressants has changed a lot. At this point, my opinion on antidepressants is that they are prescribed far more often than they are necessary. Let’s talk about the history of mental illness really quickly. Mental illness used to be caused by demons. The history of mental health treatment is wild. For starters, it wasn’t until 1895 that manic depression was established as a medical condition. Before that, most people thought that mental illness was caused by demons and spirits. Some people still think that. Then, in the early 1900s, psychotherapy was established as a way to treat sadness, mourning, and depression. 50 years later, the monoamine theory of depression was established (the whole “depression being a chemical balance” thing), and the first antidepressant was created soon after. The term “Major Depressive Disorder” wasn’t used until the 1970s, about 20 years after antidepressants first appeared on the market. The rest, as they say, is history. Antidepressants have been rising in prescription rates ever since their introduction. In particular, the number of antidepressants prescribed nearly doubled from 1996–2015. As of 2018, roughly 18% of Americans were taking antidepressants. Is that too many people, or are too many people getting depressed? Are antidepressants being overprescribed or are 2 out of every 10 people dealing with a level of depression where medical intervention is required? The thought of both possibilities being is equally terrifying to me. When I look back at my own experience with depression, anxiety, and antidepressants, I can’t help but notice the flaws of the system. Here’s what happened to me when I decided to seek treatment for my mental health: I can’t speak for an entire country of people on the true ins and outs of diagnosing mental illness. However, I can speak about my experience with getting diagnosed with a decent-sized bucked of mental disorders in one just afternoon. One Tuesday in January 2018, I woke up and went to see a psychiatrist. By noon, I had moderate depression and severe anxiety. I also was advised to be tested for ADHD, so about a week or 2 after I got told I had anxiety and depression, I also got ADHD. Then, the doctors told me that if I wanted to, I could get prescribed a bucket of pills for my symptoms. I could take meds for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. I’d been in the mental health treatment “system” for about 3 weeks. At this point, I’d spent my entire life being anxious, having panic attacks, and experiencing derealization. The offer to take some pills and have my brain feel better was better tempting. I couldn’t resist giving it a try. We started with antidepressants. Antidepressants were… fine? My first antidepressant was Lexapro. It’s a common one. I took it for about 6 months, and after a while, my depression symptoms alleviated. At around the same time, however, my life started getting better. This makes it hard for me to say why my depression was alleviated. I got a girlfriend for the first time in 3 years (since the beginning of my experience with severe depression/anxiety), I started getting good at Jiu-Jitsu (a year after I started therapy, I won a world title), and I started making friends through Jiu-Jitsu who were impacting my life in a very positive way. Mentally, I got a lot better, but I couldn’t really be sure if it was because of the pills I was taking or the daily efforts I was making. After a while, I decided to get off the pills. I didn’t like the side effects. Then, I got depressed again. Ugh. My girlfriend and I broke up. I started getting burnt out of Jiu-Jitsu and work and school. I started feeling disconnected from my friends (they were all much older than me). Everything I was doing to feel better went to crap, so I went back to the only depression treatment that I thought I could trust. I went back to my pills. And? I got better again. I started taking a different antidepressant the second time. Wellbutrin. It worked. I think. Here’s what I can’t figure out: Did I ever have serious, medical attention-required depression in the first place? Honestly, I have no idea. My anxiety has been incredibly severe at times. I probably could have benefitted from an anxiety medication at some point, but I was afraid of the addictive nature of the anti-anxiety medications. I definitely experienced depression, but I don’t know if I have “Major Depressive Disorder”. I feel like I’m in a grey area with my mental health. I don’t feel like the current mental health treatment model actually works, at least here in America the way I experienced it. I benefitted most from talk therapy, writing, getting a little older and wiser through life experience, and learning to be kinder to myself. It kind of feels like my medication probably benefitted the pocket of the person who made it more than it did my own brain. For the most part, my antidepressants just fucked up my sex life and gave me sweaty. I’m not sure I’ll ever know if it was worth it. So what’s the point? I didn’t write this to invalidate anyone’s diagnosis of any mental illness. I wrote this because life taught me that “getting diagnosed” doesn’t actually fix any of your mental health problems. All it does is validate the fact that you are struggling. What if we just validated people who struggled anyway, without forcing them into a corrupt and financially motivated system? At the very least, the best thing that came from my antidepressant experiment was that for a period of time, I got to feel seen for struggling with my mental health. Particularly as a man, this was great for me. What wasn’t great was that once I got my diagnosis, I felt labeled as a victim of mental illness. I developed a victim mentality. I also feel that my treatment providers were very quick to throw pills at me. This isn’t what really bothers me, but it’s the beginning of it. What really bothers me is that my treatment providers threw pills at me at a time in my life when I was desperate for a quick solution. If you’ve ever struggled with depression, anxiety, or similar, you know that what you really want is just to feel better. I was a vulnerable customer, and they told me that taking pills would make me feel better, so I took them. But was it really the best decision for my health? I don’t know, you don’t know, and unfortunately, it seems my treatment providers don’t know either. Only time will tell.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Does reading make you a smarter person?
Answer: I read a great book about nutrition recently. I learned a lot of valuable information. Apparently, eating too many calories can make you overweight. Apparently pizza, ice cream, and cheeseburgers are very calorically dense foods. Then, I closed the book. I felt very smart because of all my recently acquired nutritional information. Later that day (I was traveling), I ordered a pizza. I was staying in a camper-van turned Airbnb in San Diego, and I was tired from a weekend of competing and traveling, and I just wanted to relax and watch some Netflix and enjoy a pizza. After I ate the pizza, I didn’t feel awesome physically, but mentally I was very happy. Physically, I felt kind of fat. It was like I ate a whole pizza by myself or something. I know pizza is bad for me because the nutrition book said so, but I deliberately chose to eat a pizza because I wanted one. I have knowledge that pizza is not great for me, but I still ate it. I’m smart because I know that pizza is bad for me, but my actions were the same as someone who has never read a nutrition book in their life. How smart can I be, really? The point is, reading will make you smarter in some ways, but you have to apply the knowledge. You also have to know when the knowledge does not apply. After I ate my pizza, I got up the next morning and spent 3 hours at the gym wrestling and doing Jiu-Jitsu. Thanks to my trusty pizza and the discipline that I have to show up to the gym every day, no matter what I’ve eaten or drank the night before, I got through my workout no problem. One day, when I’m older, I’ll probably have to cut back on the pizza. But for now, it’s fine. Reading makes you smarter in the head, but it doesn’t make your life better until you apply the knowledge. “The art of living well and the art of dying well are one.” ― Epicurus

Question: At what age should kids start learning martial arts?
Answer: I’ve been teaching kids Jiu-Jitsu for a little over a year, and for the longest time, I thought that pretty much any kid under 7 had no business learning Jiu-Jitsu. It’s hard to learn grappling/martial arts at any age, but it’s really hard when you’re 7, have no upper body strength yet, and have the attention span of a gnat. Then, one day, a 5-year-old came into my class and completely changed the way that I think about “age” in learning martial arts. This kid is 5 years old and he can execute basic judo throws, basic takedowns, and basic attacks from closed guard. He likes Jiu-Jitsu and wants to keep learning. He asks questions that for the most part are pretty reasonable questions and he listens during instruction. He doesn’t ruin the class for the other kids. I can’t really ask for more from a 5 year old student. In reality, you’re never too young or too old to learn martial arts. Maybe 4 is a bit on the young side and 80 is a bit on the old side, but for the most part, anyone can learn valuable skills and life lessons (like discipline and respect) from martial arts training. The age a kid should start learning martial arts is the age where they can show up to a class and not ruin the class for all of the other kids. If a kid can behave themselves for the 45 minutes-1 hour of Jiu-Jitsu class, then they are old enough to be in Jiu-Jitsu class. The biggest limitation for kids learning martial arts isn’t physical ability or complexity of the activity (my kids Jiu-Jitsu class is very beginner friendly), the biggest limitation is their ability to not ruin the class for the other kids. I have some students who are 4–5 and can keep it together for a whole class, and I have 10-year-olds who make me want to pull my hair out. This, like many things in life, is not about age, it’s about maturity.

Question: Who are you beyond Quora?
Answer: Here's me, beyond Quora. When I'm not writing, I'm probably either doing Jiu-Jitsu, eating, or sleeping. I train Jiu-Jitsu 2-3 times per day, 6-7 days per week. As I've gotten older and more banged up (this sport isn't exactly great for the ole body), I've begun to vary the intensity of these training sessions, but I'm still in the gym every day multiple times per day. I also teach private lessons and seminars all over the place. That's me off Quora in a nutshell. On Quora, I feel like I'm the "martial arts self-help/life lessons dude", but that's not always who I am in real life. In real life, I'm a 24-year-old (almost 25!) Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu athlete and teacher. I'm also a writer and a ghostwriter. I've been doing Jiu-Jitsu for 7 years, and writing on the internet for nearly 2 years (November 2022 my writing career turns 2 😎). In Jiu-Jitsu, I'm currently the #13 ranked 170-pound competitor in the world (yeah, the whole world, and yeah, I feel like an imposter about it 😂). The photo above is from a pro tournament I did yesterday in Los Angeles, California, where I lost in the finals to the #10 ranked guy in the world in the final seconds. It hurt. Literally and figuratively. It was also awesome. Competing sends my emotions into overdrive. Sometimes, the pre-match feelings make me want to just give up because I'm so anxious. Sometimes, the adrenaline makes me physically stronger than I ever thought was possible. Sometimes, the wins make me so happy I cry. Same with the losses. Beyond Quora, I'm entrenched in this crazy world of fighting, constant hard training, and a deep study of trying to master one of the most complex sports in the world - submission grappling. What I love about Jiu-Jitsu is the mental challenge it gives me. I'm almost never the most athletic or explosive athlete in my division, so I'm forced to use my intellect to try to work my way toward submitting and defeating my opponents. Sometimes, I win. Sometimes, I don't. Either way, I put the same passion into Jiu-Jitsu that I put into all of my Quora answers, Medium articles, ebooks, and Substack posts. You might think it’s corny, but I don’t care. I love this shit. Beyond Quora, I'm just as passionate as I am off Quora, although probably a bit quieter. Beyond Quora, I'm an introvert. Anyway, back to fighting. I literally put my blood, sweat, and tears into martial arts, because that's the only thing I know how to do. I've been involved in combat sports since I was 12. Even though I'm a young man now, all I know how to do is to fight with the determination of a depressed chubby kid with something to prove. I try to have the same passion in my writing, although writing hasn't actually made me bleed yet. Here's to hoping it stays that way. 😅 If you want to read more about my life beyond Quora, the best thing you can do is check out my newsletter at the link below 😊

Question: What don't women understand about men?
Answer: Most men struggle to understand their own complexity. (Here’s me in a pink shirt sitting at a make-up chair before I weighed in to fight people later today. Hopefully that expresses the complexity of masculinity well enough for ya 😂) The stereotypical male-female conflict archetype is that the woman is overcomplicating the thing and the man just wants everything to be simple. I spend a lot of time in the "bro-world", where men exaggerate this archetype. Sometimes this is true, but many times, this archetype just makes men look like overly simplistic creatures who are driven by impulse. Sometimes, the inverse of the stereotype is closer to the actual fact. Sometimes it's the man who's being irrationally emotional, and he doesn't even know it. Nonetheless, people often make it seem like most men only care about sex, food, and releasing their blind rage through video games or working out or drinking beer with the homies. To me, that's always been tough to relate to. I love all the things above (for fuck's sake, I fight people for a living), but they aren't at the core of my identity. My identity is more complex than just doing my work, fighting people in Jiu-Jitsu, eating red meat, and trying to date girls I'm attracted to. Yes, all these things are very exciting to me, but if I have all of them, I'd still need to do more work to have a complete existence. It took years of therapy and journaling and working on my mind to realize that there's more to happiness as a man than lifting weights, eating beef, and getting laid. Lots of men are similar to me, but the culture doesn't validate our complex emotions. This isn't a cop out for toxic masculinity, either. Men have plenty of issues, and it's their responsibility to deal with them. We just have to deal with the additional challenge of culturally enforced emotional repression on top of the complexity of our own emotions. It's not that men are wildly complex - I'm not saying that either. I just feel like lots of men don't acknowledge the complexity of their own emotions. If they did, male-female conflict might be a bit easier to navigate.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is happiness?
Answer: Don’t let anyone fool you. Happiness is very simple. Happiness isn’t Nutella-strawberry-banana crepes (although, I kind of wish it was) or anything else you can get on the menu at the cafe up the street. Happiness is being in a state of mind where you can thoroughly enjoy the crepes. Happiness is also having the calm state of mind to enjoy going on a walk with the cute girl who you got the Nutella crepes with. It’d be weird if you kept thinking about crepes while you were on a nice walk by the lake with your super pretty lunch date. There are thousands of books written on the art of living a happy life. I’d like to write one too some day. For now, however, I’ll leave you with this: A happy life begins when you quit obsessing over what happened yesterday and and what’s happening tomorrow and who’s dating who and how many followers someone has. A happy life is on the other side of thinking. That should get you started on the right path. Have a great day 😊

Question: What are some stupid things that smart people do?
Answer: Here are 10 stupid things that smart people do every single day. Texting and driving. Cell phone use while driving causes more than 1.5 million car crashes every single year. You are 23 times more likely to crash your car if you text while driving. 38% of people text and drive. Just like… don’t do it? Going on their phones before they go to sleep. Going to bed is supposed to be a pleasant, relaxing experience, and people fuck that up by doomscrolling right before bed. Spending time sitting in your bed watching TikToks or reading tweets or Medium articles (I’ve been guilty of this one) is the antithesis of the relaxing experience you need to turn your brain off so that you rest and function properly. You probably don’t have insomnia, you’re probably on your phone too much. Using productivity as a means of social posturing. I see this a lot on Twitter. People like to brag about how much they get done. Being productive is not a personality trait. Being productive is not necessarily an indicator of proficiency at a skill. Being productive might not even make you any money. Quality over quantity. Spending money they don’t have. 30% of people are in debt. Debt is inevitable in some areas (education, home mortgage, etc), but most people don’t know the first thing about money management. It’s barely taught in schools, and it’s really hard to learn it by yourself. Money is complicated. Even some of the smartest I know people are lost when it comes to managing their cash flow. Not prioritizing sleep. If sleep wasn’t necessary, we’d have evolved past the point of needing to do it for 8 hours a day. We haven’t, but most people still think that sleeping less will help them get ahead or make more money. In reality, it’s probably just going to give them early onset dementia. Eating badly. I saw a photo of Elon Musk not wearing a shirt the other day, and one thing was clear: That brilliant man has no idea how to eat well. People were kind mean to Mr. Musk online and they shouldn’t be, but that’s not really the point here. Eating too many calories for the amount you move will make you obese. I don’t care if you’re Elon Musk or Joe from the grocery store. Obesity will make you sick. Then you will die. That’s it. Thinking the world revolves around them. People are entitled. This isn’t a new idea. Humanity is kind of an entitled species. We all want to feel safe and happy, but we don’t want to fight. Fighting is hard. You could lose. You could fail. But really, this doesn’t matter: You have to fight for the things you need in your life. No one gives you a happy life. You make one. Bullshitting with their mental health. “Mental health is real”, but for most of us, it isn’t a priority. Most people whine about how they are anxious and depressed but do nothing about it. You can drastically improve your mind with 15–30 minutes of daily mental training. 6 months of this practice just might change your life. If it doesn’t, you can yell at me. Thinking more than doing. When I say “doing”, I don’t mean working. You don’t need to work all the time. Here are some things you can do that aren’t “work” but also aren’t thinking: playing guitar, listening to music or podcasts, sleeping, meditating, writing, or cooking. Try one. Do more. Think less. Seek flow, not happiness. Watching porn. There are more than 68 million daily searches online related to pornography. I’m not even talking about hustle porn, food porn, or any of the other “appropriate” types of porn out there. Porn use has also been associated with heavy anxiety, depression, and other psychological problems. This doesn’t stop millions from watching it every single day. Porn is a drug. It’s kind of the equivalent of eating fast food, but it’s probably worse for your brain. Watch porn as often as you would eat fast food. Maybe less. For more, follow me on Twitter! 😊
