Question: What is friendship? What is a friend?
Answer: Friendship is not like fighting. Friendship is like dancing. Maybe it sounds obvious to you, but as someone who has spent their whole adult life literally fighting people every day, it took me a long time to realize this. All I did in my late teens and early 20s was fight to try to get people to like me. I thought the more gold medals I got, the more friends I’d have. I thought the more followers I had, the more friends I’d have. It worked sometimes, but the problem was that if I took a break from fighting (both literally and metaphorically), they would stop liking me and like someone else instead. In the end, I mostly lost friends. I made a few friends who I’ve managed to keep over the years, but these friends don’t really give a damn about how much winning I do. These were the friends that I didn’t constantly have to fight to keep. I didn’t have to constantly try to be interesting. I didn’t have to constantly prove my worth by beating someone in a martial arts match or by buying them stuff. I just existed, and they existed, and then after a while, we existed together. It was natural. It was not forced. I didn’t fight for these friendships, but I did make effort for them. Learning the difference between fighting and making effort was big for me. Good friendship is flowy, not violent. A friend is someone who genuinely wants you to be the best version of yourself. They are not threatened by your growth or your success. I’ve had plenty of people who wanted me to fail because my success would be a threat to their ego. These people called themselves my friends, but they were not my friends. My friends just want me to be happy—wherever that takes me. I just want my friends to be happy—wherever that takes them. Friendship is the natural closeness that you form with other people through being yourself. The more bullshit in your mind and in your life, the more difficult it is to find this natural closeness. Friends with who you are able to be yourself around are the friends you will keep. The friends you keep are the friends that you form closer bonds with. Friends are not your allies in the fight for life. Friends are your dance partners in the dance of life. Learn the difference. You’ll be a lot happier for it.

Question: Should I learn judo or jiu jitsu?
Answer: If you’re 6 and want to try and make it to the Olympics in 12 years, Judo. If you’re trying to learn how to actually fight someone, do Jiu-Jitsu. If you want to make money in martial arts, do Jiu-Jitsu. If you want to be a part of one of the fastest-growing martial arts in the world (behind probably only MMA), do Jiu-Jitsu. Judo focuses on throws and upper body attacks. In Judo, there’s also an aspect of the training called “newaza”, which translates to ground techniques. That’s basically Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Essentially, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu is newaza on steroids. This is because “newaza” is very limited. It ignores many aspects of grappling. I submitted a Judo Junior Olympian when I was just a purple belt in Jiu-Jitsu. He was quite upset about it. Leg locks are also illegal in judo. On the flipside, they are a centerpiece of learning modern Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. “Why would you ignore 50% of the human body?” is a cliche quote in BJJ at this point from BJJ legend Dean Lister (to John Danaher, who made the quote famous). Just about all Judo that I’m familiar with is done in the gi (I think there’s some no-gi Judo, it’s just uncommon). In Jiu-Jitsu, the average practitioner will practice both gi and no-gi every week. Modern Jiu-Jitsu is becoming a blend of Judo, freestyle and Greco Roman wrestling, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, sambo, and even American catch wrestling. It’s becoming really cool to watch and participate in. The other thing I like about BJJ is that the culture is very modern. BJJ is always evolving and it’s evolving very quickly. There’s no “old school martial arts bullshit”. I’m an adult. I don’t need some dude who I call “sifu” or “sensei” who tells me what moves I’m allowed to do and what is off-limits. I don’t need anyone telling me who I can’t train with and learn from. I train with friends from other academies all the time. I fly all over the world to train with people. I watch moves on Instagram and try to learn them. That’s how technical evolution happens in the modern world. Plus, now, there are even professional Jiu-Jitsu events all over the place to study and learn from. This weekend, I’m competing in one in California for $5000. Not a horrible prize for an emerging professional sport. When I was a white belt in 2015, there were only a handful of professional Jiu-Jitsu promotions in the world. Now, there are dozens. Some events are paying up to $100,000 in cash prizes. I’ve never seen this in Judo. This actually goes back to the point I made in the opening sentence. In part because there is no BJJ in the Olympics, the sport of Jiu-Jitsu is exploding. BJJ is entirely private. The early days of BJJ were financed by rich dudes who just wanted to see the art grow. The Olympics or any other large government body isn’t holding back the development of the sport, so it’s growing like crazy. People in Jiu-Jitsu don’t care about bureaucratic bullshit. People in Jiu-Jitsu do Jiu-Jitsu to escape that shit. In wrestling and judo, it’s also really hard to make money. Owning a judo school typically isn’t a super profitable business (how many working professionals want to get thrown on their heads after work?), and private wrestling schools are few and far between. There is also no money available for professional athletes in these sports. A top-of-the-line Jiu-Jitsu academy on the other hand can make 6 figures (or even more). Jiu-Jitsu as a community has also strived to create a culture that is accessible and appealing to the average person. As a result of this exploding culture, you’re seeing more and more professional Jiu-Jitsu athletes. The level of the sport is rising year after year. This year’s ADCC World Championship (Abu Dhabi Combat Club) in Las Vegas is going to be insane. You, the person reading this, can head down to your local BJJ academy tomorrow and take your first introduction class. Depending on where you go, you can probably take it for free. Jiu-Jitsu people just want you to join the culture. If the culture grows, we all live easier, get better, and learn more. That’s what Jiu-Jitsu is really about and that’s why I like it more than any other martial art.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do men with goals succeed in life and men without goals fail?
Answer: It’s not really “men with goals” versus “men without goals”. It’s “people with goals” versus “people without goals”. Obviously, “having goals” alone isn’t enough to be successful, but it’s a great start. We’ll talk more about that in a minute. To me, the guy in this picture looks like he’s trying to focus on his goals. But does he look happy? Goals alone won’t make you happy, but they can make you unhappy. If you don’t have goals, you can’t fail or succeed. You’re just existing. You’re like a blob with arms and legs floating through the multidimensional plane of existence. And actually, in terms of spirtual health, that might be a really great thing. Men with goals can succeed, but men without goals are probably a lot lower in anxiety and stress. It’s hard to stress out about stuff when nothing matters. One of my old childhood friends has no goals. He seems pretty content, but his life has stagnated in terms of progress. That’s his choice. He doesn’t have the high highs or the low lows I have, but he gets by okay. You’d have to ask him how he finds meaning in his existence. I, on the other hand, feel that goals are essential to meaning. To me, it seems that without goals, my life is essentially meaningless. At the same time, I am self-aware enough to know that “having goals” alone is not going to make my life complete. This is the dichotomy of goal-setting: Having goals can make you happy, but it might also make you sad if those goals don’t work out. Not having goals means you won’t get sad, but you also might not get happy. To put it another way, either you create meaning in your life, or your life is meaningless. I used to struggle a lot with nihilism. Perks of being raised without religion, I guess. I never believed in a higher power or anything like that, and I never believed that anything in my life was objectively meaningful. For the longest time, I thought that this meant that my life was meaningless. Because I thought it, it was so. This was my reality from 12–21, I was very depressed about it. I fought the feelings of meaninglessness, but they were persistent. I did stuff in my life, but the stuff I did didn’t matter to me. I couldn’t handle failing, so I decided that not having goals would have been safer. I never said that I wanted to be a Jiu-Jitsu world champion because wanting to be champion meant that not being a champion would be failure. I’d have rather not tried and not failed than not tried. It made me miserable. Even worse, because I wasn’t “all-in”, the results of my pursuits were always mediocre, and I was very unhappy. I was too scared to be anything, so I was nothing. Men (people) without goals cannot be anything. This is why they don’t succeed. This is why many of them are miserable. This, I believe, is the route of modern nihilism. It’s not a lack of success that makes us unhappy, but a lack of hope. Learn to be a happy failure. Let’s talk about people with goals. People who have created meaning in their lives. People who want to live better. People who want to try to be happy—like, really happy (I’m not talking about peace here, I’m not talking about joy). If you don’t try to be happy, you can’t be happy. If you don’t try to succeed, you can’t succeed. This is simple, but most people don’t let this idea sink in. Once you have “goals”—your personal antidote to nihilism—then you can begin to live a life that has more meaning and more purpose. You can make art. You can build meaningful connections (with people who have similar personal visions). You can live and work and succeed. That’s why goals matter. Goals give you a framework to create a meaningful life. That’s also why it’s so important to choose goals that are aligned with your personal values. If your value is helping people, you probably won’t get a lot of meaning out of trying to chase money or status. Setting the goal of making a butt-ton of money because a motivation YouTube video told you to would be stupid and it would make you unhappy. Choose goals that matter to you. When your “hustle” gives your life meaning, it doesn’t feel like a hustle anymore. It feels like living. Either way, you’re going to die one day. You might as well do some shit before your time comes. The potential upside is limited only by your imagination.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do people travel so much?
Answer: People romanticize travel for many different reasons. I used to do it all the time because I thought that “traveling the world” was going to make me happy. (Photo from my trip to Rome earlier this year, where I learned that traveling wasn’t going to fix the hole in my heart. 😊)  When I was in Italy 2 months ago, I ate 6 pizzas in 4 days. All I did for the 3 days that I was touring Rome and the Amalfi Coast was walk around, ride trains, eat bread, talk to people in broken Italian, and get drunk on wine with total strangers. It was supposed to be your classic European dream vacation, one that I was supposed to remember and cherish for years to come. Yet, the parts that people romanticize about travel were the parts that I hated most about this trip. I hated making small talk about why my ears are ginormous with strangers over fancy wine that I didn’t even really want to drink. I hated feeling like a slave to the bread and cheese that I was using to fuel my body all day long. I hated feeling lost and aimless as I was crawling through someone else’s home in search of my own self-discovery. I loved parts of traveling (the new experiences were cool), but it didn’t make me a happy person. Happiness is more complicated than just moving your body across the world.  The intersection of adventure and reality. I used to romanticize travel. I loved Anthony Bourdain in my late teens, so it was easy to romanticize the open road. 5 years ago, I wanted adventures, just like the ones that you’d see in movies or read about in novels. I wanted to meet fascinating strangers over wine in Rome, fall in love on the Amalfi Coast, and get my heart broken on a grey London afternoon. I didn’t care if the experiences were positive or negative, I just wanted the experiences to fill my mind with magic that I’d never seen before. Now, 5 years later, I’m realizing that I didn’t really want experiences. I just wanted to feel better. Nomadism is constantly romanticized in western culture [ https://www.kunc.org/arts-life/2021-03-06/nomadland-gives-intimate-if-romanticized-view-of-life-on-the-open-road ], but this isn’t because we actually love the idea of life “on the open road”. This is because many people today feel trapped and stuck in their lives, and the thought of leaving it all behind and traveling gives them relief from the stress of their day-to-day. When it comes to facing stress in life, there are 2 options: face the stress and grow, or run away. The second option is a whole lot easier to sell.  Trading materialism for a different kind of materialism. Young people today have different values than they used to. Today, there has been a shift from conventional materialism to experiential materialism [ https://www.becomingminimalist.com/experiences/ ]. This is best articulated through travel. Instead of buying a car or a fancy watch, young people today buy trips, concert tickets, and other experiences that they can use to feel happy about their lives. In the short term, this works, particularly because experiential happiness creates longer-lasting highs than material happiness [ https://news.utexas.edu/2020/03/09/spending-on-experiences-versus-possessions-advances-more-immediate-happiness/#:~:text=The%20researchers%20concluded%20that%20people,time%20using%20their%20material%20possessions. ]. But does this really make us happy people? Or is the commodification of experience just a band-aid for a deeper existential problem? The problem with western culture is deeper than “buying experiences vs. buying material objects”. The problem with western culture is that we are obsessed with buying things in the name of social posturing.  How to be happy (simplified). You don’t need to travel to Rome, India, or anywhere ...

Question: How can I figure out what I really want to do with my life after college?
Answer: Well, first you have to try stuff. (Me at one of my first ever Jiu-Jitsu tournaments — circa 2017 — I got choked unconscious a few hours after this picture was taken 😂) It doesn’t matter if you're graduating high school, graduating college, or if you’re just feeling lost and confused because that’s kind of what it feels like to be in your early 20s. If you want to figure out what you want to do with your life, you have to try to do stuff. Everyone’s winging it. To figure your life out, you have to start winging it. Sometimes, you’re not going to be very good at the stuff you try. That’s okay though. For example, when I was 21, I spent 6 months trying to write and perform stand up comedy. I had a 6 month break from Jiu-Jitsu to get knee surgery, so I tried something new. I thought maybe it could be my new thing. It wasn’t. I was not good at comedy. My jokes weren’t funny and performing every day made me anxious. Wasn’t my thing, but I tried. What I really learned from that experience was how to look like an idiot in public. I also tried skateboarding for a while. I wasn’t planning to become a professional skateboarder or anything, but I thought I could maybe learn a new mode of transportation and a new hobby. I fell a lot. It kinda hurt. I skateboard a little bit less now, but it’s still fun from time to time. From 19–22, I tried so many random things. I went on so many stupid coffee dates. I experienced a lot of stuff. It made specializing after college a lot easier for me. I also tried Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. That one worked out pretty well for me. I won some tournaments. I made some money. I made some awesome friends. I stuck with it, and I got my black belt after 7 years. I got a job teaching. I got to travel the US and abroad and see stuff that’d never have seen if I hadn’t tried Jiu-Jitsu. I tried, and I’m still going strong. Sometimes you try something, and it just works out for you. That’s a nice feeling. That also doesn’t mean that that’s the thing you have to do for the rest of your life. I also tried Mixed Martial Arts. For about a year when I was 19, I went to an MMA gym every day and did boxing classes, Muay Thai classes, and MMA sparring sessions with professional MMA fighters. I’ve always been a tough sparring round in the gym, so even the higher level fighters liked having me in the gym. I got to train MMA with people who were way more experienced than me. I got beat up a lot. After about a year of training, I realized that I probably wasn’t going to be the next Conor McGregor. I realized that my MMA career was probably going to involve not making a lot of money, getting brain damage, and getting beat up a lot. I realized that I could be okay at MMA, but I could be really good at Jiu-Jitsu. So, I focused on that instead. It was a good decision. I also tried writing. Not that I’m amazing at writing, but I do enjoy it. I write every day now. Writing helps my mental health, it makes me a better communicator, and it’s becoming a bit of a job for me. Some people like my writing. That’s enough for me. September will mark 1 year of writing on Quora for me. November will mark 2 years of writing on the internet. I don’t know what you’re good at. They’ll tell you that you can be anything, but they’re only partially right. You can be almost anything, but depending on the thing, you might have to sacrifice more than the average person. Talent is real, and you’re going to be better at somethings than others. I was never cut out to be a great theatrical performer. I’m too anxious. For me to become a decent comedy performer, for example, I was probably going to have to sacrifice my mental health, my martial arts career, and a lot of personal relationships. Even then, you’d probably never be watching my Netflix special. For me to become a high-level Jiu-Jitsu person, I had to sacrifice my MMA career (an easy sacrifice for me), a lot of time for training, and my physical health (I’ve gotten banged up a bit over the years). To figure your life out, you just gotta try stuff. Then you have to learn how to deal with the consequences of your actions. You have to decide what amount of sacrifice is worth it for you. That should get you started. For more, follow me on Twitter! 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How did you learn to love yourself?
Answer: Earlier this year, I wrote an answer on Quora about a girl who I thought was the love of my life who had broken my heart. (Pictured: The author, practicing self-love or whatever on the Amalfi Coast) Here’s that answer, just for some context. When I wrote this answer, I said one thing that was quite a bit problematic. I said that if my ex contacted me again, despite all of our problems and all the times she hurt me, I said that I didn’t think I’d be able to turn her away. I said: “I would take her back right now, even though doing it would be a horrible decision. Even though taking her back would destroy my mental health, drain the life out of me, and break me down, I know that if she showed up at my doorstep I couldn’t resist her.” I don’t always quote myself, but when I do, it’s usually to point out how much of a dummy I’ve been. See, the other day, my ex did contact me. I should have seen it coming, but I really didn’t. All of a sudden, I had to make a decision. Being with her forever and ever was something that I’d wanted for a long time, and now I had the opportunity for everything I thought I wanted. Instead of writing this answer, I could be on my way over to her apartment for coffee right now. However, I just couldn’t do it. For whatever reason, it didn’t feel right. I didn’t want the stress and anxiety that I had from our first relationship anymore. I didn’t want to open that door again. I don’t want to be in relationships where I feel exhausted and strung out anymore. I wasn’t rude, I didn’t say anything mean, but I did tell her that if there wasn’t anything I could do for her, I didn’t think it would be wise for us to talk to each other. I realized that I’d be better alone than I would be with someone who I know isn’t great for my mental health and happiness. I realized that I love myself enough to not chase people that I know are bad for me anymore. That was kind of a nice realization. So how did I learn how to “love myself”? I took the time to heal. I went to therapy. I wrote literally everything I felt down (you can read a lot of it here on Quora, lol). I focused on improving my mind. I learned to enjoy my alone time. I learned how to be happy in my own head. I moved (and I’m moving again soon, but more on that later). I traveled. I threw myself into martial arts and writing as if my life depended on it. This was easy because, in a way, it does. I discovered things I like about myself. I took the things I didn’t like about myself and tried to improve them. I learned to love myself the same way I learned to love my ex. I became comfortable around myself. I accepted my flaws. I treated myself to nice things for no reason other than that I wanted to. I respected myself. In the past, I would do all these things for other people, but not for myself. I changed that. I developed self-respect. This led to self-love, but not in the corny, bubble bath type of way. It was really hard. It was way easier to just throw myself into other people and hope that they’d fix my problems and insecurities. It was way easier to use “being in love” as justification for me to act like an idiot. It was easy, but it wasn’t effective for my long-term happiness. To me, self-love is when you learn to stop limiting your potential by acting like a freaking idiot.

Question: What's wrong with the fitness industry?
Answer: The fitness industry is completely disconnected from “health”. Here’s a photo of me from a few years ago, probably the leanest I’ve ever been. Sorry for the douchey picture… trying to make a point here 😂. All I did during this 6-month period of my life was work out, eat cleaner than a nun’s vocabulary, and listen to personal development podcasts. I was miserable. Life sucked. All I have from that period looking back are a few pictures of me with a nice 6 pack. I’ve always done combat sports (first wrestling, now Jiu-Jitsu), so I’ve always paid attention to my weight so that I can make weight for competitions, but I never really paid attention to aesthetics. However, there’s this myth in the fitness world that being fitter will solve all of your problems, and I drank the kool-aid. You might be a bad person, you might have terrible social skills, and you might be broke, but you if you have a 6 pack, people will be jealous of you. That’s kinda fucked up, isn’t it? Nonetheless, one summer, I decided that if I got leaner, girls would like me more. I’d be more successful if I had the body of someone who was more successful. And so, I committed to the gym harder than I ever had before. The irony is that I never had time to date anyone or work on any true personal development because I was always in the gym, either training Jiu-Jitsu or lifting weights or running or biking. I was working out for 3–6 hours per day, 6–7 days per week. My fitness was my obsession. Ultimately, this made me a worse athlete and an unhappier person. A few months after I got super duper lean, I had a bad injury, was sidelined for 6 months, and I chubbed right back up. I was more depressed than I’d ever been. That was when I experienced that episode of derealization I’ve written about a few times before. Health and fitness aren’t always the same thing. Learn to become healthy. Then you can think about fitness. The fitness industry uses extreme examples of health and fitness to sell products to you. I got really lean by working out all day long, eating great, and prioritizing my fitness over everything else. I lived an extreme lifestyle. However, health does not come from extremes. In sports, this is especially true. Optimal performance in sport does not come from zero percent body fat (in that photo, I’m probably between 10–15% body fat). Optimal performance comes from comfort. We obsess about getting out of our comfort zones, but that’s not what it’s really about. You’re not supposed to live your life in discomfort, you’re supposed to expand the area of your comfort zone so that fewer situations make you uncomfortable. If you’re struggling with insecurities about your body, hiding away by yourself doing crunches and slamming protein shakes is the antithesis of your problem. EDIT: Here’s what I look like now. This pic is a few months old, but I don’t take a ton of shirtless pics anymore because I realized I was only doing it before as a vanity metric. This is kinda the best I got 😂 This pic is a good one because it was during the off-season when I wasn’t cutting weight for a competition. In the pic below I weigh about 20 pounds more than the pic above. I’m happier. I’m also stronger in every single major lift. I could also beat the child in the pic above’s ass 😂 The point is that optimal performance body and optimal aesthetics body aren’t always the same.

Question: How do I avoid burning out?
Answer: When I was in college, juggling an internship, school, and a semi-active social life, and training Jiu-Jitsu 2–3 times per day, 5–6 days per week to compete at an international level, I lived my life in a constant state of anxiety and fatigue. However, my anxiety had very little to do with my workload and everything to do with my crappy habits. I slept about 5 hours per night. My diet consisted of protein shakes and burritos, and my idea of “winding down” was scrolling through Instagram and comparing my success to the success of famous people on the internet. Life was exhausting. I desperately wanted a way out. So, I started Googling things that would give me a solution to my problems like “signs you’re overworking”, “symptoms of overtraining”, and “how hard should I push myself?”. My search results gave me the answers I wanted. I had all the symptoms of overtraining, I had blown past all the signs of overworking, and apparently, you’re really not supposed to push yourself that hard. So, I tried working less, but this didn’t help either. All that happened from decreasing my workload was that I anxious for different reasons and I was accomplishing less of my goals. It took 5 years of trial and error, but I’ve now realized that my “overworking” was never my problem. My problem has always been a bit more complicated than just “going too hard”. Most people get tired and assume the worst. In Jiu-Jitsu, when people tell me that they’re “overtrained”, I usually look at them skeptically. I’ve been doing Jiu-Jitsu full-time for about 6 years, and I’ve experienced true overtraining 2, maybe 3 times. These bouts happened after consecutive weeks of training 2–3 times per day, weeks of not resting my body and months of not sleeping enough. My overtraining happened after weeks and weeks and weeks of overreaching. Overreaching comes first, and overtraining follows. For the non-athletes out there, it’s overreaching at work first, and then burnout follows. However, overworking isn’t really the problem for most of us. For most of us, the problem is that we aren’t resting enough. That’s an important distinction. It’s not “overtraining” or “overworking”, it’s under-recovery. It isn’t work alone that’s hurting your life, it’s your bad habits. Understanding the difference between overworking and under-resting is the key to learning how to work smarter, maximize results, and become happier while you’re doing it. The Japanese concept of “working yourself to death”. In the 1990s, there were terrifying stories circulating of Japanese businessmen and executives that were working so many hours that they would just drop dead of bodily failure. This was called “Karoshi”, which means “overwork death”. But it wasn’t really “work” that killed them. You don’t die from typing too many words. Jogging isn’t going to kill you. What kills you is the excess of activity blended with the lack of a period of dormancy. It’s not overwork, it’s overwork paired with not sleeping, resting, and allowing the mind and body to rebuild themselves. Working out doesn’t injure your body, but training every day without having proper sleep, nutrition, and hydration will destroy your body one ligament at a time. The same is true for work or any other stressor. That’s why “optimizing productivity” is actually more about what you’re doing when you aren’t working than what you’re doing when you are working. What are you doing to balance your life when no one is watching? Work, happiness, and burnout — can you balance the 3? I love my career. I write and do Jiu-Jitsu all day. It honestly feels like I don’t have a job because my job is so directly infused with my hobbies. The fact that I get any money for doing this is absolutely baffling to me. However, I often work myself to the point where I begin to hate the very things that I love the most. Like many people in my position, my passion for my career leads to burnout because I don’t think of what I’m doing as actual work. I think I’m just having fun… until I’m fantasizing about quitting Jiu-Jitsu and abandoning writing because that would mean that I’d finally get a day off to rest. Still, if I’m being honest with myself, this isn’t because I’m working too hard. This is because I am not making an active effort to add periods of rest into my day-to-day life. I work 12–16 hour days than I am proud of admitting. I also believe that framing the issue as an overwork issue creates a victim mentality, and that makes the problem worse. Calling your work problem an “overwork” problem makes you a passive onlooker in your work life. Calling your problem an “under-recovery” problem means that there’s an opportunity for you to actively fix the way you approach work. This is motivating. It’s the same problem, and honestly, it’s the same solution. However, shifting my thinking about work and recovery has made me much better at balancing my effort in the long run. We all have 24 hours in a day, but it’s not that simple. We all have 24 hours in a day, but you should probably spend 8 of them sleeping. You should block out time to see your family, read, meditate, exercise (even if exercise is your job, active recovery is still crucial), and even just schedule time to be completely dormant and lay on your bed and watch Stranger Things or something that. You’re an animal. Even if you’re a CEO, you need to schedule some play time into your daily life. When you factor in a demanding job, the constant digital reminder that you need “a side hustle”, and all other forms of stress that we inevitably experience from the onslaught of daily activities that we put ourselves through, it’s no wonder many of us are so burnt out and exhausted all the time. But it’s not our jobs or our work that are ruining our lives, it’s the fact that our jobs and our work are our lives. It’s not overworking that makes you miserable and burnt out, it’s under-doing all of the other aspects of being human. For more articles and essays like this one, check out my newsletter :)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I become less nervous and anxious?
Answer: How to be less anxious (for free): Stop "winding down" by scrolling through social media. Scrolling through Instagram or Twitter or Facebook is easy, but that doesn’t mean it’s relaxing. In my experience, the more I scroll, the more anxious I am. Just put the phone down and do something else. Exercise every day (something difficult!). Nothing makes me feel less anxious and more at peace than pushing my body to its physical limits. Weightlifting, training Jiu-Jitsu, wrestling, or even just doing some sprints on the assault bike. Sometimes it’s fun, and other times the thought of working out sounds horrible to me. Either way, exercise gets me out of my head. I’ve been involved in sports since I was 5 years old, so exercise is just a part of who I am at this point. Every time I go too long without working out, my mental health starts to suffer. Meditate (be alone with your thoughts for so long that you guys become friends). A lot of anxious people have told me that they can’t stand the idea of being alone with their thoughts. I sympathize with this (I even sleep with a fan on at night because pure silence is too much for me), but I think when it comes to dealing with anxiety, you need to have periods where you are alone with your anxiety. Anxiety is scary because you aren’t familiar with it. Your thoughts are Write. Writing is mindfulness in motion. Take your thoughts and put them on trial by putting them on paper. You don’t even have to publish your writing, but a writing habit has been the single most important thing for me in relieving my anxiety. I’ve been writing for years, long before I started publishing. Sleep more. When I was in college, I used to wake up at 5 am every day and head off to the gym to lift weights. Then, I’d go to school from 9 am - 11:30. Then, I’d go straight to Jiu-Jitsu training at noon. Then, I’d go back to school for another class at 2:30 pm. Then, I’d go back home and work on homework, and then I go back to the gym for nighttime Jiu-Jitsu training. Then, I’d go home and work on homework again. 2 days a week, I’d only train Jiu-Jitsu once per day and work for my internship instead during the daytime. Either way, my schedule was very unsustainable. I was sleeping about 6 hours per night, and I was an anxious wreck. I couldn't form personal connections because I was so overworked and anxious Eat less bullshit. If you eat like shit, you’re going to feel like shit. There are certainly more causes of anxiety than just eating a bag of Cheetos every now and then, but your habits determine the quality of your life. Eat vegetables. Prioritize protein. Don’t overdo it with the fried stuff. Your body and mind will thank you. Talk about your feelings (looking at you, guys!). Obviously, this isn't just a problem for guys, but in my experience, most guys aren’t great at talking about their feelings. Most people struggle to articulate uncomfortable emotions. This isn’t because we’re broken. This is because we don’t practice it enough. Ideally, you do this with a therapist, but even just talking about uncomfortable things with your friends will make you feel better. Some of the most anxiety-relieving conversations I’ve had have been with friends over coffee. Feeling seen does a lot for your anxiety.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do they say that misery makes great art? How so?
Answer: They say this because they’re lazy. There are a lot of artists who are “tortured”, so people assume that misery is a requisite for creating great art. This is, frankly, some bullshit. I’ll die on this hill. I even wrote a whole article about this topic on Medium one time. I’ll link it at the end of this answer if you’d like some further reading. I didn’t think that my stance on this would be triggering, but someone read my article on how pain isn’t required for great art and told me I wasn’t a true artist and then I didn’t understand their pain. Then, they unfollowed me and deleted their Medium account. Where I come from, we call that “overreacting”. I’ve been happy and I’ve been depressed, and let me tell you, happy is always better. In fact, many times when I’m struggling with depression, I simply don't have the energy to create art. It doesn’t matter how much pain I’m going through, I can’t create when I’m too depressed to get out of bed or think coherently. Sure, pain does make a good story, but it’s not the pain that people want to read about. What makes the story great is how well you tell it. You can write and tell stories and paint and make music and also have great mental health. Believing the opposite is both self-fulfilling and it contributes to the stigma of mental illness in our society. I think we can do better. You can create great art and be happy. I’ve never met anyone who “became happy” and then suddenly became terrible at art. Pain can be a catalyst for great storytelling, but so can love, joy, or nostalgia. Don’t limit yourself by thinking that you need to be miserable to be an artist. Oh, and here’s that article I wrote a while ago, give it a read if you’d like. 😊

Question: What is the most effective martial art for real world situations?
Answer: I’m a Jiu-Jitsu person, so I’m assuming most people would think that I think the best martial art for a real fight is Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. This is unfortunately not the case. The best martial art for a real fight is “mixed martial arts”, but not in the sense you’re probably thinking of. I’m not talking about the UFC here. The best martial art for real-world situations is a study of many different martial arts, like Jiu-Jitsu, boxing, wrestling, Krav Maga, Kali, judo, or Muay Thai. Hell, even the more “out there” martial arts, like Wing Chun or Tai Chi could help benefit the quest to create more well-rounded martial artists. At the end of the day, the best martial art is the one you have the most fun practicing. The most effective martial art is a combination of all martial arts aligned with your skill set and personality. That’s it.

Question: What is Substack, and should I be writing on it?
Answer: I’ve used Substack for the last year and 3 months or so. Here’s what I learned and earned in my first year on Substack: Substack is a relatively new writing platform (founded in 2017), and most writers are either just beginning to use it, or they are not using the platform to its fullest. This article is a case study of my experience of going from a complete Substack beginner with zero readers to a regular user with hundreds of weekly readers. Hopefully, you can use my mistakes and lessons to build your own newsletter faster than I have built mine. My favorite part about Substack When I decided to start a newsletter, I originally was choosing between Substack and ConvertKit. I chose Substack because it was incredibly easy to use. It almost felt like it was too easy to use. If you have a decent internet connection, can create a free newsletter on Substack in 20 minutes. If you want to make some money, you have a premium newsletter set up in an hour. Getting started on Substack is very easy. However, getting paid on Substack is a bit more of a challenge. I’ve never liked to ask for money I’m probably never going to ask anyone to “buy me a coffee” for my writing. I want to deliver good work, and I want to be paid for good work, but I don’t want people to buy me coffee because they think I’m cute or because they feel bad for me. I’ve taught Jiu-Jitsu privates before only to realize halfway through the lesson that my client was trying to fulfill some sort of fantasy. That’s not what I want. I want to create value, or at least try to. Substack allows independent writers to create a market for their own work. This is revolutionary for indie creators. Nicolas Cole talks a lot on Twitter about “category design”. Substack allows writers to create their own category for their own specific niche (my newsletter is focused on Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu), and it allows them to be paid directly for their work. Creating a Substack newsletter is essentially like creating a publication that is all about you and your brand. For newer writers who are hustling to make a living, this is crucial. The best time to go paid is sooner than you think I started on Substack in late April/early May, but I didn’t monetize my content there for 8 months. My premium newsletter was supposed to be the new project that I began at the beginning of 2022. It was a simple business plan, and I liked it because it was easy to implement. I didn’t have to overthink anything when it came to my newsletter. Currently, my newsletter consists of one free post per week, and then, the premium section (which is available for $5 per month) gives readers an extra 5 articles per month that are focused on martial arts training and performance. It’s relatively cheap to join my premium newsletter, but this is something that doesn’t yet exist in the Jiu-Jitsu world, so that was why I chose the initial price point. Slowly, it’s been growing. In my first year of having a paid newsletter through Substack, I made about $1000 directly from the newsletter. I also used the newsletter to promote my first ebook, which I published earlier this year. My only regret has been not creating the premium newsletter sooner, because this newsletter has consistently been growing over the past few months. My favorite features on Substack In addition to being a fun way to connect with your readers, promote your products, and make some money, Substack has a few features that I’ve taken advantage of in the time that I have used the platform. Guest writers. One cool feature on Substack that I’ve enjoyed using has been the “guest post” feature. Because my newsletter is martial arts-focused, I’ve been able to get friends of mine in the martial arts community to contribute articles to my newsletter. I try to do this at least once per month so that my premium readers get fresh ideas from someone other than me. Plus, editing and working with other people who like writing is fun. Substack is becoming a platform itself. As of right now, Substack says that 30% of new free subscribers and 10% of paid subscribers are coming from the Substack platform directly. This reminds me of the early days that I was on Medium. I started as a free reader on Medium, and then, as I got more invested in the platform, I decided to pay the $5 for the monthly membership. Then, I found writers on Medium I liked, and I subscribed to their newsletters. This is the life cycle of digital writing fandom. I expect this metric to grow as Substack continues to grow in popularity and relevance. Just a few months ago, Substack launched its app. Now, you can read your favorite writer’s (and discover new writers) newsletters wherever you are, either on an app or in your email. Substack is operating with a Web3 model in a Web2 world. I believe that this could be the future of digital writing. When people ask about my “blog”, I always joke that my blog “doesn’t really exist”. My blog is a concept that exists in many different places. I’ve written on Quora for nearly a year. I’ve written on Medium for nearly 2. I’ve (regrettably) published a few articles on LinkedIn as well. The other “writing” platform that I’m very bullish on is Twitter, but that’s a separate post in itself. Of everywhere I’ve posted written content, Substack is the platform that excites me the most. There’s a lot of potential over there. I believe there’s the potential to make a career over there. Like any new platform, there are some things that could stop Substack from exploding, but the reason a writer’s Substack publications don’t grow isn’t that they’re bad writers or because Substack is a bad platform. Substack is hard for writers to grow on because there isn’t a blueprint for Substack success yet. Substack is still in its infancy, and in the next 5–10 years, I believe it could become one of the biggest writing platforms on the internet. It really comes down to how we (the writers) choose to use it. Thanks to Substack’s current business model, we have the power. My biggest hope is that this doesn’t change for the worse. If you’d like to check out my Substack, click the link below. 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the power of writing?
Answer: When I started writing, I thought I was just whining. I was doing it as therapy, not because I wanted money or because I thought I could actually make anyone think a certain way about anything. I wrote about literally whatever I wanted to I wrote about mental health. I wrote about burnout. I wrote about heartbreak and breakups and love and a lot of other things I didn’t understand. I wrote about how martial arts changed my life, gave me a career, and made me the strongest version of myself. I also wrote about how martial arts destroyed my body, made me feel like I had to adopt a bullshit “tough guy” persona, and has caused me a lot of stress over the years. I definitely thought I was a lunatic the whole damn time I was doing writing in those early days, but it was fun for me. I just kept posting, even though no one read anything I wrote in the early days. For pretty much the first 6 months of my writing career, I barely made any money from it. All I got out of those first 6 months of writing was therapy and practice. Hell, I’m still not rich from writing. However, I’ve gotten something out of writing that my younger self craved so fucking desperately. I found connection with others through writing. I get a lot of messages from people on Medium and Quora about experiences they’ve had with depersonalization, depression, and anxiety. It makes me feel like I’m not a crazy person for experiencing those things. I get messages from people who I’ve never met who also do Jiu-Jitsu, either as support or to ask training questions. It makes me feel like part of a community. I even have gotten messages and had conversations with people who I know in real life about their experiences with mental health, and they only felt comfortable sharing them after reading my writing. Some of the toughest fighters I know tell me about the moments they’ve felt the weakest. It makes me feel not alone in this crazy little world. I’m a pretty imperfect human, but the idea that my writing could make a positive impact on literally anyone’s life is crazy to me. It motivates the hell out of me to keep going. The power of writing for me is that I’ve created a community for myself that motivates me to keep going through this crazy life that I’ve chosen. The power of writing is that you can literally put words on a screen or a piece of paper, and those words can inspire people to try to live happier, healthier lives. This might sound corny to you, but to me, it’s the most important thing. If you don’t get it you won’t get it. It fucking blows my mind that anyone would get any inspiration out of anything I write, and I feel overwhelmed with gratitude by every comment and message. (If I ever miss a comment or message, I promise I’m busy or distracted or didn’t get the notification 😂) That’s why I want to send as much love as I can to everyone who reads anything I ever post, even the people who write kind of mean comments. I know it’s just cuz you’re insecure, but it still hurts my feelings. Good night. (Pic above is what I look like while reading comments on my phone)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What rank should you be to teach jiu-jitsu?
Answer: I started teaching when I was a white belt—sort of. I came into Jiu-Jitsu with a wrestling background, so as a white belt, I taught people some wrestling moves here or there before and after training. Then, at blue belt, I started training full-time and competing all over the US. I started actually learning Jiu-Jitsu. By the end of my blue belt career, despite not competing for 8 months due to injury, I was ranked in the top 10 in the world. I still didn’t teach. I wanted to, but I didn’t. I covered a class once when my coach was out of town, but I did it as a favor. I didn’t get paid. I wasn’t a teacher. I was a student and nothing but. I didn’t get paid to teach until purple belt, when I started teaching private lessons. I learned a lot about self-value, entrepreneurship, and valuing your time from this period. As a brown belt, I started teaching full-time. I taught classes (mostly kids classes) and a butt-ton of private lessons. This was when I started to consider myself a teacher. About 2 months before I got my black belt, I taught my first seminar. At black belt, I mostly wear the teacher hat than the student one, but I love the days where I can to just sit and learn. It’s a treat. It’s interesting to me that some people are so set on “becoming teachers”. Don’t focus on “becoming a good teacher”. Focus on becoming a good student. Focus on mastering the material you learn. Eventually, you’ll be a teacher and you won’t even realize it. Follow me on Twitter for more! 🥋😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Is martial arts a lifestyle?
Answer: I could have had a very normal life. My parents live relatively “normal lives”. My non martial arts friends live pretty normal lives. I had a mostly normal childhood (although, probably a bit more exposure to mental illness than the average person). Doing the normal stuff—getting a regular job, going to normal social gatherings with friends, or other normal people things (like going to the movies or the mall or whatever)—was definitely an option for me. That was going to be, until the first day I walked into a Jiu-Jitsu academy. I know it sometimes sounds like that I’m bragging when I say that I “gave up a normal life for this”, but that’s not my intention. Really, I’m just trying to understand the bizarre reality that I’ve created myself. I literally fight crazy people for money. This is my job right now. Sorry if I think it’s weird. The other thing that I think that is really important to understand that the average martial artist doesn’t go through their life the same way I do. For me, martial arts is a lifestyle because it’s literally my entire life. Jiu-Jitsu is my favorite sport, my passion, and my job. For other people, martial arts is their hobby. This means that it might be part of their lifestyle, but that doesn’t mean that their whole lifestyle is martial arts-related. The beauty of martial arts is that you get out what you put in. If you want new friends, personal development, or maybe even a job, you can get that from martial arts by investing hours upon hours of your time. If you just want to get in better shape, you get that too. It’s up to you.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What one tip changed your writing forever?
Answer: This is a kind of silly quote from a rap song, but when I applied it to my writing, it changed the way I think about “pressing publish”. For years, I was terrified of submitting any of my work to judgment. Most of the time, I was too anxious about the thought of creating writing that wasn’t good that I didn’t even write in the first place. In the past, I used to write things and get berated with the normal waves of anxiety that any writer gets: If you’ve published writing before, you’ve probably struggled with these anxieties at one point or another. If you’re a newer writer, this anxiety is especially bad. My first 89 answers on Quora had a cumulative total of 20 upvotes. I felt like I was an idiot shouting into the void. Then, I started saying to myself the same thing that Young Gangsta says in the song “Scared Money”. “Scared money don't make no money”—YG I also say this to my 10-year-old students to whom I teach Jiu-Jitsu. A lot of times they’re scared to commit when they’re shooting takedowns. But that’s the thing you have to do. You have to commit. You have to accept that you might look like an idiot. It might seem dumb to you, but I internalized this quote. I love rap (to me it’s like fun, spicy poetry), and I think there are a lot of great quotes in rap songs that most people don’t think about too deeply. Their loss. For me, I’m anxious. I get worried about what people think sometimes. The best thing I ever did for my writing was to make an active effort to get over my fear of pressing publish. Scared writers don’t make no writing. It’s simple. For more thoughts on writing, martial arts, and lifestyle design, check me out on Twitter!

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do you get dates if you're boring?
Answer: To a lot of people, I’m very boring. (Here’s my sister’s dog Winston. Luckily he doesn’t think I’m boring.) Sure, I fight people for a living, but this profession is honestly far less exciting than it sounds. The day-to-day life of an athlete is a lot of bland, monotonous routine, followed by a few brief moments of excitement. I even wrote an answer a while back about all the things I don’t do as a result of my martial arts-focused lifestyle (drinking, hooking up with people, partying, etc), and a lot of people commented saying I was lame. Check here for yourself. I get it. I am not everyone’s cup of tea. Most of my days are spent going from training sessions to private lessons to writing sessions to more training sessions, scarfing down chicken and rice and protein shakes in between each session. To a lot of people, this gets boring. But I don’t really think I’m boring. My life is more disciplined than a lot of people’s, but I’m not a blob who does nothing all day. I actually like who I am. I’m a work in progress, but I don’t really want to change my personality in order to get laid. That seems kind of unethical. I’m not 17 anymore. I’m not going to change my personality to become someone who I think girls will find more attractive than the person I actually am. I did that shit in my teens and early 20s, and it always made me feel embarrassed and icky. So, I stopped. That’s why I think “how do I stop being boring so girls will like me?” is the wrong way to look at the question. The right way to think about it is “how I do stop being insecure with who I am so I can attract the right people?” I’ve found that the more I accept who I really am and lean into being myself, the easier it is for me to attract women who actually want to date me. The best moments in relationships that I’ve had were not the moments that I felt like I was trying to impress someone with my talents or with the cash in my pocket. The best moments were the ones where I was just with another person and being my weird, disciplined self. Sure, there have been times when I’ve gone out with a girl and thought she was really attractive only to realize we were incompatible due to having different lifestyles, and that was a bummer. However, in the long run, this is really not as big of a deal as you think it’s going to be. You’ll find someone new. The best way to get dates when you’re “boring” is to like yourself for who you are so that you don’t come off like some insecure chump who’s pretending to be interesting. It’s not about being “boring” or being “exciting”, it’s about finding people who accept you for you. Think about it. The more you freak out about dating, the more challenging it is.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What’s the dumbest injury you have suffered?
Answer: I’ve been involved in combat sports for nearly 13 years. I’ve experienced a lot of injuries, and many of them are dumb. I started when I was 12, and I am about to be 25. I’ve been training through all of the “dumbest” years of my life. Here are the 2 dumbest injuries I’ve suffered, because I honestly couldn’t pick between the 2: Here’s one of the few surviving photos from my white belt days in Jiu-Jitsu—circa 2016. 1. The time I tore my labrum in high school. I wasn’t a great wrestler, but I was really tough to pin. I’d lose matches by points, but I had a sense of pride about not being about to be pinned. I had a massive ego about it. I was 16. Once, after a meaningless summertime practice, I allowed my teammate to start in any position he wanted to try and put me on my back. I knew there was no way he was going to pin me, no matter where he started. He chose a grip around my shoulder, and just seconds after my other teammate yelled “Go!” he began to crank. My shoulder popped right away. I tore the labrum in my left shoulder that day, and it hasn’t been right since. Funny enough, a few months later during a match, I tore the other laburm in my other shoulder. I have 2 torn labrums, but one could have been easily avoided. 2. The time I injured my MCL… 2 days ago. I’ve been writing a lot more the last few days because I’ve had more time. On Sunday, I was training Jiu-Jitsu. I’ve been coming back from a back injury, so I got to the gym early and had my friend who’s a PT work on my back for 20 minutes or so. Then, I began to warm up and eventually train. I took every precaution for my back, and it was feeling great. So great in fact that by the end of the training, I decided that I wanted to do some wrestling. It was going great. Me and my training partner were having some great exchanges, fun scrambles, and best of all, my back was feeling great. But my partner was defending all of my attacks on his lead leg, so I set up an attack designed for his rear leg. Oh, and the mats were slippery. As I shot in for my sweep swing, I got caught in the “no-mans land” of the sweaty man, and my knee slid further that it was supposed to. I just slipped on a sweaty mat, and just like that Pop. My knee slid too far internally and the ligament stretched out. It fuckin’ hurt, but it made me more frustrated than anything else, because it was avoidable. It’s a mild injury (likely a grade 1 MCL sprain), but it’s definitely ruined my day. Worse still a good friend is coming in town to train and teach a seminar this weekend, and I’m not sure I’ll be able to do much except take him out to dinner. Hindsight, I should have saved the wrestling for a different day, when the mats weren't slippery. These are the 2 dumbest injuries from sports that I can think of. Check me out on Twitter!

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is freedom?
Answer: Today is the 4th of July (Independence Day in America), so I thought I’d write a little about what I think freedom is. In America, we make a big fuss about having “freedom”, but we still use smartphones that basically listen to all of our conversations (I see you, targeted Instagram ads). We make a big fuss about having freedom, but recently we overturned the freedom for a woman to have an abortion. We say “freedom ain’t free”, but honestly, neither are we. What America does well is provide its citizens with the illusion of freedom. To me, freedom means that I and my family have as equal opportunities for a life of prosperity as other people. I’m a white guy, so I’ve kind of got it easy. I’ve got a lot of freedom. It’d be silly for me to stand up on a soapbox and talk about unfree I am. Most of my shackles are mental. Other people aren’t so lucky. In America, we have this thing called systemic racism. You’ve probably heard of it. Maybe your country has it too. Basically, it means that people of other races do not have access to the same schools, the same safe neighborhoods, or the same healthcare. I’m simplifying a bit, but follow along. Let’s look at my hometown of Chicago for a second so that you can see what I mean. In Chicago, we have a black female lesbian mayor right now. The first black American president came from Chicago. Nonetheless, the systemic racism in Chicago runs very deep. Historically black communities in Chicago do not have as many schools, grocery stores, or police officers (though the Chicago Police Department does have a lengthy history of racist behavior, so more police probably wouldn’t help these black neighborhoods) as more wealthy communities. Schools in historically black communities are more likely to be shut down than schools in predominantly white neighborhoods. Communities in Chicago that are historically black never have gotten the outside help that they needed when they were first formed, and as a result, they’ve struggled to keep up with other communities in terms of property value. Because of this, the communities are valued less than the wealthier neighborhoods. The result of this compounded over decades is that historically black communities are less safe, there is less opportunity for growth, and worst of all, it’s very hard for people to leave. To put it bluntly, Chicago is more dangerous right now than it's ever been, and little is being done about it because the sources of the danger primarily are in communities that have a lower value. Using the definition of freedom that I used in the opening of this piece, it’s hard to say that these communities are “free”. Today there was a mass shooting in a Suburban town called Highland Park, just a few miles north of Chicago. It was a devastating event that made national news. At the same time, there have been more than 971 shootings in Chicago this year already. I haven’t seen much in the news about that. Even more tragic is that this number is down from the pandemic. It’s really hard to stand over people and tell them to dig their way out of a hole that they didn’t put themselves in when they don’t even have a shovel. So yes, freedom exists in America. You can say pretty much whatever you want besides yelling “fire” in a crowded theatre or whatever. But at the same time, your freedom is more dictated by the things that you have than the things that you don’t. It’s tough to say that a grocery store clerk living in West Garfield Park has the same amount of freedom as a CEO living in Streeterville (an upscale neighborhood in Chicago). You can say what you want and you can vote for whoever you want, but this doesn’t make you free. These rights give you the illusion of freedom. On the 4th of July, we don’t celebrate freedom. We celebrate the thought that we are free. For a lot of people, this is good enough.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I improve my writing skills?
Answer: Writing advice on the internet is overly simplistic. This isn’t because writing is easy, it’s because writing is hard. Writing is so hard to teach that for whatever reason, most people want to be paid to teach it. Most writing advice you read on the internet is really just a sales pitch for someone’s book or writing course. I don’t (currently, time will tell if I decide to sell my soul and become a writing teacher) have a course on writing, so I’ll just give you what I have time for today. Here, I’m going to give you 5 things that will give you a jump start on improving your writing skills. They’ve all helped me. These are by no means everything you need to know about writing, but these doing 5 things will help you become a better writer. (Here’s me looking tired as fuck after a long day of writing, training Jiu-Jitsu, and dealing with my sister’s dog, who, as it turns out, doesn’t like the 4th of July weekend fireworks very much. I think this dumb selfie captures the life of a writer quite well.) Edit the living hell out of your writing. I read somewhere that writers shouldn’t worry about editing their work because it’s more important to publish imperfect work than to not publish perfect work. I agree, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t take 5 minutes out of your day to proofread what you wrote. I reread everything I write before I post it. Important pieces I read out loud to myself to ensure there is flow. Don’t be lazy. Edit. Learn how to write a title (or a headline). Whether you’re trying to write articles online or books that you sell in a store, you need to master the art of titling your work. Since I write articles, here’s a tip that I use to “drill” my headline writing skills. First, I write 5 headlines in the subject line of an email and then I email all of them to myself. Then, I refresh my email. Which email do I actually want to open? That’s how I title my work. Trial and error and experience play a factor as well. Get used to rejection, but never let it stop you. I really want to get published in some cool magazine or something like a lot of the top writers on Quora and Medium, but I have to be honest. I’m not there yet. Pitching scares the hell out of me and I’ve only mustered the courage to do it a handful of times. I’m trying to apply the same mindset to rejection in writing that I apply to losing in sports. Losing is not a sign that I am a loser, losing is an indication that I can and must improve. Don’t take rejection personally. If you do this, you will give up long before you achieve any sort of success in writing (or in anything in life, for that matter). Growth mindset all the way. Drop the “starving and tortured artist” mindset. Stephen King is one of the most successful writers in the world—ever. He’s published more books than I can count. I didn’t even know what a “novella” was until a few years ago when I decided to look through his entire bibliography. King is so prolific, and that’s what has made him so great. It’s not that he did cocaine. It’s not that he had a drinking problem. It’s that he wrote every fucking day until he was undeniably one of the best in the world. The cultural perception of writers makes us all look bad. There’s this idea that all writers are these recluses who hide in their offices and whine into their keyboards. That’s bullshit. Don’t buy into that narrative. You can write and wear Jordans. You can write and be a gym rat. You can write and have awesome mental health. Writing is a medium of expression, not a symptom of mental illness or a sign that you have no money. Making an effort to drop the “tortured/starving artist mentality” changed my life as a writer. Read, but don’t overdo it. You need to read a lot if you want to be a high-level writer. I think of reading for writing the same way that I think of doing strength and conditioning in addition to Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu training. Yes, I can write if I don’t read, but reading greatly enhances my ability to write because it clears my head, exposes me to new ideas, and gives me the framework to formulate new articles in my brain. However, you shouldn’t be reading more than you’re writing. Read every day, but you should be writing at least twice as much as you’re reading. If not, your writing will struggle to surpass the hobbyist level. These are just a few writing tips that I’ve learned from the last nearly 2 years of writing on the internet. If you found any of them helpful, make sure to check out my Twitter account below, where I share thoughts on writing nearly every day of the week. 🤓

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are 10 or fewer good habits for a 24 year old that can make life better?
Answer: I’m 24, about to be 25 in August. These are 10 habits that I’ve used to become a quick learner and a happier person. Maybe they can help you too. First, let me provide a little context on how I discovered these habits and their effectiveness for me and my growth. In November of 2021, I competed in and lost in the second round of the ADCC Trials (a qualifier for the most important submission grappling tournament in the world) in a division that had more than 150 athletes. At the time, this was the largest submission grappling tournament I had ever competed in, and I had a piss-poor performance. In April of 2022 (5 months later), I competed in the second iteration of the Trials which was far more competitive, and I took 4th place in a division that had more than 250 athletes. I came in unseeded, and I upset 3 of the top 16 seeds in the tournament. Most people saw my results and wondered, “Who is this guy and where did he come from?” I wasn’t surprised though, this was something I’d obsessed over for the 5 months in between competitions. I completely changed as an athlete in 5 months. Essentially, these are the 10 most important habits that allowed me to go from losing in the second round to placing 4th at the biggest grappling tournament in North America in just 6 months. Who knows what will happen when I try again for ADCC in 2 years. 1. Study the people you wish to be like one day. I’m obsessed with analyzing the behavior patterns of world-class athletes and writers. In time, this study makes my imitation of their behavior second nature. The longer you act like a world-class performer, the sooner you will become one. 2. Seek failure every single day. You should not push your physical limits every day, but you should fail every day. Learning to fail develops a resiliency to failure, and this resiliency makes you unbreakable. When you’ve lost every single day, you begin to understand that failure is not merely an indication of inadequacy. This frees you from the anxiety of failure and allows you to maximize your preparation and performance. 3. Specialize. In Jiu-Jitsu, there are 2 “forms” that are practiced. There is gi Jiu-Jitsu (where kimono is worn) and no-gi Jiu-Jitsu, where simple athletic wear is worn in place of the kimono. After losing in the first round of my first run at the ADCC Trials, I chose to quit training in the gi. This was met with some resistance from people close to me, but nonetheless, I specialized. This specialization took my focus and discipline to the next level. “You can be anything, but you can’t be everything.” — David Allen 4. Micro-drilling. I swear by micro-drilling in everything that I do. Micro-drilling is the habit of practicing the same activity over and over again, in complete isolation. This is a drill for drilling muscle memory in your head at a low impact, meaning that there is a low risk of burnout or injury. This will train your body and mind to instantly provide the proper reaction to the proper situation. This will take your technique (in any activity) from good to great. In sports, this makes a world of difference. In writing, the main micro-drills I use are headline writing, tweet writing, and poetry writing. 5. Mindfulness. This isn’t sexy, but getting tangible results at a world-class level rarely is. Anxiety is what destroys potential. World-class athletes lose to anxiety before they even step out to compete. Many aspiring writers never publish anything because they are too anxious about the impending results. By leaving your head, you realize all of the limiting beliefs that are holding you back. I do this through mental training and meditation. 6. Visualization. Most people don’t visualize and it shows. By now, I can always tell which competitors are visualizing their performances and which are competing just to see how they do. Those who visualize important moments act at the moment as if they have been there before. The moment is not too big for them. When the moment is not too big for you and you can function under pressure the way you do in practice, all of your isolated training and hard work is able to come to fruition. 7. Dropping my sob story. Writing is my outlet for my emotions, my anxiety, and anything else that makes me upset. I need this outlet to live a full and happy life in reality. I get everything I need to get out of my head through writing, and because of that, I’m able to go through (most of) my life without my head being full of the thoughts that hold me back from realizing my potential. If I sound whiny on the internet, it’s because I’m trying to not be whiny in real life. When the “sob story” narrative is removed from my head, I’m able to channel the mind of a “winner” who can handle adversity more efficiently than I would have ever thought possible. 8. Sacrifice. Yes. I have a habit of sacrifice. Pretty much every weekend in between the 2 ADCC Trials, I sacrificed “going out” and partying or eating unhealthily because I wanted to prove that I had the ability to perform at the highest levels of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. For the last 6 weeks of my training camp, my diet was nearly perfect. I sacrificed the possibility of getting into a serious relationship in the name of this goal because it wouldn't be fair to my potential partner. I sacrificed money and time to focus on my goal. I even quit my job. This was a temporary period of my life where intense sacrifices were required for rapid progress. 9. Chasing down the people who I wanted to learn from and be like. A few months before I went to my second attempt at the ADCC Trials, I went on a training trip to Austin, Texas, where I trained with some of the top no-gi grapplers in the world today. I also took a class from John Danaher, who is widely considered to be the best Jiu-Jitsu coach in the world today. This weekend trip made me look at my sport through a more professional lens. It was also motivating and incredibly inspiring for my work ethic to surround myself with coaches like that. It made me want to go home and work in a way that would impress them. 10. Proper nutrition, sleep, and hydration. Whether you are trying to be a world-class athlete or a world-class writer or a world-class underwater basketweaver, you must master the art of optimal physical health. Part of the reason that I had such a poor performance on my first attempt at the ADCC Trials was that I had been battling back and rib injuries for the months prior. In the second attempt, I was in good physical health, had a good weight cut, and was mentally dialed in. This made all the difference. For more articles and essays like this one, check out my newsletter below.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is your favourite memory from high school?
Answer: I fucking hated pretty much all of high school. I never felt smart enough, attractive enough, fit enough, or good enough in anything I did. I was very insecure from 14–18 until I fell in love with martial arts. I was just kind of a miserable person. I had a bad attitude about everything. However, there was one thing that I did in high school with my 3 friends, 2 of our dads, and my sister (my sea star) that I fucking loved. That thing was our Sunday wiffle ball league. Our season was 6 weekends spread out between April and mid-June. Before my senior year, my dad bought us a homerun fence that we used to play our games. It was so much fucking fun. My friends and I were way too into it. It was the chance to live out our Major League Baseball dreams that we were never going to have. The “league”, which only had 3 teams and 6 total athletes, was small, but the rivalries were intense, and everyone always looked forward to playing every weekend. There was no money on the line, just bragging rights and a plastic trophy from Party City, but no one seemed to care. We dove for fly balls, swang the little plastic bat like we were trying to hit the moon, and when someone felt there was a bad call or something unfair, there were definitely some heated moments that made us a little butthurt with each other for a while. But in the end, it was all good vibes, sunshine, and some plastic baseballs while talking shit and making jokes. It was the ultimate distraction for me from the fact I had literally no idea what I wanted to do with my life. I don’t see the wiffle ball friends much anymore, but when I do, we usually pick right back up where we left off, arguing over which team was the best, which guy had the best swing, and who threw the nastiest curve ball. The world may never know the truth, but we’ll never stop laughing about it. I don’t miss high school, but I miss Sunday wiffle ball with my friends.
