Question: What is the best way to improve life?
Answer: The best way to improve your life is to escape the trap of constantly improving yourself. Self-improvement is a dirty word. Someone called me a “self-improvement writer” the other day, and honestly, it made me feel icky. Self-improvement is a community (although, that’s putting it loosely) of people who are investing time, money, and other resources in their lives in the name of becoming “better”. However, for the most part, according to the self-improvement industry’s agenda, “improving yourself” means finding a way to better fit yourself into the damaged society around you. To put it bluntly, “improving yourself” to many people really just means getting laid more, making more money, and being more popular. It means doing all the things you probably didn’t have in high school. This says more about the society we live in than the people individually, but here’s the real problem: the “improved self” doesn’t exist. The “self” doesn’t exist. You cannot improve yourself. However, you can do something much better. Why the “self” doesn’t exist. You can improve your mental health. You can improve your physical health. These are measurable aspects of your life that you can track, study, and test theories on how to improve. The value of your “self”, on the other hand, is not measurable. Different cultures around the world have different values determining what makes a valuable human, and people are expected to conform to these idealized characters. So where’s your “self”? Is the “self” how distant you are from the ideal version of yourself that you’ve created? Is the “self” the version of what you could be that is created by your mom? Is it the version created by people around you? At the end of the day, all measures of the self are subjective. This is because, at the end of the day, the self doesn’t exist. It’s a concept we use to orient our physical bodies and our minds in the world around us. How to stop improving yourself. I’ve struggled for a long time to find a good way to “end” my self-improvement journey. The truth is that if you’re not careful, you can buy books and courses and lectures until you’re broke, broken, and more existentially lost than a 17-year-old at a Slipknot concert. To end the negative and exhausting aspects of the self-improvement journey, I’ve found that I must instead begin to improve my skills in areas of my life that actually exist. The “self” is an abstract concept, whereas things like financial literacy, physical health, mental health, or if you’re me, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu competency, are all tangible things that I can improve at. Plus, improving these skills requires what is often the antithesis of self-improvement. Self-improvement requires a lack of personal satisfaction and a desire to improve, but it does not require self-acceptance. To improve your physical health, on the other hand, you must accept that your current physical health needs to be improved. You must accept yourself and love yourself enough so that you are willing to work with yourself to take yourself to the next level. You must accept. This is the first step to hopping off the hamster wheel of self-development. Does this terminology matter? You could argue that becoming a fitter, more intelligent, and more peaceful version of yourself is self-improvement, and I actually agree with you. However, by allowing yourself to fall into the ocean of self-improvement, you run the risk of drowning. Instead of merely thinking about self-improvement as the art of improving your life, it’s far more sustainable to focus on the day-to-day improvements of our abilities in different areas of our lives. This is goal-setting in a more realistic manner. Instead of “becoming a womanizer”, this is “saying “hi” to that cute girl at the coffee shop”. By escaping self-improvement, you can begin your real life. The self-improvement trap gives us this goal of “improving yourself” without actually giving us something to shoot for. The “perfect self” doesn’t exist, because the self does not exist. As we get closer to the perfect self, the goal post is pushed back, and we’re going to feel inadequate in the same ways as before. When you focus instead on learning specific skills and achieving specific goals, you are free from the overwhelming burden of “improving yourself”. Let’s look at it from a martial arts perspective. Recently, I got my black belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. I still have bad days in the gym and I still get submitted, but over time, I have seen a tangible increase in my skills in Jiu-Jitsu. The same has been true in writing. The same is true for my physical and mental fitness. Not that I’m amazing, but I am getting better in all of these areas of my life. I have improved in many different areas, but I don’t actually feel any closer to my “ideal self”. There’s a part of me that lusts after personal development as if more cold showers or more meditation would fix everything that I still struggle with. You can get your black belt in Jiu-Jitsu, but you can never get your black belt in self-improvement. Even the people who write bestselling self-help books aren’t the “best” of all of the human beings on earth. They might be some of the best writers (you know because they’ve written a great book), but they aren’t necessarily the best people. This isn’t to say that they’re bad, but it is to say that you can’t worship someone just based on their ideas and achievements alone. The point here is that your ideal self is just as flawed as your current one. The way you improve yourself without becoming trapped is to change the metrics by which you judge your growth. Your entire life is too complicated to judge as good or bad based on a few habits (you can be addicted to cocaine and also spend your weekends volunteering at a local charity), but you can certainly measure your growth in the various aspects of your life. I know some people who are great at Jiu-Jitsu and great at their jobs, but most of their lives are unexamined. They have skills in many areas, but that doesn’t mean you would consider them to be admirable people. Most of the time, it’s too hard to make grand judgments about people’s entire lives without leaving out crucial details. Life is complicated. People are complicated. This is why self-improvement doesn’t work. You can’t fix your life with some books, some cold showers, or by waking up at 5 am. These things can help you achieve certain goals, but the reality is that a complete existence requires a great deal of time, careful examination, and a lot of work. The first step to improving something that doesn’t exist is to start improving the things that do exist. Over time, you’ll likely forget all about the illusory “ideal self” that you have constantly been striving to be. For more essays like this one, check out my newsletter.

Question: Why is it better to train martial arts without a protective cup?
Answer: If you get hit in the dingus in the street, what are you gonna do? Ask the asailant to hold on a second while you recover? You have to be prepared FOR ALL REAL LIFE SCENARIOS. In Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, most people (not all, but most) train without protective cups because the likelyhood of getting wacked in the cocker spaniel is very low. MMA fighters train and compete with cups on. Boxers train and compete with cups. Kickboxers as well. Usually, it’s only grappling athletes who do not wear cups during training because the cup restricts movement and striking is not allowed in grappling. I’ve been grappling for 13 years. I’ve only been hit in the nuts a few times.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Can you lose your black belt in martial arts?
Answer: Ugh yes. This is the worst. Sometimes, I leave it at the gym. Other times, it’s hidden under a blanket in my apartment. Once I left it at a hotel I stayed at when I was traveling for a competition. I lost that one for good. Can the black belt be taken away from you? Not… really… The belt is a concept. Even if someone says “you are no longer a black belt in my eyes”, they still cannot take away the fact that you earned your black belt. The belt is a measure of skill and a reflection of the time and effort that you have put into training. It’s also not really the point of training. Even if you commit a horrible crime or something like that, you wouldn’t lose your black belt. You’d just be a shitty human who also has a black belt in martial arts. Black belts aren’t magic. They’re mostly just to hold your jacket together and keep your pants up. Everything else is semantics.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the pros and cons of learning martial arts?
Answer: This is a good question. The pros of martial arts: you will get in shape, you will learn self-defense skills, you will build confidence, you will make friends, and you may even find a new passion or career. You could inspire people through your dedication, grit, and willingness to go the extra mile. You could transform yourself from an insecure human being with so much anxiety that even leaving the house is exhausting into someone who can teach seminars and classes to complete strangers. You will become mentally more at peace. The cons of martial arts: you will probably acquire physical injuries. You might become so obsessed with martial arts that your personal life suffers. You might decide to pursue martial arts as a career, and in the beginning, this is especially not lucrative. You might work so hard that you get burnt out, and after alienating people in the pursuit of martial arts mastery, this will make you feel especially lost and alone. The key is to know what you want out of martial arts. If you’re looking for a purpose, you can find it in martial arts. If you’re looking for a hobby or an outlet or a new skill, you can find that too. As long as you don’t allow yourself to become a slave to the martial arts culture, martial arts can be the ultimate tool for personal development. For more, follow me on Twitter.

Question: What is the better workout, hitting the gym or martial arts?
Answer: In reality, it depends on your goals. For me, the answer is both. If you train martial arts, but don’t have the physical strength to apply your technique in a live situation, your martial arts training is useless. Bruce Lee wasn’t ripped just because he knew how to throw kicks and punches, he also ran constantly and did a crap-ton of push-ups. If you lift or “workout” every day, you’re probably going to have a nice-looking body, but you won’t really learn anything or develop any skills. I love lifting weights, but I love it because lifting weights makes me stronger for martial arts. I love training martial arts, and because of my physical fitness that has been crafted in the gym, I’m strong enough and flexible enough to be able to do almost technique I need. Not everyone can say this. The best workout routine is the one you can stick to that helps you reach your goals.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why are so many successful people depressed?
Answer: Success can actually cause depression. If I had to choose between winning and losing, I’d choose to win every single time. It’s more fun to get your hand raised after a match than it is to watch the other guy get his hand raised. It’s more fun to get a gold medal than it is to get a medal that’s any other color. It’s more fun to get paid than it is to watch someone else get paid. However, at the end of the day, success in anything that you do in this life feels like a double-edged sword. When I’m entrenched in the quest of trying to become successful in what I do, my self-esteem can be more erratic than Bitcoin. For those of us who struggle with anxiety and depression, this balance can be a challenge that not many people are able to relate to. Learning to manage your mind through the ups and downs of difficult personal endeavors is crucial to longevity. Without a consistent mental approach to get through ups and downs, even your greatest wins will not sustain you. This year has been crazy for me. In early April of this year, I took 4th place in one of the largest grappling tournaments in North America. That was just the beginning of what would be one of the most exciting months of my life. Just 10 days after that crazy event in Vegas was over, I re-injured my herniated L5 vertebrae, and I went from being motivated to keep competing and proving my skills to someone who was unable to bend over to tie his shoe laces. 10 days and a full dose of Prednisone after that obnoxious injury, I competed again, and I knocked off a well-established black belt in the finals of a tournament in Minnesota to win $5000. In just a month, I had 2 of the best performances of my career thus far, along with overcoming a pretty significant injury. I felt like I could do anything. I felt like all my hard work was finally paying off, and best of all, my luck wasn’t over yet. Just a few days after that win, my coach surprised me and promoted me to black belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. 7 years of training (not to mention 6 years of wrestling before that), and all of a sudden, I was a black belt. Not to mention, I was also supposed to be one of the top up-and-coming no-gi grapplers on earth. I had gone from being a complete nobody in Jiu-Jitsu to ranked in the top 20 on FloGrappling.com— the Jiu-Jitsu world’s primary media source. Not that I’m “famous” or whatever, but this has been my goal ever since I was 19 and it was finally coming to fruition. However, these achievements didn’t come without consequences. Physically, my body was feeling worn and broken down. Mentally, I was struggling to sleep, too anxious to rest, and I was barely able to sit still long enough to work on my writing. This “amazing April” set the stage for a challenging May where the wheels started to fall off the bus for me. Burnout is a complicated creature. You’d think after having all this success and attention in April that I’d be perfectly happy with my life, but the truth is that during the latter stages of this period, all I really wanted was a break. I thought that I wanted a vacation, so after competing in another tournament in Europe in early May, I scheduled a vacation in Europe for a week and a half. I thought that this would help me heal my injuries and rest my mind, but in reality, this didn’t make me feel much better. Instead, I went from feeling overwhelmed because I was doing too much to feeling overwhelmed because I wasn’t doing anything. I came back from my fancy European vacation on the Amalfi Coast thinking that I was about to be just as motivated as I was before April, but instead, I came back feeling just as exhausted as before. Within a few weeks, I was stepping past the burnout stage of exhaustion, and I was starting to feel depressed and anxious. I had to do something. I’m trying to learn to detach from my achievements. We live in an achievement-driven culture. You’re supposed to strive for your goals because these goals help you elevate your status in the social hierarchy and help give your life purpose. You’re supposed to view yourself as a product, and you’re supposed to mold that product into the best possible version. However, the problem with this way of thinking is that your perception of your life becomes correlated to your achievements. Your work ethic becomes your identity. You start to expect fulfillment from your accomplishments, when in reality, there’s more to a fulfilling life than winning medals, making money, or gaining notoriety through what you do. After doing some deeper research, I found out that this is something that a lot of people in competitive fields like business or sports struggle with. Specifically, it’s very common for athletes to struggle with depression after experiencing the highs of exciting competition. After a competition, an athlete’s depression, fatigue, and confusion metrics increase. The brain cannot handle constant excitement, and depression is how it reacts to being overwhelmed. A lot of times, it doesn’t even matter what result you achieve in a particularly exciting event. The excitement alone is enough to shock your brain into a funk. Is there a solution? So now that we know that success (especially when it’s in intense bursts) can make you depressed, what are we supposed to do about it? Should we just stop trying to succeed? Should we just abandon the pursuit of success altogether? Should we stop caring about our results and are abilities? To put it bluntly — sort of. But the key isn’t to stop striving, the key is to learn to develop a mindset where short-term success (or failure) doesn’t affect you to the point where you are living off of the dopamine you get from an exciting event. The key is to develop a routine and lifestyle that is so sustainable that it can survive both your greatest victories and your most agonizing defeats. If you live for the win on Saturday night, you’re going to feel like crap on Monday morning, when the crowd has gone home and everyone’s forgotten your name. The most important thing that you can do is to find a support system that functions effectively when you’re on top — and when you’re not. You don’t need a “team”, you need a sense of family. You don’t need a goal, you need a sense of purpose in your life. This was something that I was trying to cultivate before my “April to remember”, but I realize now that my efforts were too little, too late. I was looking for sustainability through a lifestyle that I couldn’t sustain. Without awareness of how your efforts impact your brain chemistry, you risk remaining a slave to the unpredictable dopamine highs and lows of “the grind”. Happiness lies on the other side of emotional attachment to your results. “To be even-minded is the greatest virtue.” — Heraclitus

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What's the hardest thing about learning Jiu Jitsu?
Answer: The hardest part about learning Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu is learning that no matter how good you get in Jiu-Jitsu, someone is always better. I won a world championship when I was a purple belt, and I was tapping black belts in competition as a brown belt. By the end of my brown belt career, I was ranked in the top 15 in the world in no-gi grappling (all belts). I don’t say this to brag, I say this for context. I can confidently say I’m at least okay at Jiu-Jitsu. There are still people who beat my ass. I still lose. I still fail. I recently had the chance to train with one of my Jiu-Jitsu heroes from my blue belt days who is far more accomplished than me and a bit bigger too. He ragdolled me. It was awesome. What you have to learn is that to get better at Jiu-Jitsu, you have to seek failure. The beauty of Jiu-Jitsu is that if you are training intelligently, you are able to fail over and over again without injury. All you have to do is tap out. All you have to do is learn that you don’t know everything. This is hard for people. I know it’s not easy for me.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How could we fix toxic masculinity in children?
Answer: One way we can end toxic masculinity is by cutting the bullshit. For my entire life, what most people think of as “toxic masculinity” has been the very definition that I have used to define masculinity. From the time I was 5, I remember my father telling me the different things that “real men” do and the other things that they don’t do. When I was 11, I joined the football team in my hometown, where my coach screamed at us to “not be pussies” like that was going to finally give our team a winning record. At 12, I started wrestling. Wrestling made the football team seem soft. Wrestling taught me to be strong, fierce, and fearless. Most of all, however, wrestling taught me how to hide my feelings from the world no matter what. Wrestling gave me the tools to build a front that none of my enemies (or friends, for that matter) could see through. Looking back, it was my experience with dealing with my anxiety in wrestling that laid the foundation for my 9-month experience with derealization that made me suicidal. After this experience, I resented masculinity because it hurt my mind and made connection impossible for me. But now, I don’t think of masculinity as toxic. I struggle with insecurities sometimes, but “toxic masculinity” is not the root of my anxiety anymore. Here’s how I overcame toxic masculinity in my own mind. Brutal honesty is will make you “a real man”. “Don’t be a pussy” feels like the classic term that people use when they talk about this unhealthy form of masculine expression that makes men depressed and emotionally repressed. The phrase at this point is cliche, but people still use it all the time, so I’ll use it as an example here. In fighting, this phrase is rampant. Fighting is not exactly the most progressive community on the planet. It’s insanely blue-collar, gritty, and old-fashioned. Fighters are social outcasts in many ways. I spend every day around fighters. At this point, being “a pussy” is the most common way that we get each other to push ourselves. Call it cultural misogyny if you want (it pretty much is), but it’s such a common part of the dialect in this machismo sport that simply labeling it as such does little for finding a solution. Fighters want to be together and stronger, and we will do whatever it takes to get there. For example, I’ve lost 11 pounds this week to make weight for my competition. I’ll do whatever I have to in order to become the most dangerous version of myself in a sink-or-swim world. However, I still see the issue with constantly using derogatory slang to “improve yourself”. The solution to overcoming regressive masculinity is to learn to use specific language. For example, calling yourself “a pussy” is degrading because the culture has labeled it as such. On the other hand, calling yourself “weak and pathetic” (which is what people really mean when they talk like this) is a completely different phrase, and it almost hurts more because the fluff has been removed. Calling yourself weak and pathetic is not great self-talk, but it’s better than calling yourself a “pussy” because you have removed the derogatory slang and you’ve specifically identified the sensation that you are struggling with. What would happen if men removed the slang from their emotional discord and used honest expression? This is basic Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, and that’s the first step in the solution to the genuine problem of men’s mental health. We’re looking at this all wrong. Most of the articles that I read about toxic masculinity are ridiculous. Plenty of people argue that “toxic masculinity is a good thing” because that is what “makes men into men”. Joe Rogan has basically made a career off capitalizing on this way of thinking. Lots of other people like to use “toxic masculinity” as a buzzword to springboard rants about men in their lives who are narcissists, manipulators, or mentally ill. If you don’t believe me, enter “toxic masculinity” into the search board on this site and see how many genuinely objective essays you find. Toxic masculinity isn’t a clearly defined concept, it’s a political buzzword. As a result, it has become a term people use to provoke reactions, not a term that people use to discuss mental health. Here’s what we actually know about “the state of masculinity”: Men are nearly 3.5x more likely to die from suicide than women. The highest suicide rate by demographic is in middle-aged white men. Nearly 50% of men feel more depressed than they admit in everyday life. Most men are hiding their feelings about the state of their lives from everyone around them, but why? The current culture of masculinity doesn’t inherently create narcissists, but the current culture of masculinity is deeply incomplete. It’s not toxic, it’s undeveloped. Men don’t communicate their emotions (unless it’s clouded in bullshit as an attempt to gain social clout) and as a result, they don’t grow emotionally. Emotional intelligence is a muscle, you have to practice using it to develop it. It also helps if someone shows you how to use it. Spending your whole life never talking about emotional issues and then trying to have serious relationships, for example, is the equivalent of never working out a day in your life and then trying to bench press 200 pounds. The solution begins with an objective look at men today. I sometimes have a hard time truly understanding the state of masculinity because my days are spent around fighters and “tough guys”. Machismo culture is not “a cult”, it is a big part of my life. The guys who most people write off as “tough guys” are my best friends and let me tell you, there’s nothing magical about them. They’re just regular people who insist on taking a lot of pain in the name of their goals. As an athlete, I have to find a way to make myself as tough as possible without destroying my emotional capacity. As a coach, I have to figure out a way to do this with others. Because of this, I am deeply involved in the issue of masculinity and emotional growth up close and personal every single day. As a result, I start to see masculinity as a constant crisis. Toxic masculinity is in my freakin’ face all the time, so I can’t stop thinking about it. That also might mean that the problem isn’t as severe as I think it is, but it’s definitely a real problem that affects men from all walks of life. The solution isn’t more hard work, more self-improvement crap, or even for men to “just get a therapist”, which is what a lot of people in my life have told me. I believe that the solution to masculinity today is to analyze the culture objectively and to have honest conversations about where we are going and how this is going to impact people of all backgrounds going forward. One example of this approach that I thought was really well put together is a series that The Guardian has put together in the past few years, called “Modern Masculinity”. This series looks at men from many different walks of life. It talks about controversial issues like Jordan Peterson, self-harm, and work-life balance, and it aims to answer the question “What does it mean to be a man in the modern era?”. What makes the series special to me isn’t really the content (although I do like the content), but rather the approach that it’s taking to masculinity. Honesty is the key, and that is something many men (and even our society as a whole) have been conditioned to avoid. Being a “real man” isn’t about being a man, it’s about being real. That’s what people lack in our society. We have a society that considers appearances first and everything else second. We want to know what you look like before we care about why. We want to know what’s wrong with you before we care about why. People will tell you men are weak today because they don’t have as strong of grips or whatever other crap doesn’t really make sense in order to fit the narrative that allows them to justify their actions. As someone who can deadlift over 400 pounds and fights people for a living, let me tell you this: being a man isn’t about strength, toughness, or how much beef you eat. Being a man is just the same as being a person. It’s about being honest, genuine, and kind. True strength is the ability to be kind and honest in a world that wants you to be anything but.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What's it like to have social anxiety disorder?
Answer: When you have social anxiety, even the kindest people feel like monsters. Rejection feels like dying. It’s not just “scary”. It doesn't just “make you nervous”. Rejection scares you the same way that jumping out of an airplane scares other people. To be honest, you’d rather jump out of an airplane than talk to strangers. Social anxiety makes you a little dramatic when you’re in social situations because you interpret social situations and these extreme, life or death moments. I’ve felt this way my whole life. But most people know about social anxiety by now. Most people know about the intense fear that is paired with social anxiety. We’ve all experienced it in some way. What most people don’t know about and don’t see is what happens when this anxiety goes untreated. You don’t see what happens when people lose the fight with social anxiety, because they become recluses. Social anxiety is sad in young people, but the effects of social anxiety can be devastating on adults. People know what it’s like to feel anxious about going to a party or going on a first date, but they don’t know what it’s like to watch social anxiety destroy their family members ability to relate with even those closest to them. My social anxiety is painful, but as a young person, I’m learning the habits and tricks that will allow me to fight anxiety. My dad on the other hand hasn’t been as lucky. I have social anxiety, but I force myself to go to the gym and see my friends every day. I force myself to go to parties when I get invited even though it makes me nervous. My dad on the other hand has dealt with social anxiety for so long that even some of his friends have forgotten about him. Even his wife doesn’t bother to make time for him most of the time. He’s not just avoiding social situations anymore, he’s hiding. My dad isn’t the only person who struggles with this. People with social anxiety are smart. They hide from triggers, other people, and possible exposure of their anxiety like the plague. However, what complicates this further is that my dad is also from a generation where mental health wasn’t talked about. He doesn’t know how to talk about his anxiety. I’ve probably published enough posts online about anxiety for the both of us, but unfortunately he doesn't get to reap the benefits of my meditation practice or my public therapy sessions. He can afford therapy too if he wants to, but he’s too scared to go. He’s too socially anxious to talk about his anxiety. That, I believe, is called a Catch-22 Social anxiety leaves you petrified to make any social decisions, because every decision feels wrong. Humans are social creatures, meaning that our lives require us to be social. When you have social anxiety, even just the act of living feels wrong.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why is it important to leave your comfort zone?
Answer: It’s hard to dig deep when you don’t have to. Leaving your comfort zone pushes you to dig deep, reach new goals, and become a better version of yourself. However, a lot of people are stuck in their comfort zones and don’t even realize it. Here are 5 signs that you are too comfortable in your life: You are consistently failing the same way. In Jiu-Jitsu, in the last 6 months or so I’ve been introduced to a higher level of competition. I’m fighting better guys at more important competitions now. There’s more money on the line now. Each win and each loss means more now. I’m training more than ever, traveling, and competing more than ever, but despite (what I thought were) my best efforts, I keep losing to the same type of opponent over and over again in a very similar fashion. I have 2 choices for how I can approach these types of opponents: I can either accept that I have reached my peak, or I can search for a solution to this problem. The fact that I keep running into the same problem suggests that I have been too comfortable in my habits lately. You aren’t particularly upset with your failures. If you keep running into the same problem in your relationships, you are probably the problem. If you keep running into the same problem in relationships and you aren’t striving to change yourself, it’s because you’re in a place where change isn’t demanded of you. If you are in a place where you aren’t forced to keep striving and evolving, you are likely too comfortable. While there’s nothing inherently wrong with comfort, this comfort will be the death of your goals if you aren’t careful. You are falling back into old habits. In the fall, I moved into a new apartment in Chicago. Upon moving and immersing myself in a new environment, I entered a period of profound inspiration. During the first 4 months or so in this new location, I wrote 2 ebooks, and dozens of articles, and competed in countless martial arts tournaments. I got better at everything that I did and I had quite a bit of success. However, after a while, I started resting on my laurels. I started coasting. I was finally able to quit my job to focus on Jiu-Jitsu and writing, and I took that for granted for a few months. I started coasting both in writing and training. The result was that 4 months later (May and June), I’ve been reaping the consequences of someone who didn’t work with the same discipline and tenacity. My diet suffered, my training became unstructured, and my writing became self-indulgent. Worst of all, I began wasting a lot of time. This is a result of comfort sucking the life out of the thing inside me that was making me reach. You are going through the motions. As I’ve been falling back into the old, unproductive (and destructive) habits that I used for comfort when I was depressed and aimless a little over 2 years ago, I still haven’t actually broken my routine. I’m still relatively consistent with my writing. I’m still in the gym every day. I’m still lifting weights 3 days per week in addition to my daily Jiu-Jitsu training. The difference in motivation isn’t necessarily shown in my commitment to my routine or my daily habits, the difference in motivation is shown in the results that I’m getting from my habits. I’ve been comfortable, and as a result, while I am going through the motions of the habits that got me to where I am, I felt I was lacking the drive that pushed me to where I am. It’s not enough to work out every day. You have to push yourself in the gym to get better. It’s not enough to write every day. You have to write diligently to get better. Going through the motions is a sign of excessive comfort. New challenges do not excite you. Going into the ADCC Trials this year (one of the biggest submission wrestling tournaments in all of North America), I had never been more hungry to compete. In my mind, I was ready to die before I failed. I was beyond excited to compete. The result was that I put in hours upon hours of strenuous training, smart training, and careful study of my ga,e. I pushed my limits appropriately, rested intelligently, studied my competition, obsessed over the rules, and did everything I could to have a great performance at that competition. I took 4th out of 256. That took a lot out of me, and afterward, I never took the time to make adjustments to my approach, my environment, and my mindset so that I could continue to improve. I felt burnt out but resting wasn’t an option (more competitions were on the horizon), so instead of continuing to strive, I got comfortable. I thought that if I kept on doing what I was doing, I’d continue to have good results. I was wrong.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What’s the saddest thing you had a teacher tell you or your class?
Answer: “You’re just a jock who’s been hit on the head too many times.” My science teacher told me that in high school. Looking back, from her perspective, she was kind of right. However, I don’t think she realized the weight that her words carried. See, this wasn’t the first time a teacher threw a jab at my intelligence, but it was the last. It was the last time I allowed myself to have a personal conversation with a teacher regarding my performance. As someone who’s hyperactive (I have ADHD), my teachers always would get frustrated with my behavior and my habits, and often they’d say things that kind of hurt. However, I never let it bug me until I was 17. What my science teacher said to me wasn’t the worst thing I ever heard a teacher say, but for me, it was the last straw. I don’t mean to make this a sob story, either, because other people’s teachers have definitely said meaner things to them, but my high school science teacher was the one who made me realize how much I despise organized education. This interaction was the first time as a student that I felt more like a cog in a machine than a human trying to learn stuff. This is because when she said this to me, I was slowly opening my eyes to the fact that school wasn't the single most important factor for success in life. Long story short, my teacher said this to me because I dropped her class so that I could remain eligible for sports. Remember when I said she was kind of right? I’ll let you make the decision. It was the end of my senior year, and I had a concussion from wrestling about a month earlier. During the week and a half or so where the concussion was affecting me, I couldn’t do any school work without getting a headache. This killed my academic motivation, and it also gave me a huge pile of homework that never seemed to end. I fell behind in my classes and started to perform poorly on quizzes, tests, and assignments. My grades fell. The head injury started a cycle that lasted far longer than the concussion symptoms. I became lazy in the classroom because I was so overwhelmed. This, paired with my already stressful life as a student-athlete, gave me a whole pile of new bad habits. This was also how I learned that being lazy has consequences. Eventually, the week of the biggest wrestling meet of the season came, and I had a 57% in my science class. My bad habits bit me in the butt, and though I had a quiz that week in science and an opportunity to boost my grade, I was done. I decided to play it safe drop the class so that I would remain eligible to compete in wrestling for the remainder of the season (you needed a minimum of a 60% in all classes to compete in sports at my school and I was passing all my other classes). I did this because I didn’t believe that I had what it takes to get good grades. See, since the beginning of the school year, she’d been reminding everyone how hard her class was and how hard we’d have to work to perform well in it. She was saying this while my anxiety and academic burnout were mounting near a boiling point. I’m sure she was doing this to motivate us, but for me, a student who was on the cusp of failing the class and dealing with other things in his life (a girlfriend, a sport that I loved, mental health & family issues, etc), this broke me. I didn’t want to deal with rising academic expectations because I was so stressed, so I went to my teacher and told her that I needed to drop the class because I wanted to try to make it to state in wrestling. To me, going for glory in wrestling was for more important than a science class. That’s when she told me that I was “just a dumb jock who’d been hit in the head too many times”. It was kind of a small remark, but at the time, I was drowning in stress and completely overwhelmed in every area of my life. Wrestling was hard. I was crash dieting and and gaining and losing around 10 pounds every week so that I could make weight to compete. My girlfriend and I were fighting a lot at the time. My anxiety and depression were rearing they’re ugly heads for the first time in our relationship, and this was breaking me and my “first love” apart. Plus, I was 17, and didn’t exactly know how to handle stress. While dealing with all of that, being told I was a “dumb jock” broke me academically. I internalized this idea, and it changed the course of my life for the next 5 years. I went from a kind of forgetful (ADHD, remember) C and B student to a slacker. I managed to graduate, but I almost failed out of college (and I almost killed myself in college) because I didn't think I was worthy of a degree. I learned to hate school because I never felt like I belonged there. I began to internalize the idea that I was a quitter in all areas of my life. This interaction with my teacher also changed the scope of what I did with my life. Honestly, the reason I originally decided to try to become a professional athlete was at least in a small bit because because this random lady told me I was a dumb jock, and I didn’t think I was smart enough to do much of anything else besides grapple. Once I succeeded in my goal in a world where everyone around me was doing jobs they didn’t enjoy, I realized that maybe I wasn’t stupid. Maybe I’ve just been prioritizing a bit differently. At the time, however, I felt like a freaking lunatic. It took an ADHD diagnosis (which explains why school was so hard for me in the first place), years of writing and training martial arts, and several dozen philosophy books for me to decide that while I’m maybe not the next Einstein, I’m not a complete idiot. It took me a long time to realize that maybe my teacher was just having a bad day and took it out on me. The lesson here isn’t about me. The lesson is be careful with your words, because you never know how they can affect someone. For more stories and articles from me, check out my weekly newsletter below. 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How hard is the transition from BJJ to wrestling? Can BJJ fighters make world class wrestlers eventually?
Answer: I was a mediocre wrestler growing up, and I’ve become pretty solid at BJJ. Here’s me at my tournament on Saturday. I started wrestling when I was in the 7th grade, and I stopped when I finished my senior year of high school. I started Jiu-Jitsu just a few weeks after my wrestling season ended. I was never a very good wrestler, but I had a high level of success in Jiu-Jitsu far faster than I ever did in wrestling. Everyone I trained with in Jiu-Jitsu, thought that I was a “natural”, but coming from a wrestling background, I knew the truth. Wrestling is far tougher than Jiu-Jitsu. I’m not saying Jiu-Jitsu is easier. Jiu-Jitsu is actually far more complicated than wrestling. However, wrestling instills a completely different set of values than Jiu-Jitsu, and those values are what to me seem to create universal success in athletics. The best Jiu-Jitsu athletes that I’ve competed against in Jiu-Jitsu approach Jiu-Jitsu with the tenacity and obsessive focus that is far more common in wrestling than Jiu-Jitsu. The transition from wrestling to BJJ is difficult, but not in the way that you might think. When I came into Jiu-Jitsu, I had all of the physical attributes necessary to become a good grappler because I had already been grappling for 6 years (my last 2 years or so of wrestling were at a fairly high level, too). What I lacked what the ability to learn through failure. In wrestling, failure is not an option. Losing in wrestling is seen as worse than death. Wrestling instills a hustle in you that doesn’t stop until you are keeled over, ready to puke. Wrestling teaches you that the limits you have in your mind are mostly imaginary. Jiu-Jitsu, on the other hand, exposes your limits. In Jiu-Jitsu, getting choked out (which literally simulates death), is not seen as much as dying as it is a learning opportunity. The biggest transition for me from wrestling to Jiu-Jitsu was learning to see failure (both in training and competition) not as a reflection of my own weakness as a person, but rather as data in an equation that I was trying to solve. This “problem-solving” is a core belief in Jiu-Jitsu, and while problem-solving is a factor in wrestling, the “grit” and competitive drive that wrestlers have can easily outwork a grappler who is attempting to use his brain and nothing else to win a fight. The best grapplers in the world are intelligent athletes who have the ability to “flip the switch” into fighting mode. This is a big part of why you see many wrestlers transition well to Jiu-Jitsu, but very few BJJ athletes shift to wrestling. Another big reason that the switch from BJJ to wrestling is very uncommon is that wrestling competitions for adults are few and far between. However, the ADCC World Championships are the closest thing we have. You’ll notice that the winners of this tournament are, year after year, Jiu-Jitsu athletes who have taken the time to develop their wrestling skills.

Question: Why do people fail in life?
Answer: Here are 7 reasons why most people fail to reach their goals.  Even the happiest people I know are still looking for more out of themselves. This is the modern world for crying out loud, and the idea of “good enough” doesn’t exist (which is a different article for a different day, mind you). Everyone wants to be stronger, faster, smarter, and more efficient. Everyone wants to be the best, but most people either aren’t doing what’s necessary to be the best or they just don’t know what they’re supposed to be doing. Most people are uninformed when it comes to achieving their goals. Here are the 7 most common reasons that you aren’t where you want to be. I’ll warn you in advance, some of these pills are easier to swallow than others.  Your goal doesn’t match your output. If you want to be the best at something, you need to work like a freaking maniac. People will write that off as toxic, self-help, hustle-porn BS because the cultural narrative has (thankfully) begun to shift away toward telling people to “hustle” all the time, but the truth is that exceptionally hard work is a prerequisite for any high-level goal. If you want to be the best fighter in the world, the country, or even your own city, you have to train like a damn lunatic. You have to be the first one in the gym and the last one to leave, while also working smarter and more efficiently than your opposition. If you don’t want to do that, it’s okay, but someone will. That person will likely beat you in the long run. If you want to be great at something, prove it through sustained effort and enthusiasm.  You are in an environment that holds you back. You are not inherently a product of your environment, but if you are in a place where it feels like it’s impossible to succeed, it’s probably because the environment isn’t calibrated to help people reach the goals that you have. If you want to achieve great things, you need to surround yourself with people who, at the very least, also want to achieve great things. If you’re the most ambitious person in the room, the room will be capped at your potential. Surrounding yourself with like-minded individuals is a resource that many people take for granted.  Your mentality is based on scarcity. I never understood how the “abundance mindset [ https://www.forbes.com/sites/carolinecastrillon/2020/07/12/5-ways-to-go-from-a-scarcity-to-abundance-mindset/?sh=49235cfb1197 ]” could help me as an athlete until I herniated 2 discs and popped my rib in the same week [ https://betterhumans.pub/stop-working-so-hard-and-do-this-instead-e4a320a5c7f6 ]. As I lay on my couch that weekend thinking about the overwhelming pain in my body and how I was going to miss all of my upcoming martial arts training sessions and tournaments, I realized that I had to shift from a mindset of scarcity (where I was trying to squeeze every ounce out of every day) to a mindset of “abundance”. This seems like a hippy-dippy way to view struggle, but when you learn to see the world as a place with abundant opportunities, your view of the competitive world around you changes. I had to see that there were thousands of micro-games for me to win [ https://medium.com/mind-cafe/2-simple-mental-shifts-that-completely-changed-my-life-de7c4d3fbb86 ] in order to open my mind to the fact that catastrophic failure was a prerequisite to cataclysmic victory. The abundance mindset frees you from the perceived scarcity in opportunities for success. With practice, this can free you from the anxiety that is associated with achievement.  Because your mindset is based on scarcity, you are playing short-term games. > “Play stupid games, win stupid prizes.” — Unknown If I learned anything from competitive sports, it’s that you cannot peak all the time in anything you do. For me, this was a hard thing to expect because I compete in a sport where frequent, year-round activity is a requirement for professional success, but in sports, the truth is that it is not possible to sustain a peak for more than a few months [ https://www.trainingpeaks.com/blog/how-to-hang-on-to-peak-fitness/#:~:text=You%20can%20become%20%E2%80%9Ctoo%20fit,to%20stay%20atop%20the%20peak. ]. Improvement looks more like a mountain range than a mountain, and you must develop the peace of mind to accept that and bob and weave with the peaks and valleys. Question: What is the best way to lose weight fast?
Answer: This isn’t the answer you’re looking for, but I can teach you how to lose 10 (or more) pounds in 48 hours. Here’s me on Monday of this week. I weighed about 181 pounds. On Friday, I had to get my body weight to 171 pounds to make weight for a Jiu-Jitsu competition. In order to do this, I used a technique called “water loading [ https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCCbyPgM-9I ]” which is very popular in MMA and powerlifting for rapid water weight loss. If I’m being honest, water loading is kind of bro science, but there have been some studies to verify its effectiveness at doing its job [ https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29182412/#:~:text=Novel%20methods%20of%20acute%20weight,assessing%20the%20risk%20of%20hyponatremia. ]—the job of losing a lot of water weight really fast. Here’s how it works. NOTE: This is not a diet. This is a weight loss technique used by athletes to make weight for athletic competitions. If you are going to attempt to do something like this, I recommend doing it under a doctor’s supervision.  Sunday: Bodyweight in the morning: 181 pounds. Water consumption: 2+ gallons. Dietary changes: None. The first day of the water load is the hardest, but even then, it’s not really “difficult” per se. I went to training like normal and ate relatively normal (fruits, veggies, lean meats, and light snacks when I felt hungry), but I drank about twice the amount of water I normally do. I was constantly peeing. I had a 45-minute drive to get to and from Sunday training, and I had to stop twice on my way to the gym (and once on the way back) to pee. My body was not used to being overwhelmed with this much water. Pro-tip: I used a zero-calorie water flavor enhancer to make the 2+ gallons go down easier. My flavor enhancer had sodium in it on Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday.  Monday: Bodyweight in the morning: 183 pounds. Water consumption: 2.5 gallons Dietary changes: None. The second day was a bit more challenging. After waking up and weighing even heavier than the day prior, I felt an overwhelming wave of anxiety that I wasn’t going to make weight. I stuck with the process. For this day, I continued to pee a lot and was constantly sweating. I trained hard in the morning and then did a light drilling session with a friend in the afternoon.  Tuesday: Bodyweight in the morning: 181 pounds. Water consumption: 2.5 gallons Dietary changes: First day of eating as close to zero carbs as possible. After waking up and weighing in at 181, I felt happy that the weight at least seemed to be starting to come off, but I still knew that I had a long way to go. For food, on this day broke my 16-hour fast with a skirt steak with some eggs. For dinner, I had a ribeye with greens. I had a little beef jerky as an afternoon snack. Because the carbs were low and the water was still so high, this was the day that the peeing and sweating were the worst.  Wednesday: Bodyweight in the morning: 180.8 pounds. Water consumption: 1 gallon. Dietary changes: Zero sodium, zero carbs. After waking up on Wednesday (48 hours until weigh-in) with my body weight still in the low 180s, I hit the gym for my last real training session before the competition on Saturday. In just an hour of training, I sweat out nearly 7 pounds and I was under 175 after training. Obviously, I wasn’t where I needed to be yet, but I was definitely headed in the right direction. Food was a challenge on this day because I still wanted to keep my calories high while also having zero salt and zero carbs. I used zero-calorie, zero sodium flavor product in my water (Crystal Light), and I ate mostly unsalted nut butter and celery throughout the day. For dinner, I had an unsalted chicken breast along with some unsalted asparagus. It was really hot in Chicago on this day too, so I had an extra 12 ounces of liquid with dinner (a stevia-sweetened, zero-calorie, and zero sodium soda pop, to be specific). Mentally, I still felt pretty okay on this day. I did get a bit hungry, but it wasn’t horrible. When I got on the scale that night before bed, I weighed 179 pounds.  Thursday: Bodyweight in the morning: 176.2 Water consumption: As little as possible. Dietary changes: Zero sodium, zero carbs, and as little food as possible. This is the day that was a little “unhealthy”, but this very similar to what many combat athletes around the world go through to make weight for competitions. If I’m being honest, my process was much milder than what some athletes go through. This water loading experience was a test for me to see how I would feel. My weigh-in was the first thing on Friday morning before a Saturday competition, so my friend and I made a point to get all the weight off on Thursday so that Friday would be spent eating and recovering. All I ate on this day was a plate of nuts and a little hard candy on the plane. Upon landing in New York, I was down to 175 pounds. I was feeling a bit tired from traveling and not eating, so we hit the sauna that night to get the rest of the weight off. When I went to bed on Thursday night, I weight 171.8 pounds. I felt kind of shitty, but I knew there were only a few hours left until the process was done, so I toughed it out. Dietary changes: Nothing till weigh-in, then as many carbs as possible to reflood my system with nutrients. I woke up right on weight, so my friend and I were able to get our weigh-ins done early.
