Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How does Usain Bolt (and other athletes) mentally sustain himself?
Answer: There is one psychological trait that separates elite athletes (and other top-performing humans) from the general population. I get—top athletes seem like a different breed of human. However, there’s more to being a great athlete than just magic. The world’s greatest athletes are special, but it’s not because they can kick balls into nets or do spinning slam dunks. It’s not because they’re 7 feet tall and also it’s not because they have big muscles. Athletes are special because they can do the things they do when the pressure is on and the stakes are high. What makes an athlete special is the same thing that makes a professional musician special or a professional actor special. Knowledge is great, but success is not only about knowledge. Success is about what knowledge you can recall under pressure. Furthermore, there are certain psychological factors that inhibit and prohibit the ability to induce positive performances under a great deal of stress. Athletes transcend this, and from the outside, it can seem like superhuman behavior. In reality, all it is is the ability to access “flow” at will. Some people possess psychological advantages that allow them to better tap into the “flow” experience that you have when you’re deeply lost in an activity. Here’s how you can find flow just like a world-class athlete, even if you’re like me, and have a lot of anxiety. The anxiety-excitement trope Though you might not be able to change yourself to have the ability to perform under pressure like Michael Jordan, you can perform at a very high level under pressure even if you have a lot of anxiety. This is self-help bullshit, either. This is neuroscience. If you asked your brain, anxiety and excitement are the same damn thing. The difference is the story that is attached to the emotion and the interpretation of that story. Simply put, anxiety is negative excitement. Some people have the ability to turn a high amount of anxiety into a high amount of excitement under pressure. I’ve done this in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu and it’s helped me beat some of the best athletes in the world in my sport, but I’m not the only one. 30 to 60% of elite-level athletes experience performance anxiety. In sports, we are told that it’s bad to be nervous, but pretty much all of us are nervous at some point . What separates those who perform from those who “choke” is that those who perform are able to deflect anxiety into a positive story and become excited instead. When you are excited, it’s much easier to find flow, even if the social pressure has not been alleviated. Neuroticism and flow. According to psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, author of Flow, a flow state is “a state in which people are so involved in an activity that nothing else seems to matter; the experience is so enjoyable that people will continue to do it even at great cost, for the sheer sake of doing it”. To put it simply, flow is when you get out of your head. Flow is fun, but you aren’t thinking about how it’s fun. You’re not thinking at all, you’re just doing. Neuroticism is the enemy of flow. People who experience high levels of neuroticism struggle to induce flow and therefore they are unhappy, they don’t perform well, and they don’t relieve their anxiety or improve their skills. Neuroticism can literally ruin your life. It almost ruined mine, but I was able to create a strategy that helps me stay calm under pressure. It started with martial arts, but this strategy has slowly found it’s way into everything I do. I’m a neurotic athlete. I have anxiety. I compete in a “tough-guy” sport, so it feels a little uncomfortable to say that out loud, but it’s true. Confidence doesn’t come naturally to me. I’d rather hide in a cave than talk to a stranger. I’m anxious to order at restaurants, I’m anxious to talk to strangers, and it takes me 30 minutes to an hour at least to fall asleep every night. I experienced a 9-month episode of derealization as a result of not addressing my anxiety. This anxiety also made athletic performance at a high level impossible for me for about a decade. I couldn’t hang under pressure until I was about 20 years old because when the pressure was on, I’d always draw a blank. However, since about 2017, I’ve been able to transform my anxiety into excitement in one area of my life. Jiu-Jitsu. In Jiu-Jitsu, my anxiety and excitement are one and the same. The nervous energy that I have is transformed into excitement, and it actually makes me better at what I do and it makes it easier for me to induce flow. But unlike most athletes, I am still high in neuroticism. I’m also not alone. Millions of people have anxiety, but most of them can never compete at the level that I or other anxious athletes do. So what gives? Do I have mental superpowers? In a word, no. Instead, what I have managed to do is something that most competitive athletes manage to do without thinking, and you can do it too in any aspect of your life that you apply the skill and habits. The skill is turning anxiety into excitement through mental training habits, self-awareness of your own strengths and weaknesses, and most importantly, constantly training yourself to become less neurotic in stressful situations through constant exposure therapy. Familiarity decreases anxiety and induces excitement, and this better allows you to access a flow state. The flow state is the yellow brick road to improvement. I had a conversation with my therapist one time a few years ago when I was thinking about how I’m anxious in everything I do in my entire life, except for Jiu-Jitsu. I was thinking about how I am calm and focused when it’s time to compete, but if a waiter brought me the wrong order, I’d probably just shut up and eat what I was given. “I’m just very low in neuroticism,” I said, completely serious, recalling the time I won a world championship in Jiu-Jitsu. “No,” said my therapist, “no you’re not.” Then we both laughed. Obviously, if I was truly low in neuroticism I wouldn’t be in her office every week talking about my constant anxiety that makes my head feel like it’s splitting into a million pieces. However, I was still having positive experiences with flow states in my life because I was able to get out of my head and focus in certain situations. This was because I was spending hours and hours doing Jiu-Jitsu every day. I was also practicing staying calm under pressure because I knew that this competition anxiety was a problem for me. I approached anxiety like a challenge, not an obstacle. As I started to do this in other aspects of my life, like dating or talking to strangers, or publishing writing on the internet, I noticed my anxiety decreasing in those other areas as well. Perhaps that’s the real quality that athletes have that sets them apart. It’s not that they’re low in neuroticism, it’s not that they have the mental strength that other people don’t, and it’s not that they have grit. What separates athletes is that we learn from the time we start competing that we must view all of our challenges as challenges, not roadblocks. As an athlete, you cannot afford to develop a defeatist worldview. Imagine if more people adopted the same resolve. This article follows the basic premise of some of the ideas and stories that I wrote about in my ebook that I published earlier this year. If you want to learn more about overcoming performance anxiety in anything you do in your life (whether it’s talking to strangers or competing in martial arts), this ebook will offer you research-backed methods on how to do it. To check it out, click here.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Is it okay to be weird?
Answer: Hell yeah, it is. I was never exactly supposed to be a “fighter” of any kind. I was never supposed to be a high-level athlete. I don’t have the genetic gifts that a lot of athletes have. I’m not particularly tall, I was naturally a very chubby child, and I’m not that talented. Plus, to be completely honest with you, I had options for what I could do with my life. I never had to fight anyone. Growing up, my dad always used to tell me that fighters had “rough childhoods”, and I don’t fit the bill in that regard. My parents and I have had our moments over the years, but they love me. They didn’t beat the hell out of me. I never slept on the street except for one time on accident when I was drunk in college, but that doesn’t really count. I had a relatively nice life, and I was supposed to use that nice life to get a nice career and do all these things that people say you should do. I was supposed to do what everyone else did. I was supposed to live the way everyone around me did. Instead, at 17 years old, I walked into a martial arts gym and some random guy who I had never met took one look at me and told me that one day I could fight in the UFC. As a kid who was longing for “something more” out of his life, that was enough to send me into the crazy world I live in. I’ve never looked back. When you go your own way, you’re going to feel like a lunatic. Growing up, I always struggled with anxiety and depression. I have a little bit of trauma from some things that happened when I was a kid, and I also have a genetic disposition to anxiety and depression. I also was bullied quite a bit in middle school. I hate sharing “sob stories”, but it’s important for context. Plus, despite these experiences, I never felt like I had gone through anything “tough enough” to make me strong enough to be a fighter. The early days of my martial arts career were met with a lot of resistance from childhood friends and family members because fighting was not something that people “like me” did. The people I grew up with are getting jobs at marketing agencies and building startups. They don’t work out 3 times a day, they become doctors and lawyers and entrepreneurs. When I said I wanted to become a professional Jiu-Jitsu fighter, everyone looked at me like I was a lunatic. Hell, when people look at my cauliflower ears in the grocery store nowadays, they still look at me like I’m a lunatic. Some people fight because it’s “all they have”. For some people, fighting is the only way for them to survive. I fight because while I have more, fighting is all I want. Sometimes, you can’t seek validation from your community. The most influential book in determining the course of my life has been Friedrich Nietzsche’s Thus Spoke Zarathustra. I first the stories that the book illustrates in those silly YouTube motivational videos, but it was until I was 23 that I actually read the book. My only regret is not summoning the courage to open it’s pages sooner. At 23, I had just finished college, was looking for a job with my (useless) degree in the middle of a pandemic, I had a net worth of around $1500, and I was holding onto this dream of doing Jiu-Jitsu full-time by a thread. The pandemic thwarted all of my ambitions and dreams. The pandemic led me to do a thorough cost-benefit analysis on the question of whether or not I should commit suicide. Thanks to social distancing and quarantine, I entered the work force by myself. Literally and figuratively. Thus Spoke Zarathustra brought me back to life. Of all the philosophy I’ve read, Thus Spoke Zarathustra offers the concepts that I go back to over and over again. What the book gave me wasn’t just motivation or inspiration or whatever you get in the average self-help book. What Thus Spoke Zarathustra gave me was a radical sense of a desire for independence and autonomy. Zarathustra convinced me that it was okay that I was weird and confused. Zarathustra helped me see in myself what I previously had only seen in movie characters. Zarathustra made me feel like I was a hero. Becoming a hero. About a week ago, someone who reads my blog and follows my Jiu-Jitsu closely told me that they “want to be me”. I didn’t know how to react, so I laughed. I mean, seriously, how would you react to that statement? This the reality of doing anything differently. This is the reality of being “weird”. Being weird makes you larger than life to other people. Being weird makes you a symbol for freedom in someone’s eyes. People who are too afraid or unable to live authentically will live vicariously through you, not because they are jealous of what you have, but because they are jealous of your freedom. They don’t want your life, they want the freedom that your life has. It’s funny to me because at this point, my life has nothing to do with anyone else. I’m in too deep to go back. In a way, I didn’t choose this life. It chose me. No matter how lonely, broken, or lost I get from this unique path, I cannot in good conscious give up on this path without destroying my soul. “And once you are awake, you shall remain awake eternally. ”― Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra Being weird gives you power. Being weird gave me the power to thrive in the discomfort of the martial arts world. Being weird gave me the courage to sleep in strangers basements on training trips, to fly all the way out to California on a whim to train with my Jiu-Jitsu hero, and to start some weird little blog online where I document every single aspect of this wacky journey. Maybe you think I’m being corny, and maybe you’re right, but that doesn’t mean I’m wrong. Sometimes, the cliches become cliches because they’re just too damn true to ignore. The honest truth is that the word “weirdo” is mostly just a negatively connotated word that people use to describe people who have what they want, but are too scared to admit. I’ve always thought slam poets were weird because I’ve always been jealous of their raw authentic expression. I’ve always thought the most decorated athletes in the world were weird because I couldn’t understand their unrelenting discipline. In time, I’ve worked past those insecurities, and I’m on my way to being a weirdo who’s living exactly how he wants. In the end, it pays to be weird. Embrace it.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I deal with haters in my life who want to do harm to me?
Answer: The first thing to do is recognize which type of hater you are dealing with. These are the 5 types of haters: 1. The actual real-life crazy hater. This type of hater is, for the most part, the least dangerous hater that you are going to run into. This hater is not rational. Trolls fall into this category. Sometimes, I get comments and messages from people who don’t have communication skills or common courtesy, but they freaking hate me and everything I stand for. These haters will say ridiculous things to you. They’ll find bizarre ways to talk you down, whether it’s online or in real life. They’ll scour their mind for ways to bring you down. They’ll get creative. You must let it go. These haters suck because they say mean things to your face, but they’ll also probably move on very quickly from you and start hating something else. These people are like wasps. They can be scary, but they’re mostly harmless unless you try to chase them down.  2. The hater who is living vicariously through you. In modern society, there’s this conception that you’re supposed to follow this common path with everyone around you. You’re supposed to go to school, get a job, work like a dog, have kids, raise them, play some golf, vote Republican, and eventually sit back in the nursing home and talk about the “good ole days”, which really weren’t very good at all. After that, it’s over. You die. This path is very common, and it is one of the life paths of least resistance. If you take a different path from this, or any other counter-cultural path, you encounter a lot of adversity. You encounter haters. One of the most common types of haters is someone who follows a life path that sucks the life out of them and becomes spiteful. They cope with their deep unhappiness by hating on and obsessing over someone who is following a path that is different from their own. People have a hard time with those who are different from them, especially when they look happy.  3. The hater who is pretending to be your friend. I’ve lost a lot of friends in the last couple of years. At first, I was losing my “filler” friends in exchange for a life that I created that was full of purpose, adventure, excitement, and all that jazz. I’ve done the rant about my happiness before [ https://medium.com/mind-cafe/im-scared-of-how-happy-i-ve-been-recently-c5c6d126ea70 ]. I’ve lost a lot of people because misery loves company, and I’m not miserable. Over time, even those closest to me started to become distant. I have a completely different inner circle now than I did 12 months ago. Some of my closest friends started to become visibly jealous when I was going off to travel the world to compete in martial arts every other week while they were sitting at home working jobs that were exhausting to them. At first, they simply stopped supporting me. This made me sad because I thought I had done something wrong. In time, these people actively sought to ruin my day. That’s when I realized the problem wasn’t me (in this case, at least), it was them. It hurts to lose friends, but “friends” who do not love you through your evolution are not friends at all.  4. The hater who you love. This is the hardest hater to deal with because this is the one you want to change the most. The problem with haters is that it’s very hard to win them over. The deeper their emotional tie to you, the more true that this seems to be. It’s hard to lose friends, but losing people that you deeply love and care about because of the way that you are living your life is one of the most painful experiences that you can endure throughout your personal transformation. The glow-up hurts. I’ve been on both ends of this one, with friends, family members, and lost lovers. Nothing makes you question everyth...

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I stop feeling like a fraud?
Answer: Earlier this year, I competed in one of the biggest submission grappling tournaments in North American history, the 2022 ADCC West Coast Trials. I came in relatively unknown with a chip on my shoulder, a strong training camp, relatively few injuries, and I had a good weight cut. In my preparation, nearly everything was perfect for this tournament. I beat 2 of the top 15 grapplers in the world, and 3 of the top 15 seeds in the tournament, and I finished in 4th place in all of North America. 2 weeks later, after battling a herniated disc for a week that left me sidelined and unable bendover, much less train, I beat one of the best grapplers in the world at the weight class above me to win a $5000 cash prize. After the match, my opponent was upset with the way the match went, and he screamed at the ref “he tricked you!”, because he thought that I was stalling and that I had “tricked” the referee into thinking I wasn’t stalling. I took the guy down twice and won 4–0 fair and square, but people get emotional when $5k is on the line. I won the match, but the irony of my opponent’s statement hit me a few weeks later when I was dealing with a lot of anxiety about my future matches. I felt like a fraud. I felt like I tricked the whole damn world into thinking that I was good at Jiu-Jitsu and that in reality, I was and am trash. My results in competition indicated a high level of skill, but my tendency to focus on my imperfections first led me to berate myself even after wins against high opposition week after week while battling significant injuries. I got my hand raised a bunch, but I saw the imperfections in my performances, even if the people who support me couldn’t. Even scarier, I started to get recognized a bit for my results. People started messaging me telling me that they loved watching me compete or (even scarier) that they had watched my matches and then read my blogs. I started to feel a responsibility to these people that I didn’t even know to be someone that I was convinced that I was not capable of being. People were telling me all these awesome things, but I felt like a fraud because I didn’t know if I could keep up with the quality of writing or grappling that I was delivering. I became anxious to compete again, because it seemed that the consequences of a loss would hurt my career more than a win. I became anxious because all of a sudden, I wasn’t just a kid who no one knew and no one gave a crap about. All of a sudden, there were eyes on me, and this was scary. I’ve never liked being the center of attention, and I’ve always felt like my results are never enough. This has effected my mental health a lot in the last 3 months. Just before the ADCC Trials in April, I quit my “regular job” and went all-in on my writing/Jiu-Jitsu dream that I concocted about 2 years ago. I have no safety net, no idea what I’m doing, and I feel like my world could cave in at any moment. And yet, people tell me almost every day that they are “jealous of me”. Someone even told me that they want to be me. I thought this was funny, because I’m not that impressive and I’m not that interesting. All I really do is read, write, train Jiu-Jitsu, and teach. That’s basically it. The pressure to be this larger than life figure for people around me has been emotionally draining because it’s forced me to adopt a persona that isn’t me. I feel like a fraud because I’m trying act like how I think someone who does what I do would act. I’m not acting natural because I’m not used to the newfound pressure in my life yet. I’m more anxious than normal, and this has made me a bit depressed lately as well. I never wanted attention. I’m very anxious around lots of people. Honest to God, I just wanted be great at what I do. Mind is creating a barrier to hold me back from enjoying my success and achieving more. Imposter syndrome is just thoughts, it’s not reality. This way of thinking helps me in all areas of my life. Your anxious thoughts are real, they are valid, and I feel your pain, but your anxious thoughts are not accurate depictions of reality. They are dramatized and distorted to create discomfort. They want you to be safe, but only safe in the way that they want you to be. Anxiety is a bully in your brain that follows you around and questions everything you do. Imposter syndrome is the default mindset that you adopt as a result of this bully. However, just because you have anxious thoughts or imposter syndrome, that doesn’t mean that you are bad at what you do. Just because you don’t win all the time doesn’t mean you are a loser. Just because you have anxiety doesn’t mean that your life can’t have beauty and joy and peace. Learn to separate your thoughts from reality though mindfulness, visualization, and putting your thoughts on trial. I do this through writing a lot. Learning to question my negative thoughts has changed the course of my athletic career. It has helped me go from someone who walked onto the mat already feeling like a loser to someone who can win even when his mind is telling him that he can’t. It’s not a superpower, but sometimes, it feels like it. For more of my work, check out my newsletter below. It’s free and always will be.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some things that everyone needs to unlearn?
Answer: Here are 5 common life lessons that most people would better off unlearning. As you can see, I’m a very serious pajama fighter, so I know lots of things about life. Thing to unlearn #1: Your “happiness” is the most important thing in your life. Not only is “happiness” not the most important thing in your life, the American definition of happiness kind of sucks. It’s self-centered, it’s self-serving, and for whatever reason, it’s also something that our culture is obsessed with. However, in America, when you try to make yourself happier, you actually become less happy and more disconnected. Other cultures have different definitions of happiness, meaning that for different people around the world, different actions are taken to improve life satisfaction. One definition that I like is a popular Japanese concept called “Ikigai”. Ikigai is the intersection between achievement, collectivity, personal satisfaction, and altruism. To me, it seems more holistic and less destructive that the American “pursuit of happiness” which seems to require a great deal of suffering to achieve. I believe that the more you pursue happiness, the harder it becomes to find. Thing to unlearn #2: Working hard in silence is how you “make it in life”. When I decided that I wanted to become a Jiu-Jitsu athlete, I began an intense daily training regimen that I have kept up for more than 6 years at this point. Nearly every day has had either drilling, sparring, strength training, technical study, or all of the above. At the very least, I think about how I can get better at grappling every single day. For years, instead of telling anyone about how hard I was pushing myself, I just kept working until I was at my breaking point, and then I kept going. “Suffer in silence,” I thought, channeling my inner Muhammad Ali, “one day your work will do the talking for you.” Your work never talks for you, and people who tell you that are compensating for being bad at expressing themselves. You have to speak up for yourself, it’s the only way to do it. Working hard in silence is not a path to greatness, it’s a path to isolation, depression, and feeling forgotten. The irony is that the people telling you that they are working hard in silence are not working in silence. You wouldn’t hear them if they really were. Just talk about what you do. It’s cool. We want to hear about it. Thing to unlearn #3: Failure isn’t final, but success IS final. The movie doesn’t end when you lose and it doesn’t end when you win. The movie ends when you die. But even then, it just keeps going for everyone else. I keep signing up for these Jiu-Jitsu tournaments and writing these articles that go viral (I wrote something that in May hit 2.5 million views!), and no matter what I do, none of the success has made me “set”. I never feel at peace with my effort. There’s always another mountain to climb. No matter what I do, there’s more work to do to get to where I want to be in my life. This isn’t just because I’m young, it’s because I operate from a mindset that I am not satisfied with where I’m at and that I have to improve. I’m still hungry. You’re never going to get to the top of the mountain, and because of that, you have to decide when you’re going to stop climbing. Even after you win a world championship, set a new PR at the gym, get a girlfriend, get your black belt, or write something that you’re proud of that lots of people read, there’s more work to do. The problem isn’t the work, the problem is that you are looking at the work as a temporary sacrifice to get to a destination. The work is the destination. Thing to unlearn #4: You are a “product” of your environment. You are not inherently a product of the 5 people you spend the most time with. You are not inherently a product of your environment. You are not a product. You are a person. I guess I should save the rant about the commodification of self for another time, but people really get really hung up on finding for themselves the perfect routine, the perfect diet, and the perfect life because they want to optimize their experience. They want to maximize their meat suit. Doing this sacrifices some unique about the human experience. Trying to become a “homo Deus” distorts your experience as a homo sapien. This is inevitable. I’m not saying you shouldn't try to live a great life, I’m just saying that maybe there’s more to life than trying to optimize your optimizations. I’m saying that you have to decide how much optimization you want to go for because every action has consequences. “Your body is not a temple, it’s an amusement park. Enjoy the ride.”― Anthony Bourdain Thing to unlearn #5: Your life needs to be balanced to be happy. I’ve never met any great athletes who are “balanced people”. All the best athletes that I know all work tirelessly toward their goals, alienate people, sacrifice joy for their fulfillment, and grind for wins as their life depends on it. In high-level athletics, anything less than everything you’ve got will leave you short of your potential. Sacrificing this balance is the price of being an athlete, and I believe the same is true in other endeavors. The life of an athlete is not balanced. The sensations that athletes deal with include constant exhaustion, chronic physical pain, and the anxiety of not knowing what their next move is going to be. The life of an athlete is exciting and scary and a little bit like a choose-your-own-adventure book, but it is not balanced. I know because this is my life, and while I love it, I won’t be able to do it forever. My body won’t allow it. One day, I’ll have to live a balanced life, but that day hasn’t come yet. I love what I’m doing right now, but I don’t see myself doing this at the same level in a decade. In 5–15 years, depending on my health, success, and mindset, I will probably live a different life. Maybe I will have balance then, but I will only know that it’s balanced because I am imbalanced right now. Peace has a price. For more articles like this one, join hundreds of others and sign up for my newsletter.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What does falling in love feel like?
Answer: The short answer: falling in love feels like discovering a secret that was meant just for you. The long answer: Your eyes meet when you’re on a lunch date or when you’re sitting across from each other at the coffee shop, perhaps it isn’t the first time. This time, however, the connection is different. This time, there’s a spark. This time, you want to know more about them. Despite the fact that you’re more terrified of love than a toddler on a rollercoaster, you want to learn more about this mysteriously beautiful human that life has just gifted you. But you’re too scared. You’ve been broken too many times. You’re too anxious. You’re too this. You’re too that. Instinctively, you look away. Not because you want to, but because you’ve been conditioned to. Eye contact is hard, especially when you’re anxious. I get it. Eventually, you win that internal war in your brain and muster the courage to look at them, and they’re looking back at you, smiling. It’s not so bad after all. They accept you despite your flaws, anxieties, and the fact that sometimes, it’s hard for to you accept yourself. You don’t always think you’re worthing loving, but for whatever fucking reason, they don’t agree. This is just beginning. Over the coming weeks, the wheels start to turn. A coffee date becomes lunch, and lunch becomes dinner because, for whatever reason, that’s the order that people on the dating blogs say relationship building should go in. You learn her favorite color, her favorite food, and her favorite scent. Fast forward a few weeks and you’re kissing her goodnight in front of her apartment, wishing you could freeze the moment and come back to it later. But you can’t, so you just head home with a big stupid smile on your face. Fast forward a few months after that and you’re hanging out in each other’s apartments making coffee for each other. You’re feeding her cat in the morning while she brushes her teeth, even though you don’t particularly like the cat and the cat doesn’t really like you either. You like her, so you’ll make friends with the cat. It’s fine. You accept the cat because she likes the cat. Eventually, you start to like the cat too, even though the cat peed on you in the middle of the night last week. You forgive the cat because she loves the cat. One day, months later, while she’s sleeping on your arm that’s going numb while you’re watching Avatar together, you think to yourself, “Is this too good to be true? Did I do it?” You’re used to things being too good to be true. Still, you’re a hopeless romantic deep down, and no matter how many times your heart gets trampled on, you can’t help but imagine that maybe she’s the one. You’re still too scared to attach, though. You’re still distant. Your father taught you well. Eventually, however, there’s a moment decisive that you can’t outrun. There’s a breaking point. There’s a serious conversation where you have to make a decision. She wants to know: ”where do you see this going?” “This” is a codeword for “a relationship”. You think you want to, but you’re scared. You’re scared of being hurt again. You’re scared of accidentally hurting someone again. You’re scared, but you’re sick of being scared. An internal war commences in your mind again. The intense emotions you feel in the heat of the moment cause you to dissociate from reality again. Just like that stupid song from Shrek, your thoughts start coming and they don’t stop coming. “Is this a good idea? What if it doesn’t work? What if I fuck it up? What if she fucks it up? What if this? What if that?” Your anxiety is funny like that. It always shows up just in time to shut down any and all of your strongest emotions. However, anxiety does not define you. You’ve done the work to recognize when it’s coming, and now, you can deal with. You’re nervous about this serious conversation with this girl, but anxiety does not own you. You bring yourself back to reality by taking back the power from your anxious mind. You’re not sure, but you’re way. They say when it’s love, you “just know”, but you’ve doubted everything you can for as long as you can remember. You’re not sure you’ll ever know for sure, but you’re sure you’re going to try. You aren’t sure, but you’ve decided you’re going to give it a shot. “I love you,” you say. She says it too, and now, you’re officially in love. And that’s what falling in love feels like when you’ve got a butt-ton of anxiety.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: I am 23 years old and feel like a failure who wasted many years. What can I do to quickly get myself back on track?
Answer: I’m going to be 25 in a few months, and I also feel like a failure who has wasted so many years of his life. (Here’s me trying on a weird jacket at the mall a few weeks ago. I didn’t buy it.) I’ve achieved some stuff I guess, but I still feel like a failure. I guess just have a different set of failures from what is generally considered normal. I live in cute little a studio apartment that I pay for, I have a job that I like, I’m supposedly one of the top 20 Jiu-Jitsu competitors in the world at 170 pounds (although I get imposter syndrome about that on the daily), and I recently quit my copywriting jobs to go all-in on my dream of writing and doing Jiu-Jitsu professionally. From a work standpoint, my life is in absolute chaos. I’m working in 2 unpredictable fields (professional prizefighting and digital writing) hoping that I’ll be noticed enough to make a living just being myself. I’m great at dealing with performance anxiety, and I guess that’s a good thing because I’ve been dealing with performance anxiety 24 hours a day for the last 6 months. Everything I want to do matters. Personally, I feel even more lost. I’ve been a little lonely lately. I don’t have my best friend anymore. My relationship with my family isn’t great either right now, and I don’t see how it can improve. I can’t date because I’m too scared to open up. I was going to move to California last year, but I didn’t because I was too in love with my ex-girlfriend who was teasing me with the idea of getting back together. I stayed in Chicago primarily because I wanted to work it out with her when (unbeknownst to my naive ass) she was only talking to me again because she knew that I’d do whatever it was that she told me she needed. I was a bit of a sucker for whatever she wanted because I loved her. And because codependency is a problem for me. Mostly that. I feel like a moron who’s wasted “the best years of his life” grinding away at dreams that won’t work out. I feel like a failure who is hanging on to just one more crazy dream by a thread, and if that thread goes, I’m just going to drift off into the abyss. I feel trapped and stuck, but on the outside, I look like I’m doing great. According to Instagram, life is pretty damn good right now. The biggest perk of living in a social media age is that I always look like I'm doing great because the only pictures you’ll see on there are taken when I’m full of dopamine and endorphins. I’m not trying to bore you with my sob story, but I guess my point here is that it’s okay to feel like a failure and it’s okay to feel like you’ve wasted time. The good thing is, for the most part, if you’re still breathing, there’s still more time. Here’s how I’m trying to fix my shit: It’s not just about meditating, journaling, philosophizing, or doing whatever other self-help bullshit the people on the internet or in the books say you should do. Most of that shit doesn’t work for me (at least not by itself). The first thing that does work for me is pulling out my damn whiteboard and holding myself accountable for my goals. All of my goals, even the ones I’m embarrassed to share. I write down the things I want out of life, and then I write down the habits that I think will help me achieve them. Then, I make a little bitty spreadsheet and keep track of my progress. The second thing I do is ask for some freakin’ help. I haven’t been going to therapy as much as I used to recently because I’m trying to save money, but I’m realizing that the benefits of going to therapy (for me) outweigh the cost. When I go to therapy I am able to produce work that makes the cost of therapy negligible. When I do not go to therapy I feel like I’m a fucking lunatic with no outlet. I also make sure I talk to the friends I do have and tell them I am not doing great. I don’t really trust my family when it comes to mental health stuff (they have their own problems that make them not great resources), so I rely on my friends and my therapist for support when I’m having a hard time. It’s a very Western idea to believe that your depression is entirely your problem to fix. Try to find a community. Finally, I think deeply about the cause of my negative feelings. Sometimes, depression is genetic. Sometimes, depression is an appropriate reaction to your life. Sometimes, depression is an appropriate reaction to your interpretation of your life. If you are solving the wrong problems, you will get the wrong solutions. As for myself, after thinking about it a lot, I really think that I need an environmental change. I’ve lived in Chicago for 20 years, it might be time to move on for a bit. I never wanted to live here after college. This thought has been circulating in my mind for a long time, and I think it’s part of why it’s been so hard for me to build lasting relationships here. I think my mind has been living somewhere else for a long time now. I guess my next mission is to figure out exactly where I’m supposed to be. The nice thing about being not even 25 is that I still have time. At 23 (or really any other age besides maybe on your deathbed), so do you. At least, that’s how I’m choosing to think about it. If you’d like to read more of my work, check out my blog over on Medium. 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What's the real cause behind anxiety?
Answer: When I was a little kid, I thought I had superpowers. Something kind of like Professor X or Jean Grey from the X-Men. Many of us think we have anxiety because we are “special”. I used to think this way too. My hyperactive imagination needed to develop a way to understand the weird mental sensations I was experiencing, so it came up with superpowers (probably because I watched a lot of cartoons about superheroes). I was 5. As I’ve grown up, however, I’ve realized that my anxiety is not what makes me special, but it is something that I have to deal with. My anxiety is unique to me because it focuses on my fears and insecurities. Your anxiety is unique to you. Anxiety is funny like that. I’m pretty sure that I was born with my anxiety because both of my parents are some of the most high-strung people I’ve ever met, but even then it’s possible that I’m just anxious because I was raised around high-strung people. My parents could have been high-strung because of the way they were raised or their own traumas and stressful lives. There is no chill when I see my family, and it’s not because we don’t like each other. It’s because collectively, all 4 people in my family have brains that can’t stop seeing problems. Our minds race like it’s the Indy 500, except it’s not, it’s Christmas dinner. 4 people with anxiety can find a lot of problems in a seemingly perfect day. However, there are other causes of anxiety beyond just losing the genetic lottery. I wrote an answer the other day about how about 50% of all depression cases are caused by genetics, but anxiety seems to have a lower inheritance rate. That means that most cases of anxiety are caused by trauma, stress, and other lifestyle-related factors. That sucks, but it’s also insanely motivating, even for a genetically anxious person like me. The point here is that the cause of anxiety doesn’t matter too much, because either way, the treatment is the same. I work out every day, I meditate nearly every day, I read, I write, I surround myself with great people and I have a meaningful life full of things I love, but I am still so anxious every night that it takes 45 minutes plus to fall asleep. I don’t have insomnia, I have anxiety. When I do get to sleep, I’m out like a light. I just get anxious about falling asleep. I get anxious about everything, even when it seems like there are no problems. I find problems. I hunt them down like I’m the king of the ocean and they’re little minnows swimming. It’s easy to find problems for me. However, just because I have a genetic disposition to anxiety, doesn't mean that everything is hopeless. Sometimes I used to curse my existence because of my stupid anxious brain, but in time I’ve learned to accept who I am and how I can deal with my anxiety. Dealing with anxiety is a skill. It’s a lifestyle itself. Whatever the cause is, you have to find it. Maybe it’s unprocessed trauma. Maybe it’s overwork (I often mind this is an external anxiety cause for me). Maybe it’s an unhealthy diet or something as simple as having too much coffee. The gentle balancing act is learning to view your anxiety not as a problem to be solved but as a sensation in your mind.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some good writing tips?
Answer: Slow the hell down. The reality of being a writer/athlete is that a lot of the time, I end up writing at the gym on the mats. But hey, it beats going into an office every day. The reality of trying to do both of the things that I do at a high level is that oftentimes, I am not able to give my full attention to either activity because I am preoccupied. Sometimes, I rush through my work. It’s an ADHD thing, I guess. This has been more true than ever in the past 6 months because my Jiu-Jitsu competition and travel schedule have been crazy (I’ve gone on more than 10 trips this year in 8 states and 3 countries), and while life has been exciting and I’m grateful for that, I believe my writing has suffered. I haven’t written anything I’m really proud of for around 6 months. This was the last essay I published that I am really proud of: But why? The reason that I’m feeling less than ecstatic with my recent writing work is not that the work itself is sloppy or that the ideas are bad. If anything, the opposite is true. I’ve had some really awesome experiences this year and those experiences have led to some cool stories and some new ideas that I haven’t thought about before. The truth is that the reason I haven’t loved my recent writing is that I haven’t put the obsessive focus into it that I was putting in in the past. My recent writing feels incomplete. I’ve been focusing on maintaining a consistent flow of content, even if it has meant sacrificing quality. In other words, I’ve been writing a lot and not editing that much. The result of this has been a decrease in the quality of my writing. That is NOT what you should do to become a better writer. To become a better writer, you need to slow the hell down. Hopefully this metaphor makes sense: In Jiu-Jitsu, there are professional level athletes who train 2–3 times per day, obsessively study technique, and compete at the highest levels every few weeks. I fall into this category of Jiu-Jitsu athletes. On the other end, there are people who practice Jiu-Jitsu as a hobby. These people practice a few days a week, compete at an amateur level every so often (when their schedule allows it), and really are just doing Jiu-Jitsu because they like it. Both people might love Jiu-Jitsu, but one group is going to improve much faster than the other. Writing isn’t all that different. One of my favorite writers on Quora is Sean Kernan. I read Sean’s work on Medium and Quora, and I’ve always been blown away by his ability to deliver quality content every single day, oftentimes multiple times per day. I don’t know his daily schedule, but I’m sure Sean writes a lot, and he’s been writing a lot longer than I have. He also probably doesn’t do Jiu-Jitsu 2–3 times per day. He probably writes more instead. I, on the other hand, manage 1–2 writing sessions per day, 5–6 days per week… most of the time. This is pretty good and definitely above a hobbyist writer (writing/ghostwriting makes up 50% of my income), but I can’t expect to be at the same level as the top writers in the game off of my talent and passion alone. Writing is a skill, and Sean is one of the guys who clearly has put in the work to be great at the skill. I have mad respect for that. Sometimes, I even find myself wondering “How the hell does this guy have time to write so much good stuff? Is he a bloody genius? Is Sean Kernan not a real person? Is he a collection of people? Is he the Illuminati?” While I haven’t met Sean in real life, I’m pretty sure he’s not a magician. Instead, I think that it’s very likely that he is the writing equivalent of a high-level Jiu-Jitsu competitor. He practices his craft at a greater frequency than most other writers, and as a result, he creates great work. There’s no magic. There’s probably a bit of talent, but there’s a lot of hard work and dedication to a very difficult skill. My best writing tips, in a nutshell:

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do so many people have depression nowadays?
Answer: Maybe so many people have depression because we spent the last 2 years living inside being afraid of getting sick from our closest friends and neighbors. Maybe so many people have depression because there’s a school shooting in America every damn week and it’s all the news can make time to talk about. Maybe so many people have depression because most of our lives are spent sitting in offices, commuting in traffic, and scrolling through our phones. Maybe so many people have depression because they’ve experienced trauma or abuse. Maybe so many people have depression because they’ve seen too much of the evil in the world. Maybe so many people have depression because their lives have no love. Maybe so many people have depression because their lives have no purpose. Maybe so many people have depression because their lives have no connection. Maybe so many people have depression because depression so many people have always had depression, and now we’re just recognizing it. Sometimes, (about 50% of the time) depression is a chemical imbalance in your brain you are born with. The other 50% of the time, depression is your brain’s response to what happens in your life. Either way, it’s good to be empathetic and supportive to people who are suffering from depression. Depression is real, and a lot of people deal with it. Be kind.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the harsh truths of being a man?
Answer: If you’re a man, you’re kind of expendable. This isn’t your fault, it isn’t society’s fault, and it isn’t my fault (this isn’t even my idea). You can’t make people. You can’t carry babies. If you died, someone else could impregnate someone who could carry babies. As a man, you are biologically expendable. What are you gonna do about it? There are plenty of men in the sea. There aren’t plenty of women. Dating as a guy is kind of a nightmare. You want the best quality relationship for yourself, but in order to do so, you basically have to compete with all the other guys out there in order to prove your worth as a provider, a lover, and despite what all the anti-toxic masculinity people will say, as a man. Dating is very much a numbers game, and as a man, the odds are stacked against you. What are you going to do about it? I’m scared to post this answer. This answer is kind of different from my usual stuff because I usually try to take an uplifting stance on everything that I write. I want people to read my writing and see a better version of themselves in my words. I want my writing to give people what I’m scared I’ll never have. I’m scared to post this answer because I’m pretty sure that the truth is that most of us will never “make it”. There are too many of us and not enough spots at the top. Many of us will settle for relationships we don’t love. We’ll date people who are convenient instead of those who we want, simply because the numbers didn’t work out. We’ll get jobs that pay the rent because we failed at our dreams. We’ll live lives that are okay, because our dream lives are simply not possible for people with our attributes. The truth is that you might not get what you want. The only way that you will have a shot is by making yourself someone who’s as strong, intelligent, versatile, emotionally intelligent, and durable as possible. If you choose to compete in the competitive aspects of our society, like sports, business, or certain aspects of dating, you have to become a very strong person. The harsh reality about being a man is that if you don’t, no one will notice. They’ll just forget about you. What are you gonna do about it? I hope you’ll make the right choices.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some harsh realities of life?
Answer: No matter what you do, you’re probably going to get bored at some point. For the last year and a half or so, I’ve been obsessed with “lifestyle design”. I’ve been hustling for a sense of not just independence, but control over the way that my day-to-day life unfolds. I always hated school because, in school, you have to do whatever the teacher says. I was kind of a pain in the ass to raise because growing up I followed my own agenda. I didn’t really care much about other people’s agendas because I wanted to enforce my ideas on the world. I wanted to live the life that I wanted. I was a bit of a brat and I didn’t (and don’t) like being told what to do, so I did what I wanted to. Want to know what happened? I worked hard, made smart decisions, and got a little lucky, and around 5 years later, I built the life that I want and can do pretty much whatever I want. I worked my ass off for years to live the way I want, and all of a sudden, I realized I was bored. I got pretty much everything I wanted, and it was fucking lame. I haven’t written anything that I’m proud of in almost 6 months. Last September, I challenged myself to publish on Quora every day for 6 months, and I did it. It went pretty well. That’s how I started writing on Quora. However, over time, I got bored of writing on Quora. I got bored of answering questions every day and getting yelled at by lunatics and feeling personally responsible if someone didn’t like my work. I almost left Quora in April because I was so bored, but in the end, I decided to stick around. This didn’t help the problem though. I continued publishing every day, and the result was that my answers got worse. My writing got worse. My writing became self-centered. I wrote about me for me. I didn’t care about sharing ideas and providing value anymore. I just wanted to get shit off my chest. I didn’t care about the craft anymore. The result is that rereading my posts from the last 6 months is nauseating for me. I’ve been burnt out for a long time, and I’m just realizing it now. I’m also realizing that I dealt with this burnout completely wrong. You can’t run away from your problems. You might have seen one of my recent posts about my vacation in Europe. I told myself that I was going to Europe to travel, see some sights, eat some food, and “take a break”, but the truth is that taking a 2-week vacation did very little to ease my burnout. I didn’t feel better about my life after riding around Europe and eating gelato for 2 weeks. Crazy, isn’t it? According to psychological research, taking a vacation doesn’t fix the broken shit in your life. I’ve been burnt out of my work life back home and taking a break for 2 weeks to be chubby on the beach didn’t fix that. Getting wine drunk with strangers in Rome didn’t fix that. Going to the Amalfi Coast didn’t fix that. The only way to truly confront your problems is to actually confront them. Everything gets boring if you want to be the best. Relationships get boring if you don’t find ways to keep them exciting. Jiu-Jitsu gets boring if you don’t constantly evolve. Life gets boring if you live on auto-pilot. The conundrum that we all have to deal with is the fact that new experiences are the best way to be happy, but repetition is the best way to build skills. Do you want success or joy? Do you want skill or experience? Do you want fun or focus? In order to be your best, you need a balance of the daily monotony and discipline of improvement, mixed with the variety of travel and new experiences. You need to grind, relax, and focus, but you also need to play. You need to have a little bit of fun, and honestly, that’s something I’m not very good at. Everything gets boring, but it doesn’t have to. I can’t speak for the rest of the world, but American hustle culture is obnoxious and exhausting. It’s ridiculous. You have to grind till you die, not because you want money, not because you want success, but because you need to. In my world, your identity is based on your work ethic, and that’s a dangerous place to be. It’s a dangerous place to be because one day, you’re physically not going to be able to put in the work you want to. You won’t have the energy to write new stuff every day. You won’t have the strength to constantly improve your max effort deadlift or your personal pull-up record. One day, this life is going to pass you by, and your goals, experiences, and triumphs will be just that. Your defining moments will just be moments in history. Most people probably won’t remember you or me. How are you going to deal with that?

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What overly simplistic life advice is deceptively effective if used correctly?
Answer: “Don’t give up.” I used to hate being told to not give up. I thought that being told to keep going was annoying, obvious, and even kind of toxic. Hustle Porn tells you to not give up. Stupid posters with mountains and clouds tell you to not give up. That random dude on Quora who has tape around his head tells you not to give up in like half his answers… 😁 However, in terms of improvement and development, the single act of “not giving up” will transform your odds of success. Someone who’s impossible to kill is tough to beat. For my entire life, all I’ve really wanted to do was just give up on things. For a while, I didn’t just want to give up on things. I wanted to give up on life. I was suicidal. I hate saying that because it’s almost cliche and uninteresting that a self-help-ish writer would have a period with suicidal depression, so I’m sorry in advance for being lame and typical. I just want to be honest with you. One thing I’ve never regretted is not giving up. I’ve competed in martial arts tournaments with torn knees, torn shoulders, herniated discs, mental illness, and hardly any money in my bank account (you know, which I’d need to pay rent and other “life stuff” apart from chasing my real-life Dragon Ball quest), and 9 times out of 10, this resilience has made me happier, more confident, and yes, more successful. Days before I won my world championship in Jiu-Jitsu, I was asking my friends if it was okay if I could quit Jiu-Jitsu. I almost didn’t compete in this tournament a few weeks ago because my back was fucked, but I did anyway and I won $5000 and beat one of the top athletes in the world in my sport. Before some of the biggest moments in my life, I’ve been pacing through my mind begging for a way to escape. Begging for a way out. I’ve also given up a bunch of times, too. While some of the “quits” that I’ve made have been great for me (I’ve quit some toxic relationships and quit some careers that were going nowhere), not quitting has been far more important for developing my character and improving myself. If you quit, that’s it. But what happens if you don’t? In many cases, it’s well worth spinning the wheel and trying to find out. Here’s my newsletter. If you like my writing and want to read more, check it out. We’d love to have you. 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do people write such lengthy answers on Quora?
Answer: I started writing on Quora because in July of 2021, I read Nicolas Cole’s book, The Art and Business of Online Writing. (This is not an ad for that book btw. I don’t know Mr. Cole and apart from the $9.80 I spent on buying his book, I never have given him any of my money. The book was just a great way to learn about different places to write on the internet) That book was literally the whole reason I revisited Quora after years of barely scrolling through the site. I had created a Quora account years before, but I was too anxious to publish anything and I naively thought that writing on Quora “wouldn’t be worth it”. The reason that I decided to write on Quora in the first place was because I thought it would help me get better at writing while putting myself in front of a new audience (I started writing on Medium 10 months before I posted my first Quora answer). So yes. I started writing on Quora beacuse I wanted to advance my career. That was basically the only reason. I didn’t start writing on Quora because I’m some saint who just wants to help people. I didn’t start writing on Quora because I thought it would make me money. I started writing on Quora because I thought it would help me improve my skills to the point where I could maybe make money in the future. And? I was sort of right, but it took a while. Along the way, I’ve come to love Quora for what it really is: the Wild West of Digital Writing. Quora is not a traditional “Question and Answer” site. This isn’t a site for learning basic information. It’s not a site where you’re going to learn who the 23rd president of the United States was (although, for the sake of contradicting myself, it was Benjamin Harrison). This is a storytelling website. My first 89 Quora answers got around 6000 views cumulative (and not even 30 upvotes), and my 90th answer had several hundred thousand views and nearly 1000 upvotes in just a few days. I didn’t know much about Quora at the time, and I didn’t know much about the value that you could have on a community from a single answer, but my first “viral” answer taught me a lot about what Quora is all about. I’ve gone viral on Quora a bunch of times. One of my answers has more than 2 million views. I’ve realized however, that Quora isn’t about “going viral”. It’s not about answering questions, and it’s not even about “providing value”. The point of Quora goes deeper than whatever it is you have to say. The premise of Quora isn’t “this is what I know”. The premise of Quora is “this is what happened to me, and here’s what I learned”. Each frequently visited question has dozens (oftentimes more) replies and answers, and if you read through all of these answers, you’ll read the perspectives and stories of dozens of different individuals. Individuals. People. You’ll get a bunch of different worldviews, just from clicking on one question. If you click on “How can I overcome the fear of failure?”, you’ll see my essay on middle school wrestling. You’ll see James Altucher’s story of when he quit his job. You’ll some lady’s story of how she became a doctor. You’ll see a lot of really cool stories. The reason that people write long answers here on Quora is not to be pretentious, it’s because they’ve got stories to tell. That’s it, and that’s what I love about Quora. There are barely any rules here, barely any regular people, and a lot of people with freaking awesome stories. It’s the Wild West of Digital Writing., and I think that’s badass.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do you do what you do?
Answer: Sweat. Everything is covered in sweat. Your sweat is covered in sweat. Your training partner is wearing a blanket of sweat — a not-so-carefully concocted mixture of yours, theirs, and everyone else who’s in the room with you. The training room is hotter than Hell in the summer, but you can’t see the sun. The only “landscape” you can see is a stream of sweat in the middle of the room. It took a room full of people trying to kill each other for an hour and a half to create that stream of sweat. The “River Sweat”. There’s probably some blood in there, too, if we’re being completely honest. Oh, and by the way, the work isn’t over yet. The timer is about to go — again. All you really want is a nice hot shower, maybe a smoothie, and a cappuccino, but instead, it’s time for the next round, and instead of that shower you crave so desperately you get a special shower of more sweat from your next training partner and you lock your arms around their chest. You end up waterboarding yourself with their rashguard. This isn’t torture though, this is your dream. This is way better than the alternative. You’d rather waterboard yourself with a stranger's sweat than try to fit yourself into the social boxes created by the external world around you. “This is the dream,” you think, but part of you is begging for the training session to end. It’s begging for the grind to stop. Part of you wants a smoothie and a nap, and part of you wants to be the best. Winning this internal war is what gets you up in the morning. You’re a real weirdo, aren’t you? I know that part of you loves the pain in your joints. You love walking around the grocery store with a black eye or telling people at the office that you “have a competition this weekend, so I can’t eat cake at the office or go out for drinks”. You love being different. You love having something that makes you special. You love having “an edge”. In a society that’s based on keeping up appearances, you’ve chosen the path that cares the least about appearances. Your ears look like little chicken nuggets hanging off the sides of your head. You’re a far cry from 40, but you can’t stand up without thinking about some shooting pain in your body somewhere. You don’t think of it like this, but that pain is nothing but a whisper of your mortality on these mats. Memento mori. The world cares about keeping up with appearances, but the only appearance that matters in your world is who is tapping out who. The only appearance that you care about is the perfect execution of your techniques, day after day. Your world is laced with blood, sweat, and the constant anxiety and excitement of the next match. You hate that person who you’re going to fight, but you love them. They’re trying to take everything you’ve ever worked for, but they’re just like you. You love them for that.
