Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I be happy alone?
Answer: When I was younger, I was under the impression that I needed other people to be happy. A few years after that, I began to believe that the only person that could make me happy was myself. Now, I’ve realized that the issue isn’t so black or white. Happiness is a bit complicated. You need other people, and you also need to take care of yourself. Here’s a random picture of when my sister and I had breakfast the other day. We’re weird. People love to romanticize their independence. I know because I’ve done it, I’ve seen people around me do it, and I’m a part of a culture where being “self-sufficient” is seen as the crown jewel of personal development. If you can take care of yourself, you’re supposed to be “safe”. No one can hurt you if you “love yourself”. You’re supposed to be completely self-sufficient — financially, spiritually, emotionally, and physically. When you can take care of yourself, they say that you’re supposed to be “good”. But you’re not. For the last year, I’ve been on a personal mission to create a life where I’m able to take care of myself, feel free from dependence on others, and make a living doing what I love (while traveling, going on adventures, and doing other fun stuff). I created this life, and I’m realizing now that this was only the first step in what I’ve really wanted out of my life. I don’t want to be “happy” the way it looks in the movies. A few weeks ago, I went on a really nice vacation in Italy. I spent 2 nights in Rome, 2 in a small town off the Amalfi Coast called Vietri Sul Mare, and another one in Naples. I ate pizza, drank wine, walked around, looked at a bunch of old buildings, went to the beach, and had a really nice time. But it was insanely difficult, especially the first couple of days. I missed teaching Jiu-Jitsu. I missed training. I missed trying to improve my skills in writing and Jiu-Jitsu every day. Sure, it was nice to take a break and I made an effort to enjoy every moment of it, but I had to force myself to take a break. I had to force myself to not hustle. It was really nice to not cut weight and eat pizza every day instead of salads and chicken and broccoli, but drowning yourself in wine and carbs is not real life. Fulfillment doesn’t come from bread, fulfillment comes from doing the hard stuff to make the break. A meaningful life comes from challenges. So why shouldn’t you just work yourself into the ground? It’s actually selfish to burn yourself out. In the early parts of my career as an athlete, I felt disgustingly selfish in my own skin. I’ve always had to prioritize training and work over friendships, relationships, and even my own financial security. I’ve had to make a lot of sacrifices to be decent at what I do, and the result has been a growing amount of self-sufficiency and a great deal of anxiety. After working my butt off at martial arts for more than a decade, I’m finally good enough to make a living teaching, fighting, and now, writing about it. So why am I not happy? I think it’s because the “grind” does not make me happy. I don’t “embrace the grind” because these periods of intense internal hustle, constant pushing, and the discovery of my own limits are not what make my life meaningful. What really makes me happy is giving back. Taking care of myself is cool and essential and I’m glad that I can do that, but there’s another step. I need to give back. I need to help people. Working on myself has been lovely. I feel proud of everything I’ve accomplished, and I’m going to keep working to accomplish more, but fulfillment doesn’t come from working hard at stuff alone. Fulfillment comes from working hard at stuff and then helping other people to do the same. To me, fulfillment means making the path easier for others to follow. Give them tools you never had. Taking care of yourself is cool, but you can do better than that. Self-improvement is not inherently selfish, but a lot of people make it that way. Working on yourself and meditating and journaling and doing all that stuff is a solo activity designed to enhance your individual experience, but there’s more to life than just making your own life better. Yes, you’re born alone. Yes, you die alone. However, just about every moment that you spend engaged in this world is deeply connected with other beings. Just like on an airplane, after you can take care of yourself, it’s time to work on helping take care of other people. However, what seems like happens often is that people become obsessed with their own improvement. They become obsessed with reading self-help, they become obsessed with improving themselves, and they never take the time to actually help make the world a better place. It’s as if they have a beautiful garden in a crappy town. Here’s the truth: if the world around you is on fire, it doesn’t matter if you’re driving a Bentley or a Toyota, you’re still going to burn. Some people devote their lives to service from a young age. I don’t think that’s right either, because if you make an effort to help the world but can’t actually help yourself, you become a net negative to the world because people have to spend their own resources trying to clean up your mess. To put it in martial arts terms, if I opened up my own dojo with only 6 months of training and tried to scam people (intentionally or not, it doesn’t matter) into buying lessons from me despite my incompetence, these people would eventually have to spend more money to buy more lessons from better people to correct their bad habits. Their future instructors would have to invest more time into trying to fix them. Even if I had the best intentions, I’d be a net negative in the world because of my incompetence. That’s why you have to have both for a complete existence. You have to take care of yourself, and you have to give back to the community. At this point in time, I can’t think of a better way to live.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I overcome the fear of failure?
Answer: When I was in the 7th grade, I joined my school’s wrestling team. Here’s a picture of after my first win ever. I was 12. At first, I was resistant to the idea of joining wrestling. I didn’t love physical contact from anyone when I was younger—much less so from strangers. Most boys start wrestling because their dad wrestled, but I started because I got cut from basketball and my mom wanted me to stay active during the wintertime. “Giving wrestling a try” that year would go on to change the course of my life in a million different ways, but I had no idea of that at the time. All I knew was that wrestling was really fucking hard. All I knew was that I wasn’t cut out to be anything other than mediocre in wrestling. I finished my first season with a record of 4 wins and 14 losses. This was actually a decent record for an uncoordinated, kind of chubby 12-year-old in his first year in a contact sport, and so I decided that the next year, I’d give wrestling another go. I won 4 matches my first, the next year will be even better, right? Wrong. In my second year of wrestling, I changed teams. I didn’t know it at the time, but the new team I joined was more competitive. In 8th grade wrestling, I competed more often against better opposition. I got the results I deserved. I got my ass beat worse than I ever have in any competitive experience in my life. In the entire season, I won 4 matches (although 1 was by forfeit), and I lost 28 times. Most of my losses were by pin. I got 5 4th place medals for divisions that had 4 people. I spent most of the winter of my 8th grade wrestling season getting rag-dolled, crying in the car ride home into the slushy my parents would buy me to cheer me up, and feeling miserable, alone, and isolated. My new team didn’t accept me the way the team the year before had. I didn’t make friends on the team, and I even gained a few enemies. I assumed this was because I didn’t have any skill at wrestling, and that just made me hate wrestling even more. I wasn’t motivated by all this pain. I fucking hated the sport of wrestling. I was bullied on my team, I felt alone, and I flat out sucked at wrestling. Worst of all, my mom wouldn’t let me quit. “You have to finish out the season,” she said. So I did. Wrestling beat me down to breaking point, and then it ate me up and spat me out. I was so happy when the season ended that I cried. “Thank God I never have to do that again,” I remember thinking, on my way home from my last tournament. You think that getting rag-dolled and bullied in 8th grade would have been the end of my wrestling career, but it wasn’t. Don’t ask me why, but when high school wrestling came around, I decided to give wrestling one more go. I’m so glad I did, because wrestling in high school was way more fun, way more rewarding, and changed the course of my life. I made great friends, learned a lot about myself, and I finally felt like I belonged to something—at least sort of. Best of all, getting my ass kicked over and over again on the wrestling mats taught me a valuable lesson: Results do not define you. Losing 28 matches in a wrestling season doesn’t make you a loser. Getting picked on and bullied by the bigger kids on the wrestling team doesn’t make you a victim. No single event defines the way you define yourself more than your internal monologue. Oh, and your internal monologue can be changed. Your mind can be callused and strengthened. When I compete in Jiu-Jitsu nowadays, I feel like I have a mental edge over a lot of my opponents because I know that if I lose, my life isn’t over. This sensation gives me the courage to leave it all out there every time I step on the mat, publish an article, or try to form a personal connection. Wrestling taught me to transcend my suffering and wear my heart on my sleeve. I got pinned almost 30 times in 8th grade, and I got through that. I got groped and bullied by a kid on my wrestling team who “hated my face”, and I got through that. I made it through wrestling, and I didn’t just survive—I fought it. 10 years later, I won a world title in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. 3 years after that, I became one of the top 15 grapplers in the world in my weight class. I was never a great wrestler on the mat, but wrestling gave me the mental tools to overcome anything life throws at me, To be honest, at this point, failure feels like a minor inconvenience for me. That’s an empowering sensation.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why is social media important?
Answer: Social media is important because it’s become an essential aspect of human interaction. It’s not becoming one, it is one. If you’re under 30, it’s highly likely that social media plays a significant role in your life in some way. I realize that for me, social media might be more significant than others, because, like, my whole livelihood comes through the internet, but here are just a few examples of how the internet has changed my life in a way that previous generations might not have experience with: Each of my last 3 relationships has gone something like this: Digital communication is essential for young people nowadays because we live in a digital world. Everyone communicates digitally. Maybe it’s because we’re scared to do it in person. That’s one thing the older generation seems to think. However, I think they were scared too. Alcohol has been a social lubricant for generations. I don’t call people scared if they get drunk to talk to a girl or guy they think is attractive. Also, it’s just harder to reach people nowadays. Sometimes, I find people, and they I feel like someone’s gonna get mad at me for “sliding in people’s DMs”, but I guess I don’t feel bad about it because I don’t “slide” unless I’ve met the person in real life. Social media also plays a huge role in my work life. In my work (my writing and my Jiu-Jitsu), social media is an essential aspect of sharing and promoting my services. Posting on social media organically alone (zero paid ads) has eventually allowed me to make a full-time living as an athlete and writer. Part of that is Instagram, part of that is Medium, part is Facebook, part is Quora, and part is Substack. I’m definitely addicted to social media, but I’m also addicted to Jiu-Jitsu, coffee, writing, and The point here is that in both my personal and professional lives, social media has played an essential role. Older folks will probably tell me that my methods are corrupted. I need to get off my damn phone and get in the real world. To that, I say, “how many damn nature walks do I need to take before you understand that my world is different from yours?” What if this is just how the world is now? Quora is basically a social media site. You’re reading my post about social media, on social media. These social media sites are important, and they’re only toxic when people make them toxic. In other words: Social media is not toxic. People are toxic, on social media. Don’t act like the problems with digital communication aren’t our own damn fault. Perhaps social media is “causing depression” because we are not using it as a tool to enhance our relationships, we’re using it as a surrogate to replace them.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why should I learn martial arts?
Answer: About 2 weeks ago, I got my black belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. This is what it taught me about life and why I believe martial arts can help people to become happier, more peaceful, and more successful: It all started because of a dream I had when I was around 18. When I was 18, I thought that getting my black belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu would solve all my problems. I thought that once I had a Jiu-Jitsu black belt, I could open a gym, and then a few years of hard work after that, I’d be “set”. This was a dumb thought, but it sounded nice at the time. I thought that shortly after had my black belt, I’d get some money, get myself married, have a kid, and then from there, I could just coast until death. I was so anxious about my future at 18 that all I really wanted was a life that allowed me to coast until death. The thought of working some job I hated until I died made me furious. I just wanted to feel safe, so I entered an insanely unpredictable field and decided to make that my career. At 18, I entered the unpredictable world of combat sports, and about 7 years later (I’ll be 25 this summer), I got my black belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Here’s what I actually learned about life during these 7 years of constant training. It might not be what you expect. Anxiety is like getting squished by a giant guy. In Jiu-Jitsu, when you get your guard passed, get choked, or get put in any other bad situation, you’re forced to do something. You’re forced to deal with the fact that you are in a crappy situation. Anxiety is the same way. When you have an experience with anxiety, you have to deal with the fact that you are having a really uncomfortable experience at a really uncomfortable time. You have to deal with it. There’s nothing else you can do. Sorry for the tough love. That’s going to be a theme in this one. No matter what situation you’re in, however, whether it’s the anxiety attack at the train station, cutting those last few grams to get to 77 kilos, or getting squished by some giant dude at the gym, either way, you may be anxious, but the situation will pass. It may (and probably does) feel horrible, but anxiety always goes away. It only seems to last forever at the moment. No single thing will make your existence feel complete. When I say that Jiu-Jitsu was my entire life from 18–22, most people don’t really understand what I mean by that. Everything that I did was designed to make me a better grappler. My mindset was that everything I did either made me a better grappler or a worse one. There was no in-between. Life was black and white. Life was simple. I went to school and worked a few part-time jobs here or there, but in reality, Jiu-Jitsu was the center of everything. I picked my college based on where I was going to get the highest volume of quality training while keeping my living expenses low. I picked my major based on which major would minimize workload and allow me to train more. I made sure I was at every single major tournament. I didn’t date. I didn’t see friends. I didn’t party. I didn’t drink—except for that weird 6-month phase where I was mentally going off the rails. The point is, every single thing that I did was based on being the best possible grappler that I could be, and I was absolutely miserable. I was incomplete until I started doing this little writing thing. When I started balancing writing with Jiu-Jitsu, I was able to scratch both my intellectual and physical itches, and I began to feel more mentally complete than I’d ever felt before. This was a sensation that no amount of training could give me. If I only write, I feel like something is missing. If I only do Jiu-Jitsu, I’m incomplete as well. In order to be the most dynamic version of myself, I need to train, compete, write, teach, learn, explore, and do a bunch of other stuff besides just the things that I do well and want to be successful at. Maybe other people can be happy by doing just one thing, but I can’t find happiness through one thing alone, whether that’s a relationship, sport, hobby, job, or activity. I need balance. This balance makes me better at martial arts. Martial arts taught me this balance. Professional relationships are more personal than you think. I haven’t gelled with every Jiu-Jitsu instructor that I’ve had the chance to work with. Some instructors were too hardcore for me. Others were too laid back. Some just didn’t have the knowledge to help me reach my goals. Some were basically running cults where their students worshipped the ground they walked on. For me to find a Jiu-Jitsu instructor that I actually wanted to learn from, I had to find someone who was incredibly good at Jiu-Jitsu, but also someone who was actually the kind of person who I didn’t mind being around. This last part was a challenge, to say the least, but I’m glad I found Jeff. Jeff has been doing Jiu-Jitsu for longer than I’ve been alive. He’s competed at some of the highest levels in the sport, and he’s also coached some really high-level athletes before me. I wasn’t an experimental project for him — he taught me how to be good, and that knowledge paired with my work ethic and ability has led to a pretty dynamic combination. He’s also just a great guy. That last part is really important for me because if I was in a situation where I was unhappy and unmotivated or bothered, I wouldn’t do the work to be the best that I can be. Just having a good coach isn’t enough. You need a coach who’s right for you. This same dynamic is true for all relationships you have in life. Happiness is not from winning stuff, it’s from flow. When I was coming up in the lower belts in Jiu-Jitsu, I felt a lot of pressure to be the best all the time. This started off because I had a wrestling background and was told that wrestlers were the best grapplers, but eventually, I ended up establishing a reputation as someone who just had success in competition. I didn’t actually want to be good at first, I just thought that it was the expectation. At first, I thought I was supposed to be the best in the gym. Then the best in the city, then, the state. It created a snowball effect that led to a lot of competition anxiety and lackluster performances. Eventually, my only expectation for myself was to be the best in the world in Jiu-Jitsu. Anything else meant that was I inadequate. This pressure to be the best nearly broke me until I was able to create a mindset that could handle any pressure that was thrown at me. It made me a lot tougher at 20 than most adults, and it made me seem a lot wiser and a lot older than most people my age. But mental toughness alone does not win championships. I wasn’t happy in Jiu-Jitsu until I learned to enjoy doing Jiu-Jitsu because I enjoyed doing Jiu-Jitsu, not because of the pleasure that I felt from winning. Getting rid of the pressure I put on myself made me happier, and it also made me better at Jiu-Jitsu and more successful. A little mental work goes a long way. You will never “get there”. Training is exhausting. A few weeks ago, I took the first vacation that I’ve paid for with my Jiu-Jitsu earnings, and I have complicated feelings about going home. On one hand, I’m excited to head home and chase my next goals. On the other hand, training is hard, challenges me in every way, and destroys my ego over and over again. No matter how hard I work and how much I give, I’m never “done”. I never get to relax and rest on my laurels, and if I do, the sport passes me by. Jiu-Jitsu doesn’t love me, but I love Jiu-Jitsu. That’s why I give so much to this martial art, and that’s why I will continue to find new ways to give. I only have 5–10 more years of competing at the highest levels, and after that, I’ll have to find new things to look forward to in my life. The fleeting attempts I make at significance in competitive sports make me realize that no matter how hard I try, I’m never going to have everything I want in exactly the way I want it. Even if I reach all my goals, I’ll never be the perfect athlete that I’ve created in my mind. Fulfillment is found in the fact that perfection is impossible but improvement is always possible. Getting the black belt means a lot to me, but simply getting my black belt was never my goal. With my training regiment, it was never enough to just get that belt tied around my waist. In addition, I also have a responsibility to myself to do something with my black belt. Now that I’m a black belt, I have to give back a bit. I have to teach more. I have to fight more to show that my moves and training concepts work. I have to collect more data, put myself out there, and grind more. I have to do this because I want to do it. The only thing holding me back is the fact that it’s hard. However, that’s never stopped me before.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What was a choice you made that completely changed your life?
Answer: When I was a 18 year old blue belt in Jiu-Jitsu, I competed in a competition in Chicago called the “Chicago Open”. I lost in the round of 8 (out of 32) in one of my divisions, and I got third out of 8 in the other division. Here’s the picture. There’s me on the far right with a ginormous black eye. I didn’t really know the rules of Jiu-Jitsu. I didn’t understand why there were 2 bronze medalists (I still don’t love this aspect of BJJ tournaments, but not all organizations do “bronze medal matches”). I got smoked in the semifinals by the guy who ended up taking first, but I had so much fun competing. I loved the entire process. I loved the preparation, the focus required on game day, and the learning that came afterward. This tournament lit a fire under me to keep competing in Jiu-Jitsu. It made think “I should try and take this a little further”. On a whim, I made the choice to compete in my first ever world championships while I was a sophomore in college. I was living in Eugene, Oregon, at the time. I worked a little summer job which helped me get there, and my dad (who has been my biggest fan since I was 5 years old) flew all the way across the country to watch me fight. My logic was “I got bronze in Chicago Open, I could probably win a couple matches at Worlds if I can get to the weight class below this one”. I said “fuck it”, trained like a lunatic (twice a day, 6 days a week), and lost 15 pounds to compete in this tournament. When I was in college, I experienced pretty high-functioning severe depression, and training for this tournament was the thing that gave me hope to keep on living. All I did was train, eat salads, and cry. Between the depression, the large amount of weight I had to lose (about 15 pounds in 6 weeks), and a plethora of injuries (my cauliflower ears were formed during this training camp), I experienced a lot of adversity getting ready for my first worlds. I don’t mean to make this a sob story, I just want you to understand that I was very sad during this training camp. Very sad. I was challenged a lot, but doing this tournament gave me something to look forward to. I loved that. I still didn’t know the rules of Jiu-Jitsu, I still wasn’t very good, and I was still mentally ill, but I went out and fought like my life depended on it. I guess maybe in some ways, it did. But still, I didn’t expect to win. I didn’t care much about the result. Honestly, I just wanted to win one match. That was it. The day of the tournament finally came, and I took bronze again. I got bronze at Worlds on my first try. Here’s me examining the medal like a kid looking at a new toy. I felt arrogant, but for the first time in my life, I had this thought: “Wait, am I… good at this?” This achievement was small in comparison to everything that has happened since (I was only a blue belt), but this achievement created a snowball effect that has completely changed the trajectory of my life. This was the first time that I ever felt inspired by my own hard work and sacrifice. This was the first time that I felt like all the torture I put myself through in training was worth it. This achievement made me want to give more to my sport. This was when I decided that Jiu-Jitsu was going to be my life, and I was going to do literally everything I could to make that happen. I was 19 and I had no idea what I was doing, but I knew that I could do Jiu-Jitsu. I knew that at the very least, I could be a good grappler. In time, doing Jiu-Jitsu has taught me so much about life, being a better person, and developing myself into someone I actually like being, but it hasn’t been easy. Especially around the times that the pictures above were taken, I felt like quitting all the time. But I didn’t because I loved it. Not quitting was easy, but sometimes it felt like giving up on my dreams was what I was “supposed to do”. Now, I’m a black belt and Jiu-Jitsu is my job. It’s all because at 19, after getting a bronze medal in a random tournament in Chicago, I made a choice to see if I could do “a little bit better”. About a million “a-little-bit-better’s” later, here we are.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How much does social anxiety interfere with your life?
Answer: For most of my life, I’ve been a bit of a late bloomer. This is primarily because I have a lot of anxiety. It takes me a bit of extra time to get started with things. I hesitate.I’m nervous all the freaking time. I get nervous before competing in martial arts, I get nervous before talking to strangers, and I even get nervous before writing.I I was solo-traveling internationally for the first time ever a few weeks ago, and it scared the living hell out of me. I was in a country where I didn’t speak the language, didn’t know anyone, and I had literally no idea what I’m going to do about it. It was very scary, but it’s also okay. I’ve realized that the truth is that, at the end of the day, the only thing that is really holding me back from having a good experience is the fact that I have anxiety. Everything else is minutiae. Anxiety is the only thing holding me back, and this is what I need to do about it. Scary stuff isn’t always difficult. Last week, I had to cut about 10 pounds in 5 days in order to make weight for my Jiu-Jitsu competition in Poland. I had to fly all the across the world, find and train in gyms that I have never been to before, and then fight against some of the best guys out there. No thanks to the jet lag from flying, I had a really hard time managing my weight for the competition this weekend. It was probably the most challenging weight cut of my life, and I’ve been doing this for a long time. I’ve cut weight hundreds of times, but last weekend, I almost didn’t make it. I was so hungry I couldn’t sleep, so dehydrated that even standing was a challenge, and I was already jet-lagged from the 8-hour time shift between my hometown of Chicago and Poznan, Poland, where the competition was being held.I didn’t eat anything on Thursday or Friday of last week (except for 2 protein bars!), I barely had any water, and I spent a whole hour in the sauna on Friday night. I still had to wake up and run (and spit, which is extra fun) off an entire pound when I woke up on the morning of the competition.I did everything wrong during my first international weight cut, and my body let me know that it was unhappy. I was so miserable that Friday night I was literally wishing that I could get hit by a car so that the weight cut would be ended due to injury. Even after I weighed in successfully, I couldn’t actually eat a meal for nearly 6 hours. I was forced to sip water and the Polish brand of Gatorade and nibble on bananas. This is a physical hell that is common in my sport, but for me, compared to talking to strangers, this was easy for me.I have social anxiety. Welcome to the wacky fuck-space that is my head. Easier, but not better. When I was in the late stages of cutting weight last week, I kept thinking about how terrible what I was doing was for my body.I could feel myself becoming weaker, more dehydrated, and even sicker. But for me, the physical torture is nothing compared to my actual fears. No, I’m not a masochist. I don’t enjoy cutting weight. I don’t enjoy getting beat up. I just would rather cut weight, get beat up, and fight strangers in massive martial arts tournaments than I would go into a bakery in a country where I don’t speak the language. The former is easy. The latter makes me have panic attacks. Asking for directions to the bathroom is a thought that keeps me up at night, while when it comes to fighting in martial arts, I’m as cool as a cucumber. This is a weird problem that I’m dealing with, but dealing with has made me realize that my biggest problem is not what I thought my biggest problem was. Anxiety doesn’t know logic. Anxiety is not a reasonable disorder. It’s not normal. I love the way that we talk about mental health nowadays. It’s inclusive, it’s calming, and it makes me feel more “safe”, but it’s also a bit misleading. The way that people talk about anxiety nowadays completely ignores the fact that experiences with mental health are a spectrum. It tells us that it’s normal to deal with and experience anxiety, but it does not tell us that our experiences with anxiety can be improved or relieved.Inadvertently, the way that we talk about anxiety nowadays is distorted with a defeatist worldview, and the result is that there are a lot of people who are battling anxiety under the impression that there is no way that they can beat anxiety. We feel like dealing with mental health is a losing battle. We’re told to fight our mental health symptoms, but we’re not told that we can win that fight.What if anxiety was your only problem? When I compete in martial arts, I deal with a lot of anxiety still, despite the fact that I appear calm and confident. This is because I do a lot of mental training for competitive situations. My anxiety attempts to protect me by telling me that I don’t have the skills to win. It tells me that I am not tough enough to make weight. It tells me that I’m not strong enough to defeat my opponent. It tells me that my cardio isn’t good enough to last for the entirety of a 9-minute match. Eventually, I’ve to realize that all of these doubts were thoughts in my mind. They were not accurate depictions of reality. My anxiety was painful and uncomfortable, but it was not based on reality. It was based on my insecurities. Anxiety knows that I want to do well in life, so anxiety tells me that I can’t do well in life. Anxiety is a bully in my brain that follows me around and tells me that I’m terrible at everything that I put my mind to. Realizing that is the first step to actually dealing with it. What if we could learn put all of the thoughts aside, and focused only on reality? You can’t always beat your thoughts, but you can ignore them. The anxious thoughts are a bit easier to get rid of during Jiu-Jitsu because I get lost in the “flow” of the activity I enjoy and I am able to push the thoughts away. However, my anxious thoughts do not go away as easily in real life.Whether it’s a first date, a project for a well-paying client, or any other activity that I do that’s important to me, I run the risk of getting stuck in my head and allowing my fears to dictate my experience. Then, I begin to think that my fears are actual depictions of reality, and I get stuck in my real life, as well as in my head.It’s no wonder that I experienced dissociation for 9 months straight — I was stuck in my head, and that allowed me to get stuck in my life. I was disconnected from reality because everywhere I looked both in my life and in my head was a roadblock. To make matters worse, I was beginning to realize that my thoughts were negative, and I stopped trusting them. Everything seemed like a lie, and it distorted my view of reality for quite some time. That’s why I’ve changed the way I look at anxiety. The best natural treatment for anxiety that I have is kind of dumb, but it’s undeniably effective.Before I start to do things, I ask myself “what I would do in the same situation if I had no anxiety?” If I was just living entirely in the moment, how would I behave? What would I say? What would I do?I use my imagination to create a version of myself that exists outside of my anxiety, and I strive to live the life that that version of myself would want me to live. The more that I do what my non-anxious self would want, the happier and more fulfilled I become. Living this way has also opened doors for me both in my personal and professional lives as well because I am no longer unconsciously holding myself back.I used to hold myself back in everything I did. I used to always allow fear to dictate my life, and now, while I am still anxious when I try to order an espresso in an Italian cafe, I am able to feel my fear and do it anyway.That’s pretty cool (and also not that complicated) if you ask me. Ever since I developed some sort of awareness of what mental health is and how it works, I’ve been stunned by the lack of empathy that people have toward those who are literally being attacked by their own minds. However, I also understand the feeling of being frustrated by people who just won’t do anything to improve their situations, even when all of the resources are right in front of them.I know people who have access to therapy, all the books in the world, a loving family, and enough money to buy the most expensive mental health meds, and they still can barely muster the courage to leave the house. I get frustrated when I see this, but I also feel sad, because I know what it’s like to have anxiety hold me back. I’ve been there myself and I’ve seen it in the people closest to me. I know what it’s like to have anxiety be the only thing holding me back.I’m trying to live like the only thing holding me back is a figment of my imagination, because, in some ways, it is.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do you think America is the best country in the world?
Answer: I don’t think America is the best country in the world, but I used to. When you grow up in America, you get brainwashed by everyone and their mother with the idea that the “American Dream” is the most special thing ever, that nowhere else in the world is as free as the US, and that the US is the best fucking place on earth. “Oh, and if you don’t agree with that, you can get the fuck out of my damn country.” — patriotic folks, when you express the idea that other countries have freedom too. (According to this website, Singapore is the freest country out there. The US comes in at #25, right behind the UK. I honestly don’t care that we aren’t first, but I don’t love that we act like we are.) America is fucked up, just like everywhere else. However, one thing about America that bugs me is the cultural narcissism that stops us from addressing the flaws that are deeply engrained in our culture. We have problems and we don’t talk about them. We work all the time — much more than in other countries. We are disconnected from our families and each other, and we wear that isolation as a badge of honor that means that we are successful. We also have a serious problem with gun violence, and most people don’t give a shit. We’re disconnected from our families and each other, but we also are disconnected from the tragic events that happen in front of our faces. We see mass shootings on the news all the time. When another shooting happens, people make comments about thoughts and prayers, vow to vote guns away, and then go about their day. They’re not affected because they’re dissociating from the violence as a response to the overwhelming cultural obsession with tragedy and death. We’re obsessed with death, as long as it doesn’t affect us for real. We say that America is the best country in the world, but what actually makes a country great? Is it winning wars? Is it humanitarianism? Is it having nice vacation spots and not being too expensive to travel to? I don’t know what the best country is, but after 2 and a half weeks in Europe, I can’t help but think that the “best country” isn’t the one I’m living in. But the thing is, it’s not about being “the best country”, it’s about being a better country. If you walk around telling everyone you’re the best, there isn’t much incentive to improve. I think that the truth is that Americans, despite their obsession with work and hustle, aren’t any less lazy than the rest of the world. We say that we’re the best so that we don’t have to look our flaws in the face and do the work to improve them. If America was a person, we’d tell them to change. The problem is that changing is hard work.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why is travelling so important in life?
Answer: I’ve been traveling for the last 2 weeks, and as I reach the final days of my journey, I’m realizing that traveling is not important in life unless you are able to actually learn from your travels. Nice view, isn’t it? I always wanted a life full of wild quests, grand adventures, and never-ending exploration. I always wanted my life to be “like the movies”. I always wanted to be the hero of my personal movie. I’ve always been a “get up and go” type of person. Even before I could remember, as a baby, I used to stand in my crib in the morning and shout to my mom “outside!” first thing every morning. I wanted to go to unique places, meet interesting people, and do everything you might read about in a choose your own adventure book or do in the montage scene of a movie. And so, I made it happen. for the last several years, I’ve been traveling the united states (and beyond) doing Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. This is the first time I’ve really sat down to think about what I’m doing, and while life is pretty great, it’s not exactly how I expected it would be, and I’ve been learning how to accept that and be happy anyway. Turns out, that’s the real adventure anyway. Life Isn’t Like the Movies Ever since I saw Christopher Nolan’s Tenet a few years ago, I wanted to visit the Amalfi coast. I scheduled myself a week and a few days off after my recent competition in Poland, so I decided to make a little trip to Rome and Vietri Sul Mare happen. Getting to Rome was easy. I bought a plane ticket, flew there, and then got a cab to my Airbnb, which was my home base for the next 2 days of exploration in a city I had wanted to see since my middle school Latin days. Then, the real adventure began. I took a cab from my Airbnb to the Rome train station, and then I plopped my butt on a train for 2 hours to Salerno (oh, and I almost missed the train). then, in Salerno, due to a delay, I did miss my train to the small town off the Amalfi coast where I was headed. Then, my phone’s data stopped working, so I couldn’t load my train ticket. Fuck. So, I decided to spend a euro (literally one euro) and buy another train ticket to my destination, just to make sure I didn’t get kicked off my train. I bought the ticket, and because I don’t speak Italian, I went through the whole process before realizing that I had actually bought a bus ticket. Whoops. Then, I went up to a worker at the station, and asked, “How do I get to Vietri Sul Mare”, and I held up my bus ticket (which I still thought was a train ticket). He pointed to the bus stop and said, “the white bus gets you there in 20 minutes.” I nodded and headed off to the white bus. On my way to the stop, the bus drove off. At the time, I didn’t know that that was the last thing standing between me and a smooth evening of travel to an absolutely beautiful place. “Oh well,” I thought and plopped my tired ass at the stop to wait for the next bus. About 2 minutes later, another bus came, except that this bus wasn’t white, it was red and white. I figured, “red and white is pretty close to white,” and hopped on the bus, proudly showing the driver the ticket I had purchased for 1 euro about 10 minutes earlier. “I sure hope this isn’t the wrong bus,” I thought. and sat down. Welp, I Got Lost Turns out, that was the wrong bus. it took me about 5 minutes to figure that out, but by the time I did, the bus had pulled onto the highway and was hurling itself in the other faster than I could say “arrivederci”. So at this point, I had no wi-fi or cellular data, no idea where I was going, and all I can say in Italian is “Ciao”, “Quanto?”, and “uno espresso”. If you’re reading this thinking “Chris, you are a moron…” you are right. I felt like a moron. I was lost and quite anxious. Eventually, I saw a gas station through the bus window, so I pulled the little string thing in the bus to get the driver to stop, and then I hopped off the bus and started walking toward this gas station. Then, bless my little heart, I saw a hotel. I later found out this was the last hotel for the next 30 kilometers. My eyes beamed, my heart rate slowed, and I let out a verbal sigh as I thought “finally, someone who speaks English”. I walked into the hotel, and after having this painfully embarrassing exchange in broken English, the lady there eventually was able to get me a taxi. But the taxi took a while to come, and when he did come, it wasn’t like any taxi I had ever seen before in the US. this taxi basically looked like her dad come from home to whip me over to the hotel really quick. In the end, I got to the hotel. It was lovely, and I loved the Amalfi Coast. My check-in process was just dramatic and more stressful than it should have been. This Was Just the Beginning 2 days after the story above, I went to Naples to catch my plane to London, where I’m finishing my trip with a few days of seeing people from a past life and touring the city I was born in. In Naples, my Airbnb host ghosted me (still working on getting my money back there), my phone died while trying to find a new place to stay, and then some random guy on the street kept pointing at my ears and telling me he was a doctor. Perks of having cauliflower ear, I guess. Then, I finally made it to the Naples airport, and I almost missed my flight because I couldn’t figure out how to properly check my bag. Either traveling is hard or I’m just really bad at it because I made just about every mistake in the book this week. So What Did We Learn? There is a great deal of peace in learning to accept that nearly everything in life is complete chaos. Most perceptions of order are an illusion created by the anxious mind to keep you from losing your shit. Whether you’re getting ready to compete in martial arts, getting stuck and lost in a foreign city, or just stressed out about deadlines at work, the sensation is pretty much always the same. You’re pretty much always anxious because you’re realizing you have no control over your current situation. Expanding on that logic, if you can learn to be at peace when you don’t have control, you’ll be able to thrive in even the most chaotic of circumstances. That is how you achieve true order. By dropping your preconceived notions of structure and organization and allowing yourself to become truly present in the chaos of whatever is right in front of you, you will reach true peace, true order, and a true sense of understanding. Trust me, it’s a nice feeling. Nothing is ever like the movies, but honestly, fuck the movies. This concept reminds me of this great clip from Jocko Willink’s podcast, where he talks about Anthony Bourdain’s suicide, reality, and expectations. I’d recommend giving it a watch if you struggle with being mindful and present in your everyday life. I saw it a few years ago, and it made me more self-aware and mindful than I think I wanted to be at 20. It’s one of 2 or 3 podcast clips that I will rewatch when I’m feeling down. I found this clip at a time when I myself was struggling with suicidal thoughts, a fear of growing up, and the awful sensation that my life was going to be a letdown. But the thing is, life is a letdown sometimes. It’s especially a letdown if you watch a lot of movies, social media, porn, or anything else designed to satisfy your senses and distort your view of reality. Your relationship is never as perfect as the one on TV. The food you crave is never as good as the pictures make it seem. Going on adventures isn’t as smooth and painless as movie montages make it seem. That’s the freaking point. Real love is messy. Real adventures are exhausting, make your back hurt, and can be a bit stressful. Real pizza is too hot to eat when it comes out of the oven and I couldn’t sleep my last night on the Amalfi Coast because there was a bug in my room who made it his personal mission to torture me. Everything looks better on social media or in films than it is in reality, but that doesn’t mean that the world is all nihilism and giant letdowns. Improving your mind is not about lowering your expectations. I think instead it’s about removing them. Don’t let preconceived ideas affect current experiences. You should learn from past experiences, but you also need to let the current moments stand alone. The only movie that matters is the one happening in your head right now.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How can I learn to love myself? You know all your flaws and insecurities. How do you get over them?
Answer: This isn’t how it’s supposed to work, but I actually learned how to “love myself” by obsessively loving someone else first. Here’s how that happened: (I’m also trying to become the first writer ever to get sponsored by sparkling water, so here’s a random picture of a water bottle 😊) In the past, every time I fell in love, I got hung up on something about the person I was with. They would always have some quality that would be “a deal-breaker” for me, and it was usually something small and stupid. If they didn’t like reading, didn’t like working out, or didn’t have “it” to the same degree I did, I began to feel disconnected (I soon realized that “it” was just my teenage brain’s way of defining chemistry). I dated quite a bit in college, but I never saw a future with any of the girls I dated. I saw myself getting bored—fast. Then, I met her. I met her at a Sunday Jiu-Jitsu training session one summer day, and at first, she scared the living shit out of me. She was my age, but her mind was older. It felt like she knew something I didn’t. She seemed more mature than me. She was resourceful, beautiful, and all of those other things that you’d think a 23-year-old Chris would want out of a partner. On paper, she was perfect. But of course, relationships don’t happen on paper. A few weeks into our relationship, weird stuff started happening. She fell in love a little bit too fast for me. Something felt “off”. When she got upset, she got a little bit too upset. I felt like she loved me, but I felt like something was wrong. My gut was telling me that something was wrong, but it couldn’t have been her. She was “perfect”. Sure, she fell in love too fast, but when she was kind she was so kind to me. Sure, she got a little bit too angry with me when she got drunk, but she was hot. No— she was beautiful. Sure, this warning sign, sure, that red flag, but she was everything I ever wanted. At first, I was afraid, but eventually, I decided that she might be “the one”. I cringe writing those words. You think stupid thoughts when you’re 23, deeply depressed, aimless in your life, and desperate for someone to make you feel better. Eventually, I fell in love. I thought that was supposed to be enough to fix everything. I thought love could heal the world. My ex said it could. I was hesitant at first, but I let go of myself and my anxieties eventually. Eventually, I dropped everything I stood for and decided to bet in love with someone who I had known for about 2 months. This was a stupid decision, but at the moment, it felt right. I didn’t heal, I didn’t work on my mind, I just let my love for this girl dictate the flow of my life. I’ve experienced severe anxiety, panic attacks, and derealization, so I thought that getting out of my head and being “in love with the moment” was progress, but in reality, I was just tricking myself into sacrificing myself to someone who was about to smush my heart like a bug. Our relationship was like a sinking ship, and I was the lunatic running around with a bucket trying to save it. I put in work like I never have before. I don’t know if I’ll ever put in work on a relationship like that ever again. I made all these sacrifices and did all this work, and in the end, the “love of my life” hurt me pretty darn bad (and didn’t even say sorry!). She said I was “the light of her life”, and she didn’t even say sorry. And look, let’s be real—she had her own stuff going on and struggled with her own issues, so I struggle to “hate her”. Hate doesn’t really help anyone with progress. That’s why this is complicated. I am upset about what happened. I’m upset, but I’m also grateful because this experience forced me to grow into the person I needed to be. I gave this girl so much love, so much adoration, and so much of myself that I completely forgot that I’m important too. I found this love in myself and gave it to her, so that now, as I’ve started to heal, I’m just trying to deflect the love that I had for her and give it to myself and to people that are here for me now. I’m really happy now, and I have more than enough love in my life to keep me going. In the end, it all worked out. It just took a while and hurt a lot. After I had this fucked up breakup where I felt like a weak man who was cursed to date people who didn’t give a shit about him, I learned how to prioritize my own happiness. I had a little bit of a glow-up. I got a career. I started to see some professional payoffs from my decade of martial arts training. I started living the way I always dreamed of. Although I didn’t call it that (I’ve never been won to prance around and shout about “loving yourself”), I did learn to love myself. That’s why in the end, I am grateful for that girl who broke my heart. She made me realize that there was something inside of me that wasn’t enough. She made me realize that I was using relationships to give me something that I couldn’t give myself, and I’ve started to find other ways to cultivate that love within myself. I’m starting to get that “glow” back that I had when I was in love, but I’m giving it to myself. That’s kind of cool to me. I’m still learning, but I’m making progress. I’m making progress a lot faster than I thought I would. Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some ways to have adventure in everyday life?
Answer: I think my life is quite adventurous. Here’s a photo I took this morning in Vietri Sul Mare, a little town outside of Salerno, Italy: Vietri Sul Mare is considered to be the gateway to the Amalfi Coast. Getting here was a bit of a wild ride. Here’s how I did it. First, I obsessed over one thing for about a decade. I paid for this trip with money that I made from teaching and competing in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. I got my black belt in Jiu-Jitsu last week, and before that, I was training nearly every day, several times per day, for about 7 years. Before that, I was a wrestler for 6 years. 6 years of wrestling + 7 years of Jiu-Jitsu gave me the skillset to make a living doing what I love, but it wasn’t until this week that I was able to take myself on an international vacation using the money I made from what used to be my “hobby”. I hope this isn’t the last time I get an experience like this. It’s not what you do, it’s how well and how long you practice. Then, I took a leap of faith. About a month and a half ago, I quit my real job as a social media manager for small businesses. Now, I’m all-in on the whole “writer-Jiu-Jitsu fighter” thing. I’m not stupid — I’ve been saving money for 2 years to take this shot, but I am rolling the dice by trying to do this. If I was still doing my regular job, I wouldn’t have the time to travel and do what I’m doing this week. Then, I took a vacation. Last week, I competed in this tournament in Poland. I didn’t win, but I finished in the top 8 in all of Europe. Not too bad for my first time competing internationally, but there’s certainly room for me to grow. When I get home, I will keep working on it. Right now, I’m ranked in the top 20 in the world in Jiu-Jitsu at 170 pounds. Considering that around this time last year I was making $16 an hour writing social media posts, wasn’t on anyone’s radar for being ranked in anything, and I was more heartbroken and depressed from a breakup than I’d ever been, I feel okay with taking a moment to chill by myself on the Amalfi Coast. My body and mind have been needing a little reset for a little while now. Plus, I’m 24, and I’m just getting started. In sum, you have to take a fucking shot. It’s funny to me that this trip is sponsored by my Jiu-Jitsu victories because I honestly feel like I’m still not that good at Jiu-Jitsu. There’s still so much about my career and passion that I don’t yet understand. And yet, here we are. Here’s a picture from coffee this morning: If you really want more adventure in your life, you have to stop playing it safe. You have to go all-in on your goal, even when everyone around you looks at you like you are crazy. When I left for this trip, I told my childhood best friend that I was going to Europe for Jiu-Jitsu. Instead of wishing me luck, wishing me safe travels, or even saying “see you soon!”, he said, “Well, I hope it’s worth it”. I know I’m a little sensitive, but he seemed jealous that I’m living my dream in a world where most are stuck in the trap of socially constructed obligations. You have to go all-in, and then you have to keep going. Even when you’re scared. Even when you’re anxious. Even when the future is unpredictable and grim. Even when you’re lost in a random fishing town in Italy with no cell service, no Wi-Fi, and no idea what literally anyone around you is saying. If you want adventure, you have to seek adventure. Then, you have to push past the resistance created by your natural desire for safety and comfort. Adventure is on the other side of comfort. I’ve made myself throw up from training a disgusting amount of times. I’ve had my joints destroyed and popped in fights way more than it’s normal. I’ve starved myself so much cutting weight that I cried. I’ve written so much that my wrists have literally spasmed in front of my eyes. I didn’t do these things because I’m some lunatic who likes pain. I did these things because I wanted to see how much I was really capable of. I wanted to test myself and see how much I could do. I just wanted to take a shot because I couldn’t live with myself if I didn’t. And now, I’m sitting in a moderately fancy hotel on the Amalfi Coast watching this boat drive by. I’m by myself because none of my friends or family could get off work to come with me, but I’m pretty happy (I’m going to write more about having fun with solo travel soon, btw). Ultimately, I’m happy because I proved my biggest doubter (myself) wrong. I don’t know if everyone can do what I do, but I do know that even just trying is more than worth it. P.S. I’m sorry if this answer came off as struggle porn or obnoxious hustle BS. I don’t care if you hustle. I just want you to feel at peace. I just feel proud and happy today.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How does it feel to travel alone?
Answer: I’m currently traveling alone in Europe, and it’s nerve-wracking, a little stressful, and kind of overwhelming. Although, there are times when it’s quite nice. My family went on a few family vacations when I was growing up, and I never really liked them. They always made me sad. There was always so much fighting and yelling and stress. Everyone was either drunk or screaming at each other or both. I was always excited to get home and get away from everyone. The nice thing about solo travel is that I don’t have to deal with that shit anymore. I get to make the schedule, meaning that if I don’t want to follow a schedule, then there isn’t a schedule. Today, I walked around Rome till I was tired, then I got some pizza, then some gelato. Then I got some more espresso. Then I wrote this Quora answer. That was fuckin’ it. It was nice. However, the downside of this is that I kind of miss my friends. I kind of miss people who I normally wouldn’t miss. I miss my family, even though I know they were here we wouldn’t have any fun together. That’s a weird feeling. But at the end of the day those people aren’t here, and all I’ve got is myself and all of the strangers in Italy who I don’t know yet. The nice part about home is that you know everyone, but the downside of home is that you know everyone. The beautiful part about travel is that you don’t know anyone, but the downside is that well, you don’t know anyone. You’re alone. Happiness is learning to enjoy both the company of others and your own personal solitude. Follow me on Instagram to stay updated on all my travels!

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the top hobbies that make you smarter?
Answer: Here’s a weird hobby that has made me a lot smarter: getting my ass kicked by my friends (martial arts training). Now, this hobby is my job, but for a long time, Jiu-Jitsu training was just the thing I did to pass the time. I started doing Jiu-Jitsu because I wanted a workout that would challenge me similar to how wrestling challenged me in high school. I found something that I loved more than anything else I have ever done, and though I’m biased, I think it’s made me a little smarter too. The reason that I think that my martial arts training has made me smarter is that the kind of training that I do is heavily grounded in reality. In Jiu-Jitsu, you can spar nearly every day. We don’t get together, practice some katas, and then talk about how strong we are because we have done martial arts. We fight. Every fucking day, we fight each other. Nothing exposes your limits quite like getting smashed, choked, and arm locked by people who weigh a lot less than you. When you get your ass kicked, you have to be a special kind of dumb to think that what happened to you is “okay”. For just about all of us, failure in Jiu-Jitsu (submission) is a vessel for us to learn to improve ourselves. We learn counterattacks, we learn our own submissions, and we even learn how much pain our bodies can withstand without breaking down. Learning your limits makes you more humble, and it also teaches you how you can learn things. You learn how to get better by exposing yourself to the limitations of your meat suit. I get that it’s not the easiest thing—reading, writing, physical conditioning, traveling, and meditating are some of my other favorite hobbies that help make me feel smarter—but training martial arts definitely has taught me more about life and improving the strength of my own mind than pretty much anything else that I have done. To read more of my thoughts on life, martial arts training, and happiness, check out my newsletter :)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I stop worrying?
Answer: Just let loose, man. Just “chill” and “enjoy the moment”, or whatever they say you’re supposed to do. Okay—now stop. Pull your head out of your ass and get back to reality. In reality, you have responsibilities. You have bills to pay. You have to go to work. You have to do shit. You have to make something of yourself. The experience of trying to “make something of myself” encompasses nearly all of my waking moments, and while this is a fulfilling way to spend your time, it’s getting a little exhausting. It can, and probably will break you down. That’s the long story short on why my dumb ass is stuffing his face with bread in this picture. I’m trying desperately to give myself a break from “the grind” and the daily obsession with improvement. I’m taking a little break from the chasing the constant and fleeting grasp for significance in life, and I’m trying to enjoy myself for a bit. I’m trying to “let loose”, but it’s really hard for me. It scares the hell out of me. Not working and not grinding makes me really anxious, but I’m trying to stop worrying about it. For the last year and a half, I’ve been working harder than I’ve ever worked in my life. Even though I’ve always been a pretty hard worker, I took it to another level recently. My goals have gotten bigger, so my work ethic has elevated to match these goals. I’ve been writing constantly, training Jiu-Jitsu several times per day, teaching and competing all over the world, and thankfully, my work is paying off. I recently finished in the top 4 in the biggest submission wrestling tournament in North America in April, and then I used my English citizenship to compete in Europe representing England, where I finished in the top 8. I proved to myself that I’m one of the best in the world at the thing I’m most passionate about, and doing so has literally changed my life. I currently feel more confident, happier, and more fulfilled than I have ever been. The problem is, that my current work rate is also unsustainable. You can’t write an article per day, train multiple times, and teach people while maintaining your physical and mental health. You just can’t. You need breaks sometimes, otherwise, you will break. During my last weight cut, I almost broke mentally. I wanted to give up. I retained extra water weight from my flight from the US to Europe, and I didn’t think I had it in me to keep cutting to make weight. I hated having to hang out in Poland all week this week without eating anything besides some fruit and a few protein bars. I hated it. But, I kept going because I knew that I had a break coming. I knew that whether I made weight or not, after this weekend I’d be sitting on trains riding around Europe, eating bread in various forms, and drinking cappuccinos. I kept going because there was a reason that I was forcing myself to suffer. I was not suffering just to suffer. I was suffering because I wanted to achieve my goal, and I knew that the suffering would not last forever. But now that the competition is over and it’s time for me to take this little vacation I scheduled for myself, I’m doing my very best to relax and take a break from work. You were not put on this earth to just take punishment and be miserable. There’s more to life than grinding and hustling. Or at least, I think there is. The problem is that we surround ourselves with people who have forgotten this. People forget this fact for a lot of reasons, but in my experience, the main reason is that life is hard. In the US, the “grind culture” is everything. I’ve accidentally forced myself into this existence where everything I do is about achieving more, and I stopped doing things for enjoyment. As a result, I’m worried all the time, even when I’m stuffing myself with bread. The subtle anxiety is always there. It sucks, but sometimes, you can’t make the feeling go away. You can’t always get rid of the worry. However, you can work to get rid of the compulsive behavior that comes with worry. You can fight the compulsive urge to work more, grind more, and hustle till you’re miserable. That’s why, over the next week and a half, I’m not going to the gym (unless I want to). I’m not going to write (unless I want to). I’m trying to do this “vacation” thing right, so when I get back, I feel motivated to get back to work. They say that distance makes the heart grow fonder. Let’s see if that applies to the things that I am constantly worrying about. P.S. If you have travel/food recommendations for Italy, London, and Paris, please let me know. I’ll be there over the next few weeks :)

Answer: I’m currently traveling in Europe for a Jiu-Jitsu competition, and the other day, we went to train at a local gym in town. Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best way to prepare yourself for entrepreneurship?
Answer: Sports are one of the best ways that you can prepare yourself for the cutthroat world of business. I’m a professional Jiu-Jitsu athlete. I finally feel comfortable saying that. However, Jiu-Jitsu isn’t exactly a “major sport”, and making a living in Jiu-Jitsu can be strange and difficult. Most people have never even heard of the sport that I practice for 3–6 hours every day. Some of the top Jiu-Jitsu athletes in the world are so broke that they live in their gyms. I do not live in a gym or sleep on a mat. I live in an apartment in Chicago and I sleep on a nice cushy bed. I pay for the apartment with the money I make from doing Jiu-Jitsu and writing about my experiences with doing Jiu-Jitsu. I’ve had to learn how to make money in a sport that is notoriously difficult to make a living in. I’ve had to learn about business in a place where I thought business didn’t exist. I’ve had to learn how to monetize my passion. 2 years into my “full-time” Jiu-Jitsu dream, I’m not exactly a zillionaire, but I make a living doing what I love. I wake up and make my own schedule. Here are 10 things that I have learned throughout the last 2 years as I’ve transitioned from working as a social media manager and copywriter for small businesses to working as a “pro athlete” for myself. How many internet followers you have doesn’t matter as much as you think In what I do, followers don’t pay your rent, fans do. True fans do. I only have a little over 1000 followers on Instagram, under 2000 on Medium, and about 4000 on Quora. I still make a living with my personal brand because I have a handful of people who really support me and want me to do well. I have a tribe of people who back me up. These people help me make a living doing what I love. You don’t need to go viral on TikTok or get a million Medium followers to do your thing at a high level, you just need to build a little cult. Just maybe don’t call it a cult — people don’t usually love that. Do NOT do what everyone else is doing Do what you’re good at. In my case, there aren’t that many people who write and do Jiu-Jitsu. It’s uncommon, but writing is my skill set. YouTubing is not my skill set. TikTok is not my skillset. I am a writer, a teacher, and a fighter. I spend all of my time focused on these 3 things and doing them as well as possible. Instead of contorting my skills to the market, I have spent a considerable amount of time building up my skills so that I can monetize them. Good skills are better than trendy skills. If you can do something well, you should also learn to teach it well Prizefighting is cool, but I’m aware of my limits enough to know that I can’t fight for money forever. That’s why I teach and write. These skills will outlast the limitations of my physical body. Writing, speaking, and teaching are 3 key skills for artistic entrepreneurs. Making money is not a fight. Don’t make it one People talk a lot online about how they “grind” and “fight” for their success. Most of these people have never been in real fights. Running a blog is a service industry. It’s entertainment. It is not a fight. Teaching Jiu-Jitsu is a service industry as well. These activities require collaboration with an audience, not an ego with something to prove. In service industries, I’ve found that being more aggressive is not better. Fighting is “show business”, and that’s a different skill, but teaching and writing require self-awareness and compassion instead of pure hustle and grit. If you’re an indie creator, you have to leave the cutthroat mentality to the corporate folks. You need love to succeed, not “hustle”. The thing you’re doing isn’t always the thing you’re selling Learning to extract lessons from your skill is the key to moving from a general audience to a niche. My general audience could be people who do Jiu-Jitsu or people who like to read blogs, but my specific niche is people who are interested in the combination of martial arts (or sports), life lessons, and self-improvement. In terms of monetization, specificity and value are more important than reach, but you need reach, too. You have to give value away for free to prove yourself in the digital market. Think about what you’re really writing/making content about. That’s where your audience is. Artists are broke because they won’t dance Just because you took the time to create some art (a book, a set of martial arts skills, or a song) doesn’t mean anyone has to care about it. Find out what people want and learn to dance with the market. That’s how you make a living as an artist in the modern era. Failure is worse in your head I’ve lost a lot of fights over the years. I’ve also written some shitty articles that no one read. Most of my writing has been stunningly mediocre. It’s okay though. Competitive sports, digital writing, and solopreneurship are volume-based games. The more you play, the better chances you have of winning. Stop romanticizing your artistic ability, and press “publish”. Then do it again. And again. And again. In case you needed to hear it from someone who’s been there too: individual failures (and successes, for that matter) do not define your competence. Hard work > talent I’ve been doing grappling sports for 12 years. When I win nowadays, people think I’m talented. I promise, I’m not. I’m not even really a natural athlete — just ask my parents. It just looks like I’m good now because I’ve worked super hard for a super long time. Consistency is what most people are lacking. If that offends you, it probably applies to you. You’re probably not patient enough Here’s a little story: I launched a premium newsletter last fall. For a while (about a month and a half), I had 2 subscribers. I was writing 5 extra articles per month for 2 people. I was thinking about abandoning the project because clearly, it wasn’t working the way I wanted it to. I didn’t stop though, I just kept writing articles and pumping out content for those 2 readers. I was grateful for their 5 bucks a month. Over time, I noticed that the premium subscriber number on my newsletter was slowly increasing. It wasn’t quick. It was never more than 1 in a day, but it was and has been growing. That was undeniable, and that was enough to make me realize that I had to keep going and I had to be more patient. I had to maintain my consistency over a longer period of time. I had to be more patient. Now, my premium newsletter nets me an extra $100 per month. That’s not bad for a little thing I do for fun on the side. Patience and consistency. That’s my strategy. Who knows where I’ll be in a year. Just try stuff When it comes to making a living as a pro-athlete/writer, I’ve tried nearly everything. I’ve fought for thousands of dollars countless times. I wrote an ebook. I have a newsletter. I teach seminars. I do private classes. I blog. You name it, I’ve either tried it or thought deeply about trying it. Some things have been massive successes for me, and others have been massive flops. Others have taken a while to start building. Others started off fast and died out quickly. 2 things have remained consistent though. One is me, and the other is my constant habit of “trying new stuff”. Experimentation is a requirement for growth as a creator. I quit my job almost 2 months ago and went “all-in” on the whole “Jiu-Jitsu/content creator” thing, and it’s been a wild ride thus far. The highs are incredibly validating, and the lows can make me question everything. However, the best part for me is that everything that I do when I’m working, writing, and training matters a lot. It’s all very important to me. My life is very meaningful. I’d rather be sore and tired than depressed and pissed off at the world. To me, that’s more important than any job title or career objective. That’s all I could ask for, and that's why I keep going.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the fastest way to earn money?
Answer: Last weekend, I made $5000 in a little more than 20 minutes. Here’s a picture to prove it. No, I didn’t sell drugs. I didn’t become a pornstar. I didn’t even start a business. I competed in a martial arts tournament, and I won. That’s it. I had 3 matches. The first match lasted 8 minutes. The second match went for about 2 minutes, and the 3rd and final match went for 10 minutes. I was on the mat fighting for a little more than 20 minutes. I won all 3 matches, and I was awarded a $5000 prize for my efforts. $5000 in 20 minutes of work. An easy day at the office, right? Wrong. Very wrong. There wasn’t much about this weekend that was easy, but, it was very quick. I endured quite a bit of pain, for a moderate amount of time, and I was awarded money — only because I was successful. I did make $5000 in 20 minutes, but in reality, it took me about 12 years to develop the skills to even have a chance at winning this tournament on Saturday. I made $5000 in 20 minutes, but in the long run, when it comes to my Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu “career” (a word I didn’t feel comfortable even using until about 6 months ago), I’ve lost a lot of money over the last 7 years. That’s why I wanted to write this answer about long-term goals and short-term payoffs. It takes a ridiculous amount of time to do something at a high level. I am not the most talented athlete. I’m not the most talented at anything. I don’t have magic genetics that made me a high-level athlete from a young age. When I played baseball growing up, it took me 2 years to develop enough hand-eye coordination just to hit the fucking ball. I spent the first 2 years of my baseball career celebrating foul balls and “foul tips” because they were “contact”. Contact was my indication of progress. I tried out for my school’s basketball team in middle school when I realized that the baseball thing wasn’t really working out, and I didn’t get past the first cut in basketball. Unfortunately, being 4'11 and chubby doesn’t exactly help you get the coach’s attention at basketball tryouts. After that was when I started wrestling, and I didn’t exactly have any success on the wrestling mat at first either. In 8th grade (my second year of wrestling — you know, when I was supposed to be better than my first year), I finished with 4 wins and 28 losses (more than double the amount of losses of my first year). Most of the losses were from pins. I spent most of my first 2 years involved in combat sports getting thrown around the ring, getting pinned, and then crying in the bleachers while munching on the post-competition Snickers bar that my mom or dad bought me. The point is, I wasn’t a talented wrestler, either. By my senior year of high school, I was winning more matches than I was losing, but I wasn’t winning tournaments. I never qualified for the state tournament. I wasn’t good, and I got better, but I never became great. Once wrestling was done, I started Jiu-Jitsu. This was the first time I was able to excel at something, but my success has never been linear. It takes a ridiculously strong mind to do something at a high level. When I started Jiu-Jitsu, I didn’t have any success either. I came in with a wrestling background, and that meant that I was supposed to have instant success in Jiu-Jitsu, but I didn’t. Again, I was winning more than I was losing, but I wasn’t great at Jiu-Jitsu and I didn’t have great results in Jiu-Jitsu. I was solid, but solid does not mean great. My goal wasn’t to be “solid”. My goal was to be world-class. Finally, at around 19, I started to get my “man-body”. That helped. But muscles alone weren’t enough to help me achieve my goals. I also had to develop world-class technique, precise timing, and a mind that could do all these things under intense pressure. What shifted over the course of that ridiculously long amount of time that I spent competing in martial arts was that I developed the mind of a successful martial arts competitor. I did this by studying philosophy, writing about my anxiety, practicing good habits, and yes, training a metric fuck-ton of Jiu-Jitsu on top of that. Now that I’m doing fairly well in Jiu-Jitsu, a lot of people seem to assume that I’m this talented guy who has some abilities that other people don’t have or that I just have ridiculously good luck. Those people weren’t here 11 years ago when I looked like a “roly-poly” on the mat — my dad’s words. I’ve done what I do with an intense amount of focus for a very long time. That’s pretty much it. That’s more important than talent. That’s more important than hard work. That’s more important than anything if you ask me. It takes a village to do something at a high level. Okay, this answer has been all about me so far. It’s time to shift the focus. For a long time, I was really concerned with being “self-made”. I wanted everyone to know that I had worked my ass off for everything that I achieve. I wanted everyone to know that I did it all myself. The problem is, that wouldn’t be the truth. I didn’t do this all on my own. I had a lot of help. In the picture above, the guy on my left (Jack) has been traveling with me and competing with me for nearly the last 4 years, and the guy on my right (my coach, Jeff) has been teaching me most of the Jiu-Jitsu I know since I was 17-years-old. Those are just 2 of the people that make up this village of friends and teammates that I have that help me do the things that I do at a high level. I’m just a vessel or something. Apart from just my training partners at the gym, there are also the guys who I’ve met through training out of town who have pushed me to reach for goals that I previously couldn’t have fathomed, and there are also the countless strangers who have said nice (and not-so-nice) things to me on the internet for the last year and a half that I’ve been sharing my life through writing. Both the good and bad comments motivate me in different ways. If you clicked on this answer because you wanted to learn about how to make $5000 in 20 minutes, I apologize immediately. I can’t teach you fast and easy ways to succeed. I can, however, show you that quick success does not exist. None of the things that I do well come easy to me. I could never win any grappling tournaments without training and working my butt off. I could never write good writing without editing it an obnoxious amount of times. I could never make good decisions without making stupid ones first. Maybe you’re the same way. Maybe my “advice” is useless, and maybe you’re going to go into your life and do the opposite of what I say. If that’s you, I respect it. I’ve been that guy. However, those readers are not the reason I write. I write for the people who can and are willing to learn for me. First and foremost, the person who can learn the most from the dumb shit I’ve done is myself. Here’s to not making the same mistakes over and over again.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is your biggest achievement in life?
