Answer: I’ve clicked on this question a few times, but I never felt like I could write anything worthwhile. “I won this fight this one time” didn’t seem like a valid achievement for my biggest achievement. However, last night, I got my black belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, and getting that belt means a lot to me. Getting that belt is one of the most validating achievements of my life. I’ve never worked at anything in my life like I’ve worked at Jiu-Jitsu. I’ve trained 2–3 times per day, nearly every day, for the last 6 years. All in all, it took 7 years of training Jiu-Jitsu for me to get my black belt, and I got my black belt relatively fast, compared to people who practice as a hobby. Getting your black belt in Jiu-Jitsu takes about 10 years on average. It doesn’t matter how old you are, how talented you are, or how much you train. Getting your black belt is tough. I first stepped on a Jiu-Jitsu mat at 17, and since I was 18, being one of the best in the world at Jiu-Jitsu has been my focus—my obsession. I’ve competed hundreds of times under every possible circumstance. I’ve fought on the biggest stages in Jiu-Jitsu against some of the best athletes in the sport today. I’ve fought in random middle school gyms against some of the toughest people you have never heard of. I won a world championship. I made a run through one of the toughest tournaments of all time as a “nobody” from random gym in the Midwest. I’m the 12th-ranked athlete in the world at my weight class. Until yesterday, I was the only brown belt in the rankings. But still, none of these competitive achievements phase me that much anymore. I feel happy and grateful for success and opportunities, but I’d do this if no one was watching. I’ve been doing this with no one watching for 7 years. I didn’t have any major eyes on my grappling until about a month ago. Even my world title at purple belt didn’t change my life that much. I’ve trained for so long that I stopped caring whether or not I got my black belt yesterday, the week after, or a year from now. I’ve trained for so long that the achievements I can earn stopped meaning that much to my self-esteem (although, they still impact my career quite a bit), and I now am primarily for because I want to be the best possible martial artist I can be. Maybe you think I’m lying, but I’m not. I get up in the morning and work my ass off to be better, not to be better than you or some random guy in Texas. The pursuit of championships, belts, and the clout gained through victory is a fun motivator, but I spent so many years feeling invalidated by my pursuit of these achievements that I had to learn that little thing called “intrinsic motivation”. The belt is a big achievement, but most of all, it’s an exciting achievement. However, after the excitement dies down, the belt itself doesn’t change much for me. I still have to train twice today, I still have to lose some weight for my upcoming tournament, and I still have to keep getting better at Jiu-Jitsu. I still have to figure out how I’m going to keep making a living doing this crazy sport. As a practitioner, the belt does not change that much. I’m the same dude I was yesterday. I’m not much better than I was yesterday. I just get to say “I’m a black belt” now. The belt is just validating. That’s all. It also took me almost 7 years to get. 12.5 years if you count all the wrestling I did before that. I feel good about it because I have worked my tushy off for a really long time, and people have validated my hard work. The black belt is probably the life achievement that’s most important to me, but it’s only a step toward my ultimate goal in Jiu-Jitsu. My goal was, is, and always has been to be a world-class Jiu-Jitsu black belt. Now, as a black belt, I can finally take the next step toward something I’ve been obsessed with since I was 18. I’m excited for what comes next.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Do you have a photo that presents an image that doesn't match the "reality" of what is going on?
Answer: I don’t know if you can tell, but the guy in this picture is absolutely fucking exhausted. He’s freaking out about money. He’s scared he’s not going to “make it”. He’s scared he’s going to look like an idiot in front of all the people who paid money to learn Jiu-Jitsu from him. He’s blessed and he’s happy. He’s also working his little ass off. He’s just struggling. He’s trying to figure his shit out. Mentally, I’ve been all-in on my dream since I was 17. I started reading business books before I knew what half the words meant. I started writing life advice and self-help articles just months after I’d graduated from college where I got a useless degree and spent most of my time wrestling with grown men in bathrobes. I’ve competed in martial arts all over the United States, and I’ve taught martial arts everywhere to anyone who would pay me. I taught martial arts for free. I paid to compete in competitions that no one will ever know I won or participated in. I wrote articles for basically no one but my mom. I won a world title and no one noticed. I wrote a book that no one bought. Yet somehow, I figured out a way to make my passions my full-time living. Now, I’m one of the top 12 Jiu-Jitsu athletes in the world in my weight class, I’m a professional writer, and my writing has been viewed more than 5 million times on the internet. I don’t like to toot my own horn that much, but I’m doing okay. Yet, I’m still a nervous wreck. If anything, the nerves are worse now. Now that the only thing responsible for paying my rent is my passion projects, I’m having a hard time getting out of bed. I’m sick of reading complex books. Competing and training are destroying my body. I’m beaten up. I don’t want to hustle anymore. I worked so hard for so damn long, and now, at the point in time where I need to focus most, I just want a fucking break. I love my job, I hate the stress, and I’m terrified about the future. First of all, I’ve never had such a hard time with writing. This piece has 2 components, one about each section of my career (writing and martial arts). Honestly, writing is something that I’m still kind of new at. I think I have more potential as a writer than as a fighter, but no matter what it is you are trying to do, it isn’t potential that helps you build a career doing something. What helps you make a career out of something isn’t talent, skill, or even effectiveness. What helps you make a career is consistent effectiveness sustained over a long period of time. This is something that I have not struggled with yet in writing, but I am definitely struggling with it right now. I am currently physically unable to maintain the rapid output of content that allowed me to take the early steps in the career that I just decided to go “all-in” on. I just quit my job to become a full-time writer and fighter, and now my wrists are so sore constantly writing (from “over-writing”) that I can’t write much at all. In the past, I was able to write 3000–5000 words per day, and now I can hardly manage 2000. I have to grind twice the time to write less than half of the content. Worse yet, the pain in my wrists makes it nearly impossible to find the “flow” that has allowed me to create what I feel is my best work. I’ve written so much that I constantly get messages from people telling me about how something I wrote somewhere moved them, inspired them, or gave them hope, and I can’t do anything but cry. I can barely muster the words to type a response. I’m overwhelmed with gratitude that anyone thinks anything I have written is worth a damn, but I’m terrified that I won’t ever be able to write something like that ever again. I don’t know what’s going to happen next, because I can’t write right now without severe pain in my hands and fingers. It hurts, and I can’t tell stories the way that I feel they should be told. It breaks my little heart. My body is breaking too. Jiu-Jitsu is notoriously hard on your body. Over the last 9 months, I have created an approach to training that works for me, limits injury, and still allows for maximal growth in both the technical and physical departments of the sport. The problem is that this approach is a little bit different from the approach to training that most people are using. This itself isn’t a problem, but the anxiety associated with it certainly is. I get worried that I am not keeping myself up with my competition (oh, and my competition is literally the best Jiu-Jitsu guys in the world), and even worse, I worry that I am wasting my time by taking a different approach to training than most of the people in my division. I started to feel guilty for listening to my body instead of pushing forward at all costs, and so this week I decided to go visit some friends, immerse myself in their training, and do everything that they do. This was a bad call. 2 days in, I aggravated an old injury, and now I can’t even bend over without severe pain. I know these injuries are my fault because all of the injuries that I have right now are not from freak accidents or mistakes, they’re overuse injuries. My injuries could be avoided if I continued the approach to training that has been working for me, but instead, I decided to try something different, and it backfired. Now, here I am writing this article at 15 minutes intervals because I can’t sit for more than that long without back pain, and my wrists are burning. I’m also taking intense medication that makes me tingly, exhausted, and gives me mood swings. I fucked up, and I can barely train, teach, or write, and as a result, I feel like a blob. What do I do about it? I’m sorry if I bored you with my sob story, but there is a lesson here. This isn’t my first rodeo. Every time I deal with periods where I’m unable to work and prepare the way I want, I have this initial internal struggle where I’m constantly trying to fix everything that is “wrong with me”. I will continue to live in a way that hurts, just because I want to stick with my routine. However, over time, I have sort of learned to accept that these periods where I experience low motivation are just that — periods where I am experiencing low motivation. Sure, right now I am feeling a bit more anxiety than normal about my motivation levels, but this isn’t because I fear that my motivation is gone forever. This is because I just quit my job, and when you quit your job to go all-in on your passion, you’re supposed to be extra motivated. That’s not the case with me, and as a result, my goal now must not be to force myself to work. My goal must be to allow myself to recover. The truth is that your dreams do not die when you run out of money, they don’t die when you take a break from working, and they don’t die when you struggle with your discipline. Your dreams only die when you quit. Every doubt you experience before you actually quit is a fiction created by anxiety. Do not allow anxiety to push you to quit. Motivation is fleeting, but it comes back around. Don’t forget that, and I won’t either. Hard work often pays off, but it also has a price. The price is your time, your health, your sanity, and your peace. You spend your attributes to achieve stuff, make improvements, and make money, but eventually, you’re going to run out of gas. You’re going to have to rest. You cannot constantly grind toward your goals and expect continued progress and improvements. Resting is good. I quit my job, I’ve never been less motivated, and for now, that’s okay, because my motivation always comes back. For now, I’m hoping my discipline will hold me over till then.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do you write?
Answer: I write because I am scared. I write because I want to tell you about the thing that I couldn’t tell you about if you were standing here in front of me. I write because when I wake up in the morning my mind runs and runs and runs like a train off the track. I’m scared that if I don’t get all my thoughts down, no one will remember me. I write because I want to do something artistic, but I can’t out of my head long enough to learn any other skills besides the ones I have now. Your brain changes when you dissociate for a year straight. I write because writing is the only creative pursuit that makes my life better in every single way. Sometimes, I’m nervous about the stuff that I post. My most viewed piece on Quora last week had nearly 50k views. That's about what I expect something to get if it “does well” on here. I’m desensitized to that number at this point. I’m not saying that to brag. If you were in my position, you might be too. You might also forget that 50k views mean that 50k individual people have seen something that you wrote. When you tell a personal story, like, for example, the one about your ex-girlfriend who royally fucked up your head and the way that you view life and love, you forget that now 50k people know about the traumatic event that you’re trying to process. Sometimes, writing makes me feel strong. It makes me feel like I have a voice. It makes me feel like I’m more than my actions and my thoughts. Writing makes me feel in control of my life. But other times, when I write, I don’t feel better. Sometimes, after I’m done writing I just feel like an object. Once I hit publish, my writing isn’t about me anymore. Once I shared the story about my ex-girlfriend, it stopped being my story. It became whatever the reader needed it to be. That answer inspired some people. It made some people feel good. It bugged some people. It made some people feel worried about me. Some people saw themselves in my story. Other people think I’m a fucking moron. I’m whatever you need me to be. I’m whatever you decide I am. The truth about writing is that once I hit “publish” on a piece of writing, I am not a storyteller anymore. I’m whatever you need me to be. I’m your inspiration. I’m your catalyst for change. I’m the source of your outrage. I’m the idiot who makes you feel better about your intelligence. I’m the anxious kid who makes you feel better about struggling to keep it together. I love being all that because it means that something I said has struck a chord, but I hate it too. I hate that I work so hard to give my readers something that is so hard for me to give myself. I wish I could see all the things that other people claim to see in me — good and bad. I wish I could know myself as well as random people on the internet claim to know me. I wish I could feel as strongly about the conclusions that people draw about me as they do. Instead, I feel scared. I’ve been doing this for more than a year, and I still get queasy before posting writing that’s honest for me—like this piece. I get queasy because I care. Caring literally makes me sick. I’m scared of a lot of things. I’m scared to have difficult conversations. I’m scared to tell my mom and dad that I love them. It never felt okay to say that as a kid. I’m scared of what I’ll do when my body breaks down and stops me from being able to compete in martial arts at the highest levels. I’m scared that if I stop plastering my internal mental shit all over the internet, I’ll disappear and become irrelevant. I’m scared that I’ll never “make it” as a writer or an athlete or whatever the fuck else I try to be. I am scared of a lot of shit, and that is why I write — constantly. Writing is the only thing that’s ever made me feel free from my fear. Writing is the only way I can organize my anxious brain so that I can function like a normal person. I’m one of the best Jiu-Jitsu fighters in the world right now (I finally feel confident enough to say that), but writing is the only thing that has ever made me feel truly strong. Before I started writing, I was fighting to run away from my fear. I wanted to make sure that no one knew that I was scared, so I fought and fought and fought until I didn’t feel a damn thing besides the dull pain in my neck and back. Writing is what helps me feel like a human again, instead of some deranged warrior living in a society that has deemed combat sports as violent, barbaric pursuits. Publishing is the only way that I can tell if the words and feelings that I put out there make any sense to anyone at all. That’s why I write, and that’s why I’m not stopping any time soon.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What keeps you motivated to pursue your dreams?
Answer: The 2 guys on each side of me help me stay motivated a lot more than the giant check in my hands. On Saturday, I competed in a Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu tournament with a weight limit of up to 225 pounds. At the weigh-ins on Friday night, I weighed in at 181 with my phone, wallet, and keys in my pocket. It didn’t matter. I beat out 3 tough fighters (all of whom were bigger than me), and one athlete who is considered one of the top grapplers in the world (he weighs around 200 pounds) in order to snag the $5000 grand prize. This victory is 5 times what I’ve made in a single day for Jiu-Jitsu before. I’ve spent years paying money out of my own pocket to compete. This check pays my rent nearly 7 times. Because of this check, I’m about to go buy my first pair of sneakers since I committed to this full-time Jiu-Jitsu thing a little over 2 years ago. I like sneakers. It might seem like a small thing to you, but to me, having the ability to buy something I want using money that I made doing what I love makes me want to cry. I feel like I’ve worked my whole life for these sorts of opportunity. I’ve been staying afloat financially and I’m doing pretty well for someone in my lines of work, but no one exactly thinks of writers or Jiu-Jitsu fighters as people who are rakin’ in big checks. I get that $5k doesn’t make me rich, but to me, this means that I’m at least heading in the right direction toward making a real living doing my favorite thing in the world. That helps me a lot with staying motivated. However, there’s a lot more to motivation that wads of cash and fancy pictures with giant checks. Since I spent the first part of this answer talking about how great it is that I made some money from grappling, you might not believe this, but money I make from winning doesn’t motivate me at all. It’s nice to be paid for my efforts, but I’ve been competing in grappling for free since I was 12. Training, competing, and then training again is just what I do. It’s all I know. If I lost my first match at this tournament over the weekend, I’d still have been back in the gym today. I won the bracket and took home the $5k, and we had a 6.5 hour drive home from Minneapolis last night, but I was still up at 7:30 am this morning to go teach a private lesson. After the private lesson, I drove another hour and 15 minutes to teach a class at a friend’s academy and get some training in for myself. The reason? I surround myself with awesome people. My coach (to my left in the photo above) isn’t just a coach, he’s a guy who I feel like is a good person who I actually want to hang out with. He’s not the boss of me, he’s a mentor. He teaches me shit. My friend Jack (to my right) isn’t just some guy who I know from the gym. He’s at training with me every single day, whether he wants to be or not. He competed on Saturday and won his match too. I stay motivated because I surround myself with motivated people. Sustained motivation over extended periods of time is what has given me the ability to even have a shot at winning big checks like the one in the picture. The “grind” doesn’t stop for me because it doesn’t feel like a grind. It’s fun. I like doing this. I might lose, I might get injured, or I might get burnt out, but one things for sure: I’m not giving up any time soon.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I get over anxiety?
Answer: This is a mental game that I play to deal with the feeling that everything around me is caving in. It’s called “And then what if _____”… It’s not too fun to play, but it’s really fun to win. “An Idle Mind Is the Devil’s Playground” The moment I get injured and am unable to train Jiu-Jitsu, I realize just how much time I really spend doing Jiu-Jitsu. Between live training, drilling, strength and conditioning, and studying video, I spend probably around 4–6 hours every day immersed in improving myself at Jiu-Jitsu. When you add my teaching responsibilities on top of that, plus all of my writing, it’s honestly a miracle that I have any time to even eat. I hurt my back the other day, and for the moment, I’m stuck on the sidelines. Once you remove the 4–6 hours per day I spend focused on martial arts and knock it down to about .5-1 (I still try to study tape when I’m injured), I am “gifted” with a lot of extra time, and I honestly don’t know how to handle it. I’ll spend some of the extra time writing, but I can only stare at the screen and hammer out words for so long. After I finish writing, I need to do something else, and I honestly don’t know what to do when I’m not training besides sitting and worrying about how I’m getting passed up by my competition. My competition is the best grapplers in the world, so I know that they’re working a lot harder than me when I’m not working at all. Even worse, I don't know how to structure a day that doesn’t involve training. I don’t know how to eat properly when I’m not training. I don’t know what time to get up, what time to go to bed, or how to do anything. Once Jiu-Jitsu is gone, I feel my firm grasp on my reality slipping away. It’s my discipline that keeps me sane, and injuries test my discipline in the most challenging way possible because they remove my favorite part of my discipline routine — my training. Once you take away my training routine, I start to realize that I’m a 24-year-old kid who doesn't really know much of anything about how the world works, and that’s a very scary thing to deal with, especially all by myself, away from my friends and the comfort of the gym. Luckily, I’ve Been Here Before This way of thinking has ruined my day countless times in the past. When I tore my meniscus a few years ago, I had this horrible cycle of depression that lasted for months, and eventually, it led to severe derealization — meaning that my mind was essentially cut off from reality. People often roll their eyes at this, but I promise you that derealization is real, and it’s a hell I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemies. I’ve done some kind of difficult stuff in my life, especially in sports, but without a doubt, winning my battle with derealization is the single toughest victory I have ever pulled off. Doing so gave me mental strength that I didn’t know I had. However, this bout of derealization was triggered by an injury that led to an extended break from Jiu-Jitsu. Because of this, every time I get injured now, I’m “triggered” by memories of the time that I was injured for 6 months and stuck in my head for 9. It’s scary, and I’ve had to create mental strategies that help me continue living, stay peaceful, and even stay happy when I feel like everything is about to fall apart. That’s what takes me to one of my favorite mental games. And Then What If…? My anxiety is kind of like a toddler. No matter what I say to calm its nerves, it always follows up with the same question: “And then what if _____?” (insert some horrible outcome for me) I’ve had some pretty deep internal conversations following this conversation structure, and it’s pretty much how I’ve constructed all of the strategies that I use to deal with my anxiety. It’s similar to Tim Ferriss’s “fear-setting”, but my personal twist is that I take a deeper, more existential approach to managing my fears. I analyze my fears deep down to their core. Doing this has helped me better understand my triggers, my deep-seated hopes, and my darkest fears, and it’s even helped me understand how my own brain chemistry unconsciously dictates the choices that I make. When you can consciously understand the choices that your unconscious mind is making, I believe that you are only a few steps from psychological superpowers. Here’s An Example: Let’s use my current back injury as an example. The first worry that came was “My back is probably going to hurt a bit for the next few weeks”. My anxiety took this thought and ran with it. “And then what if I’m too injured to fight at the ADCC Trials in Poland?”, screams my anxiety, thinking it cares about me and my wellbeing. If that happened, I’d simply keep training and try again at the ADCC Trials in 2024. I’ll probably be even better at Jiu-Jitsu when those come around. “And then what if your back never gets better ever?” screams my anxiety. If that happened, I’d have to accept that my athletic career was over, and then I’d figure out a new way to move forward in my life. I guess I’d become a coach. I might put on 15 pounds. The most famous Jiu-Jitsu coach in the world is so crippled in his, knee, and back that he can barely walk, I’m sure I could be a decent coach with my bad back. I won’t bore you with more of my worries, but the point here is that every time I experience a thought that makes me upset or uncomfortable, I challenge that thought. I use rational thinking to poke holes in irrational thoughts that are fucking up my peace. The result is me being happier and less anxious than I’ve ever been, and it’s pretty damn nice. Hopefully this gives you a new way to think about anxiety :)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What makes a person boring?
Answer: Boring is subjective. I wrote a list about 2 months ago about things that “are not worth it”, where I listed a lot of the habits that I have adopted in an effort to have a disciplined lifestyle. My disciplined lifestyle, unfortunately, means that I don’t drink, I don’t do drugs, I don’t hook up with strangers, and a bunch of other things that most people find “exciting”. I linked the list above if you want to read it. One comment that I got a lot was that I “must be an insanely boring person”, and while I guess that that’s a valid argument, I think it’s a little shortsighted. I don’t drink because my genetic makeup puts me at a higher risk for alcoholism than most. I don’t do drugs because when I ate a pot gummy bear a few years I spiraled into a derealization episode that made me nearly kill myself and I’m still getting past that fear. I don’t hook up with strangers because I have social anxiety and I need to be comfortable around someone before I have sex with them. The whole martial arts thing is simply a lifestyle that coincided well with my decisions. I just don’t think that a person’s interestingness should be dictated by whether or not their into IPAs or White Claws. I don’t think how wild you get is interesting. If I’m on vacation, I’ll have a drink with some friends. One day, I want to try psychedelics. Maybe after the psychedelics, hooking up with strangers will freak me out less. But being interesting is not about your small habits, it’s about the stories that you have. I write and do Jiu-Jitsu every day. That’s boring. Maybe you go to work every day. That’s also boring. The things that you do every day are not what makes you unique or interesting. What makes you interesting is the experiences and the reflections on those experiences that you have while doing those everyday things. The fact that I write every day is not interesting, but the fact that I’ve gotten 2.5 million views on Quora this month might be interesting for an aspiring writer. The fact that I do Jiu-Jitsu isn’t inherently interesting, but the things that I’ve learned from training Jiu-Jitsu (like how to properly strangle an opponent or the fact that I’m ranked #12 in the world in my weight class) might be interesting to someone who is interested in fighting. Interest is subjective, and it’s based on your current needs and wants. That’s why, if you need me, I’ll be over here being boring. I’m predictable, but I’m also constantly improving in all areas of my life. In addition to being the lamest writer on Quora, I’m also trying to write more stuff on Twitter. I promise all of my tweets are just as lame as my Quora answers. If you’d like, give me a follow! It helps me out more than you know :)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I forget someone whom I once loved deeply?
Answer: This question reminds me of my ex-girlfriend who I thought was the love of my life. She told me I was the love of her life, and I believed her. And yet, here we are. Sometimes, I wish I could forget her. If there's anything I learned from the movie in the picture above (Eternal Sunshine of a Spotless Mind), it’s that you're not supposed to forget the people you once loved, even if it hurts to not forget them. You’re supposed to learn from them. This sounds nice in a self-help-esque Quora answer, but it’s really hard to do in reality. My ex who I broke up with last year was the first woman who I really loved. It was the first time I really loved a person who isn’t my mom, my dad, or my sister. I know I really loved her because still, after everything we went through, I can’t hate her or even be mad at her. I know I loved her because I kept trying to convince myself that I wasn’t in love. This love was a neurochemical hijacking in a way I had never experienced before, and though the breakup was more than a year ago now, I still miss her a lot. I’ve dated other people since her, but I still miss her. “There are plenty of fish in the sea”, but I miss her. I would take her back right now, even though doing it would be a horrible decision. Even though taking her back would destroy my mental health, drain the life out of me, and break me down, I know that if she showed up at my doorstep I couldn’t resist her. I think that’s love. I’m only 24 and I don’t know that much, but I don’t think love is always rational. I loved this girl so damn much, and I’ll probably never see her again. I probably shouldn't ever see her again. She was sweet and sensitive, yet strong and determined. She had the duality and complexity that I’ve always craved in a partner, and I miss that so much. But she also had this dark side that terrified me. She changed a lot in the time we were together, and eventually, we grew apart. We grew apart, but that doesn’t mean I lost the memories. For a long time, I wanted the “spotless mind”, just like in the movie. I still remember when she held me one December afternoon in Milwaukee and made me feel like I didn’t have to fight my way through every moment of my life anymore. I still remember when we would sit together on Saturday afternoons after Jiu-Jitsu training and read together. I still remember when we went on drives and talked about Nietzsche, Buddha, and Viktor Frankl. I still miss that stuff, but it’s gone now. Anyway—sorry for my sob story. The point I’m trying to make is that sometimes I wish I could just rip these memories out of my head so that I didn’t have to miss this girl who probably doesn’t even think about me anymore. That’s probably the part that hurts the most. I’m sure she’s moved on. I moved on too, but sometimes it doesn’t feel that way. This past breakup forced me to change the way that I approach moving on. In the past, I’d breakup with someone and drown myself in work and training to forget them, just long enough until I stumbled upon the next girl who I could go through the same toxic cycles with. This past breakup cut me so deep that I had to actually grow. I couldn’t lie anymore. I had to forgive her for hurting me. I had to forgive myself for not being good enough and not knowing enough. I had to forgive all parties involved, but I never forgot any of what happened. The ending hurt so bad that I had no choice but to carefully analyze each mistake each of made so that I could ensure that it wouldn’t happen again. I couldn't sleep for weeks after it happened, so I had all kinds of time. This past breakup changed the way that I view every single person I interact with. It made me more careful, more mature (I think), and more protective of my own peace and wellbeing. I won’t throw myself at anyone without a bloody care ever again. I don’t want to forget these valuable lessons. I don’t want this girl’s memory to haunt me forever, but I don’t want to forget the moments that made me feel so happy and in love. After the breakup, I found myself desperately chasing women in an effort to replace the feelings that I had when I was in love, but no one could satiate my rabid insecure child the way she did. This empty feeling meant to me at the time that I needed to get her back, so I tried to do that. Long story short, it didn’t work. In time (time is the best breakup medicine), I realized that with practice, I could love myself the way my first love loved me. I realized that I wasn’t even really looking for a girlfriend or a partner, I was looking for validation and protection. It didn’t even take a therapist for me to figure why that was something I felt was lacking. With practice, writing, mindfulness, and most importantly genuine self-sufficiency (which I didn’t have during my last relationship), I was able to patch up the hole in my heart pretty well. Hopefully, with more time, I’ll be able to truly open my heart again. Until then, I’m gonna focus on writing and pajama fighting.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the benefits of playing a sport?
Answer: I've played sports for as long as I can remember. Here’s a photo from my high school wrestling days. I’m the weird one on the left. The dude on the right told me he was going to become a pilot in the Navy, and about 7 years after this photo was taken, he did. That was pretty inspiring. Anyway, here are 10 life lessons I learned from playing sports.  1. Competition isn’t everything. Once the final whistle blows, you and your soccer rivals are not enemies anymore… You’re just a bunch of people standing on a field. Without awareness, social constructs limit human connection. I don’t know… just be nice? 2. “Fatigue makes cowards of us all” — George S Patton Jr. At the beginning of the game or match, both fighters are confident. Once you start getting tired, things start to change. You have to be mentally stronger than your fatigued self is weak. 3. You aren’t entitled to victory. Sorry. You can train every day, put in hours and hours of training, spend thousands of dollars on perfect coaching, and still show up on gameday and shit the bed. Preparation does not guarantee success, it only influences it. 4. No one does anything alone. Few people are REALLY self-made, but being self-made doesn’t matter as much as everyone makes it seem. I learned how to fight through hard work and perseverance, but I also have a coach. Accepting help is not a bad thing at all. Chill. 5. Bad team members are cancerous. This one’s a little cutthroat, but nothing destroys a team quite like a member who won’t pull their weight. One bad sailor can sink a ship. 6. Rules heavily influence outcomes. In Jiu-Jitsu, different rulesets can determine who wins a match. Styles make fights. In writing, some of us are great at fiction, and some of us are great at nonfiction. Styles make books. Don’t become married to any set of rules. 7. You can learn a lot from your enemies. I always study the matches I lose and I watch my opponents even after my run through a particular tournament is ...

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do you decide what career is best for you?
Answer: I made my career out of my passion, and while I love it, this is probably not a great idea for everyone. Here are 7 things you need to know about “choosing a job that you love”. If you aren’t willing to deal with these things, maybe your hobbies are meant to be just that: hobbies. You will have to work for free. This is a hard one for people to accept because everyone is so focused on “knowing their worth” that they forget that what matters is the worth that they can provide for others. If I started charging people for guitar lessons tomorrow, no one would buy them because, well, I suck at playing the guitar. Even if I scammed someone into buying my guitar lesson course, they would not be likely to stay with me for long. I started writing online for free. I started teaching Jiu-Jitsu for free. I paid money to compete in martial arts for a decade before I got my first sponsor. In order to make money doing something, you have to learn how to demonstrate your value. Give value away for free and trust the process. Skill does not equal money. I know several Jiu-Jitsu world champions who are dead-broke. I know some talented writers who can’t sell a book. Hell, I’ve been an aspiring professional athlete still living with mom and dad and I’ve been an aspiring writer who couldn’t get anyone to buy his book. I sympathize with the struggles you face on the come up, but overcoming those struggles is not only about improving skills. Honestly, no one cares how good you are as much as you do. Learn to build, learn to create, but if you want to make a living, learn to sell. Your insecurities will probably hold you back. Overcome them before you try to build something. Very few people are operating with zero insecurities. Become aware of your insecurities and get past them — your career development depends on this. Just because you’re passionate about something doesn’t mean you’re allowed to let anxiety control you. Passion is great, but anxious passion is a predecessor to a disingenuous business model that will struggle to survive over long periods of time. Passion doesn’t pay the bills, but it can if you can get past your anxiety about whether or not your passion can pay the bills. In order to have the clear-headedness to run a business that’s based on something you love, you must make sure you are handling your anxiety well. Mental health and financial health are closely related. Act like a professional before you’re making money. Pros show up when they’re tired. They show up when they’re uninspired. They show up when the thought of working is nauseating. As an athlete, I’ve always operated with the mindset that I was a professional because being a professional athlete was my dream from the time I was 5-years-old. It was more challenging to make this shift as a writer, but doing so changed my career. I went from writing 2 articles per week to one per day. I went from being upset over bad views to seeing bad views as data. The simple shift from amateur to pro changed a lot for me. Kindness is the key to a passion-based business. This sounds a bit cliche, but people don’t actually do it. People are not kind in their business endeavors most of the time. I should know — I spent my first 2 years after college working for entrepreneurs and helping them grow their brands. The businesses that lacked kindness also lacked the ability to get off the ground. Don’t be nice, be kind. Learn the difference before you begin to build any business relationship. Be kind to everyone you work with, or quit the relationship. There should be no in-between. Learn to accept help from other people. People love to romanticize the idea of being “self-made” (especially here in America), but just about all of us are accepting some sort of help from someone. My family supports me by not fighting with me anymore when I tell them about my goals that make literally no sense to them (imagine being a parent, wanting your 19-year-old to get a degree and a salary, and he says he wants to become a professional fighter for a living…). My friends and teammates support me by showing up and pushing me in the gym every day and making me laugh when we hang out outside it. My Jiu-Jitsu sponsor helps me financially and professionally. My coach helps me technically. I have received a lot of help to get to where I’m at, and I’m eternally grateful. I’ve created a life that has a lot of love in it. Accept constant unpredictability as part of your reality. Trying to control anxiety only leads to more anxiety. When you let the anxious thoughts run wild, they’ll realize that they have no power. When you accept unpredictability as a part of your day-to-day life, it’s much harder to view it as something that negatively impacts your life. You must switch your anxiety from a problem that you deal with to an obstacle that you will overcome. I do what I do because I literally could not do anything else. I love the constant striving that is required of me in my career (I actually believe it leads me to self-transcendence, but that's for another day), and I’ve accepted that unpredictability is just part of that striving. If you cannot handle the anxiety, unpredictability, and chaos of chasing your passion, choose something more stable. Your future self will thank you for your self-awareness. There’s nothing wrong with working a normal job, having hobbies, and living a normal life, but I feel that I’ve always been destined for a passion-based career. These are just a few of the roadblocks that I’ve had to deal with in choosing my career, building it, and finally going “all-in” on my dreams of being a professional writer and fighter. Hopefully, you got some value from this. ❤️

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the simplest way to stay young?
Answer: Storytelling helps me say young. I’m only 24, so I’m probably not the top authority on “staying young”, but as I look around the people who used to be my peers, I can’t help but feel like my soul is a little younger than most people my age. Some people say I’m an old soul, but inside, I feel like a giant 11-year-old with a beard. My friends are getting “real jobs”, being anxious about who has what, and doing a lot of the things that I thought I was going to be forced to do in my mid-20s, and I’m living a martial arts movie. No “quarter-life crisis” happening over here. I’m fighting in what are giant Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu tournaments all over the world, I make a living from writing and Jiu-Jitsu, and I spend every day learning new things and sharing my knowledge with people who I meet. Most people I know complain about their jobs a lot, but I don’t. When you remove the physical damage and the occasional financial stress I get from fighting, I guess my life is pretty easy. When I was 10 years old, I wanted to be a professional athlete. Also, my favorite TV shows were Naruto and Dragon Ball Z. Nearly 15 years later, I do martial arts professionally and I get paid to compete and teach. I even had bleach blonde hair for a year and a half, like a Super Saiyan. I’m literally living the future extension of my childhood dream. This keeps me pretty young. All I did was follow my heart to a stubborn, obnoxious end, work really really hard, and get a bit lucky. I quit relationships that didn’t lead down the path I wanted. I fought injured, sick, and broken, because I wanted this dream more than I wanted to feel good. Then, after I did that for a long time, I started writing. My whole writing thing honestly came way after I started down my path. A long time ago, I thought maybe one day I could write a semi-decent book about the weird adventures I’ve been on in my life doing Jiu-Jitsu, and I didn’t want to forget my stories, so I wrote them down. I wrote essays and stories and philosophies to myself in a journal for years from the time I was around 17, but I never published anything because I was too anxious. I only started publishing because I wanted to prove to myself that I wasn’t afraid of the external judgment that comes with publishing. But now, the rush that I get from telling stories and fighting for my dreams speaks directly to that anxious 10-year-old kid I used to be who just wanted a purpose in his life. It speaks to the kid inside me that yearned for a quest. I feel young because I’m never sitting around getting old. I’m trying to grab life by the horns. I’m always experiencing new things. Maybe I’m young and naive and wrong, but right now I feel like I’m doing okay. I work like a dog for my purpose, and I wouldn't have it any other way. My joints ache, my back hurts, and sometimes I’m on edge about making money, achieving success, and whether or not I’m going to make it, but for the most part, every day is an adventure. I think that’s a good way to stay young. Wait… Was this answer supposed to be about diet and skincare routines? Whoops!

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do some intelligent people fail to achieve their potential?
Answer: After my performance at this grappling tournament in Las Vegas last week, I stumbled my way into the top 15 in the world in no-gi Jiu-Jitsu. Most people on Quora don’t follow Jiu-Jitsu, but for me, seeing myself listed amongst these athletes is a dream come true. My idols are now my rivals. This is something I’ve been working on obsessively for the last 9 months, but it’s really been 12 years in the making. Recently, I became ranked #1 in the world at my belt rank and weight class, and that was really cool, but these rankings include all belt ranks, all ages, and all athletes on earth who compete in the 170-pound division. Seeing myself on that list was a little surreal at first. But the truth is that my goal was never to be 12th in the world. I never wanted to have a “strong showing” that put my name on the map. I don’t just want to be “a tough guy”, I want to be the best. I’m a competitive athlete, and I won’t be fully at peace with my pursuit until I have achieved the top ranking. Even then, I won’t be happy, because I’ll have to defend that top ranking. The reason that many intelligent people fail to achieve their potential is that they base their happiness on their results, and they then stop pursuing their goals because their goals are not making them happy. If I let the spot that I hold on this little ranking list determine how happy I am with my life, I am going to become very frustrated and unhappy with my existence. I will probably give up on my goals and stop pursuing them altogether. I’ll get sad and quit. People make a lot of excuses as to why they don’t achieve their potential or reach their goals, but the main reason that people fail is that they get sad and quit. Sure, other factors contribute to failure, like money, a lack of talent, a lack of work ethic, a lack of discipline, etc, but none of these factors will ruin your dream quite like getting sad and quitting. If you don’t have the money to put as much time into something as you want, you might just get there slowly. If you aren’t hard-working or talented or disciplined, you might have to work harder. If something is stopping you from doing something, most smart people can figure out a way to “make it work” without giving up. Once you get sad and quit, you’re done. That’s it. A heartbroken dreamer is a tough person to help.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Does hard work really pay off?
Answer: Today I want to share the story of the time that more than 50,000 people watched me get choked out and lose on the internet. See, there are like, a lot of videos online of me getting beat up. Now, granted, each beating is one that I signed up for and was a willing participant in, but still, there are a lot of videos. However, the only video of me getting my ass kicked that matters to me is this one, from the semifinals of the 2018 IBJJF Pan Ams in Irvine, California. It’s been viewed over 40,000 times on FloGrappling’s (the largest media source in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu) Instagram page, and thousands of more times on their Facebook page. It’s been viewed at least 50,000 times. That video lit a fire under my ass that completely changed my life, but not exactly in the way you might think. Earlier that day, I walked into the tournament venue seeking a gold medal, glory, and perhaps even some internet fame of my own. Instead, I was carried out of the venue with a bronze medal around my neck, and this video went viral just several hours later. It’s tough, but this is the nature of what I do: I put myself out there and risk having my body used as a tool for someone else’s highlight reel. My opponents do the same. We’re martial artists during the digital age, and this means there’s nowhere to hide. But during the 12 months that followed the incident in California, hiding is exactly what I did. I spiraled into a mini existential crisis that involved severe depression, knee surgery, and a near-retirement from competition at the ripe age of 20. I nearly quit everything. Yet somehow, 18 months later, it was me being interviewed by FloGrappling to commemorate my first ever world championship. This is the story of how I overcame my depression and achieved the wildest dream I’ve ever had. But more importantly, this is the story of how I stopped living in the past. There are two sides to every story. What the video that I shared above doesn’t show is that I was competing in that tournament with a torn meniscus, and during the moments where I was flopping around to escape that choke, my knee was literally locked into place. I didn’t know my knee was torn, my opponent didn’t know, and the media at the tournament certainly had no idea that I was essentially fighting on one leg. They saw the opportunity for a video and just hit record. I can’t blame them, they were doing their jobs. In the 12 hours that followed the match, I was in excruciating pain and my right knee was locked into place and immobilized. We even went to Rite Aid and bought crutches so I could go for a “walk” on the beach with my friends. That afternoon, when the video went viral, I realized something that horrified me: if I didn’t bounce back from this loss, I was forever going to be known as the guy who got choked out with a made-up move. I was a loser. I was humiliated and determined to heal up and bounce back. All my friends said something along the lines of “you’ll get him next time!”. If only it were that simple. Saying I was going to heal and bounce back was one thing, and actually doing it was something else entirely. A week later, when I got an MRI at the doctor a few weeks later, he said the worst thing I could have possibly imagined: “Nothing seems to be wrong with your knee.” Considering that just a few weeks earlier I had been unable to walk, I was outraged. My body was failing me, and no one had any idea why. It didn’t get better from there. Over the next 6 months, my knee popped in and out of place countless times. At least 30 times, once even in my sleep. It was incredibly painful, and for a while, I was convinced that my athletic career was over. I was convinced my dream of becoming a Jiu-Jitsu world champion was going to die before I even turned 21. That dream was my everything, and it was slipping away. I was depressed, heartbroken, and aimless. My dream was dying, and I thought that meant that I was supposed to die too. This knee injury I believe played a significant role in triggering the episode of derealization that I wrote about on Quora a few months ago. You can read that story here. Below is how I bounced back from my knee injury and my derealization. One day in September (6 months after the Pan Ams-viral-video-incident), I injured my knee again — this time much worse than before. The doctors were finally able to locate my torn meniscus. 3 weeks later, I had surgery. 4 weeks after that, I was back on the mat like nothing had ever happened. It was ridiculous. 7 months of extreme pain, frequent “knee locks”, and an existential crisis were all compensated for in one 15-minute procedure. The mental wounds took more time to heal, but I could finally admit it to myself: I was on the comeback train. In February of 2019, now 11 months after the original injury, I was back competing, and I was happier than ever. I was doing the thing I loved most, and I was more than grateful for every second of it — I was ecstatic. But unfortunately, I still had a lot to overcome to reach my full form. “We did it.” When I came back to competition, I was finishing up undergrad, training like a professional athlete, and beginning to teach Jiu-Jitsu on the side to make extra money. I was busy. I was grateful to be back, but my workload had me incredibly burnt out and anxious for months on end. I was questioning if all of my hard work was ever going to pay off — if the journey was going to be worth the struggle. In December of 2019, it finally was. I won 6 matches and won a No-Gi Jiu-Jitsu world title at my age and belt rank. It was a wild experience. Tears were shed. When the ref raised my hand after my final match, I went straight to my close friend Jack and gave him a hug. “We did it,” I said. He’d been there for me since the beginning. He was the one who’d carried me out of the venue 18 months earlier. The dream got more surreal after that. The same media outlet that had recorded my ass-whooping 18 months earlier was now interviewing me of all people asking me about my performance, my plans for the future, and surprisingly to me, who the heck I was. To them, I seemed like an overnight success. I was dumbfounded. “How did they not remember who I was? I even had the same haircut!” That was when I realized that no one remembered my loss from years earlier except for me. No one cared that I’d gotten butt-kicked except for me. No one cared about my redemption quest from knee surgery and depression to world champ except for me. The story I had told myself was for myself, not everyone else. While I was lost in my personal legend, the world had kept on spinning. I’m done with the past. Once I achieved the biggest goal of my life, I had a huge realization: Life goes on, with or without you. For the first time ever, I understood what this actually meant. Even if you win a gold medal and got to kiss the prom queen one night, the next day comes and everyone else moves on with their lives no matter who you kissed the night before or what color your medal was. It’s not that they don’t care, it’s just that they don’t care as much as you. This is easy to understand but complicated to actually implement into your life. I know so many people who are stuck in the past, constantly reliving their “glory days”, and saddest of all, are trapped in the same mindset that they had when they were younger. They’ve stopped growing because they’re living in the past, and it’s heartbreaking. The truth is, your glory days are right now. Nothing matters except right now. Whatever happened in the past, whatever happened in the last competition, whatever conditioned you to think the way that you think right now, it’s over. Living in the past is what stops us from beginning to live in the first place. Once I achieved my goal of winning a world championship, my biggest fear wasn’t falling from grace, my biggest fear was becoming stuck in the past. “It is not death that a man should fear, but he should fear never beginning to live.” — Marcus Aurelius I realized that no matter how many titles I win, there will always be another one. There will always be another goal to throw my entire being into. If I’m not careful, I’ll do this over and over again until the day I die. I’ll never even begin to live because I’ll be constantly engrossing myself in the pursuit of external validation. I can’t have that. “It never ceases to amaze me: we all love ourselves more than other people, but care more about their opinions than our own.” — Marcus Aurelius I began my martial arts journey from a place of fear, anxiety, and ambition, but I stay on the journey because I love it. I’m free from my past successes and failures, and to me, that’s growing up. They say that life is a marathon, not a sprint. But when you experience anxiety, everything seems like a marathon. Anxiety heightens the senses, and this neurological tidal wave leaves us anxious folks feeling drained, overwhelmed, and incredibly unprepared to handle the stress of life. During my darkest periods with anxiety and depression, I felt as if I aged decades in just weeks. But though anxiety is a very real mental illness and the symptoms of anxiety are very real, the fears and cognitive distortions created by our anxiety are not real. Anxiety is a real response to not real problems. “We suffer more in imagination than in reality.” — Seneca When I hurt my knee, had an existential crisis, and lost my way, I obsessed over how I was going to redeem myself and prove to everyone that I was tough, strong, and competent. I fixated on the past, obsessed over the future, and ignored the present. It made me miserable. Becoming a world champion didn’t make me happy, being nicer to myself did. My journey through the world of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu has taught me a lot about life, but the most important lesson that I’ve learned is that no failure is final, and no success is, either. You have nothing to prove, and nothing to lose. You are here, and you are enough, as you are. When you accept that, you’ll be able to unlock your true potential. Hopefully, you don’t need to go viral to realize this.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the biggest challenges in the work you do?
Answer: For me, the hardest challenges are physical injuries. This is a short answer because my wrists and thumbs are strained so getting words out there is a challenge right now. To be a successful writer on the internet, you have to write a lot, and publish a lot. The more I write, the more my hands hurt. To be a successful grappler or to get your black belt in Jiu-Jitsu, you have to train a lot. The more I train and compete, the great risk I run for physical injuries. I have had more than my fair share of injuries in everything I do. I’m starting to think that maybe the problem isn’t the sport or the line of work and that maybe, my injuries are mostly my fault. I train too much. I try to write several thousand words per day. I fight sick and injured and take on projects I can’t handle. You might say, “hey man, just take a break,” but you know it isn’t that simple. Competitive work never is. Success is a balancing act, but it’s also destructive. If you’re trying to be the best, sustainability is a lot harder than you think.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are you tired of hearing?
Answer: I’m tired of being told “you’re only ____ years old, you don’t know anything yet”. I’m only 24. I haven’t had kids. I haven’t been married. I’ve barely even had any long term relationships. The closest thing to a “career” that I’ve had has been an international bathrobe wrestling career (Jiu-Jitsu). I can’t tell you how to do your taxes. I can’t tell you how to invest in the Dow Jones. Besides Jiu-Jitsu and writing and my own interpretations of stuff that happens to me, I don’t really know much of anything. I get it. I’m clueless in a lot of areas of my life. I’m sick of hearing about it. I’m sick of people trying to “humble me” by using my age as leverage. I believe that this intellectual posturing is a sign of a lack of wisdom, no matter how old you are. I get that I don’t know everything. Most of my life is me fucking things up, realizing I have no idea what I’m doing in all the situations that I’m pushed into, and then trying to reassess and move forward. At 24, everything I do is a learning experience. But maybe this mindset is how all of life should be lived. A few weeks back, a guy I know paid for me to come down and teach a Jiu-Jitsu seminar at his gym about 5 hours away from where I live. I was the one teaching the seminar, but I was the youngest one in the room. I’m young and I “don’t know anything”, but people are paying to learn from me. Sometimes, the people who are telling me I don’t know anything are the ones who are paying to learn from me. It just feels whack to be a part of this. A lot of people who write comments about how dumb I am have never published any writing. They’ve never been choked out in front of thousands of people (a good story for another day). A lot of people who think they know better than me are armchair quarterbacks who are using their sheer time on this earth as social leverage over me. I’ve realized that people who constantly remind you that you don’t know anything are not the people who you should be learning from. These people are more likely trying to make themselves feel better. People who attempt to use your lack of knowledge as leverage are not people who you want to learn from. The best mentors are the people who are not trying to be your mentors. The best mentor relationships are the ones you don’t have to force. If you read this and your first thought is, “this kid doesn’t know what he’s talking about”, Just know that I’ll probably re-read this in 6 months from now agree with you. I’m learning every day. Let me learn in peace. I just choose to learn in public because I’m trying to demonstrate the process of the acquisition of knowledge. Time will tell if this idea has any merit.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What made you resign from your previous job?
Answer: For the last year and a half or so, I’ve been working as a social media manager for 6–12 businesses. This was my “regular job” while I was pursuing my passions of writing and Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Last week, I said “fuck it”, and quit. Here’s why: Every time I’ve worked for someone else, the working relationship has gone up in flames. As a kid, I hated being told what to do. I hated school. I hated bosses. I’m an athlete, and for years I even had a problem taking advice from coaches and listening during technical instruction during wrestling practice. I used to make myself throw up when I was a baby just because it pissed my mom off. My amazing mother is a trooper to put up with my bullshit. Maybe I’m a demon. Maybe, I just need to march to the beat of my own drummer. My problem with authority was the leading contributing factor to my lack of success in my school years and early adulthood. I always wanted to do my own thing, and I was never allowed to. I always had to sit back and listen. I always had to follow orders. But not anymore. Now, I’m free. This is the process that I used to get to a point where I can quit my job and go all-in on my dreams of writing, teaching, and grappling: Honestly, you might not love where this answer is going… There wasn’t a secret to me becoming a “full-time writer” and a professional athlete. I didn’t discover a secret platform, create a secret product or course, or take a bunch of steroids. If anything, I mostly failed on my way here. I still fail every day. Recently, I actually wrote an e-book that hardly anyone bought. I spent most of the last fall being so injured that I couldn’t grapple or lift weights. I lost a lot of matches last year. On my year and a half-long journey to a career that I actually wanted to have, I mostly messed things up. Most of my articles received under 100 views. My first 89 Quora answers were viewed less than 6000 times, while my ensuing answers have been viewed several millions of times. All I’ve done has been practice every day, work really hard, study my game, and get a little bit lucky. That’s fuckin’ it. Now, I’m able to take the next step. I wish I could tell you there was more to it. I burned myself out, built myself back up, and then did it all over again time and time again. I’ve written and trained just about every single day for several years now for this freedom, and the “prize” that I was given was the opportunity to go “all-in” on the dream life that I designed when I was 19-years-old and living in my college dorm room. I wrote until they had to give me a job. My success on Medium/Quora during the fall gave me some higher-paying writing jobs that made my life a lot more comfortable. I did the math, and my newly acquired ghostwriting gigs would end up paying me more than double what I was being paid to write social media content previously. This made me realize that my previous employers were taking advantage of my skills and work ethic, and I felt compelled to make an escape. I felt cheated, angry, and manipulated, and this frustration gave me a chip on my shoulder that fueled some of the best writing that I believe I’ve ever put out. It was hard work. It was also dumb luck. I won’t lie to you. But at the end of the day, the most important factor to building my career online was writing was doing so much damn stuff that it was literally impossible for me to be ignored. I’ve written more than 250 articles on Medium. I’ve published more than 100 newsletters. I’ve written hundreds of Quora answers and posted a butt-ton of articles on LinkedIn and Twitter. I’ve had hundreds of grappling matches. I’ve done this stuff for so freaking long. So freaking long. I put my name out there so much that some people who were looking for a ghostwriter thought that they would give me a shot, and so far, that shot is working out. Then, I leveraged my skills close to home. Jiu-Jitsu is my first love. I train every day, I teach nearly every day, and I travel the US and beyond training and competing in various competitions. Writing and teaching give me the freedom to live the life I want, and all of my non-Jiu-Jitsu and writing clients were holding me back from the opportunities that would give me even more freedom. I also got my first real sponsor for Jiu-Jitsu this year, the guy in the picture at the top of this article. I’m lucky that I have a sponsor, but I also worked my butt off for years and years (mid-April marks 7 years of Jiu-Jitsu and 12 years of grappling for me) in order to become an athlete who was worth sponsoring. Then, I got to combine writing with Jiu-Jitsu when I was asked to start writing his company’s bi-monthly blog. It was a dream come true. Now, I’m writing articles on martial arts, ghostwriting articles, running my own blog, building my writing business, and teaching Jiu-Jitsu classes, lessons, and seminars. All of this added up to me not only not needing my previous freelance gigs, but I actually didn’t have time to do their work anymore. I had to quit these jobs so that I could focus on quality over quantity. I had to quit so that I could make my life manageable. I had to quit so that my future work would work. And so, just last week, I said “screw it”, and I did it. Now, there’s no going back. I hate being that guy who tells people “if you want what I want, you have to work for it”, but I honestly can’t tell you how else I’ve gotten to where I am. I don’t think I’m super talented, I do think I got pretty lucky, and I also worked my ass off for the life that I have created. I’ve practiced nearly every day for several hours per day for a decade for a chance to chase the life of my dreams. Only time will tell if I’m able to sustain this momentum. The story is far from over.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Does anybody actually enjoy life? People claim they do. Sure, there are some great moments here and there, but the unpredictability, relationships, stress, expectations, etc. make life a pretty crappy experience. Are these people being honest?
Answer: Last week, I fought in this giant martial arts tournament in Las Vegas. In the lead-up to the tournament, I had to lose 15 pounds. I had to train every day. I had to train 2–3 times per day every day. I’ve been doing this for 6 years. I had to lift weights. I have to push my body as hard as I possibly could without physically breaking it. I’ve chosen a career that is not stable. I do not make as much money if I lose. There is pressure, and the pressure is growing every single day. I had a good tournament last weekend, but many times, I haven’t been so fortunate. At the highest levels of competition, inches can be the difference between making a living and having to get a “real job”. Those 2 words echo in my head all the time. Weight cutting makes me wish I was dead. It’s the hardest thing for me. I love food. Last Saturday morning, I had to run and spit into a cup to lose the last pound and a half and get my body to the place where it needs to be. This is not healthy but I do it anyway. I’ve worked myself beyond the point of exhaustion so many times I’ve lost count. I’ve injured just about every joint on my body. I’ve had knee surgery. I need shoulder surgery. I have 3 herniated discs (2 in my neck and one in my lower back). My rib does some weird shit too that is concerning. I got cross-faced so hard a few years ago that my jaw now clicks on command. This sport has taken my life away from me. I’ve put every ounce of my being into Jiu-Jitsu and writing. I’ve sacrificed friends, relationships, a stable, normal career, and a bunch of other stuff for the chance at achieving glory in a sport that society looks upon with disdain. I do martial arts for a living, and because of that, some people will always see me as a meathead. They will always see me as violent. They will think less of me for pursuing my passion. This kills me inside. Okay, pause for a second. If you read that, you might have thought “this kid doesn’t understand that he has the privilege to pursue his dreams. What an ungrateful brat.” I’ve been called an ungrateful brat on Quora (or some iteration of that) a bunch of times because I choose to share my bad days with you guys. I do my best to show the good days and the bad days. The truth is that I enjoy the fuck out of my life, even when it sucks. The reason that I enjoy my life is that I am choosing my own struggles. I have to “suffer” to make weight, but because this “suffering” is voluntary, I don’t really see it as suffering. This motivates me to work harder and helps me stay motivated throughout the most grueling parts of what I try to do. I have this same mindset in writing. It sucks to write every day, but I enjoy being in the flow I find with writing more than I don’t enjoy the day-to-day “grind”. I guess this is a long-winded way of saying “embrace the grind”, but there’s more to it than that. There are extreme examples where people are forced to meet true suffering — health issues, financial strain, the death of a family member, etc, and while dealing with these things is hard, I try to deal with them by being fully immersed in the moment of whatever I’m doing. When you are more mindful, shitty shit is less shitty. Not eloquent, but hey, neither is most of life. Learn to appreciate the parts of your life that Instagram will never see.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are you grateful for at this moment?
Answer: Today, I’m grateful for my friends. Over the weekend, I competed at the 2022 ADCC West Coast Trials. For those who don’t know, ADCC (Abu Dhabi Combat Club) is the most prestigious grappling tournament in the world, and the Trials are qualifying events that happen all over the world in the lead up to the tournament. The North American Trials (particularly the West Coast Trials) are generally considered to be the most challenging of all the trials because both the popularity and competitive level of grappling in North America is considered to be the highest in the world. I went out with my friends Jackpaul and Mel (pictured above) and competed in the 77 Kilogram division. I had 256 people in my division, many of whom are considered to be the best in the world. I came into the event unseeded, and I ended up upsetting 3 of the top 16 seeds (including a few of the top 5 seeds) and ended up taking 4th place out of 256. It was a crazy weekend, and I’ve been quiet on all social platforms the last few days while I’ve been processing everything and planning my next moves. My tournament was super exciting, and I’ll talk more about it this week, but today I wanted to give my friends a little bit of a shoutout. Mel and Jack both lost their first matches early in the day on Saturday, and nonetheless, they were in my corner for every single match throughout the weekend. I’ve been the guy before who’s lost early on in major tournaments, so I understand the frustration that comes with being forced to sit and watch while your teammate continues to fight. However, you wouldn’t have been able to that detect frustration in Mel and Jack this weekend. I know they were upset with their results, but they supported the fuck out of me from the moment I stepped out on the mat Saturday morning until the final whistle of my last match on Sunday night. They were stoic as they dealt with their own defeats, and they made me feel like a champ throughout my entire tournament run. It wasn’t just about being supportive, they made me feel like a champ. I had an entourage of 2, but I felt like I had an army of support behind me. In what I do, your mental state is very important. You need to be able to remain calm, collected, and focused. My friends helped me do that. That’s why today, I’m grateful for my friends.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: If you were to teach the world one thing, what would it be?
Answer: I guess what I really want to be able to teach people how to do is how to do difficult things. Here’s a little story from one of my Jiu-Jitsu classes about how I try to help my students learn how to tackle challenges. When I joined my school’s wrestling team in middle school, my coach used to say that anyone who could walk on their hands all the down to the end of the mat would be a state champion. I could never do it. I could hardly walk more than a few steps. I was never a good hand-walker. I was also never a state champion. I was average in all things combat sports for the entirety of my youth. I didn’t win anything that mattered until I was 22. By that time, I had been involved in combat sports for more than a decade and I was doing it for the love of it. By the time I had any real success on the mat, I was already intrinsically motivated, and that gave me the work ethic to develop the skill required to have competitive success. As a side project, I still never gave up on my hand-walking, either. By the time I could walk to the end of the mat on my hands, I was already a Jiu-Jitsu world champion, and I was walking on my hands for the hell of it. I’ve realized that my wrestling lessons have helped me develop intrinsic motivation from a pretty young age, and as a coach, I try to help people do the same things. I realized this more as a coach than an athlete, but it is true in whatever you do: intrinsic motivation is the key to achieving difficult goals over extended periods of time. This is how you can teach people to develop intrinsic motivation. If you can do x, you can (maybe) do y. One thing that I hear a lot in the writing world is something along the lines of “if you write every day for 10 years, you will be a 6-figure writer”. Unfortunately, the way the market works, this is not necessarily true. You might not attain any success in writing. Nothing is guaranteed. If you write every day, that doesn’t mean that you will be the next Stephen King or Mark Manson. However, I can guarantee that if you don’t practice writing just about every day, you will definitely not achieve any success in writing. The same is true for music. The same is true for Jiu-Jitsu. In order to develop the ability to do the work required to do something incredibly well, you have to do the thing not because you want to be good, but because you love doing the thing. You must drop the results-driven approach, and seek “flow”. This is what I taught a 6-year-old how to do over the last few months. If a child can learn to flow, so can you. My work life is split about 50% between writing and teaching/competing in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Most of my teaching income comes through private lessons and teaching classes at a local academy here in Chicago, where I teach kid’s Jiu-Jitsu classes 3 days per week. I’ve done this for 6 months now, and when I first started, I had the kids “walk on their hands” for one of their warm-up exercises. As a joke, I channeled my wrestling coach told them that if they could walk all the way down to the end of the mat on their hands without falling, they’d be world champions. When we started doing “handstand walks” during class, none of them could make it more than a few feet. Most of them still can’t. Most of them are not physically developed enough yet to walk on their hands. However, some of them love walking on their hands. For a few of my students, the difficult task of walking on your hands as far as you can is their favorite part of Jiu-Jitsu class. One kid who loves this a lot is Armani. “Coach, can we walk on our hands today?” Every single day that Armani is in class, he runs over to me during warm-ups and asks me if we can walk on our hands. Every. Single. Day. The only question I get asked more than “Coach, can we play dodgeball?” is “Coach, can we walk on our hands?”. Kids are funny like that. They’re consistent. Armani is undeniably consistent. When he started walking on his hands, he couldn’t get more than a few steps. After a few months of watching me walk on my hands, getting some pointers, and practicing at home on his own, Armani was able to walk almost all the way down the mat. That was when I decided to make a friendly competition out of our daily hand-walking exercise. “Whoever is the first person to walk all the way down the mat on their hands will get a candy bar of their choice from me,” I said one day a few weeks back. After I said this, a funny thing happened. Intrinsic motivation is the key to perfection. Once I presented the students with the option to win a candy bar, some of them started to practice hand-walking before and after class. They desperately wanted that free candy. Who wouldn't? To answer my own question — Armani wouldn’t. Armani didn’t. For Armani, this extrinsic motivation did very little for him because he was already intrinsically motivated. A few classes later, Armani successfully walked all the way down to the end of the mat on his hands without a problem. After he did this, I pulled him aside. “What kind of candy bar do you want? You won.” “What do you mean?” he replied. He had completely forgotten about the challenge. He was walking on his hands every day not because he wanted to win, not because he wanted a candy bar from Coach, but because he just liked walking on his hands. He won himself a free Milky Way bar that didn’t even really need. He earned it through hard work, dedication, and most importantly, enjoying the activity that he was doing. That last point is the most important. In closing… The most important aspect of learning to do difficult things is not being gritty, being tough, or even being resilient. The most important aspect of learning to develop a high level of skills over an extended period of time is learning to enjoy the difficult skill. This is why I’m very grateful that I started wrestling when I was just 12. Legendary wrestler Dan Gable once said, “once you’ve wrestled, everything else in life is easy”. Obviously, this isn’t really true, but there is some truth to it. Becoming a successful writer, grappler, business owner, or anything is still difficult when you have wrestling experience. However, what wrestling and other physical endeavors inadvertently teach you is to love the grind for the grind itself. There were moments during my career when I was completely miserable and the thought of dying was literally more appealing than stepping onto the mat. However, now, when I look back at my wrestling days, I can’t help but reminisce about the early morning bus rides in the freezing Chicago winter, the ridiculously hard workouts at all hours of the day, and the constant soreness and hunger that I felt when wrestling was my entire life. I sense that little Armani is going to feel a similar type of way about walking on his hands one day. He’s going to think it’s hard, he’s going think it’s frustrating, but he’s also going to think it’s an incredibly fun activity to do. Learning to love doing difficult things for no other reason than the fact that they’re fun is the key to doing difficult things easily.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are the small things you can do to have a good life?
