Answer: I took this picture when I was driving down to a small town in Illinois last weekend to teach some Jiu-Jitsu. For whatever reason, I was having a moment. A moment of gratitude. I was feelin’ all touchy-feely or whatever. For a few minutes, the world felt like a warm blanket around me. I probably shouldn’t have snapped a picture while I was going 55 miles per hour down some country road I’ve never been on before in the dark, but I did it anyway. Like I said, I had a really nice moment. I didn’t feel my anxiety berating my every mood. I didn’t feel my depression reminding me that my entire life and everything I’ve ever achieved is a lie. I had no intrusive thoughts about how I’m going to cut my arm off. I had a flow state. The most important small thing that you can do to have a good life to seek flow states in small moments. I read a lot of self-help writers on the internet, and I’m scared sometimes that I’m going to end up sounding like them when I write. I’m scared that I already do. You know the type of writer I’m talking about. The writer who makes it seem like hard work can fix everything. The writer who makes it seem like the only thing standing between you and your goals is you. I’m about to compete in a grappling tournament tomorrow in Las Vegas and there are 256 guys signed up for my division. There are literally 255 guys standing between me and my goals. I can’t imagine telling people that everything in life is all in your head. But really, a good life isn’t about the 255 guys in my division, and it isn’t about the mental and physical battles that I must overcome to achieve my goals. A good life is about flow and love, and I really don’t think there’s more to it than that. The more complicated you make life, the more it sucks. This is why anxiety is so unpleasant. The huge tournament isn’t about you. The reason to do competitive things is not to win, but to flow. Winning is just a nice byproduct. Intrinsic motivation is another thing that helps you live a good life. Self-help writers write a lot of garbage. Take cold showers. Wake up at 5am. Go vegan. Read a book a week. I’ll never be able to do any of those things (unless they make vegan cheese better, for fuck’s sake that shit is awful). I grew up around mental illness, substance abuse, and a version of masculinity that made me think suicide was more socially acceptable that crying. I can’t imagine telling someone who’s depressed, addicted to drinking, or obsessed with their fragile male ego that “waking up early is going to change your life”. That’s some bullshit. I don’t know if what I write is really self-help, but I do know that at least for now, I’m thinking honestly. Honesty, flow, and love. There’s 3 small things that will actually help you live a good life. If those are too tough for you, feel free to keep waking up at 5am and preaching about how many books you read per week. We’ll see who’s happier in a decade, I guess.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: People don't really care that much about others. Why is that?
Answer: People don’t care about your shit because they’re so wrapped up in their own shit that you are just an afterthought for them. However, you can make people care about you and your stories. Here’s how: (Me trying to be the center of attention… as usual…) When I started training martial arts, I had delusions of grandeur. I was going to fight in the UFC, win Jiu-Jitsu world championships, and I was going to live and train with the best athletes in the world. My life was going to look like Dragon Ball Z, and I loved fantasizing about all the different ways my life could go. I was obsessed, and it was so much fun. Nowadays, I miss those early days. The sore muscles, early mornings in the weight room, late nights on the mat, and the thrill of stepping out to compete in my first competitions. I miss the blind ambition, the dream, and the possibility that I could be anything. That dream has come and gone. Now, that dream is a story. All the best stories begin as sparkles in your mind. In time, all our dreams fade into stories 7 years into my journey with Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, the story hasn’t quite gone the way my 18-year-old self would have hoped. I probably won’t ever even compete in mixed martial arts, and it’s much less likely that I’ll fight in the UFC. I have won a Jiu-Jitsu world championship and I have befriended and trained with some of the best athletes in the world, but I haven’t moved and joined forces with them. I still train at the same martial arts gym that I started at. I haven’t strayed too far away from roots, despite the fact that I’ve had many chances to. The dreams that I had at 18 were beautiful, but now, they’ve faded into stories. Stories are the past and stories are in the future. The only thing that is not a story is right now. Meaningful storytelling is simply the art of extracting lessons from pursuits and delivering them in a relatable and interesting framework. Okay… easier said than done. That’s why we have to go deeper. The story is just the story… sort of When I started competing in Jiu-Jitsu, I was obsessed with winning a gold medal in the International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation. For whatever reason, this was magnum opus at 19. My peers were going to school, getting careers, and partying, and I just wanted medals and some clout on the mat. I was so obsessed with achieving my goal that I couldn’t do it. Every time I came close, I’d choke under the pressure. I started competing in the IBJJF in August of 2016, and it wasn’t until August 2017 that I won my first gold medal. I failed for a year straight. It took me more than 10 tries to snag my first gold in the IBJJF, but as of last fall, I’ve won 18 IBJJF gold medals in my career. My first gold created a snowball effect and removed all the pressure that was previously derailing my performance. I thought these wins would change my life, but they really haven’t. My life changed because I changed in the pursuit of these goals. The goals are not important, the pursuit is important. The pursuit is what makes the story interesting. No matter how my matches go, the sun still goes down. Even if I get my hand raised, I still have to deal with my anxiety the next day. Even after winning the world championship in 2019, I still had to show up and go back to the gym the following Monday. No matter what happens, the story is still just that: a story. On the internet, the best stories are stories in motion. Your quest for victory is not the story. Your quest to build a successful business is not the story. Your journey to your first 1000 followers on the internet is not the story. The story never ends. The story only ends when you stop telling it. You’re allowed to take breaks, you’re allowed to try new strategies, and you’re allowed to use different resources to tell your story. None of these changes will completely derail your progress. The only thing that ruins your story is when you give up on telling it. Plus, the longer you tell your story, the more important and the more credible that story becomes. Experience, perceived credibility, and competence are the 3 pillars of meaningful storytelling. To tell a meaningful, your story must deliver on these 3 principles. Back to Jiu-Jitsu… When I started training Jiu-Jitsu at 17, all I knew was that I wanted to participate in my newfound sport for as long as I possibly could. I was less concerned with “greatness” in those early days and more concerned with survival. I was constantly scared that someone was going to take my dream away. I was insecure. However, over time and through consistent storytelling, I was able to build a bit of credibility for my Jiu-Jitsu (for both myself and others). This was in part because, since I started competing in Jiu-Jitsu in 2016, I started posting about my Jiu-Jitsu endeavors on Facebook and Instagram. I started telling the Jiu-Jitsu story in my life and on the internet. Over time, I’ve built a small, but loyal following of people who want to see me succeed. Over time, I’ve come to see my Jiu-Jitsu story as a valid pursuit — even when I’m broke, injured, and exhausted. No matter what, my Jiu-Jitsu story is a valid story. People who view the story have seen my experience either on social media or in person. My gold medals over the years have helped me to establish perceived credibility in martial arts. Finally, my hard work (which has led to my experience and perceived credibility) has created the competence that has allowed me to start to build a network for myself to make a career doing the thing I love. It only took 6 years of constant work, countless failures, painful injuries, and numerous heartbreaks for me to finally say this: I’m living the life I built. Most people do not commit 4–8 years to build a great story. However, doing so greatly increases your chances of success. I’ll end this article with this idea: No one on earth thinks about you as much as you do. However, there’s a chance that they’ll think about your stories. Your stories are really just an extension of you. So as you get to the end of this little story about me, maybe you feel a little invested. Best case scenario, maybe you care about what happens next in my story. If I made you care even a little bit, to me, that means that there is still hope for humanity. That’s the power of stories. Stories are the key to finding love in a fucked up world.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What does a 'life coach' do? Are life coaches necessary?
Answer: I actually used to be friends with someone who was a “life coach”, and their becoming a life coach was really bad for our friendship. It’s funny because a few years later, I’ve actually started to get comments from people on Medium and Quora asking if I have life coach services. Me? A life coach? Blasphemy. I will never coach anyone at life. Ever. Here’s why life coaches are bullshit. I can’t understand having the audacity to think I know what the fuck I’m doing in life. First of all, I’m currently 24-years-old, so that should automatically disqualify me from coaching anyone at life. I’ve been grappling for more than a decade at a pretty high level. I’ve competed on the international stages. I won a world title. I have nearly a thousand matches under my belt. I am definitely qualified to teach people how to wrestle each other. I’ve also written and published more than a million words in the last year. I could probably teach some people a few things about writing, maybe in a few years, I will have actual value as a writing “teacher”. However, I am not qualified to teach anyone how to date. I am not qualified to give nutritional advice (unless you want to learn how to lose 10 pounds in 3 days to make weight!). I am not qualified to teach things that I have not put an exceptional amount of work into. I have worked hard on improving = my life, but life is not like martial arts. Every life is different. There is no blueprint for how to live “the optimal human life”. The more I study life, the less and less I believe that I know about it. I’ve read writing from Nietzsche, Viktor Frankl, Miyamoto Musashi, Sun Tzu, and many more people who knew a whole lot more than I do. Reading the work of all of these thinkers, I realize that there’s more that I don’t know about life than that which I do know. Some people have the impression that I am “wise for my age”. That’s why I’ve gotten asked questions about living well by people (on Medium, Quora, and while teaching martial arts). However, wisdom is not knowing things and teaching them to people. Wisdom is knowing that which cannot be taught. That’s why I would never become a life coach, and that’s why I don’t trust people who do. “The wisdom which a wise man tries to communicate always sounds foolish.” - Herman Hesse, Siddhartha

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is your strategy to be fearless in life?
Answer: "The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation." - Henry David Thoreau Here are 10 ingredients to help you cook up a life of LOUD ABUNDANCE. Feeling pretty happy today. Even tied this bandana around my head like a doo-rag because I’m weird. Out here looking like a pirate. Whatever. Let’s dive in: 1. Spend time alone. In society today, there are CONSTANT distractions available all the time. Turn off your phone. Get away from people. Go sit with some fuckin’ trees and determine what you really want. Otherwise, everything you do after this step is contaminated. 2. Find your limits. You can't make any life changes without deciding how far you're willing to go for your freedom. Some people swear off material possessions. Others just quit drinking and eating Cheetos. Determine how much you're willing to change your life. 3. Set some goals - small first. Not an exciting step, but a necessary one. You can't do things if you don't know what you're trying to do. Small goals add up to big changes over time. 4. Write everything down. I'm biased because I write for a living, but if I didn't write down my goals and my plans on a to-do list, I'd never get anything done. I don’t usually believe in all that voodoo energy stuff, but once you've written something down, the universe has a funny way of helping you to achieve it. 5. Go against the voice in your head. My internal monologue is negative and critical. Sometimes my internal monologue wants me dead. Sorry - got a little too real for a second. I can't ignore this monologue, but I actively do the opposite of what it says. That really helps. 6. Don't celebrate your wins - cherish them. When you win, enjoy it. Celebrate a little, but don't go crazy. Don't focus on celebration, focus on appreciating when good things happen to you. Smile, appreciate your successes, and then, find the next meaningful project. 7. Seek meaning, not happiness or success. Happiness is a byproduct of meaning. Meaning comes not from doing just what feels good, but what's important. Sure, you can eat cookies and watch porn all day and make yourself "feel good", but you'll feel empty quickly. Trust me. 8. Cut the bullshit and make stuff. The happiest people are creative. My least favorite people are: 1. The "obsessed with the grind people" 2. The people who hate people #1. Neither of these kinds of people is happy. This "reality" stuff is all a game. Have some fun. 9. Realize that happiness is not a gift or a goal, it's a job. No one gives you happiness when you win something, sell something, or eat chocolate cake. Dopamine is not happiness. Happiness is a practice built on years of habits. Stop chasing happiness like it's the goal. 10. Stop trusting everything you read. Think for yourself. People don't trust religion the way they used to, but they trust influencers and digital creators (self-callout much?) as if they're the new Jesus. We're all partially wrong. A few of us are partially right. Stop trying to be right so much and stop expecting everyone around you to be right so much. Thanks for reading! Have an awesome day. 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Can you make money from a blog?
Answer: I’ve been blogging for almost 18 months now. Here are 5 blogging lessons that I wished I’d learned sooner. To answer your question: yes, you can make money from a blog. However, you probably won’t.  Most blogs do not make much money. I make a few hundred per month on Medium. I make like 20 bucks per month on Quora. I make about $30 per month with my premium newsletter. My blogging/digital writing alone is not enough for me to live and do cool stuff. It’s just not. I also write 6–7 days per week, publish writing nearly every day, and I have done so for nearly a year. I make more than most writers on Medium (and I’m a top writer in a few categories), but I am still not making a living. That’s not to dissuade you. I’m just saying, if you think this is going to be easy, you’re in for an unpleasant surprise. It’s hard as fuck — especially if writing is not a passion for you. Don’t start blogging for the money, the money is only there for the most popular blogs. Popularity comes through consistently.  You won’t strike gold, but you might build it. I had beginner's luck on Medium. I went viral after just a few months, and I thought that that meant I was going to be a famous writer and everyone was going to love me. I was an idiot. After the virality ends, you have 2 choices: 1. You can go viral again, and spend your career going from viral hit to viral hit. 2. Or, you can slowly but surely build a consistent, loyal audience over years and years of consistent writing. Going viral is exciting, but viruses don’t stay in your system forever. That’s a good thing. Build an audience slowly by putting your best foot forward every single day. — it’s better that way. Don’t strive to be a one-hit-wonder.  No platform is safe. Get over it. It seems like every other week, I see an article on Medium, an answer on Quora, a post on LinkedIn, or a tweet about how each of those platforms is “dying” and how you can’t make money on them anymore. People are saying this, but plenty of people are still making hundreds of dollars per month with each platform. Yes, it’s possible that Medium could turn into the MySpace of writing, but is it likely? I don’t think so. I think people just like saying that the sky is falling. It’s already insanely difficult to get good at writing. Writing on Medium is a separate skill in itself. Don’t waste your limited writing energy by complaining about your lack of views, lack of earnings, or how “the platform sucks”. Just write shit. Then, write more shit. You’re welcome in advance.  If no one’s reading your work, the only person you can blame is yourself. Sorry for the tough love, but some bloggers need it. The entitlement in the blogging world is ridiculous. When people don’t get views, they usually blame everyone and everything but themselves. I’ve been seeing this since I started on here. Writers blame their mom for being in the room with them while they're writing (not exaggerating — I’ve seen it). They blame the publication for publishing their article at the wrong time of day. They blame the platform (like I said in the last point) for sucking at making their stories go viral. Have you ever thought that maybe, just maybe, no one read your article because your article wasn’t that great? Even if the algorithm does suck, the story that you tell yourself will determine much of your success. Accept personal responsibility, and keep striving to do better work. This isn’t toxic advice, this is the only advice that will allow you to stick with writing long enough to do it will. A great way to test the validity of your ideas is to post the same article in multiple places. Repurpose your ideas as tweets, Quora answers, LinkedIn posts, and Medium articles/blog posts. If the idea doesn’t perform on all of these platforms, there’s really only one thing to blame, and it’s not the algorithm. Learning to blame yourself without hating yourself is the secret sauce to continued progress.  Every niche is saturated. Be yourself. You’re probably not going to be the “habits guy” as long as James Clear ...

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What can I do to change my life?
Answer: Shave your head. Okay, this answer is NOT about my hair—I try not to be that conceited. Cutting off all my hair is a metaphor here for the constant feelings of inadequacy that come with “changing your life”. Up until the other day, I was sporting a super fun bleach blonde hairdo that I absolutely adored. However, it was time for a change, so I cut the hair off. As you can see by the picture, my appearance changed quite a bit in just a few minutes throughout the duration of my haircut. But apart from my hair, not much really changed. I didn’t make a bunch of money off this haircut. I didn’t all of a sudden get messages from supermodels telling me how handsome I was. I’m a Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu competitor, and my training sessions before the haircut were pretty much the same as they were afterward. I drastically changed my appearance, and nothing changed. We live in an era where you can change nearly everything about yourself. You can change your hair, you can change your clothes, you can change your mind that’s just the way it goes… Sorry… I caught myself singing Hannah Montana. 😅 The point is that your “self” is almost entirely customizable. This is because the “self” as we know it doesn’t really exist. Your body exists. Your brain exists. Your eyeballs exist. Your consciousness does not exist. Your “self” does not exist. Your “self” is a fictional entity, and it’s pretty easy to change it. Sure, you’re stuck with some things. You’re kind of stuck with your height. If you have that gene that makes cilantro taste like soap, you’re kind of stuck with that. Other things are changeable, but maybe they aren’t worth changing. If you hate the color purple, that’s probably okay. On the other hand, you should probably change some things. If you love alcohol so much that drinking your first beer after work is the thing you look forward to most, you might want to try to change that. However, whatever you change, you’re still stuck with the same consciousness. I used to be an overweight kid who had crippling anxiety. Now, I have muscles, and for about a month earlier this year, I was the number 1 ranked Jiu-Jitsu fighter in the world in my weight class. Some people tell me this is inspiring, but I feel like an imposter. I still have panic attacks. When my anxiety spikes, I still feel like I’m walking through a dream world that I can’t escape. I still get depressed. No matter how much of ourselves we change through self-improvement, exercise, or mental health treatment, we are still ourselves, and our “selves” don’t exist. No matter what you change you are still a collection of thoughts and experiences. That’s why the best way to change the level of happiness in your life is to stop doing things and start accepting things. Prioritize and execute. Figure out what you absolutely must change. Change that stuff first. Maybe you drink too much. Put all your energy into quitting drinking. Win the drinking battle. I know alcoholism isn’t that simple, but I’m generalizing here (it’s an example please don’t yell at me). Divide and conquer. Change what you must change first, and then work your way down to smaller flaws. Quit drinking first, then focus on fixing your posture or whatever. Some battles are more important than others. However, when you change a bunch of stuff, you’ll realize that “changing your life” isn’t really what you wanted in the first place, but most of us need to figure that out for ourselves. When you change a bunch of stuff, you’ll eventually have to learn to accept some stuff. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck on the never-ending hamster wheel of self-improvement, and that wheel quickly spins out of control.

Question: What are the best tactics for dealing with haters?
Answer: “It would be really convenient if you just gave up on your dreams and goals right now. This is because if you go out and do things that you want to do, what does that mean for my excuses? How can I live with myself if you refuse to accept mediocrity? If you are happy, motivated, and hungry to do stuff, it becomes more difficult for me to justify my misery. Your success makes me jealous of my own lack of success. It makes me angry. It makes me spiteful. It makes me do things that I am not proud of.” That premise, in some way, is the origin story of every hater. If you manage to do anything well in this life, you’re forced to have to deal with critics, doubters, and people who seem to hate you for no reason at all other than the fact that you exist. How to handle these haters will determine your ability to maintain continuous improvement. This is how I deal with people who want me to fail. My first haters were my “friends”. I experienced bullying when I was a kid, but I didn’t see my childhood bullies as haters because I hated myself. I saw them as truth speakers. It took a long time to change this mindset, but over years and years of martial arts training, therapy, journaling, and a bunch of other “self-improvement stuff”, I slowly developed confidence in my abilities. I started to morph from an insecure kid who needed validation to survive into a young man who was willing and able to stand on his own. This was empowering, but it was also problematic for the people who missed the person that I “used to be”. It was problematic for my “friends” who felt threatened by growth. My growth was a sign of their stagnation. It was a strange time because I wasn’t trying to threaten anyone — I promise. I just didn’t want to feel insecure anymore. I just wanted to be happy being myself, and the result of this transformation was that I upset people who wanted me to be less than I became. My improvement made my friends’ lives uncomfortable because a lot of my friends had the same backgrounds that I did. They had similar experiences and privileges that I did, but they were unhappy, and I wasn’t anymore. My newfound lack of insecurity exemplified their insecurity when we spent time together, and as a result, we grew apart from each other. In some cases, resentment replaced the companionship that I had once clung to for survival. Misery loves company. It’s a strange experience to both lose friends and become happy at the same time. It makes you feel guilty. It makes you wonder, “Is there something wrong with feeling proud of myself? Comfortable in my room own skin? Happy?” Amongst many people nowadays, happiness is seen as the basis for division. Even worse, what if in time, I fail at my goals? What will I do when I fall flat on my face and need to talk to someone? Who will I call? Who will even pick up? Losing friends is hard, but empathy makes it harder. I’m not a sociopath. I don’t want my friends to be unhappy. I don’t want to make anyone feel bad. I don’t want to become the thing I hate. I just don’t want to be unhappy anymore, and as a result, I changed — a lot. Forget about your backup plan. Nearly every achievement is met with resistance, and insecurity makes this resistance louder in your mind. When I started publishing articles on the internet, for example, I received a lot of feedback from friends. I received good feedback from many people, and I received bad feedback from other people as well. Some people didn’t like my ideas, didn’t like my writing style, or they just wanted to take some time out of their day to comment on how “unpolished” my early writing was. In my head, the comments I really read were the bad ones. When I started writing, I had a voice, but I couldn’t spell or structure sentences for shit. This is flaw became something my critics could use to knock me down a notch as I became more confident. When I started thinking about quitting my job, some people told me to “be careful” and “make sure I had a backup plan” in case my goal of writing full-time and teaching Jiu-Jitsu didn’t work out. But I’ve never even thought about a backup plan. If I fail, this lack of a backup plan will seem naive, but for now, the fact that I am 100% all-in on going forward with my goals is part of what compels me to work as hard as I can, be as authentic as possible, and counter internal and external existence. That’s the first way that I really deal with people who I want me to fail: I don’t have a backup plan. Failure is not an option. This is my life. There are no failures, only lessons. Don’t focus on haters, focus on your thing. That’s probably why they hate you anyway. This answer is about dealing with people who don’t want you to succeed, but the more space you give haters in your mind, the less likely you are to succeed. The more you think about the contents of this article and others like it, the less likely you are to succeed. It might seem like it’s counter to everything you know about success, but haters should not be your motivators. I don’t think much about my haters — even the ones who used to be my friends. I wish them the best, I hope they end up happy and live full lives so they don’t have to be obnoxious to me, but I can’t see how using my limited energy on proving people who already don’t like me wrong can be good for my long-term health. This sounds like fancy-schmancy people-pleasing to me. Your energy is limited. You must protect it like a close loved one. Most of us don’t have time to fight with people over whether or not we’re going to be successful. Recently, for example, I’ve been feeling incredibly burned out. As a result, I have done a loose analysis of my daily schedule, and I’ve been doing my best to understand where I’m wasting time and where I could improve. The biggest waste of energy in my life is the energy that I spend fighting with my doubts and the negativity of others. Since September, I’ve been working 12–16 hour days 5 days per week, along with consistent weekend work since September, and I haven’t seen the results I’d have liked. Through my analysis, I realized that this is because I am allowing things to have space in my head that don’t deserve it. To put it bluntly, I’m not really working as much as I think I am. I’m distracted by things I can’t control. I can’t control every aspect of my experience that might be influenced by others, and that's why I’m not trying to. It’s been incredibly freeing to just “do me” for a bit. I don’t see my haters as motivators anymore. I’m not a man on a mission to prove everyone who doesn’t like me wrong. Instead, I see haters the same way I see my anxiety. I see my haters as people who need to get the heck out of my way because I’m trying to live a better life with the people who care about me the most. Haters are not your motivators. Haters are not your enemies. Haters are like pimples. Sometimes, they just show up, and you have to deal with them. Haters are rude comments. Haters are your family members giving you “the look” when you try to explain your next move. Sometimes, haters are the voice in your head that makes you feel weak inside. Haters are all of these things, but most importantly, haters are chatter. Happiness comes from peace, and peace comes from eliminating that chatter.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do you become a better writer without training?
Answer: The best thing for my writing career was taking a job teaching kids martial arts. No—that picture isn’t me. I just think it’s badass… 😂 I started working with kids last fall, and over time, the job went from something I absolutely dreaded to one of the best parts of my day. These are the biggest writing-related takeaways I’ve learned from the last 8 months of explaining complex, difficult, and sometimes even dangerous maneuvers to a room full of children between ages 4–13. Crappy stories make crappy teachers. During one of the first classes that I taught, I made the mistake of leaving my Jiu-Jitsu brown belt at home. Because of this, I wore a white belt (which is the “beginner belt) during class instead. This confused the heck out of the kids. I mean, I was supposed to be their highly qualified coach for the summer, and I was wearing a white belt? It was confusing to everyone, especially for 5-year-olds. I had to think on my feet to explain why I was wearing the white belt, so I made up this elaborate story about how I’d lost a “super fight” to someone over the weekend, and he had taken my belt from me (this would never happen in real life, my life is nothing like 1980s martial arts movies). A couple of kids (the older ones) laughed, but the younger kids actually thought that I had been “demoted” to white belt, and they became anxious and detached from the class. I only know this because one of them actually called the gym later that day to ask why I was really wearing the white belt and if I was doing okay after I’d been demoted. Even if you’ve never done martial arts before, you can understand how this was a minor fiasco at the gym. What I learned from this incident is that the words you say do not belong to you once you say them. The same is true for writing. Once you share a story with the world, it’s up to anyone to judge, distort, and make up their own thoughts about it. Their reactions to your story will dictate how they perceive you going forward. That’s why you have to be incredibly careful with your words. Writing is just really fancy teaching. Every single piece of writing is some sort of lesson. Whether it’s a blog post, a memoir, a novel, or even just a haiku, every idea communicated through writing is a lesson that we’ve learned throughout our lives. All writers are teachers in some way. The quicker that we can understand that, the better we’ll become at our craft. When I first started teaching Jiu-Jitsu, I honestly did it just for myself. Sure, I needed the money, but really, I wanted to prove to myself that I could do it because I’d always respected my teachers growing up. I wanted to satisfy my ego. The same is true for writing, I started writing for myself. I wanted to express myself, my ideas, and I wanted to prove that I could be a good writer because I’d always loved stories, movies, and books growing up. But the reasons that I started and the reason that I keep going are very different. To me, telling stories and teaching children how to armbars are one and the same — they’re both mediums of expression that can be harnessed to teach life lessons, inspire personal growth, and help people (regardless of age) live better lives. Everything I write, whether it’s fiction, a blog post, or a Jiu-Jitsu lesson plan is a lesson to help someone grow. I have a responsibility to share good lessons. Patience is the most important tool One of the most difficult parts of teaching children difficult movements like takedowns, chokes, and joint locks was that sometimes, they just couldn’t get it. No matter what I did, some of the students in the class just didn’t listen to me, didn’t do the moves that I showed, and were incredibly undisciplined. But of course, they were 5, so what was I expecting? Did I really expect 5-year-olds to master moves that have taken me 12 years of experience to develop? When I thought about it more deeply, I realized that I didn’t. When I got frustrated as a teacher, I realized that it wasn’t the students I was frustrated with, it was myself. I wanted the kids to do the moves properly because if they did, that was an indicator that I was doing a good job and that I was a good teacher. As a new teacher being considered “good” by my students and peers was very important to me. Honestly, it was insecurity. The same is true for writing. When we write, we’re impatient that success doesn’t come to us right away. We want lots of readers, lots of subscribers, and lots of money, and we want it now. As writers, we can only control our work, nothing else. The readers will eventually come, but if you don’t have the patience to fall in love with the process, you won’t last long enough to meet them. Teaching kids martial arts was a new challenge for me. It made me think about aspects of myself that I’ve never actually put time into, like my impatience, tendency to speak carelessly, and the real reasons why I choose to do the things I do. Though it wasn’t the job that was going to make me rich, it was definitely the most eye-opening gig that I’ve had in all of 2021, and I’m really glad that I took on the challenge. What surprised me most about the experience was how directly correlated teaching is to writing. I’d often spend time writing at the gym before teaching, and it really felt like when I switched from my writer hat to my teaching hat, the only shift was in my mode of expression. Teaching is verbal and writing is, well, written. That’s the biggest difference. I love teaching Jiu-Jitsu, watching people grow, and practicing my craft. I’m lucky that I’ve found a job that’s also making me better at writing. I suggest you do the same.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What should men know by age 22?
Answer: When I was 22, I was all over the place This picture sums up 22 pretty well for me. My gold medals and goofy smiles hid my craving for self-destruction, reinvention, and growth. I just wanted to burn shit, and I channeled that “burning desire” into martial arts. I was succeeding, but I was an idiot. I could fight, but I couldn’t have meaningful personal relationships, I wasn’t super kind, and I didn’t like myself, no matter what I achieved. I liked to think I was smart because I was reading Solzhenitsyn, Nietzsche, and Viktor Frankl when my college classmates were discovering weed, but not even my scholarly behavior made me smart. From ages 17–23, I was one minor injury away from binge drinking, hurting people close to me, and quitting everything I loved. I’m embarrassed how many times I fucked up my own life. Unfortunately, that was only 2 years ago, so I know I probably haven’t made as much progress with gaining knowledge as I think, but I have learned a lot in the past few years. Competing in Jiu-Jitsu all over the world, having several shitty relationships, and becoming a solopreneur at the ripe age of 23 taught me a lot about life, love, and business. Everything I do is sink or swim, and I know what it’s like to sink. Here are 7 of my favorite life lessons for young people, in the form of quotes from some of my favorite thinkers. (Warning, long answer! Felt fired up today.) “There is more wisdom in your body than in your deepest philosophy.” — Friedrich Nietzsche This quote has rung very true for me in my relationships, but also in my martial arts training. If something feels weird, it probably is. If something feels good, it probably is — at least, in small doses. If something hurts, you should stop. If something hurts other people, you should stop. Your body is not deceiving you, you’re just disconnected from what it really wants. Listen to your body’s reaction to the actions you make. These reactions tell you a lot about what you should do. Obviously, there are exceptions to this, but for the most part, listen to your body. Your mind will thank you. "Knowing how little you matter is very important for your mental health and your happiness" — Naval Ravikant In my last serious relationship, I was all-in like I had never been before. I thought she was the one. I’d never felt that way before, and I acted as such. I gave it my all. I bent my behavior to her every desire. I loved her with all my heart. I tried to protect her from everything bad in the world. I threw my desire to feel significant into my relationship, and I thought that would make me feel validated. No matter what I did, it wasn’t good enough, and it wasn't her fault or my fault. I wasn’t enough for her because we were not right for each other, and we were both making drastic strides to change that hard truth. Break-ups are one great way to learn some humility, but honestly, I’d rather be choked unconscious. “When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.” — Viktor Frankl Let’s go back to that break-up one more time. I didn’t love the situation. The breakup itself was kind of fucked up. It hurt a lot. My life was a mess for a bit. I wanted to leave my skin and live in some other reality where I didn’t have to confront the fact that I was a fucking mess of a man who didn’t know how to have a healthy relationship. I couldn’t change myself anymore after the breakup, but I did learn how to change myself. I worked on myself. I stopped seeking validation from other people. I stopped seeking—period. I got comfortable being alone. I couldn’t change my situation anymore, but I did learn to change myself. That was empowering. “Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one.” ― Marcus Aurelius Can we make it LOUDER for the people in the back? I’ve been guilty of this myself. I’ve spent too much time writing essays and articles and having conversations about what a good man should do, only to turn around and do the opposite in my real life. I’ve said that men should be honest, and then I’ve lied. I’ve said that men should be strong, and then I’ve succumbed to weakness. I’ve said that men should be kind, and then I’ve been evil. I am passionate about the value of being a good person because I know what it’s like to be a shitty person. I know what it’s like to act like a fucking turd-muffin, and my goal is to be less and less of a turd-muffin every day. I’m not perfect, but I’m trying to live well, live more, and talk less. “If you know the way broadly you will see it in everything.” ― Miyamoto Musashi This is my favorite quote of all time. Learning to wrestle as a kid taught me how to learn Jiu-Jitsu in my teens and early 20s. Learning Jiu-Jitsu taught me how to write. Learning to write taught me how to live better, love better, and be better. Everything is connected and everything is related, you just need to have the ability to see the connections. This comes from knowing “the way”. Don’t learn stuff, learn how to learn stuff. “I see in the fight club the strongest and smartest men who've ever lived. I see all this potential and I see squandering. God damn it, an entire generation pumping gas, waiting tables, slaves with white collars, advertising has us chasing cars and clothes, working jobs we hate so we can buy shit we don't need. We're the middle children of the history man, no purpose or place, we have no Great war, no Great depression, our great war is a spiritual war, our great depression is our lives, we've been all raised by television to believe that one day we'd all be millionaires and movie gods and rock stars, but we won't and we're slowly learning that fact, and we're very very pissed off.” ― Chuck Palahniuk This quote is way longer than all the others, but it’s a fucking good one. I’m so fed up with the self-help, spiritual bullshit that people force down my throat on the internet every day. The lesson I take from this quote is that my anger is valid. The fact that I feel fed up with being told to “love myself” all the time is valid. The fact that I feel I have been sold a lie is valid. However, after reading this quote, there’s only one question that matters: What are you gonna do about it? “Actual happiness always looks pretty squalid in comparison with the overcompensations for misery. And, of course, stability isn't nearly so spectacular as instability. And being contented has none of the glamour of a good fight against misfortune, none of the picturesqueness of a struggle with temptation, or a fatal overthrow by passion or doubt. Happiness is never grand.” ― Aldous Huxley Let’s keep with the fiction theme for this last one because I believe fiction often teaches us just as much about life as nonfiction. I’m sick of the idea that nonfiction is better than fiction—little expresses the human condition as well as stories. Happiness is not eating ice cream, having sex, or making money. Happiness is not hugging your mom, fishing with your dad, or finding a lovely writing flow in a coffee shop on a beautiful spring day in Chicago. Happiness is contentment. It doesn't feel amazing all the time. It’s not ecstasy, it’s not what you think it is. Happiness is when you no longer need to change the imperfections of the universe to fit your insatiable desires. Thank you for coming with me on this little rant about life, learning, and the pursuit of happiness (although, if you’ve learned anything about happiness here, it should be that happiness is not a pursuit, it’s a state of being). I’m working on a lot of new writing projects over these next few months, and I probably will not be as regularly active on Quora as I have been for the last 6 months. If you’d like to read more of my writing and stay up to date with all of my adventures, I’d love it if you joined my weekly newsletter—Who’s That? On the Mat? This is where I try to share all of my best work.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do you learn complex material quickly?
Answer: At the highest levels of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, the game is changing so fast that most people cannot keep up. The sport is going through evolutions faster than most spectators, casual fans, and even most athletes can follow. By the time you see the newest techniques being performed on the biggest stages, the next “secret move” is already on its way to the big show. We athletes like to think we’re catching up, but the top athletes in martial arts are evolving like there’s a neverending space race going on. Jiu-Jitsu athletes have 2 choices: learn the newest techniques today, or risk falling behind as your competition evolves continuously. As a result of being engrossed in this world where constant technical growth is not just helpful, but the standard, I’ve spent much of the last year focused on improving not only my skills but my ability to improve my skills faster. In what I do, learning fast is key. The problem is, I have ADHD, and I am naturally a slow learner. With that knowledge, these are 2 habits that have helped me become a faster learner than I ever thought possible. 1. I chronically emulate the best of the best at my skill. Ever since I was a child, I loved watching and studying sports. This isn’t uncommon — tons of kids all over the world watch sports and study top athletes — but my study of professional athletes was different. I studied and imitated everything about professional athletes, and I emulated their behaviors to a T. I walked the way my favorite baseball players walked. I ran the way Lionel Messi ran (although, quite a bit slower). When I was in the 7th grade, I completely changed the way that I threw a football so that I was nearly perfectly imitating that year’s Heisman Trophy winner, Tim Tebow. When I started wrestling, this knack for imitation came in handy. To learn wrestling, your coach teaches a move, and then each wrestler has to imitate the move on their drill partner during practice. Over time, this imitation of your coach’s behavior becomes emulation, and emulation over time becomes personal mastery. This single habit has allowed me to learn all of my new skills faster. Wrestling was a hard sport to learn, but over the 6 years I wrestled, I became a wrestler through obsessive imitation. By the time my wrestling career ended at the ripe age of 17, combat sports were a part of who I was. This made my transition to Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu very exciting because I was able to accelerate my learning process through my ability to quickly imitate my coaches and the athletes I watched on YouTube. Once you learn to imitate, you’re not far from emulation. Once you learn to emulate, you can become a master and even an innovator. The key is less thinking in your learning and more doing. Do first, the conceptual understanding will follow. 2. I walk on fire (without getting burned). No, I’m not Tony Robbins and I’m not going to ask you to walk on coals. Well, at least not literally. When you’re trying to develop skills, one of the most difficult and most important aspects is to develop good habits. You have to make a habit out of making good habits. You have to learn to not be lazy. You have to learn to test yourself. You have to learn to (safely) jump into the deep end, just to test and see if you can swim. If you do not do this, you will eventually be surpassed by someone who does. If you’re a writer, this means that you have to publish an obscene amount of content. You have to write blogs. You have to write articles. You have to write books. You have to write headlines, subtitles, and introductions, over and over again. You have to write in every single “environment” that you can in order to develop each aspect of your writing skills. If you’re a Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu competitor, this means that you have to compete in every single competition, hard training, and stressful environment that you physically can. This means competing in random gyms against giant people in South Carolina. This means getting up at the crack of dawn to drive 5 hours to train with guys who will probably kick your ass. This means going the extra mile, but it also means doing it healthfully. Most people don’t get that. You have to learn to outwork your competition without getting yourself injured, burned out, or broken. That is the great challenge of developing new skills. Can you make it to the top without coming to hate the thing you once loved? Most people can’t. I know several competitors who I came up through the belt ranks with on the Jiu-Jitsu competition circuit who, nowadays, are nowhere to be found. Some of them were much more talented than me, but they were not able to work with their limits to create a sustainable environment that was conducive to their growth. As a result, they burned out and quit long before they ever realized their potential. If you can create a sustainable work environment for yourself, you are on the road to becoming an unstoppable force for learning. Like Jiu-Jitsu, it seems to me that online writing is constantly changing and evolving as well. Every few weeks, I see a new article on why I have to switch to whatever new writing platform everyone is on about and why that platform is going to make me rich. While I do believe there’s a lot of hearsay and overdramatization in these posts, the fact remains that writing is always changing. The internet has sped up the growth of everything, including writing, and as a result, writers have more options than ever to monetize their words, expand their skills, and reach new audiences. If you do not do this, you risk falling behind and becoming stuck in your ways. The only solution is to adopt habits and skills that allow you to improve your existing skills while simultaneously pursuing new ones. Perhaps this is why I’ve become so addicted to the “games” of online writing and Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. They force me to constantly evolve.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What do you miss most in your life?
Answer: Today, I miss waking up feeling inspired to write every day. P.S. My new haircut really exemplifies my ginormous cauliflower ear… 😂 A few months ago, I was in a period that I felt was the most creative that I’ve ever been. I was writing literally thousands of words per day. Some days, I’d go on a “writing bender” and hammer out nearly 5000 words in a single day. I’d write 2–3 articles, multiple Quora answers, work for my clients, and then I’d still have the energy to work on my ebook (if you’re interested, the link is in my bio). I had this period of copious creative flow, and now, it’s over. The last few months just haven’t been the same. The last few months have been a grind. I’m tired. My wrists hurt. I don’t have the same discipline with writing that I did a few months ago. I want a break. Sometimes, I just want to disappear. 6 months ago, I told myself that I’d write at least 1 Quora answer every single day. That 6-month contract expires tomorrow, and I have to decide my next move. Should I still invest time in writing on Quora every single day, 7 days per week, even on holidays, travel days, and weekends, or should I take a break? Should I try and write somewhere else? It’s hard to decide. I’m also doing so much Jiu-Jitsu. I’m training 6–7 days per week between 2–5 hours per day, plus teaching. Over the next 3 months, I’ll be competing 5 times across the United States, and it’s all going to accumulate with a trip to Europe to compete in one of the biggest tournaments of the year in May. I’m on the cusp of making a full-time living from Jiu-Jitsu—so much so that I’ve quit working with several of my freelance clients. It’s an exciting time, but I am anxious. My life is a bit unstable right now. I spent the last 6 months building up emotional stability so I could withstand some financial and career instability for a bit. I’m 24. I’m supposed to take risks. I want to take risks. But at the same time, I miss that stability a bit. I miss that stability because that stability gave me the inspiration to write every day. That stability made me feel like I had the freedom to take creative risks. To do weird shit and write weird articles. To take on the weird challenge of writing a Quora answer per day every day for 6 months. Lots of artists claim to thrive in unstable environments, but I’m not like that. I need safety and stability. I need to feel like it’s okay for me to fuck up in order for me to do my best work. That’s part of why I like Jiu-Jitsu so much, actually. Jiu-Jitsu is a safe place for me to try shit, fuck up, and evolve. That’s what keeps me coming back every day. I wonder if that feeling will come back for my writing because I sure do miss it. I miss not caring whether my answers go viral or get views. I miss being a newbie.

Question: What is the most effective weight loss method or program?
Answer: Most people can’t say this, but I can: losing weight is part of my job. Most people will never lose weight professionally. As an athlete in a combat sport, my ability to generate income comes either directly from my success in competition or indirectly from strong competitive performances that lead to teaching opportunities. Competing in the right weight class is one way to ensure strong competitive performances. In what I do, being at the proper weight will help you make more money. This is probably the best motivator for weight management. In my career, I’ve had to lose weight close to a hundred times. In high school wrestling, I used to gain and lose 8–10 pounds of body weight every week. It wasn’t healthy, but I did it, and I learned a lot about the right ways to lose weight. I learned the right way from doing it the wrong way for years. I also learned that while weight loss happens in your physical body, weight loss is very, very mental. Here are the 3 best mental tricks that I use to help me lose body weight, lean out, and feel good while I do it. 1. Extremely mindful eating. When you’re dropping weight, there is no way around the fact that you have to cut calories. This is just how calories work. To gain weight, you need to be in a caloric surplus. To lose weight, you need to be in a caloric deficit. The problem is, being in an extreme caloric deficit or surplus kind of sucks. It’s just not fun. Depending on how much weight you have to gain or lose and how long you have to maintain this state, you will probably feel tired, a little “off”, and if you’re anything like me, a bit grumpy, too. This is just kind of how it works. Every time I've had to lose weight, I have had to accept a bit of discomfort in the name of reaching my athletic goals. One way that I’ve been able to deal with this a bit better has been by being mindful of when I do eat, and noticing everything I can about my “eating experience”. I notice how I feel before I eat. I notice how I feel after. I pay attention to the energy I have after eating a salad or a pile of veggies, and I pay attention to the taste of my food. Dieting has made me a much better cook because nothing is worse than a small amount of shitty food. 2. Approaching weight loss like a pro. When most people approach dieting, they approach it like a hobby. They want to lose weight, but they do not want to skip out on nights out, fancy dinner dates, or sneaky late-night runs to the Wing Stop up the street (what? Just me?). There’s nothing wrong with experiencing all that the world of food has to offer (when I’m not cutting weight, I can be a real glutton), but if you want to achieve weight loss goals, you have to look at weight loss like a job. Weight loss is probably one of the hardest jobs that you’ll ever take up. I stole this idea from Steven Pressfield’s The War of Art, a bestselling book on turning your creative “resistance” into unlimited potential, and I think it fits well in terms of dieting. Instead of “wanting” to lose weight, I look at the weight I have to lose as a part of my job that needs to be done so that I can step out and be my best when my competitions go down. It’s not a question of if I’ll lose the weight anymore, it’s just about how long it’s going to take. “The sign of the amateur is over glorification of and preoccupation with the mystery. The professional shuts up. She doesn’t talk about it. She does her work.” ― Steven Pressfield In case you needed a reminder, here's the truth about weight loss: Weight loss is simple. It’s not easy, there are no secrets.. It makes you uncomfy. It makes you tired. It might make you cry a bit, and it will definitely make you a little cranky. Welcome to the world of delayed gratification. It’s a long road, and it’s not an easy one. 3. Forgiving myself for fucking up my progress. The fitness industry is full of people who don’t know how to forgive themselves. If everyone forgave themselves for slipping up on diets and training occasionally, it’d be really hard to sell supplements that don’t work to people who don’t need them. Getting frustrated for slipping up is natural in a way — we all want to feel like we’re doing our very best, all the time — but problems arise when we start to view ourselves as less than because we have “slipped up” on our diets. We start to view weight loss as an all-or-nothing affair. This is just not true, and it’s actually less conducive to weight loss in both the long term and the short term. Last night, for example, I was well under my calorie limit for the day (I currently have about 5 pounds to lose before my next Jiu-Jitsu competition in mid-March), and I ate 3 cookies. I still finished the day under my calorie limit, but I “sinned”. I ate the cookies. I could have lost more weight yesterday, but instead, I ate the cookies. This is a great opportunity for me to hate myself. After I finished the last cookie, the thoughts of self-hatred pattered my brain like bullets. “Fuck it,” they said, “let’s just finish the whole bag of cookies. You already fucked up.” In the past, I’d have given into this voice and finished the bag. I mean, if I broke my diet, I might as well finish the job, right? Wrong. If you can learn to forgive yourself for not being perfect on your diet, your ability to lose weight quickly will reach a new level. Learn to control your mind, don’t let it control you. In October of last year, I lost 17 pounds in 3 weeks to make weight for the ADCC Trials. I wrote about it on Quora. You can read about it here: Chris Wojcik's answer to How can I lose weight quickly? I didn’t have the best tournament of my life, but I got the weight off, and my weight cut did not impact my performance. Throughout all of my weight cuts in my career, I’ve been using these same strategies, but often on autopilot. This last cut, I was observant of the mental tricks and strategies that help me lose weight smoothly and with minimal stress. I am now applying them once again. With all these tricks, the most important mindset shift is this: learning to control your mind is the first step to learning to control your body.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why are intelligent people not confident?
Answer: This is Georges St-Pierre. He’s arguably the greatest MMA fighter of all time. Apart from being an all-around bad mother fucker, Georges is also known for being one of the most skilled martial artists of all time. He challenged himself in many disciplines of combat sports and sought to become a true mixed martial artist. This success across disciplines to me is proof that he’s an incredibly intelligent athlete. He also admitted that when he fights, he gets scared. In a sport like MMA, it’s usually thought that fear is an emotion that you are not allowed to feel, but Georges proves that wrong. He gets scared and still kicks ass. When you’re getting ready for a fight, the natural human response is fear—anxiety. Less intelligent people disguise this fear through blind confidence, but Georges St-Pierre used this fear to fuel him to become the most technically developed fighter many people have ever seen. He’s smart, and he feels fear because he realized the magnitude of what he was trying to do. He felt fear and he felt unconfident, but he just didn’t allow these feelings to dictate the way that he approached his endeavors. He was smart enough to figure out a way to deal with his lack of confidence. I’m not as badass as Georges St-Pierre, but before I compete in my own martial arts matches, I am always nervous and a bit insecure. I’m scared to boast about my own abilities because while I’m not a genius, I’m smart enough to realize that everything I have built can be taken away in a moment. For about a month earlier this year, I was the number 1 ranked athlete in my weight class and belt rank, and I still felt anxious about the guys who are chomping at the bit for “a piece of me”. Sure, I’ll talk shit when I’m with my friends, but when comes time for me to fight a stranger in a competition with a prize on the line, I always struggled with being a bit too hesitant. Thinking too much has been my Achilles heel for my entire life. Even though I’ve built confidence through years of successful competitive performances and results, my analytical brain does a great job of always finding ways to make me doubt myself. Intelligent people struggle with confidence because, well, they think a lot. Thinking is a natural predecessor to doubt. However, thinking a lot also helps us to solve problems. You have to work to build a confident mind, and even if you’re smart, it’s possible. One of my favorite quotes is “if you’re so smart, figure out a way to be happy” from author Raj Raghunathan. People used to tell me I was depressed because I was “smart”, and I never liked that. It made me want to be dumb. Instead, I’ve spent a lot of time figuring out how to build lasting happiness for myself. I also think you can rephrase this thought process for the issue of confidence: “If you’re so smart, figure out a way to be confident.”

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is your advice to a 23 year old man who had a miserable life and gets tired of it and wants a better life?
Answer: Your own will is rarely enough to pull you out of misery. You need to find a team. You need to find a community. For me, it was getting a therapist, becoming engrossed in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, and spending less time around people who left me emotionally drained. After you join a community, I recommend doing these 7 things to improve your life. If you’re miserable, they will work wonders. Learn how to eat healthily. For me, I learned that refined sugar is bad for my athletic performance (shocker), but also detrimental for my mental health. If you eat like shit, you’re gonna feel like shit. Learn how to sleep well and manage your stress. Many people claim to be insomniacs, but in reality, they’re just overworked and overstressed and have never learned how to compartmentalize their life. Keep work stress out of relationships. Keep relationship stress away from work. Work out regularly. You don’t need to become Mr. Olympia, but hitting the gym makes you live longer. I don't care if you don’t like to work out. Go workout today so you don’t die of a heart attack when you’re 50. Find a job that doesn’t suck. Plenty of people have jobs they hate. As a freelance writer turned entrepreneur, I get this. In the short term, it’s easier to do what other people want you to do even if you don’t like it if you’re getting paid. In the long run, this will make you miserable. Find a job you love. If you have a boss, get a boss you respect. Learn to be comfortable alone. We’re born alone and we die alone. Do not run from that. Accept it. People are awesome, or they are horrible. Do not let other people’s emotions dictate the quality of your experience. Learn to work with other people to achieve common goals. I know I just said you need to learn to be comfortable alone, but I don’t think you should go live in the woods and meditate for 8 years. Learn to become a valued member of teams. Maybe you can even become a leader one day. When I started Jiu-Jitsu, I never thought I’d actually become a coach or someone that people look up to, and now it’s sort of happening. Beautiful things happen when we learn to work together. It should go without saying, but if you’re depressed or anxious, seeing a therapist, a psychiatrist, or a doctor to improve your mental health is key. I’m not telling you working out, eating vegetables, and sleeping will make your problems go away, but they will make your life better. 23 isn’t too late. 30 isn’t too late. 60 isn’t too late. However old you are, right now isn’t too late. You don’t have forever, but you have today.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How does one succeed in life?
Answer: I don’t know how to be successful in everything, but I do know that to be a successful fighter, writer, and business owner, you have to be a little bit delusional. You have to be stable and realistic in your delusions. For example, if you’re me, about 10 minutes before the picture above was taken, for example, you have to look at your 175 pound self in the bathroom mirror (after you take your last nervous pee), recognize that you’re about to compete against a guy who probably weighs around 50 pounds more than you. Then go out and compete anyway with full belief that you will win. If you do not have the ability to develop this belief, you can kiss your chances of victory goodbye. I won the match above btw. If you’re a writer, you also have to be delusional. You have to convince yourself that what you have to say is insanely valuable. You have to convince yourself that in a world with nearly 8 billion people on it, your perspective is for whatever reason going to be the thing that people are going to click on and read. What are you, crazy? Successful “creativity” is the intersection between fantasy and reality. To do anything well, you must have mental stability and peace, but when you have an active imagination, this can be a challenge. This is the process that I use to work with my imagination to create the best reality possible for me to live in. I used to live in a dream world. Most children have “imaginary friends” that they play with or have snacks with after school, but growing up, I had imaginary worlds that I would live in for hours on end. I’ve always been anxious, and my fantasy worlds were a safe place that I could escape to as a way to make myself feel better. Nothing when wrong in my imagination. There was no pain, no bullies, and no rejection. Everyone was kind and worked together for common goals. These worlds were my safe haven for many years. Even as a young adult, when I got anxious, I found myself craving the safety that I used to feel when I would go hide in my head. I had notebooks detailing my fictional worlds. I constructed elaborate fantasies that didn’t even involve me, they were just a distraction from the anxiety that I felt as a child. However, my elaborate imagination also scared the crap out of me, because I thought that there was something “wrong” with me. I had enough self-awareness to realize that not everyone had imaginations the same way I did, and I was afraid that I was going to become “delusional” or “crazy”, like the people I’d seen on TV. I was scared that one day I’d go too far off the deep end and that I’d never recover. I had to learn how to use my imagination in the real world. The best part about having an imagination is also the worst part. Your imagination is a tool. If you can learn to harness it, you can develop a high level of creativity, competence, and even confidence. The problem is, in a world that cares primarily about your “real world” achievements, a mind that is very active on matters that do not exist can become a very dangerous thing. It can make you anxious, depressed, confused, misunderstood, and even outcasted. Sometimes, it’s our socially constructed societies that outcast us. Other times, we outcast ourselves. This is because, for many of us, we confuse our tool of imagination as a crucial aspect of our identity. We become our imaginations, and this holds us back from being successful, happy, and the most creative that we can be. In reality, having a vivid imagination does not make you creative. Creativity is the intersection between your imagination and reality. Growing up is a pain. In the war of creativity, reality is undefeated. No matter how confident I imagine myself before my match against that guy above who was much bigger than me, I always am brought back to earth the moment the giant man and I tie up to begin the match. When you feel 230 pounds pulling on your neck, you can’t help but be brought back to the reality that you’re really not as powerful as you are in your imagination. This is the exposure of your limits, and it can very humbling. Learning to navigate this discomfort and constant ego-bruising is both the hardest part of growing up and the secret to becoming a successful, creative human being in adulthood. The hardest (and most important) part of growing up is recognizing that you’re not as great (or as horrible) as your imagination convinces you that you are. The hardest part of growing up is realizing that you’re not special. You’re not special, but that’s awesome. Perceived significance is the root of much social anxiety. When I go out on the mat to compete in Jiu-Jitsu, it feels like everyone is emotionally invested in watching my every step. It feels like I’m under tremendous pressure. It feels like I’m this very important person and that if I don’t succeed, everyone is going to know how much of a big fat loser I really am. However, that’s not the truth. That’s just my anxiety. It sucks and it feels crappy, but anxiety is not the truth. Anxiety is a disorder. Your imagination and your anxiety are very closely related because both constructs feed off the idea that you’re “special”. They both feed of your ego. Successful creativity is when you’re able to get past the distracting thoughts created by your ego (imagination and anxiety) and actively problem-solve. This is why it’s so hard to be a good artist, athlete, or entrepreneur. All of these endeavors require the individual to harness inspiration from their imagination, overcome doubt from their anxiety, and then become immersed in the real world, and find a way to make their fantasy fit into our collective reality. To become better than other people at stuff (“successful”), you have to kill your ego. That's kind of ironic, but it’s true. If you’re so caught up in your head that you cannot function creatively, competitively, or entrepreneurially, you will always exist in a reality that is so different from the base reality that you will struggle to leave your mark on it. If you’re fighting with your imagination, it’s tough to fight the 230-pound dude sitting in front of you. It’s hard to creatively solve problems. It’s hard to write. It’s hard to paint. It’s hard to do anything when you’re fighting your head. Creative flow comes from the sacrifice of the ego. By freeing yourself from the narratives that your imagination plays through your mind, you will be able to create new storylines in reality.
