Question: What is some dating advice for men?
Answer: The biggest obstacle for most men in romantic relationships is themselves. Dating is hard work. You have to put yourself out there. You have to risk rejection. You have to invest time and often money. Sometimes, you will invest time and money, and you won’t even get a rejection. You’ll just get ghosted. Welcome to the real world. It’s not all lucky charms and chocolate chip cookies. It kind of sucks. That is the nature of most interpersonal relationships, and I’m tired of the collective agreement that as a culture we should just sit around and complain about how we can’t find partners. This defeatist attitude plagues a lot of people, especially guys. I will not support it. Dating is hard for everyone. The early stages of dating are absolutely terrible. You never know if you’re going to get ghosted, ignored, or rejected out of the blue. One time, I went on a date with an absolutely beautiful girl at a juice bar, and we had a nice time. On the next day, I went to the coffee shop next door to the juice bar for an afternoon pick me up, and this girl was sitting there on a date with another guy. She was having a much better time with him than she did with me. Our awkward eye contact gave me all the clarity I needed. We didn’t talk again after that interaction. I had thought it was going well, and I clearly was wrong. A few weeks ago, I talked on the phone with a girl I met on a dating app, and we made plans to get a smoothie this week. She said “I’ll text you tomorrow!” and then we said goodnight. She never texted me and I never heard from her again. Dating is hard. Dating is mostly rejection, spending money, and making awkward small talk with someone you don’t know. Connections are hard to make. I get that it kind of sucks, but do you really have a better idea? If you don’t want to invest in relationships, don’t invest in them. I read an article the other day that made me laugh because the writer was so dead right. I can’t find it anymore, but the premise of the article was that if you’re not going to invest in your dates, there’s no point in going on them. Dating is an investment, and cheap investments have cheap rewards. This isn’t just true with dating, this is true with all relationships that you have in your life. Sure, not all relationships require you to wine and dine (I’m definitely not wining and dining with my buddies from Jiu-Jitsu any time soon), but you do have to make an effort in all your relationships. If you stop making effort, the relationships will fizzle out. Relationships have risks, and if you don’t want to take the risks, don’t have the relationship. You can sit at home and live a safe life with no rejection, no financial investment, and no risk, and you will most likely be miserable. Don’t whine about danger from the safety of your risk-free environment. If you’re scared to lose, don’t play the game. If that pisses you off, it’s probably because you’re insecure, and not because dating is broken. I hate being the bearer of tough love, but that’s the only solution I have to this dating problem. The world will not bend to your anxieties and insecurities. “The mass of men live lives of quiet desperation” — Henry David Thoreau I’ve lost a lot of friends this year. One thing that I started doing last fall was treating my friendships similarly to the way that I treat my romantic relationships. In the past, I used to put my romantic relationships on a pedestal above everything else, and I saw my friendships as relationships that were stable, but dull. One day in around October of last year, I realized that most of my friends weren’t all that invested in spending time with me. I had this painful realization that many of my friends liked being around me and liked being associated with me, but they didn’t like spending time with me. I was remaining friends with these people not because I liked them, but because I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t like that about myself. So, I got comfortable being alone. My last serious relationship ended basically because my girlfriend went on vacation with a man who had a history of predatory behavior, and she lied to me about it. She told me that I just didn’t understand her “energy”, and I was upset. The situation made me feel lost, heartbroken, betrayed, angry, and sad all at once. This situation made me look at my entire dating history, and I slowly began to realize that I had a pretty significant history of “trauma-bonding” along with codependent relationships. This was kind of a tough realization for me, and I needed to take a break from dating. I was so shaken up about the whole thing that I literally could not look at women from a romantic point of view for quite some time. I wasn’t angry with women, but I was terrified by the idea of having another romantic relationship. But when this happened, I didn’t write a whiny article about how “dating is so hard”. I didn’t blame women, the culture, or even my own personal shortcomings for my problems. I focused less on rage and more on me. I just tried to get better and make myself feel more secure. I decided that I never wanted to feel codependent again. Saying “dating is hard” is not a unique perspective. What are you going to do about your dating challenges? Dating is a nightmare, but dating is not nearly the most difficult part of the human experience, and it’s overly dramatic (and kind of obnoxious?) to think that is. Yes, it’s hard to find a partner. It’s hard to coexist with people. It’s hard to overcome your anxiety and put yourself out there to women that you’re attracted to. It’s hard. But, so is getting a good career. So is being healthy. So is having healthy family relationships. Honestly, trying to have any sort of emotional connection with my parents is one of the hardest parts of my entire life. I’d rather go on 50,000 first dates than talk to my mom and dad about my feelings. However, I’m actively working on this insecurity, not whining about it online for money. My point is that quitting dating doesn’t change anything besides the fact that you are guaranteed to not date anyone. Whining about how hard dating is doesn’t make dating easier. It doesn’t make the world a better place. Words have power, and by spewing hate and negativity, that power can change people’s lives in all the worst ways. Use your words for good. Offer perspective. Offer advice. I believe that the way to make dating easier is to understand dating as a game, learn the rules of the game, and then work to become good at the game within its rules. That, however, is an answer for another day.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What would you do with your life if money were no object?
Answer: Honestly, if I didn’t need money, my life would look very similar to how it does now. I’d still get up and go train Jiu-Jitsu just about every day. I’d still write every day. I’d still teach Jiu-Jitsu. I’d still do all of these things just about every day. The difference would be, if I didn’t need money, I wouldn’t work so hard. I’d take more rest days. I’d stop working when I’m tired. I wouldn’t force myself to push myself to the brink of my limits. I’d work really hard because I loved it, but I would stop when that love faded. In real life, I have to persist with writing and Jiu-Jitsu even if I’m burned out and exhausted because, well, I need these 2 activities to eat. I’m not complaining. It could be worse. I’d just have less joint pain if money were no object.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why are you able to live a good life?
Answer: I’m able to live a good life because I surround myself with people who want to see me succeed. This weekend my friend Jen flew me out to DC, let me teach classes and a seminar at her school, and let me stay with her for free. They even took me out to dinner and showed me around DC last night. I’ve worked really hard at Jiu-Jitsu for a long time, and it’s humbling and flattering to get pampered a bit and feel as if all those hours in the gym, on the road, and on the competition circuit weren’t for nothing. Living a good life comes from being good to people and working hard. A good life is simple. Friends make life easier and better.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Does money really buy happiness?
Answer: No, money can’t buy happiness. At least, not lasting happiness. Money can buy you this ice cream pint, and this ice cream pint made me pretty happy for a while, but money can’t buy lasting happiness. Not even lasting money can buy you lasting happiness. To me, lasting happiness comes from a healthy body, a life full of love and adventure, and gratitude for the entirety of the human experience. Happiness is peace. You don’t become happy from doing stuff or buying stuff. Money buys ice cream, not happiness. Ice cream is a metaphor here.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are your favorite photos of yourself?
Answer: I don’t usually love the pictures of myself, but I like this one. It has my sisters doggo in it. His name is Winston. He’s a goober. I may have made him mildly uncomfortable by taking this.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What's your dream job?
Answer: Ever since I was 5 years old, all I ever wanted to be was a professional athlete. I’ll never forget when I told my dad about my dream to play professional sports when I was about 6, and he told me “anything is possible, but you might want to focus on things that are more probable”. That stung a little bit. The truth hurts. This isn’t a knock on my dad — he’s my biggest cheerleader nowadays — but the point is, to most people, the thought of me being a professional athlete was a little bit silly. I was an overweight kid who cried when he lost during recess football. I wasn’t pro athlete “material”. Nonetheless, I never considered an alternative career path. I had tunnel-fucking-vision on making a living through sports. The only sport that I was ever “decent” growing up was wrestling, but even on the wrestling mat, I still wasn’t particularly impressive. I didn’t even qualify for the state championship my senior year of high school. I improved a lot at wrestling — from 4–28 my first year to a winning record (barely) my senior year of high school — but I wasn’t going to wrestle in college, and the Olympics were out of the question. When I was 17, I stumbled into an MMA gym for the first time, and I really just wanted to get the same “high” that I got from wrestling growing up. I did not start training MMA or Jiu-Jitsu because I thought I could make a living doing it. I was told there was “no money in grappling”. On a whim, I signed up for the world Jiu-Jitsu championships in 2016, mostly because I wanted to say that I “competed at worlds”. Somehow, I took 3rd at the world championships (looking back, this was mostly dumb luck, but it was amazing for my confidence). After I got a bronze medal at the world championships, something shifted in my mind and I began to approach Jiu-Jitsu like a professional. I wasn’t a pro, but I had the mindset of a pro. I was training as if I was a professional athlete, but I was still paying out of my pocket to compete, travel, and train. This is just how Jiu-Jitsu works at the lower levels. This is how all dream jobs seem to work. You’re an amateur first. You have to earn the opportunity to do what you love for money. In 2019, when I won a world title at purple belt, I had to pay to compete at the event, fly out to California, and I had to pay for my victory pizza afterward. This is just how my sport works. I didn’t get frustrated by this, I just saw it as a necessary step on the path to becoming a professional athlete. At the time, I had a few sponsors, my savings, and I taught a few private lessons each week, but I was not making a living. I was not a professional athlete. I was a glorified amateur. That’s actually why I started copywriting. Life costs money, and I couldn’t support my dreams on ambition alone. The shift from amateur to pro didn’t happen overnight, but it’s slowly been happening for me over the last 2 years as Jiu-Jitsu is growing into a professional sport. Last weekend, I fought in an event that paid $5000 to the winner, along with bonus prizes to other athletes for impressive performances. All of a sudden, I’m looking at my competition calendar, and I will be competing in events for a cumulative of nearly $10,000 in prize money over the next month, and if things continue to go well, more great opportunities could be on the horizon. Performing well in these events could also give me the opportunity to teach more, and make additional income through my teaching. Somehow, I’m doin’ the damn thing.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why are there so many losers that have never had a girlfriend?
Answer: Here’s a picture of me, being an actual loser. This was Saturday. Since I was a loser in this match, does that mean that I am a loser in my whole life? I hope not. I’ve also had plenty of girlfriends. Honestly, I’ve probably had too many girlfriends at this point (wow, nice humblebrag, bro), and I really don’t feel like a “winner” when it comes to dating. This question sounds like it was written with a lot of hate if I’m being honest. Being a winner doesn’t always mean getting laid. Being a loser sometimes doesn’t mean you will never get laid. People have a hard time getting girlfriends for a lot of reasons, but I don’t think your relationship status is what dictates whether or not you are a loser in life. The reason that there are so many losers who have never had a girlfriend is that we’re all losers in our lives at some point or another. I just don’t think that “loser” or “winner” is a good place to base your identity.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Which is the best mix, wrestling and bjj or judo and bjj?
Answer: Depends on your goal, but I’d argue wrestling is almost always better. Some people who read my answers are very self-defense minded, and for them, I’d suggest basic wrestling along with BJJ. You’re not going to hip throw drunk people in bars. You’re just not. If you’re interested in competitive grappling, BJJ mixed with wrestling is the way the of future of the sport. My training currently is primarily Jiu-Jitsu with a heavy focus on wrestling. If you want to get in the cage and fight MMA I’d also recommend wrestling. Besides Ronda Rousey, I can’t think of any Judoka who had much MMA success, while I can name A LOT of wrestlers who have succeeded in MMA. If you’re interested in training gi Jiu-Jitsu, I’d recommend learning some Judo, I guess, but you could still counteract most Judo with effective wrestling. Wrestling, in my opinion, is the best base for MMA. A tough wrestler who doesn’t mind a scrap is a tough match up for ANYONE. I’m team wrestling all day, but I also have a lot of respect for high level Judoka. Judo is a TOUGH sport.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why is Brazilian jiu-jitsu so tough for newcomers?
Answer: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu is tough, period. Jiu-Jitsu is especially tough for beginners because just like with any skill, when you begin practicing, you most likely won’t be very good. Being not good at things is not fun. It’s tough. This is already a challenge, but in Jiu-Jitsu class, you also have the option to spar every single day, and it’s pretty clear that sparring is one of the most important tools for getting better at Jiu-Jitsu. As a result, most Jiu-Jitsu beginners spend most of their time sparring with people who are far more experienced than them. This is tough because you get beat up a lot. Even if you tap early to avoid injury, you still are receiving a lot of negative feedback. You feel like a loser. This is also tough. If you’re obnoxiously competitive like me, this is more tough than getting beat up. Those who elect not to spar struggle to make progress. Those who elect to spar often get frustrated or injured and quit long before they can make progress that validates their hard work. The key as a beginner is to learn to let your ego go a bit. Allow yourself to get beat up and learn. Find other reasons to enjoy training besides just being victorious all the time. Honestly, no one cares who the best gym warrior is. As I always tell my students, “you can’t win in training. There are no medals for “winning” in class.” Jiu-Jitsu is tough because delayed gratification is tough.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How will you describe life in 3 sentence?
Answer: At the beginning, you learn from the people who have been assigned to you. Then, you keep the good and unlearn the bad and try to make your own way. Then, you give back and make the world a better place. I’m currently on step 2 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Where are all the popular kids in your high school now?
Answer: Well, I went to this BBQ last summer where I bumped into a few former high school classmates who were definitely way more popular than I was. I didn’t want to go (the thought of seeing people I knew) but I went because it was at a friend’s new apartment. A lot of the popular kids from my high school now work as “consultants” somewhere or lots of other fancy jobs. They make good money. They work too many hours. Most of them don’t hate their jobs, but they wish their jobs didn’t take up so much time. After work, they go to happy hour and talk about the things that they’re “gonna” do when they have more free time. They’re probably not going to do any of them. After happy hour, they go home, turn on Netflix, watch some mind-numbing TV, and then go to bed. My life, on the other hand is a martial arts movie. I get to travel the world with my best friends and do my favorite thing. I go on adventures. I’ve sacrificed things for sure, but I’m happy with where I’m at right now. Maybe one day I’ll figure out what a “consultant” actually does. Seems like they make a lot of money.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the most important thing you have learned about leadership?
Answer: The first “leadership” opportunity I had was helping to run a kid's Jiu-Jitsu program in Chicago. Here are 6 of the most important lessons on leadership that I learned from trying to teach tiny people how to fight. A nice, low-quality photo from belt promotions last fall. Teams are only as strong as their weakest link. Some of my Jiu-Jitsu students are 4. The other day, a girl told me she wasn’t tall enough to lock the bathroom door at the gym. The day before that, a student told me about how proud he was that he weighed 43 pounds. These are tiny humans. It would be pretty easy for me as a teacher to simply disregard these small students and focus more on my bigger, more advanced students. However, this would be bad for the class as a whole because the neglected students would become resentful and disruptive to the learning environment. This is why I try to give energy to all students in the class because everyone is at different levels of skill, competence, and learning aptitude. Yes, I have favorite students. I’m human. I just try to make sure the students can’t tell who my favorites are. Most importantly, I focus on building from the bottom up. If you want respect as a leader, earn it. I’ve won a world championship at purple belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Throughout my career, I’ve medaled at major championships 6 times, and I’ve won a bunch of other smaller tournaments as well. I’m not the best competitor of all time by any means, but I have won and accomplished some seemingly impressive things in my time on the mat. However, the truth is that my students (who are 6, remember) really don’t give a crap about me and my medals. They don’t care what belt I am. They don’t care that I go train with world champions whenever I can. They are looking for other qualities that they can respect me for, besides just my prowess as a fighter. Kindness, consistency, and being able to relate to my students are great qualities for any leader start with that do not involve competence of skill. People want to learn from people like them, not people who think they’re above them. Even kids. Especially kids. Silence speaks louder than words. I don’t like to yell. I don’t like being yelled at, so I try to make a conscious effort to never actually “yell” at students in my class. Yelling escalates conflict, and conflict leads to resistance from students. Unless there is a fire in the room or an urgent situation, I don’t really see why negative yelling is good for anyone. Yelling creates apprehension, which leads to resistance. Resistance increases all problems in your situation, and this makes you more likely to have consistent conflict. Sometimes, I will yell “good job!”, because I noticed my coach doing that growing up and I found it really encouraging. Positive reinforcement at a high volume is good. Negative criticism (for lack of a better term) should be brought on gently. When there is conflict in my class, I find that silence is better for finding solutions and deescalating the situation. If there was a serious problem in the class, like a fire, panicking would only make it worse. Why would it be okay to panic over comparatively small problems, like minor misbehavior? Your team can sense your fatigue. People around you can tell when you’re tired, and they can tell when you are slacking off. They can also tell when you’re fighting your fatigue resiliently. The second sentence is more important than the first one. Some days, when I come into teach, I’ve already trained twice that day, worked, had phone calls, taught private lessons, or wrote. On rare occasions, I’ve already done all of the above by the time it’s time to teach my kiddos how to do armbars. People can sense when I’m allowing this fatigue to get to me. On the days that I’m too tired and “a little out of it”, the kids are out of it too. As a leader or teacher of any type, you have to keep it together. People can sense when you’re off, and their behavior will reflect the energy you put into their development. Grit is a contagion. It is not taught. My Jiu-Jitsu coach, Jeff, is one of the grittiest individuals I have ever met. Grit, by definition, is the combination of “passion and perseverance” that allows someone to stick with a given activity for a very long time. Jeff has over 25 years of MMA and Jiu-Jitsu experience. At his first MMA fight (which took place when I was an infant), there were no weigh-ins and gloves were optional. Point is, he’s a tough dude, not to mention a really smart guy and a fantastic coach. However, right now I’m focused on his grit. If I sit there and tell people to be tough, it doesn’t really inspire them to be tougher themselves. It ends up looking silly, hypocritical, and unhelpful for the entire room. Jeff doesn’t tell his students to be tough — ever. He just is tough, and that is what inspired me to become someone who can persist through injuries, compete under pressure, and keep putting myself out there no matter what. This is what I strive to create in my students, through leading by example. You must learn to see the individuals in the group. Your team only exists because you have decided that it does. Think about that for a second. Teams are socially constructed. The Chicago Bulls are different from the Los Angeles Lakers because we have decided that they are. As a coach, teacher, or leader, you have to learn to relate to people both individually and as a group. People need to feel seen when they work with a team. If you spend too much time focusing on the team and not enough time on the individuals, people will stop learning, start acting out, and become unhappy. Love makes people work together. Give people on your team a little bit of love. Unless you’re running an empire in the 1500s, it’s better to be loved than feared.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What does anxiety feel like?
Answer: Anxiety feels like chronic inadequacy. You go through life just like everyone else, but you can’t help but feel like something about your experience is different from everyone else. You’ve seen the movies, so you hope that it’s because you’re “special”. Something is wrong with everything, and you don’t know why you can see the problems that no one else can seem to find. The mountains above, for example, are very imperfect. Nature is beautiful but deeply flawed. This makes your anxious brain uneasy. As you grow up, you figure have a “gift” for analysis and problem-solving, but to you, the gift feels more like a curse. “It’s okay,” you think. Maybe you feel this way because you’re going to achieve something great one day. All the highest achievers in the movies are a little “different”. You know you’re a little different, you just don’t know why. You decide to sit back and wait. Your moment is coming. You wait for it. But the moment never comes. Your time to shine never smacks you in the face. That girl who you thought would notice your “gift” never notices your existence because you never even said “hi” to her. The teacher who told you you had “potential” never gives you an opportunity to prove it because you were too petrified to raise your hand in class. You never got into Harvard, either. You didn’t finish most of the ACT. You couldn’t stop sweating on the paper. You can’t understand why you’re such a failure. You thought you had a “gift”. You thought that there was some reason your head was constantly spinning with thoughts and analysis. You thought you knew something that everyone else didn’t, but it turns out you didn’t know much of anything at all. You thought there was a reason that your head left your body whenever you felt uncomfortable, but now you think that this happens to everyone. You thought you were special, but you realize now that you’re not. Your ego struggles with this idea. All of a sudden, life feels meaningless. If you aren’t special, what’s the fucking point? Everything is wrong. Everything needs to be improved. Especially you. You’re very wrong. You really need to be improved. You realize that you need to act. You’ve lived in fear long enough. You become obsessed with improving yourself. Obsessed. You wake up at 5 am to study stuff you don’t even want to learn. You write in your journal every day about the things you think successful people write about. You work out every single day. You become obsessed with proving your success, and by some miracle, you start achieving shit. You get pretty good at sports. You go to college. You finally get a girlfriend. You get muscles. You get abs. You study “the good life”, and a year later, you can recite Aristotle and Miyamoto Musashi and Nietzsche. Suddenly, people want to be around you. Some people say they “want to be you”. This is strange to you because you become the person you are by striving to not be yourself. You keep striving for more. You keep improving yourself. You grind on the hamster wheel of improvement so much that the wheel itself starts to break down. Your impressive physique starts to break down due to overtraining. Soon, you’ll have more injuries than muscles. The strong mind that you’ve been cultivating through extreme discipline starts to break down due to exhaustion. You’re married to the discipline, but it’s an abusive marriage. You’d rather be dead than continue to improve yourself. You’d rather crash your car into a bridge than take another cold shower. People love your dedication and focus, but all you want is a fucking break. Suicide seems like an intelligent response to the reality that you’ve created for your life. Slowly, you start to realize that nothing is ever going to “cure” your anxiety. Meditating helps. Exercise helps. Surrounding yourself with good people helps too. However, no matter what you do, nothing will cure your anxiety for good. To most, this seems hopeless, but to you, it seems to be freeing. Finally, you can take a break, because no amount of work is going to cure your sense of “something being wrong”. You realize you can’t fix an imperfect world, and you start to think that maybe the world is supposed to be imperfect. For the first time in your life, you start to accept yourself a little bit. “This is called healing,” you think. Anxiety is overanalysis. Anxiety is panic attacks. Anxiety is that sense of unease that you get when you meet someone new. You can’t figure out why, but with anxiety, something “just seems off” all the time. I was going to write about all the things I do to counteract my anxiety, but that wasn’t the question. The question is “what does anxiety feel like?”. Anxiety feels like a lot. The cure for anxiety is also a lot.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Share something you're grateful for today?
Answer: Here’s a picture of my dad and me from the 2016 IBJJF No-Gi World Jiu-Jitsu Championships. This was the first-ever world championship tournament that I competed in. I was a 19-year-old blue belt. When I signed up for this tournament, if I’m being completely honest, I didn’t know the rules of Jiu-Jitsu. I was really scared. By some luck of the draw (literally, I got a lucky draw in the bracket that made winning matches a bit easier), I managed to take 3rd place in the world championship with about a year of Jiu-Jitsu training under my belt. I was living in Oregon at the time, and my dad flew all the way out from Chicago just to watch me compete. He didn’t coach me. He didn’t yell at me. He didn’t give me a motivational speech. He just hung out with me for the weekend. My dad is not a “wrestling-dad”. My mom was not a “wrestling-mom”. My parents were never emotionally invested in my athletic career, but they also supported it. I’m incredibly grateful for that. Here’s why: Last night, I was teaching my kids Jiu-Jitsu class, and one of the guys who I was coaching with started screaming at his son during the class. He embarrassed his son in front of all his friends, all of the other students, and all of the parents watching the class. The worst part is, he didn't think of it this way. He thought he was “toughening him up”. I hadn’t noticed it before, but it occurred to me last night that he does that pretty often, and it also occurred to me that the kid probably doesn't love being yelled at by my dad every time he makes a wrong move at Jiu-Jitsu practice. When I wrestled as a kid, my parents never told me what to do on the mat. They never wrestled, and any advice that had was going to be counterintuitive. They were smart enough to know that. My parents made me tough in other ways. My childhood was easy in a lot of ways, but I still had some challenges. I went to a good school. I grew up in a 2 parent household. I got to play sports throughout high school. But still, emotionally, a lot of things were hard. My dad has a lot of trauma from his youth, and he struggles with it a lot. He didn’t exactly learn how to talk about or deal with mental health from his abusive parents who both had severe drinking problems. This makes it hard for him to control his emotions. It makes him drink more than he should to cope with his PTSD. My dad isn’t perfect, but compared to the situation he was raised in, he’s a hero. He also taught me some really important lessons. My dad showed me how to be tough by going through life and thriving despite all of the pain that he has experienced. He also showed me that you can go through hell and come out the other side a kind person. He showed me that you can be tough and thoughtful. Kind and strong. Here’s me and my mom from a trip we took to New York for a Jiu-Jitsu tournament in 2017. I won 2 gold medals and a $400 cash prize this weekend. It was one of the first times I won money in sports. I felt really proud because I paid for her flight and for our Airbnb on this trip. My mom is tough as fuck. She swam a mile the day before I was born. My mom taught me how to be tough by beating breast cancer when I was just 4 years old. She taught me to be tough by being tough herself. One of my earliest memories (I was about 4 or 5) is going into the bathroom of our house to pee one night and finding my mom and dad, both covered in blood, tending to the wounds from one of the surgeries she had. It was a bit shocking, and that was a really hard period for my family, but we got through it. My parents taught me how to get through shit. Sometimes, when you are getting through shit, it hurts. Sometimes you yell. Sometimes you scream. Sometimes you cuss. Sometimes you cry into a pillow. You’re allowed to do all those things. You just don’t quit, unless you’ve got a damn good reason to. I don't want to sound like I’m romanticizing anything, but my parents are tough as fuck, and I’m glad that they didn’t ruin my favorite sport while trying to instill mental strength into my brain. I’m grateful for my mom and dad because they taught me a lot of incredible lessons over the years. They taught me how to be tough. They taught me to be a good person. They also backed off and let me make my own failures. My hobbies were my hobbies. My sport was my sport. My career is my career. My anxiety is my anxiety. I have to deal with my shit if I want to be okay. No one is coming to save me. In a generation of helicopter parents, I appreciate the fact that I was allowed to fall flat on my face a bunch because I’ve learned a lot from those experiences. My parents taught me that you can be successful and imperfect. You can be fucked up and that makes you perfect. My mom and dad and I aren’t as close as we used to be, but maybe that’s just part of trying to be your own person. I guess this is growing up. I’m also grateful for my sister (my sea star) because one day, she’s all that I’ll have left.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Does failure always lead to success?
Answer: No. Sometimes failure just leads to more failure. In order to learn to turn your failures into successes, you have to learn from your failures. You have to reflect. I do this by meditating on the failure. I do this by writing about the failure. I try something, and if I fail, I make notes of the things that went wrong in my preparation, my execution, and I also make notes of which elements are outside of my control. Usually, failure precedes success. I have never been a natural at anything I did. Before I won any wrestling or Jiu-Jitsu tournaments in my life, I lost a lot.
